meaning: Can, Should, It'd be good if
summary: A hypothetical phrase that highlights or asks questions about what would be good.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばいい
text: In contrast to ばよかった, which is used for expressing regret about something that someone wishes had been done, ばいい highlights that the speaker is hoping for a particular result, in relation to something that has not happened yet. This translates as 'It'd be good if (A)'.
To use ばいい, add the conjunction particle ば, to the end of the normal verb conjugation used for ば, and then attach the い-Adjective, いい.

Although ばいい literally means 'if (A), it's good', it can also be used to give advice, and has a meaning that is similar to 'should (A)' in these situations. It is generally quite a soft way of giving advice.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たらいい・といい (N3, It would be nice if, It would be good if, Should, I hope): All three expressions share the base meaning of 'it would be good if (A)' and can be used to express wishes or give suggestions. たらいい・といい tend to sound stronger or more assertive than ばいい, which feels lighter or less serious in tone. While often interchangeable, in questions like どうすればいい？・どうしたらいい？ ('What should I do?'), といい is not usable.

たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): Both たほうがいい and ばいい are used to give suggestions. たほうがいい is a straightforward 'You should…', while ばいい adds a nuance of 'All you have to do is...' or 'Why don't you just...?' Depending on context, ばいい can sound more friendly, but it can also sound a bit pushy. Unlike たほうがいい, ばいい is commonly to be paired with のに to express 'It would be good if (A), but (A) isn't possible).'

ないほうがいい (N5, It'd be better not to, Shouldn't do): ないほうがいい is used to advise against doing something, similar to 'You shouldn't…'. It's a common expression that reflects the speaker's personal or subjective opinion. In contrast, ばいい suggests doing something, with a nuance like 'All you have to do is...' or 'Why don't you just...?' Unlike ないほうがいい, ばいい is often paired with のに to express 'It would be good if (A), but (A) isn't possible).'

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): Both can be used to give advice or suggestions, but the tone differs. ことだ sounds more formal or authoritative, as if stating a rule or guideline. In contrast, ばいい is more casual and conversational, often used among friends. Additionally, ばいい can be used in contrary-to-fact suggestions, such as 行けばいいのに ('You should go but you won't'). ことだ cannot be used this way.

といい (N4, I hope, I wish, You should, It would be good): When followed by いい, both ば and と express 'if you do (A), it would be good', but with different nuances. ば conveys uncertainty and is used for unlikely events, e.g. 'It would be nice if (A)', implying that it probably won't happen. と is stronger, often implying hope, e.g. 'I hope (A) happens.' Depending on context, といい can also suggest 'You should (A).'.

はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): はずだ indicates something is expected based on information or logic, as in 行けるはずだ ('I should be able to go.'). ばいい expresses hope or a hypothetical good outcome, like 行ければいい ('It'd be nice if I could go.'). One is based on reasoning, the other on desire.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たらいい・といい
text: When any of the conjunction particles that carry the meaning of 'if' (たら, ば, or と) are paired with the い-Adjective, いい, they will express the desired result of the speaker. These all translate to 'it would be nice if (A)'. However, the speaker's level of certainty about the result being 'good' will change slightly, depending on the particle.
ばいい - Hypothetically, (A) happening would be good. (Lowest strength/certainty)
たらいい - When (A) happens, it will be good. (Medium strength/certainty)
といい - The result of (A) is good. (Strongest/most certain)
To use ば, たら, or と with いい, first add the conjunction particle to the end of any verb, and then attach the い-Adjective, いい.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ばいい (N3, Can, Should, It'd be good if): All three expressions share the base meaning of 'it would be good if (A)' and can be used to express wishes or give suggestions. たらいい・といい tend to sound stronger or more assertive than ばいい, which feels lighter or less serious in tone. While often interchangeable, in questions like どうすればいい？・どうしたらいい？ ('What should I do?'), といい is not usable.

たらどう (N4, Why don't you...?, What if you did...?): たらどう is a gentle, open-ended suggestion, e.g. 休んだらどう？('Why don't you take a break?'). たらいい・といい can also suggest, but sounds more like advice, e.g. 休んだらいいよ ('You should take a break.'). It can also express hope, like 雨が止むといいね = 'I hope the rain stops.'.

ばよかった (N4, Should have, I wish, It would have been better to): ばよかった and たらいい・といい are similar in that both express the speaker's wish or hope. ばよかった is used when expressing regret over something that happened (or didn't happen) in the past, e.g. 行けばよかった ('I wish I had gone.') which implies 'but I didn't'. In contrast, たらいい・といい typically expresses something the speaker hopes will happen in the future, e.g. 明日晴れるといいけど ('I hope it's sunny tomorrow.').

ないほうがいい (N5, It'd be better not to, Shouldn't do): ないほうがいい is used to advise against doing something, similar to 'You shouldn't…' in English. たらいい and といい can also be used to give advice, but they often express the speaker's wish or hope for something to happen, similar to 'I hope' or 'It'd be nice if…'. Unlike ないほうがいい, they can be used for situations outside a person's control.

たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): たほうがいい is a common expression used to give advice or make suggestions, often reflecting the speaker's personal opinion on what would be better. たらいい・といい carry similar meanings, but often expresses the speaker's wish for something to happen, similar to 'I hope' or 'It'd be nice if…' Because of this, only たらいい・といい can be used with things out of a person's control.

といい (N4, I hope, I wish, You should, It would be good): Both といい and たらいい can express 'if you do (A), it would be good'. but differ in nuance. たら is less certain, often used for things that may or may not happen, e.g. 'It would be nice if (A).'. と is more definite and can imply hope, e.g. 'I hope (A).'. Depending on the context, といい can also suggest 'You should (A).'.

はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): はずだ expresses confident expectation, as in 雨が降るはずだ ('It should rain.'). たらいい and といい express hope or desire without implying it will happen, e.g. 雨が降るといい ('I hope it rains.'). The difference lies in expectation vs. wish. Thus, といい is often used even when the speaker is not confident the thing will happen.

meaning: During, While, Throughout, In the process of
summary: An expression that highlights an action in process, or the entire scope of something. To be within or throughout (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 中
text: As a suffix, {中|ちゅう} is frequently used to highlight a period of time (or space). By attaching the case marking particle に to 中, the sentence can be modified to show that (B) is happening/existing throughout the timeframe/space of (A). This is often translated as 'throughout (A), (B)', or 'during (A), (B)'. First, let's take a look at {中|ちゅう} being used to show events that are in process.

Now, to show that a (B) event is happening within (A), simply add the case marking particle に to show a 'temporal location'. This will be done by attaching に to the end of any noun that you would like to indicate as the being the 'space' within which another thing exists/occurs.
In these examples, we can see that {中|ちゅう}に is sometimes read/said as {中|じゅう}に. The basic rule for when to use ちゅう or when to use じゅう is as follows:

{中|ちゅう}に - Expresses a very specific (usually small) amount of time/space, or something that is not always the same (an amount of time/space that can change, depending on the person/situation). This 'thing' that ちゅう highlights is usually a 'process', and therefore means that (A) is 'in the process' of happening.
Examples - A meeting, class, visit to somewhere.

{中|じゅう}に - Expresses a predetermined amount of time/space that will always remain the same, regardless of the person/situation. Therefore, じゅう does not highlight a 'process', but focuses on the 'length' or 'space' itself. This tends to mean 'all throughout', as it focuses on the full amount of time/space.
Examples - A day, year, house, town or country.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: There is also a difference between {音読|おんよ}み (Chinese readings of words), and {訓読|くんよ}み (Japanese readings of words).
じゅう is used more frequently with {訓読|くんよ}み - ({今年中|ことしじゅう}, {夏休|なつやす}み{中|じゅう}, {今晩中|こんばんじゅう}).
ちゅう is used more frequently with {音読|おんよ}み - ({水中|すいちゅう}, {会議中|かいぎちゅう}, {試合中|しあいちゅう}).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら勉強する 'listen to music while studying'. In contrast, 中 attaches to nouns to express 'while doing X,' and there is no requirement that what follows must be an action performed by the same subject, e.g. 会議中に電話がかかってきた ('A phone call came in while I was in a meeting.').

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): ているところだ and 中 are similar in that both express being in the middle of doing something, but they function differently grammatically. ているところだ is used with verbs, e.g. 今、食事をしているところです ('Now I'm in the middle of eating.'). In contrast, 中 attaches to the end of nouns and expresses a similar meaning, e.g. 今、食事中です, which means essentially the same thing but is more concise.

うちに (N3, While, During): Both expressions refer to a continued state, but in different ways. うちに means 'do (B) while (A),' that is, during the ideal time or condition for (A), e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.') In contrast, 中 attaches to nouns and simply means 'during (A)' or 'in the middle of (A)', e.g. 会議中 ('in the middle of a meeting'), 授業中に携帯が鳴った ('My phone rang during class.')

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): Both patterns express being in the middle of an action, but differ in how they are used. 中 attaches to nouns to indicate 'in the process of' or 'during.' For example, 今、食事中です means 'I'm in the middle of eating.' ているあいだに refers to something happening while another action or state is ongoing. For example, ご飯を食べているあいだに電話が鳴った and 食事中に電話が鳴った are equivalent in meaning.

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): Both express a continued state or action, but are used differently. 中 attaches only to nouns and means 'in the middle of (A)', e.g. 会議中 ('in the middle of a meeting'), 使用中 ('in use'). の間に attaches to nouns (as-is), verbs/adjectives (with の removed), and な-adjectives (with な instead of の), and means 'while doing (A), (B)', e.g. 映画を観ている間に電話が鳴った ('While I was watching a movie, the phone rang.')

最中に (N3, In the middle of): Both express a continued state or action, but are used differently. 中 attaches only to nouns and means 'in the middle of (A)', e.g. 会議中 ('in the middle of a meeting'), 使用中 ('in use'). 最中に is used with verbs in the ている form or with nouns (using の) to mean 'right in the middle of (A), (B)', e.g. 食べている最中に話し掛けられた ('I was spoken to when I was right in the middle of eating.')

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot', and can describe one-time or repeated actions. 中 attaches to nouns and describes an action or state in progress, e.g. 勉強中 'now studying' or 使用中 'currently in use'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About の間に
text: {間|あいだ}に is an expression that can be used with almost any type of word, to highlight that (A) is the period/space within which something else will or did happen/exist. It may also be a period/space 'until' something else will or did happen/exist. It is a combination of the noun {間|あいだ}, and the case marking particle に.
When used with verbs or い-Adjectives, {間|あいだ}に will simply follow the verb/adjective. However, の will be required after nouns, while な will be required after な-Adjectives.
When {間|あいだ}に is being used to express the period/space 'until' something happens/exists, it will be paired with まで.

With {間|あいだ}に, the (B) action/location is usually something that can or did happen/exist at a 'specific' point during (A), and does/did not take up the whole time-frame/space of (A). In this way, it can translate more literally as 'in the span of (A)'. This comes from the kanji {間|あいだ}'s common meaning as 'an interval'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～ところに・～ところへ (N2, At the time, When, While, Timing): ～ところに・～ところへ and の間に both express the idea of 'while', but with different nuance. ～ところに／へ emphasizes a scene or moment into which something else happens, e.g. ゲームをしているところへ兄が部屋に入ってきた ('While I was playing a game, my brother entered the room.') の間に, by contrast, simply describes one event taking place during another, without emphasizing a specific situation or setting.

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): 間(あいだ) means 'period' or 'space', and in addition to its literal meaning, it is used in expressions meaning 'while' or 'between', e.g. 1月と4月の間に 'between January and April'. In the ているあいだに form, the focus is on something happening during another ongoing action. For example, 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was studying.').

最中に (N3, In the middle of): Both の間に and 最中に express 'while (A), (B)', but with slightly different nuance. 最中に is more emphatic, implying that (B) happened right in the middle of (A). In contrast, の間に simply states that (B) occurred during the general span of (A), and sounds more objective.

ついでに (N3, While you are at it, On the occasion): ついでに and の間に can both express the idea of 'while', but are used in different contexts. ついでに implies taking advantage of one action to do another, e.g. 買い物のついでに銀行に寄った ('I stopped by the bank while shopping.') の間に, by contrast, means 'during/while (A), (B)' without the added nuance of 'while you're at it' that comes with ついでに.

ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, 間に can follow various words or phrases to express doing something while a certain state or condition persists, e.g. 若い間にマラソンを走りたい ('I want to run a marathon while I'm young.').

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): Both express a continued state or action, but are used differently. 中 attaches only to nouns and means 'in the middle of (A)', e.g. 会議中 ('in the middle of a meeting'), 使用中 ('in use'). の間に attaches to nouns (as-is), verbs/adjectives (with の removed), and な-adjectives (with な instead of の), and means 'while doing (A), (B)', e.g. 映画を観ている間に電話が鳴った ('While I was watching a movie, the phone rang.')

うちに (N3, While, During): Both の間に and うちに can express 'while' or 'during', but are used in different contexts. の間に simply conveys the idea of 'while (A), (B)', e.g. 映画を観ている間に眠ってしまった ('I fell asleep while/during watching a movie.') In contrast, うちに carries the nuance of doing something during an ideal time or condition, e.g. 明るいうちに帰ろう ('Let's go home while it's light out.')

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is occupied with it, e.g. 映画を観ているところだ ('I'm in the middle of watching a movie.'). In contrast, の間に is used to express that something else happened at some point during the duration of that action, e.g. 映画を観ている間に父が帰ってきました ('My father came home while I was watching a movie.').

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like the English 'when'. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot'. In contrast, の間に is used with nouns, and describes a period within which something happens, similar to the English 'while' or 'during', e.g. 冬休みの間に ('during winter break').

meaning: While, During
summary: A grammar point which highlights (A) as being the optimal time to do (B), or that (B) happened at some imprecise time within (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About うちに
text: When うち, (sometimes seen using the kanji {内|うち}, or {裡|うち}) is paired with the case marking particle に, it expresses a period/space 'within' which something else will/should happen/exist. It quite often (but not always) carries the nuance of (A) being the 'best', or the 'optimal' time/space within which (B) could occur/exist. In English, うちに can simply be translated as 'while', or 'during'.
うちに may be paired with the dictionary or ている form of verbs, the plain form of い-Adjectives, nouns followed by の, or な-Adjectives that are followed by な.
Unlike {間|あいだ}に, うちに expresses something that can happen/exist anywhere 'within' the span of (A), and is therefore non-specific as to where (B) is located.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The kanji {裡|うち} refers literally to the inner walls/lining of something, and anything that is enclosed within that space. This can be thought of as where the 'non-specificity' of うち comes from, in regard to where within that space something is.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, うちに can follow various words or phrases to express doing something while a certain state or condition persists, e.g. 若いうちにマラソンを走りたい ('I want to run a marathon while I'm young.').

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is occupied with it, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating dinner.'). In contrast, うちに describes doing an action while a certain state is ongoing, often with the nuance that it's the ideal time, e.g. 熱いうちに食べましょう ('Let's eat it while it's hot.').

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): Both expressions refer to a continued state, but in different ways. うちに means 'do (B) while (A),' that is, during the ideal time or condition for (A), e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.') In contrast, 中 attaches to nouns and simply means 'during (A)' or 'in the middle of (A)', e.g. 会議中 ('in the middle of a meeting'), 授業中に携帯が鳴った ('My phone rang during class.')

最中に (N3, In the middle of): Both can be translated as 'while', but differ in nuance. うちに emphasizes doing something before a condition changes, e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.') 最中に highlights something occurring in the very middle of another action, e.g. 会議の最中に電話が鳴った ('The phone rang in the middle of the meeting.')

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): Both の間に and うちに can express 'while' or 'during', but are used in different contexts. の間に simply conveys the idea of 'while (A), (B)', e.g. 映画を観ている間に眠ってしまった ('I fell asleep while/during watching a movie.') In contrast, うちに carries the nuance of doing something during an ideal time or condition, e.g. 明るいうちに帰ろう ('Let's go home while it's light out.')

ついでに (N3, While you are at it, On the occasion): Both can be translated as 'while', but with different implications. ついでに means 'while you're at it' and adds a convenient extra action, e.g. 買い物のついでに銀行に寄った ('I stopped by the bank while shopping.') うちに emphasizes doing something before a condition changes, e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.')

ないうちに (N3, Before it becomes, Before ~ occurs, Without): うちに means 'while' a state persists, implying that an action is taken during that time, e.g. 明るいうちに帰る ('Go home while it's still light.') ないうちに means 'before' a negative state ends, emphasizing the importance of acting before something happens, e.g. 雨が降らないうちに出かける ('Leave before it rains.') Both suggest taking action while a condition remains unchanged.

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot', and can describe one-time or repeated actions. うちに means 'while' or 'during,' often with the nuance that it's the ideal or only time to act, e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.').

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): Both patterns can express the idea of 'while,' but differ in nuance. ているあいだに refers to something happening during another ongoing action. For example, 勉強しているあいだに電話がかかってきた means 'The phone rang while I was studying.' うちに emphasizes doing something while a particular state still lasts. For example, 早いうちに帰ろう means 'Let's go home while it's still early.'

meaning: Before it becomes, Before ~ occurs, Without
summary: A construction that highlights a period of time in which (A) didn't happen, or wasn't noticed, often leading to a negative result.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ないうちに
text: In contrast to うちに, which is often used to express the 'optimal', or 'best' time within which something should occur, ないうちに expresses the time within which something 'does not' occur, and results in (or causes) something negative, or will cause something negative if not dealt with. This means that 'before (A) happens (B)', or 'without (A) happening, (B).
うちに will be paired with verbs in their ない (negative) form, before the (B) phrase highlights something that 'is done to prevent (A) from happening', or 'happened unfortunately during (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: まえに (N5, Before, In front of): ないうちに and まえに both mean doing something before another event, but with different nuances. まえに simply marks one action happening before another. ないうちに adds the sense of doing something while there's still time. For example, 暗くならないうちに帰ろう means 'Let's go home before it gets dark,' with the nuance that it's better to leave while it's still light out.

うちに (N3, While, During): うちに means 'while' a state persists, implying that an action is taken during that time, e.g. 明るいうちに帰る ('Go home while it's still light.') ないうちに means 'before' a negative state ends, emphasizing the importance of acting before something happens, e.g. 雨が降らないうちに出かける ('Leave before it rains.') Both suggest taking action while a condition remains unchanged.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About べき
text: The auxiliary verb べき, being the attributive form of べし, is a structure in Japanese that is often paired with verbs to express that something 'ought to be done'. It implies some sort of moral obligation, or that (A) is the only reasonable course of action. This comes from the kanji {可|べ}き, which carries the meaning of being something 'permissible' (indicating that any other action would not be acceptable).
べき will be paired with the plain (non-past) form of a verb, before being followed by either だ, or another noun.

べき is also sometimes translated as 'must do (A)', or 'should do (A)' but it is important to remember that it will always have the nuance of being the only 'permissible' choice, and is therefore very strong.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: In modern Japanese, there are only 18 auxiliary verbs, of which べき is not one. べし (the standard form) is considered to be a classical auxiliary verb. Due to this, べき (and べし) are often referred to as classical auxiliary verbs.

sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: べく (N1, For the purpose of, In order to, To ensure): Both expressions are similar in that they are both derived from the classical Japanese べし and relate to expectations, but they differ in precise meaning. べく typically expresses an action performed for a particular purpose, e.g. 上達すべく毎日練習しています ('I practice every day in hopes of getting better.'), while べき expresses a societal expectation in the sense of saying that something is how it 'should' be, e.g. 言いたいことがある時は本人に言うべきです ('When you have something to say, you should tell the person concerned.')

ものだ (N3, Supposed to, Should, That's the way it is): Both express what one 'should' do, but with different nuance. べき reflects personal or moral judgment, e.g. 約束は守るべきだ ('You should keep your promises.') ものだ conveys social or cultural expectations, e.g. 子どもは早く寝るものだ ('Children are supposed to go to bed early.')

ないと (N4, Must, Have to): ないと and べき both express a sense of necessity, but with different nuances. ないと focuses on immediate or practical obligation, like 行かないと ('I've got to go.'). べき expresses moral or logical duty, as in 行くべきだ ('You should go.').

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): Both express obligation, but differ in tone. ことだ is used to offer advice or general suggestions, e.g. 無理をしないことだ ('You should take it easy.') べき is stronger, implying moral or logical necessity, e.g. 約束は守るべきだ ('You should keep your promises.')

たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): たほうがいい is used to give advice or make a suggestion, often expressing the speaker's subjective opinion on what they believe would be better. It's commonly used in everyday conversation. べき has a similar meaning, but is more formal and has a stronger nuance of expectation about what 'should' be done, rather than a personal opinion.

はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): はずだ and べき can both be translated as 'should', but they differ in nuance. はずだ expresses an expectation based on evidence or reasoning, like 明日来るはずだ ('He should come tomorrow.'). In contrast, べき expresses obligation or social correctness, as in 来るべきだ ('You should come.').

ないほうがいい (N5, It'd be better not to, Shouldn't do): ないほうがいい is used to advise against doing something, similar 'You shouldn't…' in English. It is a common expression that reflects the speaker's personal or subjective opinion. べき has the opposite meaning ('You should,') and is more formal. It carries the nuance of stating what 'ought to' be done based on social norms, rather than giving personal judgment or advice.

べきではない (N3, Should not, Must not, Ought not to): べき expresses strong obligation or moral judgment, as in doing something because it is right or proper, e.g. 約束は守るべきだ ('You should keep your promises.') べきではない is the negative form, used to advise against actions considered wrong or inappropriate, e.g. 人を見た目で判断すべきではない ('You shouldn't judge people by appearances.')

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About べきではない
text: As an extension of the auxiliary verb べき, that is partnered with verbs to convey 'ought to do (A)', べきではない (or べきじゃない) highlights the opposite, and means 'ought not to (A)', 'should not (A)', or 'must not (A)'. Just like べき, it is quite strong, and implies that doing (A) would be considered improper/incorrect.
べきではない (or べきじゃない) will be paired with the plain (non-past) form of a verb.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なければいけない (N4, Must do, Have to do): These express contrasting meanings: なければいけない 'must' vs. べきではない 'should not'. The former implies necessity or rule, while the latter carries a tone of moral or social advice, e.g. 行かなければいけない ('You must go.') vs. 行くべきではない ('You shouldn't go.').

なくちゃ・なきゃ (N5, Must do, Have to do): なくちゃ and なきゃ are casual ways to express obligation, similar to 'I need to…' or 'I have to…' in English. In contrast, べきではない has the opposite meaning—'should not' or 'ought not'—and is more formal. It conveys a sense of societal expectation or what is considered proper, rather than reflecting the speaker's immediate or personal needs.

はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): はずだ expresses an assumption or expectation based on reason or context, e.g. 雨が降るはずだ ('It should rain.'). In contrast, べきではない expresses a strong sense of moral or social obligation not to do something, e.g. 嘘をつくべきではない ('You shouldn't lie.').

たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): たほうがいい is used to give advice or make a suggestion, often expressing the speaker's subjective opinion on what they believe would be better. It's commonly used in everyday conversation. In contrast, べきではない has the opposite meaning and is more formal. It conveys an expectation or rule about what 'should not' be done, rather than a personal opinion.

なければならない (N4, Must do, Have to do): These are opposites: なければならない 'must' vs. べきではない 'should not'. The former suggests a rule or necessity; the latter implies social or moral advice, e.g. 行かなければならない ('You must go.') as compared to 行くべきではない ('You ought not to / shouldn't go.').

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): ことだ suggests what one should do as advice or a general guideline, e.g. 無理をしないことだ ('You should take it easy.') べきではない expresses the opposite, indicating what one should not do based on moral or social expectations, e.g. 人を見た目で判断すべきではない ('You shouldn't judge people by appearances.')

ものだ (N3, Supposed to, Should, That's the way it is): ものだ expresses general or societal expectations, e.g. 子どもは早く寝るものだ ('Children are supposed to go to bed early.') べきではない carries the opposite nuance, conveying that one should not do something based on moral or social reasoning, e.g. 人を見た目で判断すべきではない ('You shouldn't judge people by appearances.')

てはいけない (N5, Must not, May not): てはいけない expresses prohibition, meaning something 'must not' or 'cannot' be done. In contrast, べきではない suggests that something 'should not' be done, often implying it's improper or that there's a better option. While both express negative recommendations, てはいけない is more authoritative and used for rules, whereas べきではない carries a more subjective nuance.

ないほうがいい (N5, It'd be better not to, Shouldn't do): ないほうがいい is used to advise or suggest not doing something, similar to 'You shouldn't…' It is a common expression that reflects the speaker's personal or subjective opinion. べきではない can carry a similar meaning but is more formal, with a nuance of stating what one 'ought not to' or 'should not' do based on social norms or what is considered proper, rather than personal advice.

べき (N3, Must, Should, Ought to): べき expresses strong obligation or moral judgment, as in doing something because it is right or proper, e.g. 約束は守るべきだ ('You should keep your promises.') べきではない is the negative form, used to advise against actions considered wrong or inappropriate, e.g. 人を見た目で判断すべきではない ('You shouldn't judge people by appearances.')

meaning: As for, Speaking of, Casual は (Sentence topic marker)
summary: A casual way of marking the general topic of a sentence.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About って
text: Although って can be used as a casual quotation marker in Japanese (replacing と), it is also frequently used as a casual topic marker (replacing は). This is something that occurs primarily in spoken language, and will come directly after the sentence topic, in exactly the same way as the adverbial particle は usually would.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Used primarily in spoken language

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: は (N5, As for... (Highlights sentence topic)): って is used in casual conversation to introduce a topic informally. It comes from the quotation particle と and can carry the nuance of 'speaking of…'. は is a more standard and flexible topic marker, used in both casual and formal situations, including writing. Unlike って, は can also carry a contrastive nuance.

なんか・なんて (N3, Such as, Things like, Emphasis): って casually introduces or refers back to a topic, e.g. あの人って優しいよね ('That person is really kind, huh?') なんか・なんて adds a dismissive or emotional tone, often implying downplaying or surprise, e.g. 私なんかにできるかな ('Can someone like me really do it?')

といえば (N3, Speaking of, If it were the case that): Both can mean 'speaking of (A)', but differ in tone and usage. といえば often refers back to something just mentioned or known to both speaker and listener, e.g. 京都といえば、お寺が有名だね ('Speaking of Kyoto, its temples are famous.') って is a casual form used in everyday conversation, often functioning like は to casually introduce a topic, e.g. この映画って最高！ ('That movie is amazing!')

meaning: Very, Quite, Considerably
summary: A word that expresses a very high level of (A), by stating that it is at the most center of what would be expected of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About  なかなか
text: なかなか (or {中々|なかなか} in kanji) is an adverb in Japanese that is frequently translated as 'very', or 'considerably'. It is regularly paired directly with other adjectives, or before nouns (with の coming between なかなか and the noun).

なかなか can also sometimes have the nuance of being something that is {軽視|けいし}しがたい. This basically translates as 'difficult to dismiss', but is a bit closer to English expressions like 'nothing to scoff at', or 'not to be taken lightly'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: なかなか, coming from the kanji {中|なか} meaning 'within', can be thought to mean the 'middle' or 'most' (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なかなか～ない (N3, Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from): なかなか means 'quite' or 'fairly' when used with positive expressions, e.g. なかなか面白い映画だった ('It was quite an interesting movie.') In contrast, なかなか～ない expresses difficulty or delay, meaning 'not easily' or 'hardly', e.g. 仕事がなかなか終わらない ('The work just won't end.')

あまりに (N3, So much...that, (Way) too...): Both emphasize degree, but differ in nuance. なかなか suggests something is quite or surprisingly so, often with a positive tone, e.g. なかなか面白い映画だった ('It was quite an interesting movie.') あまりに means 'too much' or 'excessively', and is often negative in tone, e.g. あまりに寒くて出かけられなかった ('It was too cold to go out.')

けっこう (N5, Quite, A lot, Fairly, Rather): Both なかなか and けっこう are adverbs used to express extent. In affirmative sentences, they can both mean 'quite' or 'rather.' A key difference is that なかなか is often used in negative sentences to express difficulty in doing something. Meanwhile, けっこう can be used alone (especially as けっこうです) to politely decline something, like saying 'I'm fine.'

かなり (N3, Quite, Considerably, Pretty, Fairly): When used in affirmative sentences, なかなか and かなり both convey the nuance that something exceeds expectations, e.g. なかなか美味しい ('It's quite tasty.') or かなり美味しい (essentially the same meaning). The main difference is that なかなか is often used in negative expressions to suggest that something is not easily done, e.g. なかなかうまくいかない ('It just won't go well.'), while かなり is not used this way.

あまり (N3, So much...that): Both express degree, but with different implications. なかなか implies something is quite or unexpectedly good, e.g. なかなかいい店だね ('This place is surprisingly good.') あまり highlights an excessive degree that leads to an unintended or negative result, e.g. 緊張のあまり声が震えた ('I was so nervous my voice shook.')

あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): なかなか and あまり～ない both express degree, but in opposite directions. なかなか implies exceeding expectations, e.g. なかなか美味しい ('It's quite tasty.'). In contrast, あまり～ない suggests a lesser degree, or falling short of expectations, e.g. あまり美味しくない ('It's not very tasty.').

のなかで (N4, In, Among, Within): Though both contain なか, their meanings are different. なかなか is often used in negatives to express difficulty, like 'not easily' (なかなかできません), or in positives to mean 'quite' (なかなかいい). In contrast, のなかで means 'among' and is used when referring to one or more members of a group. For example, 果物の中でりんごが一番好き means 'Among fruits, I like apples the best.'.

meaning: So much...that
summary: A structure that often highlights an excessive amount of (A) that causes a negative result.
formation: ［い］Adjective［さ］+ の + あまり + (Negative Result) Phrase
［い］Adjective［み］+ の + あまり + (Negative Result) Phrase
［な］Adjective + な + あまり + (Negative Result) Phrase
Noun + の + あまり + (Negative Result) Phrase

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About あまり
text: As a noun, あまり means 'excess', and refers to an amount of something that is in surplus. This noun is quite often used after many different types of words, to indicate that something happened/exists to an excessive degree (which then resulted in something negative occurring). By itself, {余|あま}り is not negative. However, this grammar point can be thought of as a set phrase that is generally used in negative situations.

To use あまり, you will need to attach it to the end of the following structures. A verb, an い-Adjective (that has been turned into a noun through the use of さ or み) followed by の, a な-Adjective followed by な, or a noun followed by の. Then, after あまり, a (B) phrase will highlight what the negative result was.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: こそ (N3, For sure, For certain, Even more so, Underlined or bolded text): Both express emphasis, but in different ways. あまり is a noun that emphasizes an extreme degree leading to an unintended result, e.g. 悲しみのあまり泣き出した ('She burst into tears from too much sadness.') こそ is a particle that stresses importance or exclusivity, e.g. 今日こそ早く寝よう ('Today, for sure, I'll go to bed early.')

すぎる (N5, Too much, Very): Both すぎる and あまり express that something is excessive, but they differ in usage and nuance. すぎる attaches to the stem of verbs and adjectives, while あまり follows plain-form verbs, nouns with の, or な-adjectives with な. Though すぎる can imply something negative, あまり more clearly emphasizes that the excess leads to a negative consequence.

からこそ (N3, Emphasized because, Precisely because): あまり follows a noun or verb phrase and shows that an extreme state leads to an unintended result, e.g. 緊張のあまり声が出なかった ('I was so nervous I couldn't speak.') からこそ attaches after the reason and emphasizes it as the precise cause, e.g. 緊張したからこそ全力を出せた ('It was precisely because I was nervous that I gave it my all.')

あまりに (N3, So much...that, (Way) too...): Both mean 'too much', but differ in nuance. あまりに emphasizes intensity and doesn't necessarily imply a result, e.g. あまりに暑い日だった ('It was an extremely hot day.') あまり highlights excess that leads to a (usually undesirable) outcome, e.g. 暑さのあまり眠れなかった ('I couldn't sleep due to the extreme heat.')

Adj限りだ (N1, Extremely, Really, Very, As ... as one can be): Both emphasize extremity, but with different focuses. Adjective + 限りだ expresses a strong feeling at its peak, e.g. 悲しい限りだ ('I'm as sad as can be.') あまり indicates that excess leads to a (usually undesirable) result, e.g. 悲しみのあまり声が出なかった ('I couldn't speak due to extreme sadness.')

なかなか (N3, Very, Quite, Considerably): Both express degree, but with different implications. なかなか implies something is quite or unexpectedly good, e.g. なかなかいい店だね ('This place is surprisingly good.') あまり highlights an excessive degree that leads to an unintended or negative result, e.g. 緊張のあまり声が震えた ('I was so nervous my voice shook.')

あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): あまり has the base meaning of 'excess', but its nuance changes with context. Together with a negative word in the form あまり～ない, it means 'not very (A)', e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'). Used affirmatively, it implies something of an excessive degree, e.g. 緊張のあまりうまくできなかった ('I was so nervous I couldn't do it well.').

meaning: Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from
summary: A phrase that expresses a very low level of (A), by stating that it is nowhere near the center of what would be expected of (A).
formation: なかなか + Phrase + Verb［ない］

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なかなか～ない
text: When used positively, なかなか means to be 'very', or 'considerably' something. However, when used in a sentence that has a verb in the ない (or ありません) form, it carries the meaning of 'not at all', 'hardly', or 'far from'. Quite often, this expression is used to highlight something that the speaker expects should happen, but for some reason does/is not.
To use なかなか (or {中々|なかなか} in its kanji form), なかなか will be put at the beginning of a phrase (or directly before the negative verb), before further describing the situation.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なかなか (N3, Very, Quite, Considerably): なかなか means 'quite' or 'fairly' when used with positive expressions, e.g. なかなか面白い映画だった ('It was quite an interesting movie.') In contrast, なかなか～ない expresses difficulty or delay, meaning 'not easily' or 'hardly', e.g. 仕事がなかなか終わらない ('The work just won't end.')

すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): なかなか～ない expresses that something is not easily done, often implying difficulty or repeated effort. For example, なかなかうまく話せない ('I just can't speak well.') has the nuance that the speaker is trying but not succeeding. In contrast, すこしも～ない means 'not even a little.' 少しも話せない means 'I can't speak at all.', focusing on the absence of ability without any implication of effort or struggle.

めったに〜ない (N3, Hardly, Rarely, Seldom): めったに〜ない and なかなか〜ない both express rarity, but with different nuance. めったに〜ない means something rarely happens and carries a neutral or negative tone. なかなか〜ない, while also indicating rarity, emphasizes difficulty or persistence, often despite effort. It suggests that the situation is hard to bring about, rather than simply uncommon.

全く～ない (N3, Not~at all): Both express rarity or lack of frequency, but with different focus. 全く〜ない means something happens infrequently, e.g. 全く外食しない ('I hardly ever eat out.') なかなか〜ない suggests it doesn't happen easily or readily, often due to circumstances, e.g. 忙しくてなかなか外食できない ('I can't easily eat out because I'm so busy.')

別に〜ない (N3, Not really, Not particularly, It's not like...): Both negate expectations, but in different ways. 別に〜ない downplays something as not particularly important, e.g. 別に怒ってないよ ('I'm not especially mad.') なかなか〜ない indicates that something doesn't happen easily, e.g. なかなか怒らない人だね ('He's not someone who gets angry easily.')

あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): なかなか～ない and あまり～ない both express negation, but with different nuance. なかなか～ない implies difficulty or delay despite effort, e.g. なかなか話せない ('I can't speak easily.', implying difficulty despite effort). あまり～ない simply indicates a lower degree, e.g. あまり話せない ('I can't speak very much/well.').

meaning: According to
summary: A semi-formal expression that highlights information that is according to (A), or stems from (A).
formation: Verb + ところ + によると(1)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About によると・によれば
text: によると, a combination of the case marking particle に, the う - Verb よる, and the conjunction particle と, is a phrase that is used to express that something is 'according to (A)', or 'going off (A)'. In these cases, (A) is considered to be the source of some form of information which will be conveyed in the (B) part of the sentence.
This expression will be used after nouns, or with verbs that have been paired with ところ (to indicate the 'place' where the information came from).
In newspapers and in articles, the more formal によりますと variant can also regularly be seen.
However, this structure is not limited to using と, and the same meaning can be conveyed with によれば. This is just よる in its conjunctive form that pairs with the conjunction particle ば.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: よる is almost always written in hiragana alone. However, there are several different kanji that can be used to represent this verb. Each of these kanji have slightly different nuances, but they generally all represent the same 'base' meaning. This meaning is that '(B)'s foundation is (A)'. The most common kanji used for よる are as follows:
{依|よ}る - (B) depends on (A).
{拠|よ}る - (B) extends from (A).
{因|よ}る - (B) results from (A).
{由|よ}る - (B) is due to (A).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Remember that ことによると is a set expression meaning "perhaps"!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: によって・による (N3, By means of, According to, Depending on, Because of, Due to): Both derive from よる ('to be based on'), but are used differently. によると・によれば means 'according to' and is used to report information, e.g. 天気予報によると雨が降るそうです ('According to the weather forecast, it will rain.') によって・による often means 'depending on' and has broader uses, including cause, method, or basis, e.g. 人によって考え方が違う ('Ways of thinking vary depending on the person.')

にもとづいて (N3, Based on, In accordance with): によると・によれば reports second-hand information, e.g. 新聞によると事件があったそうです ('According to the newspaper, there was an incident.') にもとづいて indicates that an action is grounded in something like rules or facts, e.g. 法律にもとづいて判断する ('Make a decision based on the law.')

にしたがって (N2, As, Following, As then, According to, In accordance with): Both can translate as 'according to', but differ in usage. にしたがって means 'in accordance with' or 'following' something, e.g. 説明書に従って組み立てた ('I assembled it according to the manual.') によると・によれば expresses reported information, e.g. 説明書によると操作は簡単です ('According to the manual, the operation is simple.')

をもとに (N2, Based on, From, According to): Both involve a basis or source, but differ in usage. によると・によれば reports information, e.g. 天気予報によると雨が降るそうです ('According to the weather forecast, it will rain.') をもとに means doing something based on a source or foundation, e.g. 事実をもとに小説のストーリーを考えた ('I thought up a story for a novel based on true events.')

meaning: By means of, According to, Depending on, Because of, Due to
summary: A semi-formal expression that highlights information that is according to (A), or stems from (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About によって・による
text: によって, による, and により are all different versions of the same expression, that can basically be translated as 'according to (A)', or 'depending on (A)'. This uses the same よる as seen in the grammar pattern によると. They will be used in the following way:

によって - Generally used before a comma (although not always). Acts as the separation point between the (A) and (B) parts of a sentence. Made up of the case marking particle に, and the う - Verb よる in its て form.
による - Generally used at the end of a sentence, to highlight that the previous statement depends on (A).
により - Almost always used before a comma. Acts as the separation point between the (A) and (B) parts of a sentence. Made up of the case marking particle に, and the う - Verb よる in its conjunctive form.
To use any of these constructions, attach them to the end of a noun that you want to express as being the 'dependent' thing.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Although よる is almost always written in hiragana, there are several different kanji that use this reading. They all share similar meanings. Learn more about this in the によると grammar point.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: によると・によれば (N3, According to): Both derive from よる ('to be based on'), but are used differently. によると・によれば means 'according to' and is used to report information, e.g. 天気予報によると雨が降るそうです ('According to the weather forecast, it will rain.') によって・による often means 'depending on' and has broader uses, including cause, method, or basis, e.g. 人によって考え方が違う ('Ways of thinking vary depending on the person.')

ために (N3, Due to, Because of, As a result of): Both can express cause, but with different perspectives. ために often reflects the speaker's point of view, e.g. 試合は台風のために中止になった ('The game was canceled in light of the typhoon.') によって typically conveys an external or objective cause, e.g. 台風によって多くの家が壊れた ('Many houses were damaged due to the typhoon.')

でできる・からできる (N4, Made of, Made from, Produced from, Come from): でできる・からできる expresses that something is made or composed of a certain ingredient, e.g. この家は木でできている ('This house is made from wood.'). In one usage, によって can be used with verbs like 作る or できる with a similar meaning, e.g., 木によって作られた家 'a house made from wood'. In other uses, によって can also mark the person or method by which something is made, while でできる・からできる cannot.

次第 (N3, As soon as): Both describe how one thing leads to another, but with different nuance. 次第 emphasizes immediacy, e.g. 方法が決まり次第連絡します ('I'll contact you as soon as the method is decided.') によって・による shows variation or dependence, e.g. 方法によって結果が変わる ('The result changes depending on the method.')

〜かは〜によって違う (N3, Depends on, Changes depending on, Differ depending on): Both express variation depending on conditions, and 〜かは〜によって違う includes によって as part of its structure. summary: A slightly formal phrase which means in whole, but is primarily used with negative phrases to mean not at all.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 全く～ない
text: 全く～ない is an expression that combines the adverb {全|まった}く, with a phrase that uses another word in its ない form. It is often translated as 'not at all (A)'. Literally, it is closer to 'completely not (A)', or 'entirely not (A)', coming from the kanji {全|ぜん}'s meaning of 'whole'.
Like many other adverbs, まったく may be used at the beginning of a sentence, or directly before the word that it is describing as being 'not at all' (A).
It is common to see this expression using both the kanji form, and plain hiragana form of {全|まった}く, so both should be learned early.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): Both 全く～ない and あまり～ない express negation, but differ in degree. 全く～ない indicates a complete absence, e.g. 全く寒くない ('It's not cold at all.'). あまり～ない suggests a lesser degree, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.').

決して〜ない (N3, Never, By no means): While both 決して〜ない and 全く〜ない express negation, their nuances differ. 決して〜ない is a stronger, more emphatic expression meaning 'never' or 'by no means', and often carries an emotional or resolute tone. 全く〜ない translates as 'not at all' and conveys a more general or objective negation. The choice between them depends on context and the speaker's emotional stance.

なかなか～ない (N3, Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from): Both express rarity or lack of frequency, but with different focus. 全く〜ない means something happens infrequently, e.g. 全く外食しない ('I hardly ever eat out.') なかなか〜ない suggests it doesn't happen easily or readily, often due to circumstances, e.g. 忙しくてなかなか外食できない ('I can't easily eat out because I'm so busy.')

とても～ない (N3, Not ~ at all, Cannot ~ at all): 全く～ない and とても～ない both express strong negation, but differ in nuance. 全く～ない is used to completely deny or negate something, indicating total absence or lack. とても～ない, on the other hand, implies an extreme state or condition that makes something impossible, adding a nuance of implausibility or incapability.

すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): 全く～ない and すこしも～ない are emphatic negatives that can both mean 'not at all' or 'not even a little'. For example, 全く飲まない and 少しも飲まない both mean 'I don't drink at all.' or 'I don't drink even a little.'. While often interchangeable, すこしも may sound unnatural when there's no nuance of amount or degree. For example, 全く行ったことがない ('I haven't gone at all.'), which wouldn't fit with すこしも.

ぜんぜん (N4, (Not) at all): Both ぜんぜん (with a negative verb) and 全く～ない mean 'not at all,' e.g. ぜんぜんできない and 全くできない both mean 'I can't do it at all.', with ぜんぜん being more casual in tone. In modern speech, both can occasionally appear with affirmative forms, e.g. ぜんぜん大丈夫 ('It's completely fine.'), though this was traditionally considered improper use.

meaning: Should, Ought
summary: A particle construction that is often used for presenting orders or expectations from an authority.
formation: Verb［ない］ + こと + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことだ
text: As a sentence ending particle, こと has two primary functions. These are as follows:
{願望|がんぼう}や{軽|かる}い{命令|めいれい}を{表|あらわ}す - Highlighting a desire or weak command.
{感嘆|かんたん}や{疑問|ぎもん}を{表|あらわ}す - Highlighting astonishment or doubt.
We will focus on the first meaning in this grammar point, as the 'astonishment' nuance is not as commonly used in modern Japanese, and is primarily used only by women.

At the end of a sentence, こと will be paired with the dictionary (or ない) form of a verb, to highlight a particular action that either should, or should not occur. It is usually grouped with the auxiliary verb だ, although this is not always the case. This construction is most often translated as 'should/should not (A)', or 'ought to/not (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものだ (N3, Supposed to, Should, That's the way it is): Both express what should be done, but with different nuance. ことだ is used to give firm advice, e.g. 諦めずに続けることだ ('You should keep going without giving up.') ものだ expresses general expectations or norms, e.g. 仕事は地道に頑張り続けるものだ ('One is expected to keep working steadily.')

たほうがいい (N5, It'd be better to, Should do): たほうがいい is a common expression used to give advice or make suggestions, often reflecting the speaker's personal opinion on what would be better. ことだ may appear similar but is more formal, carrying a stronger nuance of expectation, implying 'this is how things are (or should be,' rather than a personal suggestion.

ないほうがいい (N5, It'd be better not to, Shouldn't do): ないほうがいい is used to suggest not doing something, similar to 'You shouldn't…' in English. It's a common expression that often reflects the speaker's personal or subjective opinion. In contrast, ことだ expresses the opposite idea, meaning 'should' or 'ought to,' and is more formal. It carries the nuance of stating a rule or general expectation rather than personal advice.

命令形 (N4, (Verb)!, Do (something)!): The imperative or command form (命令形) gives direct, blunt commands, e.g. 止まれ ('Stop!'). It can sound harsh unless softened with particles like よ, e.g. 頑張れよ ('Try harder, okay?'). In contrast, ことだ offers soft advice, e.g. 早起きすることだ ('You should wake up early.'), and is often used when giving recommendations or suggestions.

べき (N3, Must, Should, Ought to): Both express obligation, but differ in tone. ことだ is used to offer advice or general suggestions, e.g. 無理をしないことだ ('You should take it easy.') べき is stronger, implying moral or logical necessity, e.g. 約束は守るべきだ ('You should keep your promises.')

ばいい (N3, Can, Should, It'd be good if): Both can be used to give advice or suggestions, but the tone differs. ことだ sounds more formal or authoritative, as if stating a rule or guideline. In contrast, ばいい is more casual and conversational, often used among friends. Additionally, ばいい can be used in contrary-to-fact suggestions, such as 行けばいいのに ('You should go but you won't'). ことだ cannot be used this way.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): ことはない downplays the need for action and is often used to reassure, e.g. 焦ることはない ('There's no need to rush.') ことだ gives firm advice and carries an authoritative tone, e.g. 焦らずに進めることだ ('You should proceed calmly.') ことはない can also mean that something never occurs, which is a usage unrelated to ことだ, e.g. 彼と会うことはない ('I never see him.')

べきではない (N3, Should not, Must not, Ought not to): ことだ suggests what one should do as advice or a general guideline, e.g. 無理をしないことだ ('You should take it easy.') べきではない expresses the opposite, indicating what one should not do based on moral or social expectations, e.g. 人を見た目で判断すべきではない ('You shouldn't judge people by appearances.')

わけだ (N3, For that reason, No wonder, As you'd expect, Naturally, Thus, This is why): Both express reasoning in a broad sense, but are used differently. わけだ explains why something is the case, e.g. 暖房が壊れているのか。だから寒いわけだ ('So the heater's broken. That explains why it's cold.') ことだ gives strong advice or instruction, e.g. 寒いなら暖房をつけることだ ('If it's cold, you should turn on the heater.')

なければならない (N4, Must do, Have to do): ことだ is used for light advice ('should' or 'ought to'), e.g. 毎日早起きすることだ ('You should get up early every day.'). なければならない expresses stronger obligation, like 'must' or 'have to', often implying consequences. ７時に起きなければならない ('You must get up at 7.').

てはならない (N2, Must not, Cannot, Should not): Both carry an authoritative tone, as if stating a rule, but have opposite meanings. ことだ gives strong advice or recommendations, e.g. 約束は守ることだ ('You should keep your promises.') てはならない expresses strict prohibition, e.g. 約束を破ってはならない ('You must not break your promises.')

meaning: I heard that, It is said that
summary: An expression that highlights how (A) seems to be, based on what someone has heard.
formation: Noun + だ + そう + だ
Noun + だ + そう + です (polite)
［な］Adjective + だ + そう + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そうだ
text: The auxiliary verb そうだ has two primary functions in Japanese. It can convey one of the following things:
Hearsay: {伝聞|でんぶん} - Highlighting things that have been heard from other people.
Appearance: {様態|ようたい} - Highlighting the way that things 'appear', or 'seem'.

The appearance nuance is covered in another lesson, so we will focus on hearsay in this grammar point. When used to repeat statements that have been heard from other people/sources, そうだ (or そうです) will be paired with the plain form of a verb or い-Adjective, or a noun/な-Adjective followed by だ.
そうだ always implies that the speaker is not 100% certain about the validity of the information that they are conveying. Due to this, it does not sound as confident as other expressions, like ようだ.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In order to avoid confusion between the そうだ that is used for repeating information, and the そうだ that is used for making observations, the following differences will need to be memorized.
Verbs -
{降|ふ}るそうだ - Unaltered verb, そうだ that is repeating information.
{降|ふ}りそうだ - Conjunctive form, そうだ that is used for making observations.
い-Adjectives -
{寒|さむ}いそうだ - Unaltered adjective, そうだ that is repeating information.
{寒|さむ}そうだ - い removed, そうだ that is used for making observations.
Nouns and な-Adjectives -
{綺麗|きれい}だそうだ - だ is used before そうだ. This is repeating information.
{綺麗|きれい}そうだ - No だ between the な-Adjective and そうだ. This is making an observation.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Do not confuse with the form of そう used with word stems.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようだ (N4, It seems that, It appears that, It looks like): While both of these forms express information indirectly, they differ in the source of the information. ようだ simply means 'it appears that...', and can cover information gleaned from a variety of sources. In contrast, (だ)そうだ is typically used specifically to indicate hearsay (i.e. 'I heard that...'/'someone said that...').

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): らしい ① and そうだ both convey information heard from another source, but with different nuances. らしい ① suggests hearsay with some degree of certainty, implying the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 'Apparently it's (A)'. In contrast, そうだ is more neutral, simply meaning 'I heard (A).' or 'They say (A).'. They also connect differently to nouns and な-Adjectives, e.g. 大変らしい vs. 大変だそうだ (both meaning 'It seems difficult.').

んだって (N3, I heard that, He or She said that): Both express hearsay, but with different tone and usage. んだって is very casual, often used in everyday conversation, and carries an explanatory tone due to んだ, e.g. 明日休みなんだって ('They said tomorrow's a day off, you know.') そうだ is more neutral and indirect, with no explanatory nuance, e.g. 明日休みだそうだ ('I heard tomorrow's a day off.')

ということだ (N3, I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that): Both convey hearsay, but differ in tone and formality. そうだ is used to directly pass on something you've heard, e.g. 明日は休みだそうだ ('I heard he has tomorrow off.') ということだ is more formal and often sounds more confident or declarative. It can also carry a nuance of explanation or conclusion, e.g. 明日は休みになるということだ ('So that means / They say we'll have tomorrow off.')

といわれている (N4, It is said that, Is known as): といわれている and そうだ both report something heard, but differ in nuance. といわれている is more general and formal, e.g. 'It is said that (A)'. On the other hand, そうだ often implies someone specific said it and is more casual, e.g., 雨が降るそうだ ('I heard it's going to rain.').

とか (N2, I heard that… something like, They said ... or something ): Both can relay hearsay, but with different levels of certainty. とか adds a nuance of vagueness or uncertainty, e.g. 来月引っ越すとか ('I heard they might be moving next month, or something.') そうだ also conveys hearsay, but with less ambiguity, e.g. 来月引っ越すそうだ ('I heard they're moving next month.')

ときいた (N4, I heard that): Both ときいた and そうだ express hearsay, but with different nuances. ときいた means 'I heard (A).' and conveys information directly heard by the speaker, e.g., 高いときいた ('I heard it was expensive.'). In contrast, そうだ reports hearsay in a more abstract fashion, similar to 'They say (A).' in English.

meaning: Having done..., If...is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so
summary: A sentence starter which highlights that upon the previous (A) being done, the uncontrollable result of (B) then also happened. Going off (A) being done, (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About すると
text: すると, a combination of する and the conjunction particle と, is generally considered to be an abbreviation of そうすると, and means that 'once (A) is done, (B)', or 'upon (A), (B)'. すると is usually used at the beginning of a new sentence, to highlight something that occurred due to the circumstances mentioned in the previous sentence/statement.
As a standalone statement, すると is classified as a conjunction.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そうすると (N3, Having done that..., If that is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): すると is often considered an abbreviated form of そうすると, and both are typically used at the beginning of a sentence to express something that occurred or logically followed from what came before, similar to 'upon (A), (B)' in English. Both can also be used to summarize or draw a conclusion from the previous statement, like saying 'so that means (A).'

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): The two Japanese phrases, すると and そのため(に), are used in different contexts. すると is used to indicate a natural or logical outcome or consequence of a certain action, it is often translated as 'and then', 'if', or 'when'. On the other hand, そのため(に) is commonly used to express the cause or reason for a certain outcome, it is often translated as 'for that reason', 'because of that' or 'hence'.

と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): と marks a natural result, while すると is a transition word meaning 'thereupon' or 'and then'. It's often used at the beginning of a new sentence to show what happened next. For example, ドアを開けた。すると、猫がいた ('I opened the door. And there was a cat.'

それに (N4, And, Besides, Moreover, In addition): すると and それに are both sentence starters but differ in usage. すると shows result or reaction, e.g. 雨が降った。すると傘を差した ('It started raining. Then he opened an umbrella.'). それに is additive and neutral: 雨が降っていた。それに寒かった ('It was raining. And cold too.').

そこで (N3, Accordingly, Now, Therefore, To that end): Both describe what follows from a previous situation, but with different nuance. そこで introduces an intentional response to a situation, e.g. 雨が降ってきた。そこで傘をさした ('It started raining, so I opened my umbrella.') すると shows a natural or immediate result, e.g. 雨が降ってきた。すると子供が泣き出した ('It started raining. Then the child started crying.')

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そうすると
text: そうすると, a combination of {然|そ}う (an adverb meaning 'like that', or 'as such') する and the conjunction particle と, expresses that 'once (A) was done, (B)', or 'upon (A), (B)'. そうすると is usually used at the beginning of a new sentence, to highlight something that occurred due to the circumstances mentioned in the previous sentence/statement.
As a stand-alone statement, そうすると is classified as a conjunction.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Although {然|そ}う has a kanji form, this particular word will almost always be written in hiragana. This is true for many different expressions that use そう, not just そうすると.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と (N4, If, When, Whenever, And, [Conditional]): と marks a natural condition, while そうすると is used to explain what would happen in that case. It means 'if that happens' or 'then...' and often introduces a result. For example, 早く寝なさい。そうすると、明日は元気になるよ ('Go to bed early. Then you'll feel good tomorrow.')

すると (N3, Having done..., If...is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): すると is often considered an abbreviated form of そうすると, and both are typically used at the beginning of a sentence to express something that occurred or logically followed from what came before, similar to 'upon (A), (B)' in English. Both can also be used to summarize or draw a conclusion from the previous statement, like saying 'so that means (A).'

sections.heading: About のはXの方だ
text: のは～の{方|ほう}だ is an expression used to show that (A) (usually despite expectations) is (B). It can be translated as 'the one that (A), is (B)'. This phrase is made up of the following parts:
のは - Used for nominalization (creating a noun phrase). は highlights contrast between two (or more) elements.
の{方|ほう} - A combination of の, the case marking particle, and {方|ほう}, a noun meaning 'side', or 'direction'.
だ (or です) - The auxiliary verb used for 'determining' something.

The literal meaning of this grammar point is something similar to 'that which is (A), is on the side of (B)'. By saying that something is on the 'side' of (B), it comes across more gently than expressly stating that it 'is (B)'.
To use this construction, attach のは to the end of a phrase, and then follow it with a noun + の{方|ほう}だ. Note that のは will become なのは if the final word before のは is a noun.

text: わけではない (N3, It doesn't mean that, It is not the case, It's not like): のはXの方だ emphatically states what is true or relevant, often in contrast with something else, e.g. 勝ったのは彼の方だ ('He was the one who won.') わけではない, by contrast, qualifies or softens a statement, e.g. 彼が勝ったわけではない ('It's not that he won.') One affirms directly; the other downplays or denies.

Adjective + の(は) (N5, The 'one' that... (Indefinite pronoun, Adjective nominalization)): Both structures single out and highlight something. That is, expressing '(A) is the one that (B)'. Adjective + の(は) is the simpler form, e.g. 新しいのはどっち？ ('Which one is new?') のはXの方だ expands on this to specify and contrast. A common use is in insistent apologies, e.g. いいえ、謝らないといけないのは僕のほうだ ('No, I'm the one who needs to apologize.')

こそ (N3, For sure, For certain, Even more so, Underlined or bolded text): Both structures single out and highlight something, but in different ways. のはXの方だ highlights contrast between options and is often used in apologies, e.g. 悪いのは僕の方だ ('I'm the one that's at fault.') こそ emphasizes exclusivity or importance, e.g. 私こそ謝るべきだ ('I, and no one else, should apologize.')

meaning: Model, Type, Pattern, Kind, Shape, Size(d)
summary: A suffix which defines the shape, pattern, or model of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Noun＋型
text: {型|がた}, or sometimes {形|がた}, are two kanji that are often used as a suffix, to identify that something is 'shaped', or 'sized' according to (A). The primary reading of both of these kanji is かた, but becomes がた due to {連濁|れんだく} (sound changes due to conjugation). {型|がた} can be attached directly to the end of nouns, or to い-Adjectives. Occasionally, {型|かた} will be used after the case marking particle の. In these cases, because it is connected to の, and not directly to the noun, it will be read as かた, not がた.

Although there are two different kanji that can be used in this expression, {型|がた} will be used far more frequently than {形|がた}. This is primarily due to the base meanings that these kanji have. Those meanings are as follows:
{型|がた} - Form (in regard to design, pattern, type, or model).
{形|がた} - Shape (in regard to physical shapes only. Square, rectangle, triangle, etc).
Due to this, {型|がた} is used when describing any form/pattern that is abstract, while {形|がた} is primarily only used for describing very basic (visible) shapes.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): Both describe attributes, but with different focuses. 型 emphasizes form or category, e.g. 家族型の会社 ('A family-style company') らしい expresses what seems typical or characteristic of something, often based on impression, e.g. 家族らしい雰囲気 ('A family-like atmosphere', warm and loving, as one might expect from a family)

風 (N4, -style, Way, Fashion): Both describe style or appearance, but with different nuance. 型 refers to a concrete type, model, or category, e.g. 新型のスマホ ('A new model of smartphone') 風 suggests resemblance or outward style, often subjective or superficial, e.g. 昔風の家 ('A house in the old-fashioned style')

的 (N3, ~ly・~like・~al, Typical): Both attach to nouns to form descriptive modifiers, but differ in meaning. 型 refers to a fixed or functional type, e.g. 日本型の経営 ('The Japanese style of management') 的 turns nouns into な-adjectives meaning 'related to' or 'having the quality of', e.g. 経済 → 経済的な問題 ('An economic problem')

meaning: (Please) try to, (Please) look
summary: An honorific expression used to ask someone to attempt to do (A), or to peruse at their leisure.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てごらん
text: てご{覧|らん} is an honorific language expression in Japanese that is used in a similar way to なさい. It is usually translated as 'please try to (A)', where (A) is the verb that ご{覧|らん} is connected to, through the use of the conjunction particle て.

However, despite being translated as 'please try to (A)', the literal meaning of {覧|らん} is 'to look', or 'to peruse' (to look at one's own leisure, without needing to rush). Due to this, てごらん can be thought of as being quite similar to てみる 'to try', but with the added emphasis of 'try as you like, when it suits you'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないでください (N5, Please don't (Polite request)): ないでください is a polite way to ask someone not to do something. It's neutral and appropriate for strangers or people of equal status. In contrast, てごらん is a gentle request form often used by adults to children, etc., that adds a nuance of 'Give this a try' or 'Try doing this (to see how you like it).'

てください (N5, Please do (Polite request)): てください is a basic way to express a polite request ('Please do…'). For example, 食べてください would mean 'Please eat (this).' It is polite and neutral, and can be used with strangers or people equal in status to you. てごらん is a gentle request form often used by adults to children, etc., that adds a nuance of 'Give this a try' or 'Try doing this (to see how you like it).'

な (N5, Do not, Don't (Prohibitive)): The dictionary/non-past form of a verb + な expresses a blunt command not to do something. In contrast, てごらん is a gentle encouragement to try doing something. For example, 食べるな！ means 'Don't eat it!' while 食べてごらん means 'Try eating it' Both are used toward someone of lower status, such as an adult speaking to a child.

てみる (N4, To try to): てみる expresses trying something to see what it's like, similar to the English 'try (doing)', e.g. 食べてみる ('I'll try eating it.'). てごらん is a more directive form that encourages someone else to try something, e.g. 食べてごらん ('Try eating it.' as a gentle request). てごらん is often used by adults to children, or superiors to subordinates. Among peers, something like 食べてみて would be more common.

なさい (N4, Command to do): Both are command forms, but with different tones. なさい is a polite but direct command, often used by teachers or parents, e.g. 食べなさい ('Eat.'). てごらん is softer and gently encourages someone to give something a try, e.g. 食べてごらん ('Try eating it'). Both are typically used from adults to children, or superiors to subordinates.

meaning: To have the honor of doing, To take the liberty of doing, To do (polite, formal)
summary: An expression used to politely inform someone that you will perform a specific action after obtaining their permission.
formation: Verb［causative・て］+ いただきます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About させてもらう
text: させてもらう or させていただく is a polite phrase used when the speaker wants to respectfully say they will do something. It is made up of the causative form of a verb plus the receiving word もらう (or the more humble いただく).

させてもらう literally means 'I receive you allowing me to do (A)', however, in practice, it can be thought of as similar to English phrases such as 'To take the liberty of doing (A)' or 'To have the honor of doing (A)'.
Although it is not necessary to mention either party, if they are mentioned then the person who is acting can be marked by が and the person who is 'allowing' the action will be marked by に.
As もらう and いただく are verbs, this pattern can be used in any combination that may normally be seen with verbs. For example, させてもらいたい or させてもらいませんか may also be seen.

Compared to other respectful phrases which are to do with one's own actions, such as いたす, させてもらう implies receiving permission from the other party and a level of gratitude from the speaker. This implication makes it sound softer than other similar phrases.
As this can be seen as doubling-up, it is avoided by some speakers in formal situations, although it is still commonly seen in retail and business situations.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: As させてもらう is already a humble phrase, it can be seen as 'double-keigo' to use it in combination with certain respectful or humble words.

meaning: Combined particles
summary: A particle construction which shows the ownership or relationship of (B) with where (A) is from, going, done with, done until, etc.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Particle + の
text: In Japanese, many particles are often grouped together with the case marking particle の. The primary function of this is to form a link between noun (A), and noun (B). In each of these cases, noun (B) will be considered to have all of the qualities described by noun (A), and the first particle that follows it.
The particle that comes before の will always be something that adds some form of immediate information about noun (A). The most common ones are as follows:
Noun (A) から の Noun (B) - The (B) that is 'from' (A).
Noun (A) と の Noun (B) - The (B) that is 'grouped with' (A).
Noun (A) へ の Noun (B) - The (B) that is 'toward' (A).
Noun (A) で の Noun (B) - The (B) that is 'done with' (A).
Noun (A) まで の Noun (B) - The (B) that is 'until' (A).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Because noun (A) is describing noun (B), noun (B) will be considered as the subject of the statement. Due to this, particles that usually mark subjects, topics, or objects of actions cannot be paired directly with の. This includes に, も, は, が, and を.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Adjective + の(は) (N5, The 'one' that... (Indefinite pronoun, Adjective nominalization)): Particle + の is used when particles like から, と, へ, で, or まで combine with の to describe a noun. For example, 先生への手紙 means 'a letter to (my) teacher,' and 駅までの道 means 'the road to the station.' Adjective + の(は) is a pattern where の replaces a noun, allowing the adjective to form a descriptive phrase. For example, 高いのはこれです means 'This is the expensive one.'

の (N5, Verb nominalizer, The one who..., That which...): In the phrase AのB, の indicates a relationship between A and B, either possession (e.g., ジョンの本 = 'John's book') or description (e.g., 日本人の学生 = 'A Japanese student'). Particle + の is a variation where a phrase with a particle describes another noun (e.g., 先生からの手紙 = 'A letter from the teacher'). Note that particles like に, も, は, が, and を are typically not used in this construction.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About である
text: である (or であります) is a construction in Japanese that is considered to be the formal equivalent of だ. This should not be confused with the polite speech word です, as である is simply a combination of the conjunctive form of だ, and the う - Verb, ある.
である may be used in any place that だ would usually be used, but is most likely to be found at the end of sentences/statements.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Primarily used in literary work

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たる (N1, To be (in a position of), As a, For): Both are formal forms of 'to be' used in writing. である is the standard formal equivalent of だ, e.g. 彼は学生である ('He is a student.') たる emphasizes qualification or the qualities appropriate to a role, e.g. 指導者たる者 ('A person worthy of being a leader')

です (N5, To be, Is): です is often used as the polite form of だ, which is similar in meaning to 'is' or 'to be' in English. It's polite but not overly formal, and it's often used in both speech and writing. In contrast, である is a formal (but not polite) expression mainly used in writing or formal speeches. One key difference is that である can appear in front of nouns in modifying clauses, like in 日本人である留学生 ('an exchange student who is Japanese').

がある (N5, To be, There is): がある expresses the existence or possession of inanimate objects, similar to saying 'there is' or 'I have' in English. In contrast, である is comparable to (and is, in fact, an alternate form of) the casual だ or polite です, and is therefore equivalent to the English "it is". In other words, ピアノがある means 'There's a piano' or 'I have a piano', but ピアノである means 'It's a piano' in formal/written language (the spoken polite equivalent would be ピアノです).

だ (N5, To be, Is): The main difference between だ and である is formality. だ is casual and common in conversation, while である is more formal and mainly used in writing. Both だ and である follow nouns or noun phrases, but である has a more literary tone. である slight differs from the verb ある (to exist) in that である is a fixed connector.
