sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ところが
text: ところが is a conjunction in Japanese that is a combination of the noun, ところ 'place', and the conjunction particle が. It is used to highlight that (A) was expected, but the unexpected result (B) occurred. It is usually translated as 'however', or 'despite that'.
ところが is most often used at the beginning of a new sentence, before highlighting something that is contrary to what was described in the previous sentence.
This use of が in Japanese is referred to as {確定|かくてい}の{逆接|ぎゃくせつ}, which basically means 'a contradictory conclusion'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Sometimes, ところが is referred to as a conjunction particle itself, disregarding the combination of ところ and が. This is similar to ところで, another conjunction particle that has a slightly different meaning, and is frequently translated as 'by the way'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それでも (N4, But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless): それでも and ところが both show contrast, like 'even so' or 'and yet'. それでも has a neutral tone and simply adds something that goes against the previous statement. ところが implies something unexpected or surprising happened, especially outside the speaker's control.

だが・ですが (N4, But, Still, However, Nevertheless): Both だが・ですが and ところが express contrast, but with different nuances. だが・ですが is a neutral transition similar to 'but' or 'however,' and can appear in various positions within a sentence. ところが usually comes at the start of a sentence and emphasizes an unexpected or surprising result, often appearing in storytelling or narration.

それにしても (N2, Nevertheless, Even so): Both express contrast, but with different nuance. ところが introduces an unexpected result, e.g. 試合に勝つと思った。ところが負けた ('I thought we'd win the game. But we lost.') それにしても acknowledges the situation but adds an emotional reaction or further judgment, e.g. 仕方がない。それにしても悔しい ('It can't be helped. Even so, it's frustrating.')

が (N5, But, However): Both ところが and が express contrast or contradiction. ところが is used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize a contrast between expectation and reality. In contrast, が is used after a phrase or at the end of a sentence to express simple contrast, or sometimes to add information or context without implying surprise or expectation.

けれども (N5, But, Although): Both ところが and けれども are linking phrases used to express contrast. けれども (or the casual form けど) shows a simple contrast or transition, similar to 'but' in English, and can appear mid-sentence or at the end. In contrast, ところが is typically used at the beginning of a sentence and adds a strong nuance of surprise or something unexpected.

却って (N3, All the more, On the contrary, Conversely): Both introduce unexpected outcomes, but differ in type of surprise. 却って means the result was the opposite of what was intended or expected, e.g. 謝ったら却って怒られた ('When I apologized, I was yelled at instead.') ところが highlights a surprising turn of events, though not necessarily the exact opposite, e.g. 田中さんに電話をかけた。ところがもう出発していた ('I called Tanaka. But he had already departed.')

けど・だけど (N5, But, However): Both ところが and けど・だけど express contrast or contradiction. The key difference is that ところが is used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize a contrast between the expected result and reality, and is more formal. In contrast, けど・だけど are used after a phrase or at the end of a sentence to express simple contrast or contradiction.

meaning: By the way, Incidentally
summary: A grammar point that uses the situation or place of (A) as a good point to incidentally start talking about a new topic.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ところで
text: ところで is a conjunction particle that is made up of the noun, ところ 'place', and the case marking particle で. It is used in a similar way to 'by the way', or 'incidentally' in English, but will only be used for introducing new topics, not continuing within the same topic.
ところで will primarily appear at the beginning of a sentence, before making a statement or asking a question about something unrelated.
The literal translation of ところで is closer to 'and with that', and implies that something (within the previous topic) suddenly reminded the speaker of another thing (that happens to be a new topic).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: When ところで appears after the past tense of a verb as たところで, it carries a different meaning, and will express that something isn't the case, despite (A). This is an advanced grammar point that will be covered at another stage.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: といえば (N3, Speaking of, If it were the case that): Both can be used to shift the topic, but といえば is used after a noun to bring up something related or comment on that thing, e.g. 京都といえば、有名なお寺が多いね ('Speaking of Kyoto, there many famous temples, aren't there.'). In contrast, ところで typically starts a new sentence to introduce an unrelated topic, e.g. ところで、週末の予定は？ ('By the way, what are your plans for the weekend?').

そういえば (N2, Speaking of which, By the way, Come to think of it): Both can be used at the beginning of a sentence to introduce a new topic, but with different nuance. ところで marks a clear, unrelated shift, similar to 'by the way' in English, e.g. ところで、週末は何してた？ ('By the way, what did you do this weekend?') そういえば recalls something related to the current topic, e.g. そういえば、田中さんに会ったよ ('Speaking of which, I saw Tanaka.')

sections.heading: About ほど
text: ほど, coming from the kanji {程|ほど} 'an extent', is used for describing rough estimates about the 'amount' of something. However, unlike expressions such as くらい (which focuses more on the speaker's uncertainty about the exact number), ほど puts emphasis on the upper (or lower) limit of something as having been 'reached'. Due to this, it is usually translated as 'so much that (A)', or 'to the extent that (A)'.
ほど can be added on to the end of the attributive form of any word. The attributive form being the form that is able to be partnered directly with nouns.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ば〜ほど (N3, The more…the more): ほど (sometimes written in kanji as 程) has the basic meaning of 'extent'. ば〜ほど shows a proportional relationship, similar to 'the more (A), the more (B)', e.g. 練習すればするほど上手になる ('The more you practice, the better you get.') When used alone, ほど means 'so much that (A)' or 'to the extent of (A)', e.g. 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.' / 'It was so quiet that I was surprised.')

くらい ② (N3, To the extent that, So…that, About the only thing that...): Both くらい and ほど can express extent in the sense of 'so much that (A)' or 'to the extent of (A)', and are often interchangeable, e.g. 驚くくらい静かだった / 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.') くらい (also written as ぐらい) tends to sound slightly more colloquial, and each word has other uses where they may not be interchangeable.

ほど～ない (N3, Is not as…as, Isn't... like..., Not to the extent of...): ほど (sometimes seen in kanji as 程) has the basic meaning of 'extent'. ほど〜ない is used for comparisons meaning 'not as (A) as (B)', e.g. 彼ほど背が高くない ('I'm not as tall as him.'). When used alone, ほど means 'so much that (A)' or 'to the extent of (A)', e.g. 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.' or 'It was so quiet that I was surprised.').

は～くらいです (N3, About the only, To the extent that): Both relate to expressing extent, but with different emphasis. は～くらいです highlights something as the only or most notable case, like 'about the only (A) is (B)', e.g. できるのは田中さんくらいです ('Mr. Tanaka's about the only person who can do it.') ほど expresses extent or intensity, e.g. 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.')

くらい ① (N5, About, Approximately): くらい (often ぐらい in speech) expresses an approximate degree or extent. It's often used with number + counter expressions (the くらい① form), as in 10分くらいかかった = 'It took about ten minutes.' ほど can be used similarly, but is more formal and carries the nuance of an upper limit—e.g., 10分ほど implies 'about, but no more than ten minutes.'

まで (N4, Even, To even, To the extent of): まで and ほど both mean 'to the extent of,' but with different uses. まで emphasizes inclusion or a surprising limit, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.'). ほど means 'so much that' and often describes degree or intensity, e.g. 痛いほど分かる ('I understand to the point that it hurts.').

meaning: The more…the more
summary: A phrase that highlights a hypothetical (A), and how something will increase or decrease as much as (A) does.
formation: （［な］Adjective + なら（ば））+ ［な］Adjective(*) + な + ほど
（［な］Adjective + であれば）+ ［な］Adjective(*) + である + ほど
（Noun + であれば）+ Noun(*) + である + ほど
(*) The same Adjective, Verb or Noun has to be repeated

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ば〜ほど
text: ば～ほど is a combination of the conjunction particle ば, and the noun ほど. It is used in a similar way to 'the more ~ the more' in English. Literally, it just highlights that 'if it is (A), then the limit of (A) will be controlled only by its extent'.

To use ば～ほど, ば will be paired with the hypothetical form of any verb/い-Adjective (or noun/な-Adjective with なら on the end), before the same word will be repeated in its attributive form. After this, a (B) part of the sentence will highlight what the expected result of (A) is.
As である (the formal version of だ) may replace な with な-Adjectives (or なら with nouns), sometimes である will be used instead of な/なら, in regard to both nouns and な-Adjectives.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The conditional part of the structure is sometimes omitted. この豆を食べれば食べるほど痩せるらしい。→ この豆を食べるほど痩せるらしい。

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ほど (N3, The more, About, To the extent that, So much… that): ほど (sometimes written in kanji as 程) has the basic meaning of 'extent'. ば〜ほど shows a proportional relationship, similar to 'the more (A), the more (B)', e.g. 練習すればするほど上手になる ('The more you practice, the better you get.') When used alone, ほど means 'so much that (A)' or 'to the extent of (A)', e.g. 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.' / 'It was so quiet that I was surprised.')

どんどん (N4, Progressively, Rapidly increasing, More and more): どんどん is an adverb that implies rapid or dramatic change, often in leaps and bounds, e.g. どんどん大きくなる 'grow rapidly'. 〜ば〜ほど is a structure that shows proportional change, like 'the more (A), the more (B)' in English. For example, 大きくなればなるほどいい ('The bigger it gets, the better.').

一方だ (N3, More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er): Both can be used to describe change, but with different patterns. ば〜ほど expresses a proportional relationship between two things, like 'the more (A), the more (B)', e.g. 練習すればするほど上手になる ('The more you practice, the better you get.') 一方だ shows a continuous, one-way change in a single direction, e.g. 物価は上がる一方だ ('Prices just keep rising.')

ますます (N3, Increasingly, More and more, Decreasingly, Less and less, Keep -ing): They are similar in that both describe change, but ば〜ほど specifically expresses a proportional relationship between two things, like the English 'the more (A), the more (B)', e.g. 見れば見るほど好きになる ('The more I look, the more I like it.'). In contrast, ますます simply emphasizes continued intensification, e.g. 彼の人気はますます高まっている ('His popularity is steadily rising.')

ば (N4, If… then, (Conditional)): ば is a conditional form that emphasizes the condition needed for a result, e.g. 勉強すればうまくなるよ ('If you study, you'll get better.'). ば〜ほど builds on this to mean 'the more (A), the more (B)' e.g. 勉強すればするほど、うまくなる ('The more you study, the better you'll get.').

meaning: Is not as…as, Isn't... like..., Not to the extent of...
summary: A grammar point that highlights the extent of (A) as insufficient to cause (B).
formation: (1) ［い］Adjective［ない］、［な］Adjective + ではない、［な］Adjective + じゃない

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ほど～ない
text: Another expression that uses the noun ほど 'an extent' in Japanese, is ほど～ない. In the (A) part of a sentence, an extent will be highlighted, before the (B) part of the sentence will use ない to negate that extent, saying that it has not been reached. This phrase can be translated as 'it isn't like (A)', 'it's not to the point of (A)'. Literally it means 'if (A) is the extent, then (B) is not true'.
ほど will regularly be used after a verb or noun, while ない is more likely to be used after a verb, い-Adjective, or な-Adjective (as it is describing something about ほど).

While this grammar point may be used for expressing that an extent has not been reached, it is also frequently used for making comparisons between two things. In these cases, it states that 'the example/limit of (A) is something that cannot be reached/repeated by (B)'. This is similar to '(B) is not as ~ as (A)' in English.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: より～のほうが (N5, To be more ~ than ~): Both ほど～ない and より～のほうが express comparisons, but from different angles. ほど～ない is a negative comparison, meaning 'not as...as' (e.g. Xほどおいしくない = 'not as tasty as X'). より～のほうが is a positive comparison, meaning 'more...than' (e.g. AよりBのほうがおいしい = 'B is tastier than A').

ほど (N3, The more, About, To the extent that, So much… that): ほど (sometimes seen in kanji as 程) has the basic meaning of 'extent'. ほど〜ない is used for comparisons meaning 'not as (A) as (B)', e.g. 彼ほど背が高くない ('I'm not as tall as him.'). When used alone, ほど means 'so much that (A)' or 'to the extent of (A)', e.g. 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.' or 'It was so quiet that I was surprised.').

まで (N4, Even, To even, To the extent of): Both grammar points share the idea of 'to the extent of,' but are used differently. ほど～ない makes negative comparisons, e.g. ジョンはトムほど強くない ('John isn't as strong as Tom.'). まで emphasizes something going beyond expectations, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.').

より (N4, More than, Over): Both expressions are used for comparisons. ほど～ない makes negative comparisons, e.g. ジョンはトムほど強くない ('John isn't as strong as Tom.'). より is used for positive comparisons, e.g. トムはジョンより強い ('Tom is stronger than John.'). Note that ほど follows the greater of the two options, while より follows the lesser.

pattern: では・それでは・じゃあ
meaning: If so, Well (then), In that case
summary: A common phrase used to say and with that, usually in order to start a new topic, or excuse oneself.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About では・それでは・じゃあ
text: では and じゃあ are both abbreviations of それでは, and used as conjunctions in Japanese. This structure may be considered as a combination of それ, the case marking particle で, and the binding (adverbial) particle は, but is commonly treated as a single word. それでは, では and じゃ is the order of use from most formal to least formal.

それでは has two primary functions. It can be used to continue in the same topic, showing that '(B) is a result of (A)'. Or it may be used to change the conversation topic completely, showing that '(A) is at a good point to become (B)'. In each of these cases, it can be translated as 'and with that' in English. 'If so', 'well then', and 'in that case' are also common translations.
The translation of 'in that case' is most commonly used when one person is making an assumption/drawing a conclusion about something that someone else has just said.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: さ - Interjection (N3, All right, There we go, Now, You see, Well (I don't know, let me see)): Both can appear at the beginning of a sentence to mark a transition. では・それでは・じゃあ signal a shift or next step based on context, e.g. じゃあ、行こうか ('Well then, shall we go?') さ (often extended as さあ) adds an encouraging or prompting tone, e.g. さあ、そろそろ行こうか！ ('Come on, let's get going!')

それなら (N2, Then, If that's the case): それなら and それでは can both be used at the start of a sentence as transition markers meaning in that case or well then. それなら expresses a response to a specific condition, as in それなら行きません (In that case, I won’t go). それでは can overlap in usage, but it can also mean well then or and with that, often used to wrap up a topic, as in それでは、失礼します (Well then, excuse me), which それなら cannot convey.3

さて (N3, Well, Well then): Both mark transitions, but with slightly different nuance. さて is used to shift to a new topic or proceed to the next step, e.g. さて、次の話題に入りましょう ('Now then, let's move on to the next topic.') では・それでは・じゃあ reference the previous context and often lead into a decision or conclusion, similar to 'well then' or 'in that case', e.g. それでは、始めましょう ('Well then, let's begin.')

meaning: In order to
summary: A structure which indicates the desired result of (A), and then what is required to lead toward that end.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About のに
text: Regarded as a conjunction particle by itself, のに is simply a fusion of the case marking particles の and に. のに has two primary functions in Japanese. It can be used to show that something is the opposite of what is expected for (A) (translated as 'despite'), or it can be used to show that something is required for (A) to be realized (translated as 'in order to'). We will focus on the 'in order to' meaning in this lesson.
To use のに, simply attach it to the base (non-past) form of a verb that you would like to express as being the 'goal', before following it with the conditions required to meet that goal.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ため(に) (N3, For, For the sake of, In order to): Both can mean 'in order to' when expressing purpose and are often interchangeable in that usage, e.g. 健康維持のために運動する / 健康を維持するのに運動する ('I exercise in order to maintain my health.') However, ために can also express cause in certain contexts, which のに cannot, e.g. 雨のために試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled due to rain.')

には (N2, In order to, In regard to, For): Both can express purpose, e.g. 日本語を勉強するのに文プロを使っている ('I'm using Bunpro to study Japanese.') 日本語をマスターするには時間がかかる ('To master Japanese it takes time.') のに follows dictionary-form verbs, while には can follow either verbs or nouns. には is also used more broadly to mean 'in regard to' or 'for', where the idea of purpose doesn't apply, e.g. 子どもには難しい ('It's difficult for children.')

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ため(に)
text: ため (or {為|ため} in its kanji form) is a noun in Japanese that can be translated quite closely to 'sake' in English. However, it is classified as a non-independent word in Japanese, and must always be connected to another word which illustrates the 'sake' that ため is highlighting. The case marking particle に will often be added after ため, to show that (A) is a goal that something will be done to reach.
Due to this, ために can be translated as 'for the sake of (A)', or 'in order to (A)'.
To use ために, attach it to the end of verb in its non-past form, or a noun followed by の.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): These share the same core construction, using ため(に) to express 'in order to (A)' or 'due to (A)'. ため(に) is used within a sentence after a noun, verb, or adjective phrase. そのため is used at the beginning of a sentence to mean 'for that reason' or 'due to that', referring back to what was just said.

のに (N3, In order to): Both can mean 'in order to' when expressing purpose and are often interchangeable in that usage, e.g. 健康維持のために運動する / 健康を維持するのに運動する ('I exercise in order to maintain my health.') However, ために can also express cause in certain contexts, which のに cannot, e.g. 雨のために試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled due to rain.')

わけだ (N3, For that reason, No wonder, As you'd expect, Naturally, Thus, This is why): わけだ and ため(に) are similar in that both can be used when expressing a reason, but they mean quite different things. わけだ is used when drawing a conclusion, like the English 'so that's why (A)', while ため(に) on the other hand means 'for the sake of (A)' or 'due to (A)'.

向き (N3, Suitable for, Facing): Both can be translated as 'for (A)', but differ in nuance. 向き attaches directly to a noun and suggests suitability, e.g. 子ども向きの本 ('A book suitable for children') ため(に) connects to nouns with の and suggests intended benefit or purpose, e.g. 子どものための本 ('A book for children [designed to benefit them]')

んがため(に) (N1, In order to, To, For the purpose of): んがため(に) can be considered an old-fashioned, literary form of ため(に). While both can express the idea of 'for the purpose of (A)' or 'in order to (A)', for example 生きんがために食べる 'eat (in order) to live' sounds like a much more formal and poetic version of 生きるために食べる (same meaning).

には (N2, In order to, In regard to, For): Both can express purpose, similar to 'in order to' or 'for that reason', e.g. 海外に行くためにパスポートを取った ('I got a passport in order to go abroad.') 海外に行くにはパスポートが必要だ ('A passport is necessary to go abroad.') Unlike ため(に), には also has broader uses, such as marking scope or perspective, e.g. 子どもには難しい ('It's difficult for children.')

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ために
text: ため (or {為|ため} in its kanji form) is a noun in Japanese that can be translated quite closely to 'sake' in English. However, it is classified as a non-independent word in Japanese, and must always be connected to another word which illustrates the 'sake' that ため is highlighting. The case marking particle に will often be added after ため, to show that (A) is a goal that something will be done to reach.

However, when used with verbs in the past tense, ために more frequently highlights that something happened 'due to (A)', rather than 'for the sake of (A)'. Because of this, a more accurate description of ため in all situations is 'in light of (A)'. This expresses that (A) is the primary or major event/thing that resulted in (B).

To use ために as 'in light of', 'as a result of', or 'because of', attach it to the end of verb in its past form, or a noun follow by の. It may also be used after い-Adjectives or な-Adjectives in their attributive form.

This 'in light of (A)' nuance can be used in reference to things that have already happened (as above), or in reference to something that is considered as the purpose of an action (as in our other ために grammar point).

sections.label: Caution

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: によって・による (N3, By means of, According to, Depending on, Because of, Due to): Both can express cause, but with different perspectives. ために often reflects the speaker's point of view, e.g. 試合は台風のために中止になった ('The game was canceled in light of the typhoon.') によって typically conveys an external or objective cause, e.g. 台風によって多くの家が壊れた ('Many houses were damaged due to the typhoon.')

にあって (N1, At, In the (place or situation), Under ~ conditions or circumstances, During, Suited to): Both express reason or cause, but with different constraints. ために connects to nouns with の and means 'due to (A)' or 'for the purpose of (A)'. にあって attaches directly to a noun and is limited to situations, positions, or conditions, e.g. 非常時にあって ('in a state of emergency') It cannot be used with general nouns the way ために can.

ゆえに (N1, Because, The reason is, Due to, Therefore, So): Both relate cause and result, but their structures are different. ゆえに can be used as a sentence-level connector meaning ‘therefore’, drawing a conclusion from a stated reason, as in 予算が不足している。ゆえに延期した (‘The budget was insufficient; therefore, it was postponed.’). ために is a grammatical form meaning ‘because of' or 'due to’ and comes within a sentence to similarly express purpose, e.g. 雨のために試合が中止になった (‘The game was canceled due to the rain.’).

せいで (N3, Because of, Due to, Blame): ために and せいで can both mean 'due to (A)', but with a difference in tone. せいで almost always implies a negative or undesirable result. ために can be used with either positive or negative nuance. Also, ために can mean 'for the purpose of (A)', which せいで cannot.

おかげで (N3, Thanks to, Because of): ために and せいで can both express the idea of 'due to (A)', but they differ in that おかげで almost always describes a desirable result, while ために can be used with either a positive or negative nuance. ために can also, in some cases, mean 'for the purpose of (A)', while おかげで cannot be used in this way.

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): そのため(に) can be seen as a more specific version of ために. ために follows a noun, verb, or adjective phrase to express purpose or reason. そのため(に) appears at the beginning of a sentence and means 'due to that' or 'in order to do that', referring back to what was previously said.

につき (N2, Due to, On account of, Each or every): Both ために and につき can express 'due to (A)', but differ in tone and usage. ために requires の to connect to nouns, e.g. 悪天候のため ('Due to bad weather') につき connects directly and sounds stiffer or more formal, e.g. 悪天候につき (Same meaning) Unlike ために, につき cannot be used to express purpose.

その結果 (N3, As a result): ために and その結果 both express a cause/effect relationship, but in different ways. ために is used within a sentence following a noun, verb, or adjective, and can mean either 'due to (A)' or 'in order to (A)'. その結果 comes at the beginning of a sentence and always means 'as a result of that', referring back to the previous statement.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About という
text: という is a combination of the case marking particle と, and the う - Verb {言|い}う. It is a set expression that primarily uses only hiragana. という connects two nouns, and means 'the (B) that is called (A)', or 'the (B) known as (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: といわれている (N4, It is said that, Is known as): という is versatile: AというB = 'a (B) called (A)' or to show hearsay, e.g. 面白いという本 'a book said to be interesting'. といわれている is more formal and emphasizes that something is generally said or believed by many people, especially in written or academic contexts.

いわゆる (N2, What is called, So-called, Generally known): いわゆる and という both convey the idea of something being referred to by a name, but they function differently. いわゆる comes before a noun to mean 'the so-called (A)'. という appears between two nouns in the form AというB ('a B called A'). Because they serve different grammatical roles, they can appear together, e.g. いわゆる外来語というもの ('What is known as a so-called loanword')

というのは (N3, ~ Known as ~ is, ~ Called ~ is, ~ Means ~, Because): Both expressions contain the same という, but are used differently. という is used to name or describe something, typically in the form AというB ('a B called A'). In contrast, というのは introduces something as a topic for explanation or comment, e.g. 人生というのは ('This thing we call life') While という is followed by a single noun, というのは is followed by a phrase that elaborates on the topic.

ということ (N4, ~ing, The ~ that ~ (Nominalization)): ということ turns phrases into nouns and is often used to clarify or restate something, e.g. 日本に行くということ 'the fact that (he) is going to Japan'. という by itself links a phrase or name to a noun, as in ポチという犬 'a dog named Pochi' or 来年日本に行くという学生 'a student who is going to Japan'.

meaning: I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that
summary: A construction that expresses an entire phrase as either hearsay, a rumor, or one's explanation of (A).
formation: Phrase + ということ + だ
Phrase + ということ + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ということだ
text: Like ということ, an expression used for nominalizing a phrase in the fashion of 'the ~ that ~', ということだ makes use of the auxiliary verb だ (or です), and stresses that the nominalized phrase 'is' the case. This phrase is often translated as 'I heard that', or 'it is said that', but literally, it is closer to 'it is that it's ~'. The だ is what gives this expression a high degree of certainty, therefore implying that the speaker has heard the statement elsewhere, and is sure of its validity.
ということだ can be added to the end of any phrase that the speaker wants to highlight as being something that is known.
ということだ is regularly paired with other expressions that show the 'source' of information, such as によると, or によれば.
When ということだ is being used to express hearsay (statements that cannot easily be proven), it can be rephrased as とのことだ. The literal difference between these two phrases is as follows:
ということだ - It can be explained that (A) is ~ (more emphasis on the information).
とのことだ - The statement of (A) has been applied to ~ (more emphasis on the source that 'applied' the information).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Can be rephrased to とのことだ if expresses hearsay.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とか (N2, I heard that… something like, They said ... or something ): Both can report hearsay, but with different tone. とか is casual and vague, often implying uncertainty, similar to 'I heard / They say (A), or something.' ということだ is more formal and declarative, closer to 'The word is (A).' ということだ can also be used to draw conclusions (i.e. 'that means (A)'), which とか cannot.

だって (N3, I heard/was said, Because, But, Even or also, Even if or even though): Both can be used to report hearsay (i.e. 'they say (A)'), but differ in tone and nuance. ということだ is more formal and can carry the nuance of summarizing or confidently reporting what the speaker heard. だって is much more casual and light, and can also be used at the beginning of a sentence with an emphatic 'but I mean (A)' nuance, which is something ということだ cannot do.

とされている (N4, To be considered, To be deemed, Be regarded as, Be accepted as, To be said, To be accredited with): とされている and ということだ both report other people's opinions. ということだ has a nuance of direct hearsay: 'They say that (A)'. On the other hand, とされている presents something as generally believed or accepted. It's less about quoting someone and more about shared public perception.

そうだ (N3, I heard that, It is said that): Both convey hearsay, but differ in tone and formality. そうだ is used to directly pass on something you've heard, e.g. 明日は休みだそうだ ('I heard he has tomorrow off.') ということだ is more formal and often sounds more confident or declarative. It can also carry a nuance of explanation or conclusion, e.g. 明日は休みになるということだ ('So that means / They say we'll have tomorrow off.')

ということ (N4, ~ing, The ~ that ~ (Nominalization)): ということ turns phrases into nouns and often clarifies what was said, e.g. 日本に行くということ 'the fact that he's going to Japan'. Adding だ forms ということだ, which is used to report information second-hand, e.g. 来年から海外に住むということだ ('I hear he'll be living abroad from next year.').

ことなの (N3, (A) is (Description of A), (A) means that (Description of A)): Both use こと to summarize information, but with different nuances. ことなの means 'it's that (A)' and is often used to clarify or define something, as in '(A) means (B)' or 'that means (A).' ということだ can also be used in this way, but additionally functions to report hearsay, e.g. 'I hear / They say (A).' ことなの, without the quoting function of という, is not used to report what others have said.

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): ということだ and らしい ① both convey information from another source, but differ in nuance and formality. らしい ① conveys hearsay with a nuance of confidence, e.g. 雨が降るらしい ('Apparently, it's going to rain.'). In contrast, ということだ literally means 'It is said that (A).' or 'The word is that (A).', and sounds more formal and confident than らしい ①.

summary: A structure that presents the thing referred to as (A), before defining it further.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About というのは
text: というのは is a phrase that combines the case marking particle と, the う - Verb {言|い}う, and the nominalizing particle combination のは. Together, they are usually translated as 'the ~ known as ~ is ~', or 'the ~ called ~ is ~'. Sometimes, it can even simply be '~ means ~'. In essence, というのは is just a way to turn an entire phrase into a noun, before explaining that noun further. This explanation of (A) will either be to give a definition of it, or to give a reason for it.
To use というのは, attach it to the end of a phrase that you would like to indicate as being something that will be explained further '(A)', and then follow it with your definition/reason, '(B)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ということは (N2, That means, That is to say): というのは and ということは are similar in that both take a phrase and turn it into a topic for further explanation. While sometimes interchangeable, というのは is typically followed by a definition or reason. ということは is primarily used to rephrase, clarify, or draw a conclusion from the previous statement.

いわゆる (N2, What is called, So-called, Generally known): いわゆる and という both express the idea of something being 'called' something, but they are used very differently. いわゆる precedes a noun to mean 'the so-called (A)'. というのは takes a word or phrase and introduces it as a topic to be defined or explained. Because they serve different roles, they can be used together, e.g. いわゆる五月病というのは ('This thing known as the so-called May blues is...')

ことなの (N3, (A) is (Description of A), (A) means that (Description of A)): ことなの and というのは can both be used in explanations, but differ in position and role. ことなの appears at the end of a sentence to emphasize a conclusion or explanation. Literally, 'it's that it's (A)'. というのは follows a noun or phrase to introduce it as a topic to be explained. They can be used together, e.g. 人生というのはこういうことなんだ ('This thing we call life... this is what it means.')

～と言っても (N3, Although ~ might say that ~): ～と言っても typically qualifies or corrects an impression based on a previous statement, while ～というのは explains or defines something more directly. For example, 忙しいと言っても一日中じゃない ('I say I'm busy, but not all day') vs. 留学というのは海外の学校で勉強することです ('What we call study abroad means studying at a school in a foreign country').

ということ (N4, ~ing, The ~ that ~ (Nominalization)): ということ and というのは both turn phrases into nouns. ということ is often used to clarify what was said, while というのは introduces a topic for further explanation or comment. というのは can also start a sentence to mean 'what I mean is (A)' or 'that is to say (A)'.

という (N3, Called, Named, Known as, As much as): Both expressions contain the same という, but are used differently. という is used to name or describe something, typically in the form AというB ('a B called A'). In contrast, というのは introduces something as a topic for explanation or comment, e.g. 人生というのは ('This thing we call life') While という is followed by a single noun, というのは is followed by a phrase that elaborates on the topic.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 的
text: {的|てき} is a {接語尾|せつごび} (suffix) in Japanese that has two primary uses. The first use is very similar to 'as' or 'for' in English, and means 'considering/within the category of (A), (B)'. The second use primarily relates to people, and will be covered later. As a single word, {的|てき} is often likened to adjective endings such as '~ly', '~like', and '~al'.

To use {的|てき}, attach it to the end of a noun that you want to express as being the focus point of either a verb or a noun that will come later in the sentence. When describing a noun, {的|てき} will be followed by な (meaning that it becomes a な-Adjective). When describing a verb, it will be followed by に (making it an adverb).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): 的 and らしい both describe being 'like' something, but differ in usage and nuance. 的 is highly versatile, converting nouns into な-Adjectives, e.g. 感情的な 'emotional' or 定期的に 'regularly'. In contrast, らしい expresses embodying the ideal or typical qualities of something, e.g. 春らしい天気 'spring-like weather'.

風 (N4, -style, Way, Fashion): 風 (ふう) and 的 (てき) are suffixes that turn nouns into descriptors. 風 suggests a style or 'air,' and is more limited in use, e.g. 日本風 or 和風 'Japanese-style'. 的 is broader, used for both adjectives and adverbs, e.g. 感情的 'emotional' and 定期的に 'regularly'.

っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): 的 and っぽい are similar in that both can be attached to nouns to turn them into adjectives (or adverbs, in the forms 的に and っぽく). They differ grammatically (的 functions as a な-adjective, while っぽい is an い-adjective), and in nuance. 的 has a wider range of uses, similar to English endings like '-al', '-ly', etc., e.g. 感情 'emotion' vs. 感情的 'emotional'. っぽい is narrower in use, and often carries a derogatory meaning, e.g. 子供っぽい 'childish'.

Noun＋型 (N3, Model, Type, Pattern, Kind, Shape, Size(d)): Both attach to nouns to form descriptive modifiers, but differ in meaning. 型 refers to a fixed or functional type, e.g. 日本型の経営 ('The Japanese style of management') 的 turns nouns into な-adjectives meaning 'related to' or 'having the quality of', e.g. 経済 → 経済的な問題 ('An economic problem')

ぎみ (N3, Looking, Feeling a little, Touch of, Tending to, Slightly): 的 and ぎみ (気味) are similar in that both can be attached to nouns to turn them into adjectives, but they differ in nuance and usage. 的 has a wider range of uses, similar to English endings like '-al', '-ly', etc., e.g. 感情 'emotion' vs. 感情的 'emotional'. In contrast, ぎみ has the specific meaning of 'slightly (A)' or 'showing tendencies of (A)', and typically expresses a subjective judgment about a condition, e.g. 疲れ気味 'a bit tired'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About もの・もん
text: もの, an extremely common noun in Japanese that means 'thing', can also be used as a sentence ending particle. In these cases, it adds a small amount of emotion to a statement, and presents it as a reason. Due to this, もの is usually translated as 'because', or 'cause'. Literally, it just means 'it's an (A) thing!'. もの is quite casual, so should be avoided in formal situations.
To use もの as 'because', attach it to the end of the plain form of any word.
To emphasize もの even further, the explanatory んだ (after a verb or い-Adjective), or なんだ (after a な-Adjective or noun) will often be used.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Can sound childish/cute

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものだから (N2, Because, The reason is): These two are closely related and use the same もの (with もん as a more casual variant) to express reason. もの・もん is often used at the end of a sentence in a casual or even childish tone to give a personal reason, e.g. 'because (A)'. ものだから is a slightly more formal expression, often used to explain or justify an action or situation in a softer, less direct way.

なぜなら〜から (N3, Because, The reason is, That is because): なぜなら〜から and もの・もん are similar in that both can express a reason, but they differ significantly in tone and formality. なぜなら～から is a formal and objective way of stating a reason, similar to saying, 'as for why, it is because (A)'. In contrast, もの・もん is casual or colloquial, sometimes even childish, and conveys a personal, subjective tone, like saying, 'because' or ''cause (A)'.

ことだから (N2, It is exactly because): Both もの・もん and ことだから can be used to give reasons, but they differ in tone and intent. もの・もん is casual, colloquial, and subjective, used to express personal feelings or justifications, like 'because (A)'. ことだから, on the other hand, has a more objective and emphatic feel, often meaning 'it is precisely because (A) that (B)'. In some contexts, ことだから can also imply 'considering (A), then (B)'.

ので (N5, Because, So, Since, The reason being): ので expresses a cause or reason, similar to 'A, so B' in English. もの or もん (the latter being more casual) can also express a reason, adding emphasis or emotion, like the English 'because.' The main difference is that ので sounds more objective and can be used mid-sentence, while もの or もん typically comes at the end of a sentence and conveys a more personal or emotional tone.

から (N5, Because, Since): から expresses a cause or reason, similar to 'A, so B' in English. もの or もん (with もん being more casual) can also express an emphatic or emotional reason, similar to 'because' in English. The main difference is that から can be used mid-sentence, while もの or もん typically appears at the end of a sentence and conveys a more personal or emotional tone.

ものですから・もので (N2, Because, My excuse is, My explanation is): These expressions also share the same root as もの・もん, but differ in tone and formality. もの・もん is casual and subjective, typically used for personal justifications like 'cause (A)'. ものですから or もので adds a more objective or polite tone, and is commonly used in formal or semi-formal situations when offering explanations or justifications for one's actions or circumstances.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ものだ
text: もの (or {物|もの} in its kanji form) is classified as a {形式名詞|けいしきめいし} (dummy noun) in Japanese. This just means a noun that is used in a similar way to 'thing' in English. もの regularly refers to things that do not have their own name, or are difficult to name due to their complexity. When もの is combined with the auxiliary verb だ, it implies that the previously mentioned (A) is something that 'is what it is'. This is often used in relation to customs, conventions, common sense, or to highlight results that would naturally be expected in any given situation.
To use ものだ, attach it to the end of the attributive form of any word/word that ends a phrase that you would like to highlight as being an obvious piece of information.

ものだ as 'supposed to', or 'the way it is' can also be used to negate a phrase, and say that it is 'something that isn't expected', or 'shouldn't be the case'. To do this, だ will be replaced with ではない, or じゃない.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものだから (N2, Because, The reason is): Both expressions use the same ものだ, with the only difference being the presence or absence of から 'because/since'. Therefore, ものだ is used at the end of a sentence to express the idea of how something is or should be. In contrast, ものだから presents a reason or an explanation for something, and is often used when justifying a certain action or situation. ものだ can also be used to express obligation, while ものだから is not used this way.

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): Both express what should be done, but with different nuance. ことだ is used to give firm advice, e.g. 諦めずに続けることだ ('You should keep going without giving up.') ものだ expresses general expectations or norms, e.g. 仕事は地道に頑張り続けるものだ ('One is expected to keep working steadily.')

べき (N3, Must, Should, Ought to): Both express what one 'should' do, but with different nuance. べき reflects personal or moral judgment, e.g. 約束は守るべきだ ('You should keep your promises.') ものだ conveys social or cultural expectations, e.g. 子どもは早く寝るものだ ('Children are supposed to go to bed early.')

べきではない (N3, Should not, Must not, Ought not to): ものだ expresses general or societal expectations, e.g. 子どもは早く寝るものだ ('Children are supposed to go to bed early.') べきではない carries the opposite nuance, conveying that one should not do something based on moral or social reasoning, e.g. 人を見た目で判断すべきではない ('You shouldn't judge people by appearances.')

ものですから・もので (N2, Because, My excuse is, My explanation is): While both expressions contain もの, they are used with very different nuances. ものですから・もので offers a reason, and is often used to explain or justify one's personal actions or situation, e.g. 忙しかったものですから 'I was busy, so...'. In contrast, ものだ is used to express a natural tendency or general truth, e.g. １２月は仕事が忙しいものです ('Work is busy in December.', implying that's just the way it is).

はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): はずだ conveys a specific expectation or prediction based on current evidence, like 雨が降るはずだ ('It should rain.'). ものだ expresses a general rule or common tendency, like 雨は春によく降るものだ ('It often rains in spring.'). The former is situational, while the latter is habitual or cultural.

meaning: In the middle of
summary: A phrase that expresses (A) as being right in the middle of occuring, or at the highest intensity.
formation: Verb［ている］+ 最中（さいちゅう）に + Phrase
Noun + の + 最中（さいちゅう）に + Phrase
Verb［ている］(1) + 最中（さいちゅう） + だ
Verb［ている］(1) + 最中（さいちゅう） + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 最中に
text: While {中|ちゅう}に highlights that something is in the process of happening (when used in relation to events/actions), {最中|さいちゅう}に strengthens that meaning further, to show that something is 'right in the middle of happening'. As the kanji {最|さい} means 'utmost', we can see that the literal meaning is 'utmost middle'. This can be translated in a similar way to phrases like 'at the height of (A)', or 'in the midst of (A)', in English.
When using {最中|さいちゅう}に, a (B) part of the sentence will usually highlight something else that happened during (A), somehow interrupting or disturbing it.
To use {最中|さいちゅう}に, attach it to the end of the ている form of a verb, or a noun followed by の.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the general time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. It can be used with nouns as in 雨の時 'when it rains', verbs as in 父が帰ってきた時 'when Dad came home', or adjectives as in 暑い時 'when it's hot', and can describe one-time or repeated actions. In contrast, 最中に describes something happening right in the middle of another action/event, e.g. 食事の最中に電話がなった ('My phone rang while I was in the middle of eating.').

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): ているところだ conveys that an action is in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is busy with it, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べているところだ ('I'm in the middle of eating dinner.'). In contrast, 最中に is used to express that something else happened during that action, e.g. 晩ご飯を食べている最中に電話がかかってきた ('The phone rang while I was right in the middle of eating dinner.').

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): Both の間に and 最中に express 'while (A), (B)', but with slightly different nuance. 最中に is more emphatic, implying that (B) happened right in the middle of (A). In contrast, の間に simply states that (B) occurred during the general span of (A), and sounds more objective.

うちに (N3, While, During): Both can be translated as 'while', but differ in nuance. うちに emphasizes doing something before a condition changes, e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.') 最中に highlights something occurring in the very middle of another action, e.g. 会議の最中に電話が鳴った ('The phone rang in the middle of the meeting.')

中 (N3, During, While, Throughout, In the process of): Both express a continued state or action, but are used differently. 中 attaches only to nouns and means 'in the middle of (A)', e.g. 会議中 ('in the middle of a meeting'), 使用中 ('in use'). 最中に is used with verbs in the ている form or with nouns (using の) to mean 'right in the middle of (A), (B)', e.g. 食べている最中に話し掛けられた ('I was spoken to when I was right in the middle of eating.')

～ところに・～ところへ (N2, At the time, When, While, Timing): Both describe an interruption during an action, but with different focus. ～ところに・～ところへ highlights timing or the moment of interruption, e.g. 出かけようとしたところに電話がかかってきた ('Just as I was about to leave, the phone rang.') 最中に stresses that the action was in full progress, e.g. 晩ご飯を作っている最中に電話が鳴った ('The phone rang when I was right in the middle of making dinner.')

途中に・途中で (N2, On the way, Partway, In the middle of): 最中に and 途中に・途中で both mean 'in the middle of', but differ in nuance. 最中に emphasizes being right in the middle of something, e.g. 晩ご飯を作っている最中に電話が鳴った ('The phone rang when I was right in the middle of making dinner.') 途中に・途中で can overlap but also means 'on the way', e.g. 学校に行く途中で友達に会った ('I ran into a friend on the way to school.')

meaning: After, Upon
summary: A slightly formal expression that highlights something that logically occurs after or upon (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 上で
text: {上|うえ}で is an expression in Japanese that is used after the past form of verbs, or nouns followed by の. It shows that something will happen 'after (A)', or 'upon (A)'. This grammar point is used in a similar way to its literal meaning, which is 'with the above/previous (A), (B)'. {上|うえ} as 'above', and で as 'with', in で's use as a case marking particle.

{上|うえ}で is a structure that is primarily used in formal settings. Due to this, it will not be used in casual conversations very often. It also strongly hints at (A) being a requirement for (B), or (A) being something that would logically be expected before (B).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In A上でB: A cannot be passive

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 上に (N2, As well, Besides, In addition to): Both use 上 but differ quite a bit in meaning. 上に adds information, like '(B) in addition to (or 'on top of') (A)', typically within the same general category, e.g. 彼は親切な上に頭もいい ('He's smart in addition to being kind.'). In contrast, 上で expresses an action happening after (lit. 'upon') another action or condition being realized, e.g. 社長に相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after consulting the president.').

てから (N5, Once...is done, Once...happens, After doing): てから and 上で both convey a sequence of events, but their nuances differ. てから simply indicates that one event follows another. In contrast, 上で emphasizes that the first action or event was a necessary precondition for the second event. Also, 上で is more formal than てから, and often used in business situations or writing.

た末・の末 (N2, After, As a conclusion of): Both can express the idea of 'after doing (A), (B)', but 上で focuses on process or sequence (lit. 'upon' doing), e.g. 話し合った上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after discussing it.'). In contrast, た末・の末 emphasizes an outcome after prolonged effort or struggle, e.g. 悩んだ末に転職した ('After much deliberation, I changed jobs.').

て初めて (N3, For the first time, Not until, Only after, Only when, Only because): Both show one action leading to another, but with different focus. て初めて marks a first experience or realization, e.g. 大人になって初めて分かった ('I only understood after becoming an adult.') 上で shows a necessary step before the next action, e.g. 社長に相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after consulting the president.')

あとで (N4, After, Later): Both 上で and あとで express that one action follows another, but with different nuances. あとで simply shows sequence, like 'after doing (A)'. 上で implies the first action is a necessary step for the second, similar to 'upon doing (A)', and is more formal, often used in writing or business contexts.

たら (N4, When, From when, Just when, If): Both 上で and たら can describe sequences or conditions, but with different nuance. 上で implies that one action is a prerequisite for another, such as 社長と相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after discussing it with the president.'). たら is more general and covers a wider range of temporal and conditional uses, as in 晴れたら散歩に行こう ('If it's sunny, let's go for a walk.').

meaning: Thanks to, Because of
summary: A phrase gives thanks to (A) for causing some particular result, sometimes sarcastically.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About おかげで
text: おかげで (or お{陰|かげ}で in kanji) is an expression that is used to show thanks or appreciation in Japanese. It is usually translated simply as 'thanks to (A)', or 'because of (A)'. おかげで is a combination of the polite prefix お, the noun {陰|かげ} 'shade', and the case marking particle で.
おかげで can be used after any word in its attributive form.
Literally, お{陰|かげ}で means 'in the shade of (A)'. This implies that (B) was only made possible due to (A) creating the ideal situation for it to occur.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: せいで (N3, Because of, Due to, Blame): Both mean 'because of', but with opposite tone. おかげで expresses a thankful cause, e.g. 先生のおかげで合格できた ('Thanks to my teacher, I passed.') せいで places blame for something negative, e.g. 雨のせいで試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled because of the rain.')

ために (N3, Due to, Because of, As a result of): ために and せいで can both express the idea of 'due to (A)', but they differ in that おかげで almost always describes a desirable result, while ために can be used with either a positive or negative nuance. ために can also, in some cases, mean 'for the purpose of (A)', while おかげで cannot be used in this way.

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): Both express cause and effect, but with different tone and usage. おかげで implies a positive result and gratitude, e.g. 先生のおかげで合格できた ('Thanks to my teacher, I passed.') そのため(に) is neutral, objective, and often appears at the start of a sentence. It can also mean 'for that purpose'.

につき (N2, Due to, On account of, Each or every): Both express cause, but differ in tone and formality. おかげで implies a positive result with gratitude, e.g. 先生のおかげで合格できました ('Thanks to my teacher, I passed.') につき states a neutral reason, often used in formal notices, e.g. 雨天につき中止します ('Due to rain, it is canceled.') It also only follows nouns.

meaning: Based on, In accordance with
summary: An expression showing that something is based on (A), by expressing the foundation to which it adheres.
formation: Noun + に基（もと）づいた + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にもとづいて
text: In order to say that one thing is 'based on' another in Japanese, the expression に{基|もと}づいて will be used. This is a combination of the case marking particle に, the う - Verb, {基|もと}づく 'to originate from', and the conjunction particle て. This expression regularly highlights some kind of judgement/conclusion that the speaker has made, using (A) as their base.
To use に{基|もと}づいて, put the noun (or noun phrase) that you would like to identify as a 'basis' before に{基|もと}づいて, and then express your judgment/conclusion in part (B) of the sentence.
Alternatively, the past form of {基|もと}づく may be used when connected directly to a second noun. (A) に{基|もと}づいた (B) directly expresses that (B) is based on (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: によると・によれば (N3, According to): によると・によれば reports second-hand information, e.g. 新聞によると事件があったそうです ('According to the newspaper, there was an incident.') にもとづいて indicates that an action is grounded in something like rules or facts, e.g. 法律にもとづいて判断する ('Make a decision based on the law.')

を踏まえて (N1, Based on, Considering, Keeping in mind, Taking into account, Therefore): Both have a general meaning of 'based on', but with slightly different nuances. にもとづいて typically shows strict reliance on a fixed source like rules or data, e.g. 法律にもとづいて判断する 'ake a decision based on the law'. を踏まえて means taking something into account as a reference or consideration, e.g. アンケートの結果を踏まえて調節する 'make adjustments taking the survey results into consideration'.

をもとに (N2, Based on, From, According to): These phrases both mean 'based on' and can overlap, but differ slightly. にもとづいて is more formal and tends to show a concrete or logical foundation for an action or product. をもとに is less formal (but still used in formal contexts) and can indicate a general basis or inspiration where にもとづいて may not fit.

にしたがって (N2, As, Following, As then, According to, In accordance with): Both are formal expressions meaning 'in accordance with (A)', but differ in usage. にもとづいて shows the foundation for an action, e.g. 法律にもとづいて判断する 'make a decision based on the law.' にしたがって can overlap, but often shows related change, e.g. 年を取るにしたがって目が悪くなっていく 'Eyesight deteriorates with age.' In this case, もとづいて would not be used.

に合わせて・に合った (N3, In accordance with, Matching, Fitting, Suitable for, Adjust or tune to): Both express a general sense of basing an action on something, but their specific nuances differ. に合わせて・に合った conveys adapting or matching to something. For example: 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ = 'Choose clothes based on the season.' In contrast, にもとづいて typically expresses the grounding or foundation for some action. For example, 経験にもとづいて判断する = 'Make a decision based on experience.'

からして (N2, Even..., Judging from, Based on): While both patterns can be translated into English as 'based on', they have very different meanings. からして means 'based on (A), (B)', and expresses the logical basis for the speaker's judgment or opinion. For example, 匂いからして美味しそう = 'From the smell, it seems tasty.' In contrast, にもとづいて expresses the foundation or basis for another action. For example: 経験に基づいて判断する = 'Make a decision based on experience.'

meaning: Aspect, Respect, Point, Way, In terms of, In that, From the point of view
summary: An expression which highlights that with the specific aspect or point of (A), (B) is true.
formation: Phrase + という + 点（てん）(で)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 点
text: {点|てん} is a kanji that is regularly used to express a specific 'point', 'spot', 'aspect', or something similar. When attached to the end of the attributive form of another word, it will highlight that word as a point of interest within the sentence. This is regularly translated as 'from the aspect of (A)', 'in respect to (A)', 'in terms of (A)', and other similar phrases that simply draw attention to something.

To use {点|てん}, attach it to the attributive form of another word, a noun followed by の, or a phrase followed by という. In many cases, {点|てん} will be followed by the case marking particle で, but other particles may be used depending whether {点|てん} is being conveyed as a subject, object, destination, or something being utilized.

Sometimes, で (as 'with' or 'at') may be replaced with expressions such as について 'in relation to (A)', or からいうと 'speaking from (A)'. So long as the grammar structure that accompanies {点|てん} is also used to highlight something specific (and can be paired with a noun), it will sound natural.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にしたら (N2, From the point of view of): にしたら and 点 are similar in that both can express the idea of a standpoint, but differ in nuance. にしたら expresses an opinion from a personal or empathetic point of view, e.g. 子どもにしたら大事件だ ('For a child, it's a big deal.'). In contrast, 点 will typically highlight a reference point for objective analysis, e.g. 安全性の点では問題がある ('There's a problem from a safety standpoint.').

ことから (N3, From the fact that): ことから is used to draw a logical conclusion from a fact or observation, e.g. 顔色が悪いことから風邪を引いていると分かった 'From the fact that his face was pale, I could tell he had caught a cold.' 点 comments on a specific point without implying a conclusion, e.g. 安さという点でこのスマホのほうがいい 'This smartphone is better from the perspective of low price.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なぜなら〜から
text: When combined with the conjunction particle から, なぜなら (or なぜならば) forms a set pattern that can be translated as 'why (A), that is because (B)'. Essentially, it is a way to highlight that a 'because' is coming at the end of the sentence, drawing attention to it.

なぜなら itself is a conjunction that is a combination of the adverb, なぜ 'why', and the hypothetical form of だ, なら. Literally, なぜなら～から is similar to 'why is (A) so, (B) is the cause'. This sounds quite dramatic in English, but is a perfectly natural way of emphasizing a statement/fact in Japanese.
To use なぜなら～から, state that fact/important piece of information as (A). Then, at the beginning of a new sentence, なぜなら will be followed by the reason/cause, with から finishing the sentence.
The primary function of なぜなら in Japanese (as opposed to simply using から or ので by itself) is to gain the attention of the listener, and inform them that important information is coming.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もの・もん (N3, Because, Cause): なぜなら〜から and もの・もん are similar in that both can express a reason, but they differ significantly in tone and formality. なぜなら～から is a formal and objective way of stating a reason, similar to saying, 'as for why, it is because (A)'. In contrast, もの・もん is casual or colloquial, sometimes even childish, and conveys a personal, subjective tone, like saying, 'because' or ''cause (A)'.

だって (N3, I heard/was said, Because, But, Even or also, Even if or even though): Both can be used to express reasons, but だって is highly casual, colloquial, and emotional, while なぜなら〜から is formal and objective-sounding. Also, なぜなら〜から begins a sentence, and clearly introduces a reason for something just stated, while だって can be used in sentence-final position. Depending on usage, だって can also have the meanings of 'I hear' and 'even though', which なぜなら〜から does not have.

～かというと ② (N3, If you ask me..., If I had to say, If I were to say, If I were to choose one, I'd rather): These phrases are related in that they can be used similarly, as なぜなら〜から could be rephrased as なぜかというと. They are different in that なぜなら〜から always explicitly states a reason for something, like 'as for why, it's because (A)', while ～かというと② can simply be used to comment on something, e.g. 好きか嫌いかというと 'if I were to say whether I like it or dislike it'.

ことだから (N2, It is exactly because): These phrases are similar in that both express a reason with a degree of certainty, but they differ in specific usage and nuance. なぜなら〜から is used at the beginning of a sentence to provide a reason for something previously said, explicitly saying 'as for why, (A)'. ことだから is used at the end of a phrase with the reason following, conveying 'it is precisely because (A) that (B)'.

ので (N5, Because, So, Since, The reason being): Both ので and なぜなら〜から express reasons or causes. ので is more objective and straightforward, used in both casual and formal contexts, similar to 'A, so B' in English. なぜなら〜から emphasizes the reason more strongly, typically used in writing or formal speech, with a nuance of 'As for why, it's because...' and often used for detailed explanations.

ものですから・もので (N2, Because, My excuse is, My explanation is): These phrases are similar in that both express a reason, but they differ in tone and usage. なぜなら〜から provides a clear, objective explanation for something just mentioned. ことだから is often used in expressions like '彼のことだから', meaning 'because it's him', highlighting a reason based on someone's typical behavior or the nature of a situation.

ものだから (N2, Because, The reason is): These phrases are related in that both can be used to express a reason, though they differ in tone, nuance, and usage. なぜなら〜から is more formal and objective, and is used at the beginning of a sentence to provide a reason for something previously said. In contrast, ものだから is used at the end of a phrase or sentence, and typically has a nuance of providing a justification or excuse for one's behavior or the situation.

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): Both expressions relate to cause and effect, but in opposite directions: なぜなら〜から gives the reason for something previously stated, while そのため(に) introduces the result of a prior situation. Additionally, そのために can also express purpose, a meaning なぜなら〜から does not carry.

～かというと ① (N3, Why? Well..., Why? Because..., If you ask me why..., The reason why is..., It is because...): These phrases are related in that they can be used similarly, as なぜなら〜から could be rephrased as なぜかというと. They are different in that なぜなら〜から always states the reason for something previously said, like 'as for why that is, it's because (A)', while ～かというと① can be used to clarify what you are explaining, for example by saying なぜ嫌いかというと 'as for why I dislike it'.

から (N5, Because, Since): Both から and なぜなら〜から express reasons or causes. から is straightforward and casual, used in both casual conversations and formal speech, similar to 'A, so B.' In contrast, なぜなら〜から emphasizes the reason more strongly, often used in writing or formal speech with the nuance of 'As for why, it's because...' and typically when explaining a point in detail.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About こそ
text: こそ is an adverbial particle in Japanese that primarily replaces either を or が. Its main role is to highlight the preceding noun (or noun phrase) as being the most important piece of information in relation to the rest of the sentence. In English, this is an effect that is primarily achieved through things like bold text, underlining, or emphasizing a particular word in speech. If we were to make a direct comparison to an English statement, then things like 'precisely because it's (A)', or 'rather it is due to (A)', are quite similar to こそ's function.
こそ can be used directly after any noun that would usually take the を, or が particles, so long as that particular piece of information needs to be emphasized.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although こそ is able to replace が or は, the nuance will usually come across as more similar to が, due to the fact that が puts emphasis on a specific point, while は nominates general topics. To make things easier, the three particles can be thought of in the following way:
は- Weakly highlights specific information.
が- Strongly highlights specific information.
こそ- Very strongly highlights specific information.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: こそ replaces particles を and が.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なんか・なんて (N3, Such as, Things like, Emphasis): Both add emphasis, but with opposite nuance. なんか・なんて often downplays or dismisses, while こそ highlights importance or exclusivity. The former can feel self-deprecating or casual, while the latter stresses that something uniquely applies. Compare 私なんかできるのかな？ ('I wonder if someone like me could do it?') versus 彼こそできる ('Him, if no one else, can do it.')

からこそ (N3, Emphasized because, Precisely because): Both use こそ for emphasis, but からこそ highlights a reason or cause, meaning 'precisely because', e.g. 努力したからこそできた ('I could do it precisely because I worked hard.'). こそ on its own emphasizes the word it follows, framing it as precisely the one, e.g. 彼こそできる ('He, if no one else, can do it.')

あまり (N3, So much...that): Both express emphasis, but in different ways. あまり is a noun that emphasizes an extreme degree leading to an unintended result, e.g. 悲しみのあまり泣き出した ('She burst into tears from too much sadness.') こそ is a particle that stresses importance or exclusivity, e.g. 今日こそ早く寝よう ('Today, for sure, I'll go to bed early.')

のはXの方だ (N3, It is...that..., It is...who..., ...is the one that..., ...is the one who...): Both structures single out and highlight something, but in different ways. のはXの方だ highlights contrast between options and is often used in apologies, e.g. 悪いのは僕の方だ ('I'm the one that's at fault.') こそ emphasizes exclusivity or importance, e.g. 私こそ謝るべきだ ('I, and no one else, should apologize.')

～てこそ (N2, Only if, Because, By, Unless, Until): Both involve the same こそ, but one attaches to nouns and the other to verb + て form. こそ emphasizes a specific word or element, often to contrast or highlight, e.g. 彼こそできる ('He, if nobody else, can do it.'). In contrast, ～てこそ focuses a condition that must be met for something to be true, e.g. 大人になってこそ分かる 'understand only after becoming an adult'.

より (N4, More than, Over): より expresses a general comparison, like 'more than (A)' or '~er,' e.g. 月曜日より水曜日がいい ('Wednesday is better than Monday.') or 走るより野球をするのが好き ('I prefer playing baseball to running.'). In contrast, こそ adds emphasis, highlighting something as especially important, e.g. 月曜日こそ図書館に行きたい ('Monday is precisely when I want to go to the library.').

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): こそ and なら can look similar after a noun, e.g. 彼こそできる vs. 彼ならできる, but differ in nuance. こそ is emphatic, suggesting that something someone is 'the one', e.g. 彼こそできる ('He's exactly the one who can do it.'). なら implies a conditional focus, e.g. 彼ならできる ('If it's him we're talking about, he can do it.'), without the nuance of excluding other possibilities that こそ can have.

meaning: Emphasized because, Precisely because
summary: A phrase emphasizing that precisely from (A), (B). In a similar way to capitalizing a word in English.
formation: Noun + だ + からこそ + Phrase

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About からこそ
text: Traditionally, the adverbial particle こそ is used to emphasize whatever noun (or noun phrase) it is attached to. However, when combined with the conjunction particle から, it focuses on emphasizing the 'reason' for something. This structure is very similar to phrases like 'precisely because (A)' in English.
からこそ is an expression that is primarily used after either verbs or nouns. In the case of nouns, the noun will need to be followed by the auxiliary verb だ, before からこそ is added.
With からこそ, there may be several reasons for why something is the way it is, but こそ will show that there is a 'foremost' reason that should be considered before anything else.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～ばこそ (N1, Precisely because, Only because, Because, Due to, Only if): Despite appearing different, ～ばこそ and からこそ are essentially synonymous in meaning, both expressing an reason for something, i.e. 'it is precisely because of (A) that (B)'. The main difference is that ～ばこそ is a highly formal and literary expression found primarily in writing, while からこそ is far more common and used in everyday speech as well as writing.

こそ (N3, For sure, For certain, Even more so, Underlined or bolded text): Both use こそ for emphasis, but からこそ highlights a reason or cause, meaning 'precisely because', e.g. 努力したからこそできた ('I could do it precisely because I worked hard.'). こそ on its own emphasizes the word it follows, framing it as precisely the one, e.g. 彼こそできる ('He, if no one else, can do it.')

あまり (N3, So much...that): あまり follows a noun or verb phrase and shows that an extreme state leads to an unintended result, e.g. 緊張のあまり声が出なかった ('I was so nervous I couldn't speak.') からこそ attaches after the reason and emphasizes it as the precise cause, e.g. 緊張したからこそ全力を出せた ('It was precisely because I was nervous that I gave it my all.')

ものだから (N2, Because, The reason is): からこそ and ものだから are similar in that both can be used in expressing a reason. They differ in that からこそ is used to specifically emphasize the reason, like saying 'it is precisely because of (A) that (B)', while ものだから is not as emphatic, and is generally used when providing an explanation or excuse for one's actions or a situation.

～てこそ (N2, Only if, Because, By, Unless, Until): Both からこそ and ～てこそ emphasize cause and effect, but they differ in nuance. からこそ highlights a specific reason with a strong emphasis, e.g. 努力したからこそ合格できた ('I was able to pass precisely because I worked hard'). In contrast, ～てこそ indicates that only after a certain condition is fulfilled can something else happen, e.g. 努力してこそ意味がある ('It only has meaning after putting in effort').

から (N5, Because, Since): から expresses a reason or cause, similar to 'because of A, B' or 'A, so B' in English. The reason comes before から, with the result after. からこそ is the same から followed by the emphatic こそ, highlighting that the given reason is precisely or solely responsible for what follows. It's used for strong arguments or emphatic points.

ことだから (N2, It is exactly because): からこそ and ことだから are similar in that both can emphatically state a reason. However, ことだから is typically used to make a prediction or assumption based on a person's known behavior or character, e.g. 田中さんのことだからできると思う ('Because it's Tanaka, I think he can do it'). In contrast, からこそ is more broadly used to emphasize a specific reason, e.g. 努力したからこそできた ('I could do it precisely because I worked hard').

meaning: Just, Only, Nothing but
summary: A slightly formal way of subjectively expressing the only thing that is happening. Nothing but (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばかり
text: When used after verbs followed by the conjunction particle て, or nouns, the adverbial particle ばかり highlights that 'nothing but (A) is being done', or 'only (A) exists'. In relation to verbs, てばかり is often followed by いる, as a modified version of the standard ている. However, adding いる is not a requirement, and the same nuance may be conveyed without it.

When a sentence consists of a part (A) and a part (B), ばかり will be followed by either で (with verbs or nouns), or いて (only with verbs). This is when ばかり appears directly before the sentence conjunction point, and other combinations are possible (such as ばかりだから).
It should be noted that the で with ばかり here is not the particle で, but the conjunctive form of the auxiliary verb, だ.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: ばかり is rarely seen using kanji, but it originally comes from {許|ばか}り (sometimes {計|はか}り). This kanji means 'to let off', or 'to let through', and implies that (A) is the only thing that is being 'permitted' in a specific situation.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ばっかり, ばっか, ばかし, and ばっかし are all fairly common casual variations of ばかり

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しか～ない (N4, There's only, Nothing but): ばかり and しか～ない can both mean 'only' or 'nothing but', but their usage and nuance differ. ばかり is used with affirmative verb forms and can imply excess. For example, 漫画ばかり読む 'to read only manga' has a sense of reading manga all the time. In contrast, しか～ない is used with negative verbs and expresses 'nothing but' in a more objective sense. For example, 漫画しか読まない simply states that nothing else is read.

だけでなく(て)～も (N3, Not only ~ but ~ also, Not just ~ but ~ also): ばかり emphasizes exclusivity, meaning 'only' or 'nothing but', e.g. 肉ばかり食べている ('He eats nothing but meat'). だけでなく～も expresses inclusion, meaning 'not only…but also', e.g. 肉だけでなく野菜も食べている ('He eats not only meat but also vegetables'). Compared to だけ, ばかり often carries a stronger nuance of excess or doing something too much.

ばかりに (N3, Simply because, Only because, Just because, Simply on account of): ばかり means 'only' or 'just', often with a neutral or excessive nuance, e.g. 寝てばかりいる ('He does nothing but sleep'). ばかりに adds a nuance of regret, expressing that something bad happened solely because of one reason, e.g. 寝坊したばかりに電車に乗り遅れた ('I missed the train just because I overslept').

ばかりだ (N3, (Only) continue to, Keep on -ing, More and more): ばかり means 'only' or 'just', often suggesting repetition or excess, e.g. 文句ばかり言っている ('He does nothing but complain.'). ばかりだ builds on that to express that a situation continues to worsen or progress in one direction, e.g. 状況は悪くなるばかりだ ('The situation keeps getting worse.').

だけしか (N3, To emphasize '~only', Nothing but): ばかり and だけしか are similar in that both can express limitation, but ばかり emphasizes the idea of excessiveness of a single thing, e.g. 漫画ばかり読む 'do nothing but read manga', while だけしか emphatically stresses insufficiency, e.g. 千円だけしかない ('I have only 1,000 yen.').

ばかりでなく (N3, Not only…but also, As well as): ばかり means 'only' or 'nothing but', emphasizing exclusivity, e.g. 甘いものばかり食べている ('He eats nothing but sweets.'). ばかりでなく means 'not only…but also', adding inclusivity, e.g. 甘いものばかりでなく野菜も食べなさい ('Don't eat only sweets, but vegetables too.').

わ〜わ（で） (N1, And...so, And...because, Since): Both describe a situation dominated by repeated or excessive actions, but the nuance differs. わ〜わ（で） emphasizes noisy, uncontrolled, or emotionally charged repetition, often highlighting disorder or annoyance, as in 子どもたちが泣くわ叫ぶわで大変だった ('The children were crying and shouting nonstop, and it was a mess.'). ばかり focuses on one action happening repeatedly or continuing in the same direction, often with frustration or resignation, as in 彼は文句言ってばかりいる ('He does nothing but complain.').

だけ (N5, Only, Just): Both ばかり and だけ express limitation, similar to 'only,' but with different nuances. 漫画だけ読んだ means '(He) read only comic books,' while 漫画ばかり読んだ implies '(He) read nothing but comic books,' with a suggestion that other reading would be better. だけ connects to the dictionary form, while ばかり connects to the verb's て form.

meaning: (Only) continue to, Keep on -ing, More and more
summary: A slightly formal phrase that presents some kind of trend that is only intensifying further.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばかりだ
text: Occasionally, the adverbial particle ばかり is combined with verbs in their attributive form, to show that (A) is the only thing that is occuring. It may also imply that (A) is happening 'more and more', or that 'it keeps on (A)'. This phrase utilizes ばかり's standard meaning of 'only', and combines it with the auxiliary verb だ (or です).
As can be seen with these sentences, this use of ばかり is paired almost exclusively with verbs that describe some form of change (higher/lower, stronger/weaker, better/worse, faster/slower, etc).
If the speaker would like to express further information in a (B) part of the sentence, だ will simply get changed to its conjunctive form で, before continuing.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つづける (N4, To continue): つづける and ばかりだ both show continuation, but with different nuances. つづける attaches to verb stems and shows simple ongoing action, e.g. 減り続けている 'is continuing to decrease'. ばかりだ adds the sense of 'more and more,' often negatively, e.g. 減るばかりだ 'keeps on decreasing'.

てくる (N4, To come to, To become, To continue, To be starting to, Has been ~ing): ばかりだ attaches to the dictionary (non-past) form of a verb and is used to show that an action, often a negative one, keeps happening or is the only thing happening. In contrast, てくる combines the て-form of a verb with くる to describe an action that began in the past and has continued to the present. Unlike ばかりだ, てくる can be used for both positive and negative situations.

ばかり (N3, Just, Only, Nothing but): ばかり means 'only' or 'just', often suggesting repetition or excess, e.g. 文句ばかり言っている ('He does nothing but complain.'). ばかりだ builds on that to express that a situation continues to worsen or progress in one direction, e.g. 状況は悪くなるばかりだ ('The situation keeps getting worse.').

一方だ (N3, More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er): ばかりだ and 一方だ are similar in that both express continuous or progressive change. However, ばかりだ is typically used with negative developments and often carries a more subjective tone, e.g. 状況は悪くなるばかりだ ('The situation keeps getting worse'). 一方だ, on the other hand, sounds more neutral or objective, and doesn't necessarily imply a negative trend, e.g. 人口は増える一方だ ('The population keeps increasing').
