sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばかりに
text: When paired with the case marking particle に, ばかり regularly conveys the meaning of 'simply because', or 'just because'. Literally, this expression means that 'even with just (A), (B) is/was able to occur'. This phrase is regularly paired with the past form of verbs, indicating that something that has already taken place, led to some other result.
To use ばかりに, simply attach the expression to the end of any word in its attributive form.

It should be noted that this particular grammar pattern has a strong tendency to be used with results that are negative. However, this is not a requirement. A high level of eagerness/enthusiasm can also be expressed when paired with grammar points like たい, or ほしい.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ばっかり, ばっか, ばかし, and ばっかし are all fairly common casual variations of ばかり

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からといって (N2, Just because): They may seem similar because both can be translated as 'just because', but mean very different things. ばかりに expresses, often with regret, a negative outcome caused by a single reason, e.g. 一回遅刻したばかりにクビになった ('I was fired just because I was late once.'). In contrast, からといって means 'just because (A), it doesn't mean (B)', e.g. お金持ちだからといって幸せとは限らない ('Just because someone is rich doesn't mean they're happy.').

ばかり (N3, Just, Only, Nothing but): ばかり means 'only' or 'just', often with a neutral or excessive nuance, e.g. 寝てばかりいる ('He does nothing but sleep'). ばかりに adds a nuance of regret, expressing that something bad happened solely because of one reason, e.g. 寝坊したばかりに電車に乗り遅れた ('I missed the train just because I overslept').

につき (N2, Due to, On account of, Each or every): These expressions are loosely related in that both indicate a reason. ばかりに conveys that a specific cause led to a negative outcome, often with a nuance of regret, e.g. 忘れ物をしたばかりに受験できなかった ('Just because I forgot something, I couldn't take the exam'). につき, by contrast, is a formal, neutral expression often used in official contexts, e.g. 工事中につき通行止め ('Road closed due to construction').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことがある
text: ことがある is an expression in Japanese that combines the noun こと with the case marking particle が, and the う - Verb, ある. It is often translated as 'to be possible', 'to occasionally occur', or 'to sometimes occur'. However, the more literal translation of ことがある is '(A) is a thing that exists'.
ことがある may be paired with the attributive form of any other word.

Occasionally, が may be replaced by も. In these situations, it implies that '(A) is also a thing that exists'. Basically this just highlights that (A) is something that needs to be considered (among other things).

sections.label: Caution

たことがある

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき marks the time of an action or event, like 'when' in English, e.g. 雨の時 or 雨が降るとき 'when it rains'. ことがある expresses something that happens occasionally, e.g. 雨が降ることがある ('There are occasions when it rains.'). Because they express different concepts, the two can be combined, as in: 時間がないとき、コンビニ弁当を食べることがある ('When I don't have time, there are occasions when I eat a convenience store lunch box.').

たことがある (N5, Have done before): With a non-past verb, ことがある expresses that something happens occasionally or from time to time, similar to saying 'There are times when…' In contrast, たことがある uses the past tense to describe a completed experience. For example, 日本に行ったことがある means 'I've been to Japan.' It refers to something that has happened at least once, without implying it occurred repeatedly.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): These two expressions can be opposite in meaning. ことはない means that something never happens or is not necessary, e.g. 彼と話すことはない ('There are no occasions where I talk to him'), while ことがある indicates occasional occurrence, e.g. 道に迷うことがある ('I sometimes get lost'). Note that ことはない can also express 'no need to', e.g. 心配することはない ('There's no need to worry'), which is unrelated to any use of ことがある.

meaning: To decide on, Have decided to
summary: An expression that shows that the thing which is (A) has been decided upon, or will be done.
formation: Verb［ない］+ ことにします (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことにする
text: In a similar way to how にする means to 'decide on' something, ことにする means to decide on a situation, or course of action. This grammar point is a combination of {事|こと} 'thing' in its role as a nominalizer (a word that creates a noun-phrase), and にする 'to make it (A)'. Literally this grammar structure can be translated as 'to do (A)', or 'to make it (A)'.

ことにする may be used with verb-phrases that are either in the affirmative, or negative (using ない) forms. As こと itself is a noun, the verb (or auxiliary verb) that comes before it will need to be in its attributive form.
にする is a strong expression, which tends to make the speaker sound like they are fairly resolute in their decision.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): ことにする and ようにする are closely related but have different nuances. ことにする is used to express a resolution or decision, e.g. 来年、マラソンを走ることにした ('I decided to run a marathon next year.'). In contrast, ようにする expresses making an effort to carry out an action and is often used for ongoing intentions or habits, e.g. 毎朝走るようにしている ('I'm trying to run every morning.').

にする (N5, To decide on, To choose, To make something into, To view something as): Both にする and ことにする share the same core meaning: making a choice or decision. にする is used when choosing a thing and follows a noun, like ビールにする ('I'll have a beer'). ことにする follows plain-form verbs and expresses the speaker's decision to do or not do something, like 行くことにする or 行かないことにする.

ことになる (N3, It will end up being, It is the result of, It has been decided that): These expressions are similar in that both are used to express decisions. ことになる conveys that something has been decided or will happen due to external factors, e.g. 来月転勤することになった ('It's been decided that I'll be transferred next month'), while ことにする describes something the speaker has decided of their own power, e.g. 来月仕事を辞めることにした ('I've decided to quit my job next month').

～にする・～くする (N4, Adjective + する, To make something/someone (more)): ～にする・～くする and ことにする both involve making something a certain way, but differ in usage. ～にする and ～くする are used with nouns and な-Adjectives, e.g. 綺麗にする 'make clean' and 甘くする 'make sweet'. ことにする, used with verbs, implies deciding on an action, e.g. いくことにする 'decide to go'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことなの
text: When the noun こと (or {事|こと} in its kanji form) is combined with なの, it conveys an explanatory meaning that is similar to what can be seen in the んです・のです grammar pattern. As with んです, ことなの transforms 'it is (A)', into 'it is that it is (A)', simply emphasizing the point.

ことなの may be seen in several different forms, and is quite often used in conjunction with というのは. In these types of sentences, というのは will present the topic, before ことなの will be used to show the conclusion that the speaker has drawn about that topic.
This expression may be used with any word in its attributive form, nouns followed by の, or な-Adjectives followed by な.
という may also be used directly before ことなの. However, this is not always the case, and is even more unlikely when it was already utilized in the first half of the sentence.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: As というのは is quite long, it will often be shortened to って or とは in casual speech.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: というのは (N3, ~ Known as ~ is, ~ Called ~ is, ~ Means ~, Because): ことなの and というのは can both be used in explanations, but differ in position and role. ことなの appears at the end of a sentence to emphasize a conclusion or explanation. Literally, 'it's that it's (A)'. というのは follows a noun or phrase to introduce it as a topic to be explained. They can be used together, e.g. 人生というのはこういうことなんだ ('This thing we call life... this is what it means.')

ということ (N4, ~ing, The ~ that ~ (Nominalization)): ことなの combines こと with the explanatory ～んです／のです form and is used to give or ask for background with an emphatic, explanatory tone. ということ also turns a phrase into a noun, meaning 'the fact that' or 'the act of (A)', but is typically used to clarify something without the added emphasis of ん／の.

ということだ (N3, I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that): Both use こと to summarize information, but with different nuances. ことなの means 'it's that (A)' and is often used to clarify or define something, as in '(A) means (B)' or 'that means (A).' ということだ can also be used in this way, but additionally functions to report hearsay, e.g. 'I hear / They say (A).' ことなの, without the quoting function of という, is not used to report what others have said.

ということは (N2, That means, That is to say): These two expressions are similar in that both can be used when offering or seeking explanations. ことなの is used at the end of a phrase or sentence, often to clarify a particular point, e.g. 今日は来ないということなの？ ('So does that mean he's not coming today?'), while ということは begins a sentence and sets up a conclusion based on what was just said, e.g. ということは、今日は来ないんだ ('So that means he's not coming today').

こと (N4, Converting a verb into a noun): These related expressions both use the noun こと, or 事 in kanji. On its own, こと turns a verb or adjective into a noun phrase, e.g. 食べる 'to eat' becomes 食べること 'the act of eating'. When combined with the explanatory/emphatic なの, it conveys meaning or definition, e.g. 'It means that (A)' or '(A) is how it is.'

meaning: It will end up being, It is the result of, It has been decided that
summary: A grammar point which expresses that something will end up being the thing which is (A), or result in (A).
formation: ［な］Adjective + な + ことになります (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことになる
text: ことになる is an expression that combines the nominalizing use of こと (creating a noun-phrase), with the case marking particle に, and the う - Verb なる 'to become'. This expression can be translated as 'to become (A)', but has the nuance that someone/thing caused (A) to become that way. Due to this, it may also be translated as 'it has been decided that (A)', or 'it will end up being (A)'.
ことになる is primarily used with verbs and い-Adjectives in their attributive form. It may also be used with な-Adjectives followed by な.
The 'it has been decided that (A)' meaning only applies to verbs, as only verbs will be enacted by someone/thing.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: This structure is a good example of why なる is often viewed as the intransitive form of する. する conveys that someone is performing an action (transitive), while なる implies that something is the result of an action (intransitive). This is why the (A) phrase in ことになる is usually determined to have been decided/performed by someone else, while still focusing on exactly 'what' (A) became.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The "something has been decided" meaning only applies to verbs!

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にする (N5, To decide on, To choose, To make something into, To view something as): Both にする and ことになる relate to decisions but differ in agency. にする is used when the speaker actively chooses something, often in daily situations like deciding what to eat, similar to 'I'll go with X.' ことになる, on the other hand, expresses decisions made by others or by circumstance, like saying 'It's been decided that X.'

ことにする (N3, To decide on, Have decided to): These expressions are similar in that both are used to express decisions. ことになる conveys that something has been decided or will happen due to external factors, e.g. 来月転勤することになった ('It's been decided that I'll be transferred next month'), while ことにする describes something the speaker has decided of their own power, e.g. 来月仕事を辞めることにした ('I've decided to quit my job next month').

ことになっている (N2, To be expected to, To be scheduled to): These are closely related patterns with a slight but clear nuance difference. ことになる expresses that something has been decided or will happen, often beyond the speaker's control, e.g. 転勤することになった ('It's been decided that I'll be transferred'), while ことになっている is typically used to refer to an established or habitual rule, e.g. 会議を行うことになっている ('It's been decided we'll hold a meeting').

に決まっている (N2, Surely, Bound to, Certainly, Be decided): These patterns are related in that both center around the idea of something being decided. ことになる expresses that something has been decided or will happen, often beyond the speaker's control, e.g. 転勤することになった ('It's been decided that I'll be transferred'), while に決まっている expresses that something is decisively true, e.g. 勝つに決まっている ('They'll definitely win').

ようになる (N4, To reach the point that, To come to be that, To turn into): Both ようになる and ことになる express something becoming a certain way, but with different nuances. ようになる describes a change in state, e.g. 話せるようになった ('I became able to speak.') ことになる, on the other hand, conveys a decision made, often outside the speaker's control, e.g. 辞めることになった ('It was decided that I/he/she would quit.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～は～で有名
text: In order to describe what certain things/places are famous for, ～は～で{有名|ゆうめい} is a common expression that will be used. This construction is made up of the adverbial particle は, the case marking particle で, and {有名|ゆうめい}, a noun that may also be used as an な-Adjective.
～は～で有名 is usually translated as '(A) is famous for (B)', but literally means 'with (B), (A) is famous/renowned'. The structure may be broken down in the following way:
(A) は - Presents (A) as the topic.
(B) で - With (B), in で's use as 'with'.
{有名|ゆうめい}だ - Is famous.
As can be seen from these examples, こと (or の) may precede で{有名|ゆうめい}. This is quite common when an entire phrase is being described as the famous aspect of (A), rather than a single word.

meaning: There is no need to, Never happens
summary: An expression that shows that (A) is a thing that either never occurs, or is not called for.
formation: Verb + ことはありません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことはない
text: ことはない is an expression that has two primary purposes in Japanese. To convey that there is 'no need for (A)', or that '(A) never happens'. In these cases, (A) is a verb that will appear directly before こと. ことはない is often used to reassure someone that something will not come to pass.

In this expression, the adverbial particle は is working to present (A) as the extent (a regular role of adverbial particles), while the {形容詞|けいようし} ない negates that extent. This negation is up to interpretation, with the literal meaning simply being 'There is no (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 決して〜ない (N3, Never, By no means): Both express negation, but differ in tone and nuance. ことはない suggests that something never happens, or literally that 'there are no cases of (A)', e.g. 忘れることはない ('There's no way I'll forget'), while 決して〜ない adds strong emphasis, meaning 'never' or 'by no means', and could even be used together with ことはない, e.g. 決して忘れることはない ('I will by no means forget').

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): ことはない downplays the need for action and is often used to reassure, e.g. 焦ることはない ('There's no need to rush.') ことだ gives firm advice and carries an authoritative tone, e.g. 焦らずに進めることだ ('You should proceed calmly.') ことはない can also mean that something never occurs, which is a usage unrelated to ことだ, e.g. 彼と会うことはない ('I never see him.')

わけがない (N3, There is no way, There is no reason, It is impossible, Cannot be): These expressions are similar in that both emphatically express negation, but they differ in nuance. ことはない implies something never happens, or literally 'there are no cases of (A)', e.g. 二度と会うことはない ('I'll never talk to him again / a second time.'). In contrast, わけがない expresses strong denial or impossibility, e.g. 負けるわけがない ('There's no way I can lose.')

ことがある (N3, Something is possible, Sometimes, Occasionally, There are times when): These two expressions can be opposite in meaning. ことはない means that something never happens or is not necessary, e.g. 彼と話すことはない ('There are no occasions where I talk to him'), while ことがある indicates occasional occurrence, e.g. 道に迷うことがある ('I sometimes get lost'). Note that ことはない can also express 'no need to', e.g. 心配することはない ('There's no need to worry'), which is unrelated to any use of ことがある.

までもない (N1, There is no need to, Do not have to, It is not necessary to, Needless to): Both can serve as emphatic ways to express 'there is no need to', e.g. 心配する（までもない/ことはない） ('There is no need to worry.'). Note however that ことはない can also be used to mean that something never happens (lit. 'there are no cases of'), e.g. 彼と会うことはない ('I never meet him.'), while までもない is not used in this sense and will always have the 'no need' meaning.

すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): ことはない and すこしも～ない are both emphatic negatives, but with different nuances. ことはない means 'There's no need to (A).' or 'There are no instances of (A).'. For example, 心配することはない ('There's no need to worry.'), and 彼と話すことはない ('There are no occasions when I talk to him.'). In contrast, すこしも～ない emphasizes absence of degree or amount, e.g., すこしも心配していない ('I'm not even a little bit worried.').

はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): ことはない has two primary uses: one is to express that there is no need to do something, e.g. 心配することはない ('There's no need to worry.'), and the other is to say that something simply doesn't happen, e.g. 彼と会うことはない ('There are no cases where I meet him.'). In contrast, はずがない expresses the speaker's strong denial or disbelief regarding some possibility, e.g. 負けるはずがない ('There's no way / It's highly unlikely we will lose.').

なくてもいい (N4, Don't have to): ことはない and なくてもいい can overlap when expressing 'There is no need to...' or 'You don't have to...' For example, 心配することはない and 心配しなくてもいい both mean 'There's no need to worry.' However, ことはない can also be used to express that something never happens. For example, 彼と話すことはない means 'I never talk to him,' which is not a use for なくてもいい.

ひつようがある (N4, It is necessary to): These forms are opposites in meaning. ひつようがある shows something must be done, as in 行く必要がある ('You need to go.'). ことはない reassures that something doesn't need to be done, as in 行くことはない ('You don't need to go.'). One expresses necessity, the other expresses lack of it.

meaning: Although ~ might say that ~
summary: A grammar point highlighting that although, or even if (A) is said, (B) is more accurate.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About  ～と言っても
text: As a construction that combines と{言|い}う (presenting the previous statement as a quotation) and ても, meaning 'even if (A)', or 'even though (A)', と{言|い}っても will mean 'even if I say (A)', or 'although I say (A)'. This expression is used when the speaker wants to highlight (A), but draw the listener's attention to (B), in order to clarify something.

This expression may be used after any word in almost any tense, due to the case marking particle と being used in its quotation role. However, な-Adjectives and nouns will sometimes be followed by だ (although it is regularly omitted).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: といえば (N3, Speaking of, If it were the case that): While both relate to things that have just been mentioned, ～と言っても softens or qualifies assumptions, while といえば introduces a related topic. For example, 旅行と言っても日帰りだった ('Even though I say vacation, it was just a day trip') vs. 夏といえば海ですね ('If we're speaking of summer, the beach comes to mind').

というのは (N3, ~ Known as ~ is, ~ Called ~ is, ~ Means ~, Because): ～と言っても typically qualifies or corrects an impression based on a previous statement, while ～というのは explains or defines something more directly. For example, 忙しいと言っても一日中じゃない ('I say I'm busy, but not all day') vs. 留学というのは海外の学校で勉強することです ('What we call study abroad means studying at a school in a foreign country').

にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): Both ～と言っても and にしても can be translated as 'even though' or 'even if', but they differ in nuance. ～と言っても is used to downplay or soften expectations, e.g. 運動と言ってもウォーキング程度です ('Even though I say exercise, it's just walking'), while にしても has the nuance of 'even considering (A), (B)' or 'no matter if (A), (B)', e.g. 忙しいにしても連絡してほしい ('Even if they're busy, I'd at least like to be contacted').

といえども (N1, Even (if), Although, Even though): といえども is essentially a more formal/written-style variant of the more casual/colloquial と言っても, with both meaning 'even if one says'. Though they can overlap in usage, と言っても is perhaps more commonly used when referring to something actually said, e.g. 安いと言っても5000円はする ('Although I say it's cheap, it does cost 5,000 yen.'), while といえども is often used figuratively with no explicit sense of quotation, e.g. 名人(だ)といえども失敗する時もある ('Although he's a master, he sometimes fails.').

meaning: Speaking of, If it were the case that
summary: A hypothetical grammar point that is used when (A) suddenly reminds the speaker of something related.
formation: (1) と言（い）うと、と言（い）ったら

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About といえば
text: と{言|い}えば, と{言|い}うと, and と{言|い}ったら are all expressions that are translated quite closely to 'speaking of (A)', or 'if it were the case that (A)'. Each of these structures has a slightly different nuance, but are largely used in the same situations.
と{言|い}えば - More hypothetical, 'were it (A)'.
と{言|い}うと - More concrete, 'if it's (A)'.
と{言|い}ったら - More situational, 'when it's (A)'.

These constructions are most commonly used after nouns, in response to something that has already been mentioned in the conversation (usually by someone else). The thing that has already been said is quite often the 'trigger' for someone remembering something, causing them to interject with と{言|い}えば.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ところで (N3, By the way, Incidentally): Both can be used to shift the topic, but といえば is used after a noun to bring up something related or comment on that thing, e.g. 京都といえば、有名なお寺が多いね ('Speaking of Kyoto, there many famous temples, aren't there.'). In contrast, ところで typically starts a new sentence to introduce an unrelated topic, e.g. ところで、週末の予定は？ ('By the way, what are your plans for the weekend?').

は (N5, As for... (Highlights sentence topic)): Both といえば and は can introduce the topic of a sentence. といえば is used when referencing something previously mentioned or known, often implying that more information will follow ('speaking of…'). は is broader and can also suggest contrast, as in 'バナナは食べたけど…' ('I ate the banana, but [not the apple]'). といえば doesn't create contrast in this way.

～と言っても (N3, Although ~ might say that ~): While both relate to things that have just been mentioned, ～と言っても softens or qualifies assumptions, while といえば introduces a related topic. For example, 旅行と言っても日帰りだった ('Even though I say vacation, it was just a day trip') vs. 夏といえば海ですね ('If we're speaking of summer, the beach comes to mind').

って (N3, As for, Speaking of, Casual は (Sentence topic marker)): Both can mean 'speaking of (A)', but differ in tone and usage. といえば often refers back to something just mentioned or known to both speaker and listener, e.g. 京都といえば、お寺が有名だね ('Speaking of Kyoto, its temples are famous.') って is a casual form used in everyday conversation, often functioning like は to casually introduce a topic, e.g. この映画って最高！ ('That movie is amazing!')

そういえば (N2, Speaking of which, By the way, Come to think of it): These expressions are similar in that both can be used to shift the topic, but といえば is typically used following a noun to introduce something connected to that topic, while そういえば recalls something the speaker just remembered. For example, 夏といえば花火だね ('Speaking of summer, fireworks come to mind') vs. そういえば、明日は休みだった ('Oh right, we have a holiday tomorrow').

meaning: To do for one another, Mutually, With
summary: A common expression used to highlight when (A) is done mutually among all involved, or for one another.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 合う
text: When following the conjunctive form of another verb, the う - Verb {合|あ}う means to do that action in concert with another person/group. This is often translated as 'to mutually do (A)', or 'to do (A) for one another'. Realistically, it just means 'to do (A) reciprocally', with involvement from both sides being required. In this usage, {合|あ}う is considered to be a suffix.
This construction is often used with expressions like お{互|たが}いに 'mutually', which simply emphasizes the point.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と共に (N3, Together with, At the same time, As well as): Both relate to the idea of doing something 'together', but with different nuances and usage. 合う attaches to verb stems to convey mutual interaction, e.g. 助け合う ('help each other'), while と共に means '(A) happens together with (B)' in the sense of co-existence or simultaneity, e.g. 年を取ると共に考え方も変わった ('My thinking changed as I grew up').

pattern: に合わせて・に合った
meaning: In accordance with, Matching, Fitting, Suitable for, Adjust or tune to
summary: A construction used to show that something is done to fit with (A), or to match (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に合わせて・に合った
text: When the る - Verb {合|あ}わせる (sometimes {併|あわ}せる) is seen in the form {合|あ}わせて, it conveys that something has been made to 'match (A)' or 'fit with (A)'. (A) being a noun that appears before に, followed by {合|あ}わせて. This structure can also have the nuance of 'in accordance with (A)', highlighting that (A) is the governing factor.
It is also possible to see the う - Verb {合|あ}う used in its past tense form, linking an (A) noun to a (B) noun. This has a similar meaning, but is closer to '(B) that has met (A)'.
In sentences that use either of these expressions, more information is usually given about why something is happening in accordance with (A), or what the purpose of (B) meeting (A) is/was.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 向け (N3, Intended for, Aimed at): Both relate to the idea of being suited to something else, but with different nuances. に合わせて・に合った implies active adjustment to suit a person or situation, e.g. 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ ('Choose clothes to match the season'), while 向け describes being made for or targeted toward a certain group, e.g. 子供向けのアニメ ('A cartoon for children').

にもとづいて (N3, Based on, In accordance with): Both express a general sense of basing an action on something, but their specific nuances differ. に合わせて・に合った conveys adapting or matching to something. For example: 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ = 'Choose clothes based on the season.' In contrast, にもとづいて typically expresses the grounding or foundation for some action. For example, 経験にもとづいて判断する = 'Make a decision based on experience.'

に応じて (N2, Depending or based on, According to, In response to, Suitable for or to): Both relate to the idea of one thing being dependent on another, but with different nuance and formality level. に応じて is a formal expression and conveys variation or response depending on conditions, e.g. 必要に応じてサポートする ('Support as needed'), while に合わせて・に合った is less formal and implies actively adjusting to match or suit something, e.g. 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ ('Choose clothes to match the season').

向き (N3, Suitable for, Facing): Both relate to the idea of being suited to something else, but with different nuances. に合わせて・に合った implies active adjustment to suit a person or situation, e.g. 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ ('Choose clothes to match the season'), while 向き describes suitability or appropriateness by nature, e.g. 初心者向きの本 ('A book suitable for beginners').

にしたがって (N2, As, Following, As then, According to, In accordance with): Both relate to the idea of being in accordance with something else, but with different nuances and usage. に合わせて・に合った follows a noun and implies adjustment to suit a person or situation, e.g. 相手に合わせて話し方を変える ('Adjust your way of speaking to the other person'), while にしたがって shows something happening in response or proportion to another change, e.g. 年を取るにしたがって体力が落ちる ('As you age, your stamina declines').

meaning: Concerning, About, Regarding
summary: A phrase that expresses a topic adhering to (A), and therefore being about it.
formation: Noun + について + の + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About について
text: について is a combination of the case marking particle に, the う-Verb {就|つ}く 'to assume a position', and the conjunction particle て. It is most often translated as 'about (A)', or 'concerning (A)', with the literal translation being closer to 'taking the position of (A)', or 'assuming the topic of (A)'.
について may be used after nouns, or noun-phrases (phrases that use こと, の, etc).
について may also appear before の + noun. In this use, it means '(B) that is about (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It is rare to see について actually using the kanji {就|つ}. について itself is regularly considered as a single compound word, rather than a combination of its parts.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: において・における (N3, In, On, At, Regarding, In terms of): While they appear similar in form, these expressions have different nuance and meaning. について means 'concerning (A)' and often marks a topic of discussion, question, and so on, e.g. 日本文化について話す ('Talk about Japanese culture'), while において・における is a formal equivalent of で and often indicates the location or context something happens, e.g. 会議において発表する ('Announce at the meeting').

にかかわる (N2, To relate to, To have to do with, Concerning, Depends on): Both patterns relate to a topic, but differ in meaning, tone, and grammatical usage. について means 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)' and attaches to verb phrases, e.g. スポーツについて話す ('Talk about sports'), while にかかわる is more formal and attaches to nouns, typically describing a more serious or consequential relationship, such as one involving life, health, or major repercussions, e.g. 命にかかわる問題 ('A life-threatening issue').

に取って (N3, To, For, Concerning): These two phrases appear similar but are used quite differently. について means 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)' and indicates the topic of a speech, discussion, etc., e.g. ゲームについて話す ('Speak about games'), while に取って (often written in hiragana as にとって) means 'to/for (A)' or 'as far as (A) is concerned' and is typically used to express perspective or point of view, e.g. 私にとって大切な人 ('An important person to me').

に関する・に関して (N3, Related to, About, Regarding): Both patterns mean 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)' and show a relationship between (A) and the following phrase, but with some differences. について is neutral in formality and attaches to verb phrases, e.g. 歴史について学ぶ ('Learn about history'), while に関する・に関して is somewhat more formal and can modify verbs (in に関して form) or nouns directly, e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('A book about history'), which について cannot do.

にかけては (N2, When it comes to, Regarding, Concerning): Both について and にかけては can be translated as 'about' or 'regarding', but they differ in specificity and usage. について typically marks the topic of a discussion, question, or the like, e.g. 日本文化について話す ('Talk about Japanese culture'), while にかけては highlights someone's strength or expertise in a specific area, often with praise, e.g. 料理にかけては彼が一番 ('When it comes to cooking, he's the best').

につき (N2, Due to, On account of, Each or every): Though similar in that both use に with a form of the verb つく, these patterns differ in meaning and formality level. について means 'concerning (A)' and typically marks the topic of a discussion, question, or so forth, e.g. 日本文化について話す ('Talk about Japanese culture'), while につき is a formal way to express a reason or condition, often used in official announcements, e.g. 悪天候につき中止する ('Cancel due to bad weather').

にまつわる (N1, Surrounding, Related or relating to, Associated with, Connected to): Both introduce a topic, but the nuance is different. にまつわる means ‘associated with' and is used for things indirectly connected through stories, episodes, or background, as in この神社には狐にまつわる話が多い ('There are many stories associated with foxes at this shrine.'). について is a neutral topic marker meaning 'about' or 'regarding,' used simply to state what is being discussed, as in 日本の歴史について勉強している (‘I am studying about Japanese history.').

に対して (N3, In contrast to, While, In regard to, Whereas): Both に対して and について express a relationship between (A) and (B), but differ in nuance and usage. について means 'about (A)' and marks the topic of a statement, e.g. 日本について学ぶ ('Learn about Japan'), while に対して means 'toward (A)' and expresses direction or stance, e.g. 親に対する気持ち ('Feelings toward parents') or 優しい人に対して ('Toward kind people').

meaning: Figure, Shape, Appearance, Looks, Wearing, Dressed in, Presence
summary: An expression highlighting someone having the figure of (A), often in relation to dress or presence.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～(の)姿
text: When the noun {姿|すがた} 'figure' is used as a suffix, it describes the outward appearance of someone. This may be in relation to what the person is wearing, their overall shape, body type, or style. {姿|すがた} is often translated as '(A) looking', 'wearing (A)', 'clad in (A)', or 'performing (A)'.
{姿|すがた} may be used after verbs in their attributive form, or after nouns followed by the case marking particle の.

{姿|すがた} is a word that focuses primarily on the way that someone appears to the observer. Therefore, it is also often used to describe the observer's impression of who they are looking at, in regard to their presence, or lack thereof.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): Both relate to appearance, but with quite different nuances. ～(の)姿 refers to someone's outward form, posture, or visual state, e.g. 彼女の頑張っている姿 ('The sight/figure of her working hard'). In contrast, ～らしい② is used to describe traits or appearances typical of a category or role, e.g. 男らしい ('Manly'). While 姿 describes the appearance or form itself, ～らしい② is about how that form embodies social or cultural norms.

にみえる (N4, To look, To seem, To appear): Both expressions relate to appearance, but with different nuance and usage. ～(の)姿 refers to someone's outward form, posture, or visual state, e.g. 彼女の頑張っている姿 ('The sight/figure of her working hard'), while ～ように見える expresses how something visually seems or appears to the speaker, e.g. 彼は悲しそうに見える ('He looks sad') or 葉っぱに見える ('It looks like a leaf').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と言える
text: と{言|い}える is a common expression that utilizes the potential form of the verb {言|い}う 'to say', to highlight that it is possible for something to be said. This phrase is often used to express a general idea about something that the speaker believes to be correct. と{言|い}える translates as 'it is fair to say (A)', or 'one could say (A)'.
As the case marking particle と is being used in its {引用|いんよう} (citation) use, と{言|い}える may follow any direct phrase/statement.

と{言|い}える is regularly seen paired with grammar patterns like だろう, or でしょう. This makes the overall statement more friendly, by considering the listener's thoughts about the issue being presented. と{言|い}えるだろう can simply be translated as 'can we not say (A)?', or '(A) can be said, right?'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The speaker is usually relatively confident about their statement when using と{言|い}える, but the usage of a form that expresses conjecture shows that they are open to the possibility of being wrong, thus softening the tone.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: と言える by itself makes the statement much more frank

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: といってもいい (N4, You could say, You might say): Both と言える and といってもいい can express a meaning similar to the English 'it can/might be said that (A)' with the difference being the degree of assertiveness. と言える is a firmer statement, literally meaning '(A) can be said.'. In contrast, といってもいい sounds more tentative, implying that it would be fine/acceptable to say the thing in question, but allowing for the possibility that other views/opinions may also be valid.

sections.heading: About ちゃんと・きちんと
text: In Japanese, two {副詞|ふくし} (adverbs) that are used to express very similar ideas are ちゃんと, and きちんと. These words may be used either at the beginning of a sentence (to modify the meaning of the whole sentence), or before verbs. ちゃんと and きちんと both translate quite closely to 'properly', or 'neatly'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そのため(に)
text: そのために is a frequently used conjunction in Japanese that utilizes その, the noun ため 'reason' (occasionally seen as {為|ため}), and the case marking particle に. そのために is most commonly translated as 'for that reason', or 'to that end'.
そのために will be used at the beginning of a new sentence, to highlight something that will be done/occur due to the circumstances/goal of something in the first sentence. に is often omitted.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: {為|ため} is an exceptionally flexible kanji in Japanese. In addition to ため it is occasionally used for する 'to do', なる 'to become', なす 'to bring about', and つくる 'to make'. The kanji itself means 'to put (something) to use', with heavy emphasis on whatever new state/result will be arrived at afterwards. This meaning can be seen reflected in all of {為|ため}'s readings.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: すると (N3, Having done..., If...is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): The two Japanese phrases, すると and そのため(に), are used in different contexts. すると is used to indicate a natural or logical outcome or consequence of a certain action, it is often translated as 'and then', 'if', or 'when'. On the other hand, そのため(に) is commonly used to express the cause or reason for a certain outcome, it is often translated as 'for that reason', 'because of that' or 'hence'.

ため(に) (N3, For, For the sake of, In order to): These share the same core construction, using ため(に) to express 'in order to (A)' or 'due to (A)'. ため(に) is used within a sentence after a noun, verb, or adjective phrase. そのため is used at the beginning of a sentence to mean 'for that reason' or 'due to that', referring back to what was just said.

という理由で (N3, For (that) reason; on the grounds of (that), With the reasoning, Under the pretext of, Due to): Both introduce reasons, but そのため(に) shows a direct consequence or effect from what was previously stated, while という理由で introduces a reason more abstractly and with a greater degree of formality. They also differ in how they connect the reason to the consequence, with そのため(に) always appearing at the beginning of a sentence, and という理由で being able to appear either at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence.

それで (N4, Because of that, So?, And then?, Therefore, With that): そのため(に) and それで both show cause and effect. それで is casual and used in everyday speech: 道が混んでた。それで遅れた ('The road was crowded, so I was late.'). そのため is more formal and can also express purpose, e.g. 健康のため、運動している 'I'm exercising for my health.').

おかげで (N3, Thanks to, Because of): Both express cause and effect, but with different tone and usage. おかげで implies a positive result and gratitude, e.g. 先生のおかげで合格できた ('Thanks to my teacher, I passed.') そのため(に) is neutral, objective, and often appears at the start of a sentence. It can also mean 'for that purpose'.

そこで (N3, Accordingly, Now, Therefore, To that end): Both are typically used at the beginning of a sentence to show what follows from a certain cause or situation. そのため(に) more clearly states the relation and can mean either 'due to that' or 'for that purpose', while そこで is less clear about the relationship between the previous thought and what follows, similar to the English 'as such' or 'in light of that'.

ために (N3, Due to, Because of, As a result of): そのため(に) can be seen as a more specific version of ために. ために follows a noun, verb, or adjective phrase to express purpose or reason. そのため(に) appears at the beginning of a sentence and means 'due to that' or 'in order to do that', referring back to what was previously said.

なぜなら〜から (N3, Because, The reason is, That is because): Both expressions relate to cause and effect, but in opposite directions: なぜなら〜から gives the reason for something previously stated, while そのため(に) introduces the result of a prior situation. Additionally, そのために can also express purpose, a meaning なぜなら〜から does not carry.

せいで (N3, Because of, Due to, Blame): Both せいで and そのため(に) show cause and effect, but せいで follows a word or phrase and implies a negative result or blame, e.g. 台風のせいで試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled because of the typhoon'), while そのため(に) is used at the beginning of the sentence and neutrally shows a logical result of whatever was previously stated. そのため(に) can also express 'for the purpose of (A)', which is a nuance せいで cannot have.

その結果 (N3, As a result): These expressions are similar in that both are used at the beginning of a sentence to express the effect of a cause mentioned just previously. そのため(に) implies a direct, logical cause, like the English 'due to that', while その結果 focuses on the ultimate condition or situation brought about by the cause, like 'as a result of that'. そのため(に) can also express 'for the purpose of (A)', which is a nuance その結果 cannot have.

meaning: As a result
summary: A grammar point which highlights something that is a result of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About その結果
text: その{結果|けっか} is a conjunction in Japanese that is used to highlight the result of something that has been previously said. The noun {結果|けっか} itself means 'result'. This expression translates as 'as a result of (A)', or 'resulting from (A)'.
その{結果|けっか} will be used at the beginning of a new sentence, before a (B) phrase will highlight the result of (A).

その{結果|けっか} may be used to highlight either positive, or negative results interchangeably. However, the (B) part of the sentence almost always focuses on a new 'situation' or 'condition' that has been created due to (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 結果・の結果 (N2, As a result of): Both expressions use 結果 to express a resulting situation or condition, like the English 'as a result', but differ in how they connect to the cause. その結果 is used at the beginning of a sentence and points back to something just mentioned, while 結果・の結果 is used in mid-sentence and connects directly to an explicitly mentioned cause, either by attaching to a verb or to a noun with の.

そこで (N3, Accordingly, Now, Therefore, To that end): These expressions are similar in that both are used at the beginning of a sentence and can express the outcome of a situation, but they differ in nuance. そこで is relatively vague about the connection between the two events, like the English 'as such' or 'accordingly', while その結果 more specifically conveys that a situation or condition results from the previously mentioned cause.

したがって (N2, Therefore, Thus, As a result): その結果 and したがって are similar in that both express a result or consequence with a relatively formal tone. その結果 emphasizes the resulting situation or condition, similar to the English 'as a result of that', while したがって implies a logical conclusion, which may or may not necessarily be a 'resulting' situation.

ために (N3, Due to, Because of, As a result of): ために and その結果 both express a cause/effect relationship, but in different ways. ために is used within a sentence following a noun, verb, or adjective, and can mean either 'due to (A)' or 'in order to (A)'. その結果 comes at the beginning of a sentence and always means 'as a result of that', referring back to the previous statement.

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): These expressions are similar in that both are used at the beginning of a sentence to express the effect of a cause mentioned just previously. そのため(に) implies a direct, logical cause, like the English 'due to that', while その結果 focuses on the ultimate condition or situation brought about by the cause, like 'as a result of that'. そのため(に) can also express 'for the purpose of (A)', which is a nuance その結果 cannot have.

meaning: Compared to, When compared to
summary: A grammar point used to make direct comparisons or contrasts between (A) and (B).
formation: (1) に比（くら）べたら、に比（くら）べれば、に比（くら）べると

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に比べて
text: に{比|くら}べて is a set expression in Japanese, used when comparing one thing to another. It is often simply translated as '(A) compared to (B)', or 'when comparing (A) to (B)'. {比|くら}べる is a る - Verb that means 'to compare', or 'to contrast'.
に{比|くら}べて will be attached directly after a noun, before the (B) part of the sentence will explain the comparison that is being made.

Occasionally, the case marking particle と will be used instead of に. に and と are largely interchangeable in this expression, with に focusing slightly more on the changes/differences between similar features of (A) and (B). Alternatively と often mutually contrasts (A) and (B), discussing their individual/unique characteristics.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 割に (N3, Although, Despite, Rather...for, Unexpectedly, Comparatively, Considering): Both are used in making comparisons, but に比べて is used to directly compare and contrast two things, e.g. このスマホはあのスマホに比べて安い ('This smartphone is cheaper than that one'), while 割に expresses a gap between expectation and reality, e.g. 値段の割に美味しい ('It's tasty considering the price'). The former makes a neutral comparison; the latter evaluates something against an assumed standard.

にしては (N3, (Even) considering, (Even) for): Both are used in making comparisons, but にしては expresses when something is unexpectedly different from what one would assume based on a certain condition, e.g. 子供にしては大人しい ('He is quiet for a child'), while に比べて simply compares or contrasts, e.g. この問題は前のに比べて簡単だ ('This problem is easier than the previous one'). にしては implies something contrary to expectations, while に比べて does not.

meaning: No matter how
summary: A grammar point that highlights that no matter how much (A), the result cannot be avoided.
formation: どんな + （に） + Noun + でも

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About どんなに〜ても
text: As explained in the そんな grammar point, the こそあど{言葉|ことば} may occasionally be seen in the forms こんな, そんな, あんな, or どんな. どんな itself is an abbreviation of どのような, meaning 'in what way', or 'what kind of'. When partnered with に (creating an adverb), and ても, どんなに～ても is used to express the extent of something that is insufficient. It can be translated as 'no matter how (A), (B)'.
どんなに may be attached to any type of word, so long as that word is then followed by でも (in the case of nouns or な-Adjectives) or ても (in the case of い-Adjectives or verbs).
どんなに～ても can literally be translated as 'even if (A) is in however/whatever (way), (B)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): Both どんなに〜ても and にしても introduce conditions contrary to results, but with different focuses. どんなに〜ても emphasizes an unchanging outcome despite extreme conditions, e.g. どんなに高くても買います ('I'll buy it no matter how expensive it is'), while にしても is used more flexibly to acknowledge a point while suggesting a contrast or reservation, e.g. 行くにしても、今日は無理だ ('Even if I go, today's not possible').

いくら〜でも (N3, No matter how (much)): Both express 'no matter how', but どんなに〜ても is used with qualities or actions, e.g. どんなに忙しくても行きます ('No matter how busy I am, I'll go'), while いくら〜でも is used with amounts or quantities, e.g. いくら頼んでも無理です ('No matter how much you ask, it's impossible').

どうしても (N3, Regardless of, No matter what): どんなに〜ても means 'no matter how' and emphasizes that an outcome remains unchanged even under extreme or difficult conditions, e.g. どんなに努力しても勝てない ('No matter how hard I try, I can't win'). On the other hand, どうしても expresses strong intent or inevitability, often meaning 'no matter what' or 'at any cost', e.g. どうしても行きたい ('I want to go no matter what'). It can reflect either persistence or a lack of alternatives.

にも～ない (N1, Cannot... even if one wants or tries, Would like but cannot, Wants or tries but cannot): Both にも〜ない and どんなに〜ても deal with limitations, but in different ways. どんなに〜ても focuses on the resilience or constancy of an outcome despite extreme efforts or conditions, e.g. どんなに頑張っても無理だった ('No matter how hard I tried, it was impossible'), while にも〜ない expresses helplessness or inability despite intent, often paired with verbs of volition or emotion, e.g. 寝ようにも寝られない ('I can't sleep even if I try').

meaning: No matter how (much)
summary: A phrase that highlights that no matter what number of (A), the result will not change.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About いくら〜でも
text: In a similar way to どんなに～ても, いくら～でも is regularly translated to 'no matter how (A), (B)'. However, unlike どんな (which is an abbreviation of どのような), いくら is a noun that comes from the kanji {幾|いく}ら, meaning 'how much'. When partnered with ても (with verbs and い-Adjectives), or でも (with nouns and な-Adjectives), the literal meaning means 'however much (A), (B)'.
With いくら～でも, the (B) part of the phrase will usually highlight something that is being negated, giving the phrase it's 'no matter how much' nuance.

Despite this trend of being used in sentences that contain ない or ありません, いくら～でも may also be seen in positive sentences. In these cases, despite not being negative, the (B) phrase will still be something that is surprising/unexpected in some way (due to its extent or amount).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: どんなに〜ても (N3, No matter how): Both express 'no matter how', but どんなに〜ても is used with qualities or actions, e.g. どんなに忙しくても行きます ('No matter how busy I am, I'll go'), while いくら〜でも is used with amounts or quantities, e.g. いくら頼んでも無理です ('No matter how much you ask, it's impossible').

どうしても (N3, Regardless of, No matter what): どうしても and いくら〜でも both express emphasis but in different ways. どうしても is used when something must happen or when the speaker is determined, e.g. どうしても行きたい ('I want to go no matter what'). いくら〜でも means 'no matter how much' or 'how many', often used with amounts or degrees to show that the outcome won't change, e.g. いくら頼んでも無理です ('No matter how much you ask, it's impossible').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 〜かは〜によって違う
text: ～かは～によって{違|ちが}う is an expression in Japanese that appears quite complex at first, but is actually quite simple when broken down into its parts. かは is a combination of the case marking particle か in its role as a quotation, paired with the adverbial particle は, highlighting the topic of the sentence. Together these can be translated as 'whether (A)'.
によって{違|ちが}う is made up of the case marking particle に (highlighting a location), the て form of よる (a う - Verb), followed by {違|ちが}う 'to differ', (another う - Verb).

All together, this can be translated as '(A) depends on (B)'. More accurately though, the meaning is 'whether (A) will differ depending on (B)'. かは is regularly used after an entire phrase, followed by a noun and then によって{違|ちが}う.
Alternatively, かどうか may be used instead of かは. This changes the nuance from 'whether (A)', to 'whether or not (A)'. When translated directly, かどうか is quite similar to 'whether (A) or however'.

Finally, this expression may also be seen without {違|ちが}う. In a sentence like this, 'differs' is simply removed, becoming 'whether (A) will depend on (B)'. As conjugation between the verbs is no longer required, によって will become による.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 次第だ・次第で (N2, Depending on, So): The grammar point 次第だ／次第で is used to indicate that a situation or course of action depends on something specified, often involving uncontrollable events or conditions. On the other hand, 〜かは〜によって違う expresses that the result or state changes depending on certain conditions or variables, focusing on how outcomes differ based on those factors.

によって・による (N3, By means of, According to, Depending on, Because of, Due to): Both express variation depending on conditions, and 〜かは〜によって違う includes によって as part of its structure. The key difference lies in grammatical structure: 好きか嫌いかは人によって違う ('Whether someone likes it depends on the person.') vs. 好き嫌いは人による ('Likes and dislikes depend on the person.')

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かなり
text: かなり is an adverb that is used to convey a 'considerable' amount of something. It is often translated as 'quite', 'fairly', 'considerably', or 'pretty'. かなり will almost always appear directly before a phrase, or directly before a noun (in which case の will come between the noun and かなり).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なかなか (N3, Very, Quite, Considerably): When used in affirmative sentences, なかなか and かなり both convey the nuance that something exceeds expectations, e.g. なかなか美味しい ('It's quite tasty.') or かなり美味しい (essentially the same meaning). The main difference is that なかなか is often used in negative expressions to suggest that something is not easily done, e.g. なかなかうまくいかない ('It just won't go well.'), while かなり is not used this way.

summary: A structure that expresses an excessive amount of (A) that led to (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About あまりに
text: Being the adverbial form of {余|あま}る 'excess', あまりに is a grammar structure that is used to convey an 'excessive' amount of something that caused a certain result. あまりに will almost always be used in sentences expressing some sort of surprise/shock about the degree of (A). Often, あまりに is translated simply as 'so much (A) that (B)', or 'way too much (A)'.
In the last example, we can see that あまり will be followed by の when linked to a noun. Occasionally, にも will be used instead of に. This just emphasizes the 'excess' of (A) further.

As the literal meaning of あまりに is quite close to 'excessively', it may be easier to remember this translation, rather than 'so much (A) that (B)'. Usually, 'it is excessively (A), so (B)' will cover most possible nuances.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なかなか (N3, Very, Quite, Considerably): Both emphasize degree, but differ in nuance. なかなか suggests something is quite or surprisingly so, often with a positive tone, e.g. なかなか面白い映画だった ('It was quite an interesting movie.') あまりに means 'too much' or 'excessively', and is often negative in tone, e.g. あまりに寒くて出かけられなかった ('It was too cold to go out.')

あまり (N3, So much...that): Both mean 'too much', but differ in nuance. あまりに emphasizes intensity and doesn't necessarily imply a result, e.g. あまりに暑い日だった ('It was an extremely hot day.') あまり highlights excess that leads to a (usually undesirable) outcome, e.g. 暑さのあまり眠れなかった ('I couldn't sleep due to the extreme heat.')

すぎる (N5, Too much, Very): Both すぎる and あまりに express that something is excessive or 'too much.' すぎる attaches to the stem of verbs or adjectives (e.g. 早すぎる), while あまりに comes before them (e.g. あまりに早い). They can also be combined for emphasis (e.g. あまりに早すぎる). Compared to すぎる, あまりに often carries a nuance of surprise or emotional reaction.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About わけだ
text: One of the most misunderstood words in Japanese is {訳|わけ}. Of the many ways it can be translated, the most common are 'reason', 'cause', 'meaning', or 'conclusion'. Despite this, it may be beneficial to consider it almost identical to an equally versatile English word 'so'.

In all of its uses, わけ simply highlights the plain existence/determination of something in the same way that 'so' does in English. This can be seen in its most basic form in わけだ. A combination of わけ and the auxiliary verb だ.

わけだ will be used at the end of sentences, and is sometimes preceded by という. This use is often translated as 'for the reason of (A)', 'no wonder its (A)', or 'its (A), as you'd expect'. Realistically though, it just means 'it is so that it's (A)', or 'so it's (A)'.

Due to わけ being a noun, it will need to follow the attributive form of whatever word comes before it. As we can see 'so' and わけ have an extremely close pattern of nuances, ranging from 'because', all the way through to simple emphasis (like with 'naturally', and 'as you'd expect').
わけ may also be used in questions, implying that the speaker is trying to determine something that they have heard. わけだね 'so its (A) right?', and わけですか 'so is it that (A)?' are good examples of this.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: はずだ (N4, Bound to (be), Expected to (be), Should be (able)): Both express logical conclusions, but with different emphasis. はずだ conveys expectation or prediction, as in 来るはずだ ('He should come.'). わけだ explains a reason behind something known or observed, like 来るわけだ ('So that's why he's coming.'). はずだ leans future-oriented, わけだ explanatory.

ことだ (N3, Should, Ought): Both express reasoning in a broad sense, but are used differently. わけだ explains why something is the case, e.g. 暖房が壊れているのか。だから寒いわけだ ('So the heater's broken. That explains why it's cold.') ことだ gives strong advice or instruction, e.g. 寒いなら暖房をつけることだ ('If it's cold, you should turn on the heater.')

ため(に) (N3, For, For the sake of, In order to): わけだ and ため(に) are similar in that both can be used when expressing a reason, but they mean quite different things. わけだ is used when drawing a conclusion, like the English 'so that's why (A)', while ため(に) on the other hand means 'for the sake of (A)' or 'due to (A)'.

だけに (N2, As might be expected, Because, All the more because, It's only natural): Both だけに and わけだ can be used to draw conclusions, but differ in tone and focus. だけに emphasizes an expected result based on a known condition, e.g. 忙しい人だけに来ないと思った ('Precisely because he's a busy man, I thought he wouldn't come'), while わけだ indicates the speaker's realization based on something previously expressed or observed, e.g. だから来ないわけだ ('So that's why he's not coming').

だけのことはある (N2, No wonder, Not surprising that, As expected): Both だけのことはある and わけだ can be used when drawing conclusions, but function differently. だけのことはある affirms that an outcome is appropriate or deserved in a positive sense, e.g. プロだけのことはある ('It's as expected from a pro'), while わけだ signals the speaker's understanding or conclusion, e.g. だから負けたわけだ ('So that's why we lost'). The latter conveys realization, in either a positive or negative sense.

はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): はずがない denies something based on logic or evidence, while わけだ draws a conclusion or explains a reason. sections.label: About
sections.heading: About わけではない
text: As mentioned in the {訳|わけ}だ grammar point, わけ is a noun that is used for strong determination/conclusion in Japanese, in the same way that 'so' is in English. Naturally, this determination may sometimes be negative, as is the case with わけではない. ではない being the conjugated form of the auxiliary verb だ, the adverbial particle は, and the い-Adjective ない.

わけではない may be translated as 'it doesn't mean that (A)', or 'it's not the case that (A)'. Although, 'it is not necessarily so that it's (A)', or 'so it's not (A)' are closer to the actual nuance of わけ. わけではない can be used at the end of any sentence, so long as the word before わけ is in attributive form.
As always, では may be replaced by じゃ.

text: はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): はずがない strongly rejects something as being true. わけではない denies an assumption while leaving room for nuance. For example, 雨が降るはずがない ('There's no way it will.') vs. 雨が降るわけではない ('It's not that it will rain.'), implying e.g. that the weather might be poor in other ways, etc.

のはXの方だ (N3, It is...that..., It is...who..., ...is the one that..., ...is the one who...): のはXの方だ emphatically states what is true or relevant, often in contrast with something else, e.g. 勝ったのは彼の方だ ('He was the one who won.') わけではない, by contrast, qualifies or softens a statement, e.g. 彼が勝ったわけではない ('It's not that he won.') One affirms directly; the other downplays or denies.

というわけではない (N2, It is not that, It doesn't mean that, It is not always the case): Both わけではない and というわけではない express the idea of 'it doesn't mean that (A)' or 'it's not necessarily the case that (A)', but differ in usage and nuance. わけではない attaches directly to a verb or adjective phrase to deny a specific assumption or conclusion, while というわけではない uses the quoting particle と and often adds a nuance of clarification or softening of an implied statement.

わけがない (N3, There is no way, There is no reason, It is impossible, Cannot be): Both of these patterns with わけ express negation, but with different nuances. わけではない denies a possible interpretation or assumption, e.g. 'it's not the case that (A)', while わけがない is a stronger, categorical denial, meaning 'there's no way that (A)' or '(A) is impossible'.

とは限らない (N3, Not necessarily so, Is not always true, There is no guarantee that): Both とは限らない and わけではない challenge assumptions, but in different ways. わけではない denies a specific inference or interpretation, e.g. 'it's not the case that (A)', while とは限らない emphasizes exceptions, e.g. 'just because (A), it's not always (B)'.

というものでもない (N2, There is no guarantee that…, Not necessarily): Both というものでもない and わけではない express that something isn't necessarily true, but differ in tone. わけではない directly denies a potential assumption, while というものでもない has a more indirect or reflective nuance, often meaning 'it's not always necessarily the case that (A)'.

meaning: At the same time as, The instant, The moment, As well as
summary: An expression that points out when two or more events take place or coexist at the same time, or same moment.
formation: Verb［る］ + と同時（どうじ）に
［な］Adjective + である + と同時（どうじ）に
Noun + （である) + と同時（どうじ）に

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と同時に
text: To convey that things are happening at the same time in Japanese, と{同時|どうじ}に will often be used. This is a combination of the case marking particle と in its listing particle use, {同時|どうじ}, a noun meaning 'the same time', and に, the case marking particle marking a location.

と{同時|どうじ}に translates as 'at the same time as (A)', 'the instant that (A)', or 'as well as (A)'. In sentences that use this grammar structure, (A) is considered to be the primary event, but any (B) or (C) events are not considered any less important.
In the case of nouns and な-Adjectives, である is often omitted.

While the literal meaning of と{同時|どうじ}に is 'at the same time', this expression is also regularly used when listing multiple roles or functions that someone/thing has. This comes across as 'as well as', but still carries the 'at the same time nuance'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なり (N1, As soon as, The moment, When): Both と同時に and なり follow the plain form of verbs and describe events occurring in close succession, but their nuance differs. と同時に means 'at the same time as' and emphasizes actual simultaneity. In contrast, なり highlights immediate consequence, something happening as soon as the first action occurs, and often implies a reflexive or automatic response.

と共に (N3, Together with, At the same time, As well as): と同時に and と共に can both mean 'together with' or 'at the same time as', but their nuance differs. と同時に emphasizes temporal simultaneity in neutral or factual contexts, while と共に often conveys shared action, emotional resonance, or development over time.

でもある (N3, Be also, It also is): でもある and と同時に can both express the idea of 'also' or '(A) as well as (B)', though they function differently. と同時に follows the first item of information, while でもある follows the additional information. Because they appear in different parts of a sentence, they can also be used together. For example, ピアニストであると同時に、作曲家でもあります ('In addition to being a pianist, he is also a composer').

とき (N4, When, At the time of): とき expresses the general time of an action or event, like 'when' in English. と同時に means 'at the same time as' and emphasizes simultaneity. For example, 帰ってきた時 means 'when (I) came home', while 帰ってきたと同時に means 'the moment (I) came home' or 'as soon as (I) came home'.

たとたんに (N3, The instant or moment, As soon as, Just as): Both と同時に and たとたんに describe closely linked events, but they differ in focus. と同時に emphasizes simultaneity or coordination, while たとたんに conveys a sudden, often unexpected result following a completed action. Their grammar structure also differs: と同時に follows the non-past form, while たとたんに follows the past tense.

meaning: Almost, Nearly, About to, On the verge of
summary: A construction indicating the place or situation in which (A) was about to, or on the verge of happening.
formation: Verb［ない］+ ところだった
Verb［ない］+ ところでした (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ところだった ①
text: As explained in the ところ grammar point, ところ is a noun that is often used to highlight the situation within which a verb is 'about to' happen (when that verb appears in its non-past form). However when followed by だった, it emphasizes that the thing that was 'about to' happen never actually eventuated (or that another more important event happened at that moment). This can be translated as 'to almost (A)', or 'to be on the verge of (A)'.
The verb that ところ is paired with may also be seen grouped with the auxiliary verb ない. In this case, it implies that something was 'about not' to happen (but then did).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ところだった ② (N2, Was just about to do something, Was in the middle of...): ところだった can be used with two closely related nuances. The more literal meaning expresses the idea of 'was just about to (A)', as in: 昼ご飯を食べるところだった ('I was just about to eat lunch.'). The more figurative meaning conveys that something nearly happened but ultimately didn't, similar to 'I almost (A)' or 'I nearly (A)' in English, as in: 死ぬところだった ('I almost died' [but didn't]).

るところだ (N4, About to, On the verge of): るところだ and ところだった① both express that an action is or was about to happen, but differ in outcome. るところだ means the action is about to occur and likely will. ところだった① means it was on the verge of happening, but didn't in the end.

meaning: I heard/was said, Because, But, Even or also, Even if or even though
summary: A very casual expression used to give reasons, say but, or sometimes even to relay things heard from others.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だって
text: だって is a colloquial combination of the auxiliary verb だ, and the adverbial particle とて in Japanese (a combination of the particles と, and て). It has a wide range of uses, but primarily exclaims that something is the 'premise' for whatever has been said, or will be said next. This 'exclamation' is usually translated as 'I heard', 'cause', 'but', or 'even if'. The meaning that will be conveyed is determined primarily by where だって appears in a sentence.

When placed at the beginning of a sentence, だって highlights the speaker's (usually) displeasure about something that has just been said, before following it with an explanation or counterpoint. This だって is quite similar to でも.

At the end of a sentence, だって is used to express hearsay, in a similar way to 'I heard that', or 'it was said that', in English. In these cases it will be preceded by なん. なんだって always appears after a noun, or a phrase that has been nominalized (with の or こと).

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The adverbial particle とて itself is an abbreviation of expressions like と{言|い}って, and と{思|おも}って. だとて (the full construction) may also be used, but is almost always replaced by だって, as it is far easier to say.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Used in casual language; has a childish/naive nuance

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: んだって (N3, I heard that, He or She said that): Both expressions involve だって, but their usage differs. んだって appears at the end of a sentence and means 'I hear (A)' or 'they say (A)', with an explanatory nuance added by ん. In contrast, だって is more flexible. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, and has several meanings. It can function as a casual 'because', 'even though', or 'they say (A)', depending on context.

たって (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter how): These are two expressions that can look very similar, or even identical in some cases, as たって when used with nouns will become だって. As an overall guideline, だって is a casual expression used to express 'I hear (A)' or 'they say (A)', or as a colloquial 'because', while たって is one way to say 'even though (A)' or 'even (A)', similar to ても or でも.

ということだ (N3, I heard that, Rumor has it that, It is said that, It means that): Both can be used to report hearsay (i.e. 'they say (A)'), but differ in tone and nuance. ということだ is more formal and can carry the nuance of summarizing or confidently reporting what the speaker heard. だって is much more casual and light, and can also be used at the beginning of a sentence with an emphatic 'but I mean (A)' nuance, which is something ということだ cannot do.

なぜなら〜から (N3, Because, The reason is, That is because): Both can be used to express reasons, but だって is highly casual, colloquial, and emotional, while なぜなら〜から is formal and objective-sounding. Also, なぜなら〜から begins a sentence, and clearly introduces a reason for something just stated, while だって can be used in sentence-final position. Depending on usage, だって can also have the meanings of 'I hear' and 'even though', which なぜなら〜から does not have.

それでも (N4, But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless): だって and それでも both express contradiction. だって is casual and often used at the start of a sentence to offer an objection, e.g., だって疲れたもん ('But I'm tired!'). それでも is less casual and shows contrast with a neutral tone, e.g., 雨だった。それでも行った ('It was rainy, but I still went.').

ときいた (N4, I heard that): Both ときいた and だって express hearsay, but differ in tone and formality. ときいた means 'I heard that (A)' and is neutral and conveys information directly heard by the speaker, while だって is casual and emphatic, often used in conversation to mean something like 'They say (A).' or 'I'm telling you (A).'.

meaning: I heard that, He or She said that
summary: A very casual way to quote something that has been said.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About んだって
text: When used at the end of sentences, だって often expresses something that has been heard by the speaker. This particular use of だって will always be paired with ん or なん.
As だって is a grouping of the auxiliary verb だ, and the adverbial particle って, なんだって primarily expresses the following:
なん - Presents an explanation.
だ - Determines something to be true.
って - An abbreviation of と{言|い}って 'is said' or と{思|おも}って 'is thought'.
In this way, it translates quite similarly to 'it is that (A) was said/thought'. Realistically though, it is used in the same way as 'I heard that (A)', or 'it's thought that (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: なんだって usually comes across as being quite casual, so is best used in conversations with friends.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ときいた (N4, I heard that): Both ときいた and んだって express hearsay, but with different nuances and formality. ときいた means 'I heard (A).' and conveys information directly heard by the speaker, e.g. 高いときいた ('I heard it was expensive.'). In contrast, んだって is casual and adds an explanatory nuance, like 'They say (A).' or 'I heard that (A).', e.g. 高いんだって ('They say it's expensive, you know.').

だって (N3, I heard/was said, Because, But, Even or also, Even if or even though): Both expressions involve だって, but their usage differs. んだって appears at the end of a sentence and means 'I hear (A)' or 'they say (A)', with an explanatory nuance added by ん. In contrast, だって is more flexible. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, and has several meanings. It can function as a casual 'because', 'even though', or 'they say (A)', depending on context.

そうだ (N3, I heard that, It is said that): Both express hearsay, but with different tone and usage. んだって is very casual, often used in everyday conversation, and carries an explanatory tone due to んだ, e.g. 明日休みなんだって ('They said tomorrow's a day off, you know.') そうだ is more neutral and indirect, with no explanatory nuance, e.g. 明日休みだそうだ ('I heard tomorrow's a day off.')

って (N5, Casual quotation): って (a contracted form of と) is a casual quoting particle used to mark direct or indirect speech, thoughts, feelings, or to introduce a topic. んだって, which combines って with the explanatory ん・の, is used to express 'I heard' or 'He/she/they said.' While って can follow any word, んだって requires な before な-Adjectives or nouns.

とか (N2, I heard that… something like, They said ... or something ): These two expressions are similar in that both can serve as casual expressions of hearsay, i.e. 'they say (A)' or 'I hear (A)'. The difference is that んだって has a slightly more explanatory and emphatic nuance due to the presence of ん, while とか has an uncertain or non-specific tone, i.e. 'I hear (A) or something', because of the presence of the question particle か.

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): んだって and らしい ① both convey information from another source, but with different nuances and levels of formality. らしい ① suggests hearsay with a nuance of certainty, indicating the speaker believes it to be true, e.g. 'Apparently it's (A).'. In contrast, んだって is highly casual and includes an explanatory nuance, similar to 'He/she/they said/say (A), you know.'.

meaning: (Not) involved with, (Not) concerned with, (No) connection with, (No) relationship with, (Not) related to
summary: A common expression used when a relationship or connection exists, or does not exist with (A).
formation: Noun + に(1) + 関係（かんけい） + がある(2)
Noun + に(1) + 関係（かんけい）+ が(3)ある(2) + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 関係がある
text: When the noun {関係|かんけい} 'a relation' is paired with がある 'to have', it will be received in a similar way to phrases like 'involved with (A)', 'concerning (A)', or 'in relation to (A)'. {関係|かんけい}がある will often be preceded by the case marking particle に, expressing the location 'where' the connection exists.
に itself will always be preceded by a noun or noun-phrase.
Alternatively, に can be replaced by other case marking particles such as と or の. Each has a slightly different nuance, but are used quite interchangeably.
に{関係|かんけい}がある - Relating to (A).
と{関係|かんけい}がある - Related with (A).
の{関係|かんけい}がある - Having a relation with (A).
Naturally, ある may be replaced by ない, to express that there is 'no relation' between (A) and (B).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: に関する・に関して (N3, Related to, About, Regarding): Both express the idea of connection, but differ in usage and nuance. に関する・に関して attaches to nouns to mean 'about (A)' or 'regarding (A)', e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('a book about history') or 歴史に関して勉強する ('study about history'). 関係がある conveys a looser connection, meaning 'is related to (A)', and unlike に関する・に関して, can be used with と as well as に, in sentence-final position, or with ない to express a lack of connection.

meaning: Related to, About, Regarding
summary: A phrase that shows that some thought or action is in connection to (A).
formation: Noun + に関（かん）する + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に関する・に関して
text: に{関|かん}する and に{関|かん}して are two grammar patterns in Japanese that are regularly used to show when (B) is 'about' or 'related to' (A). {関|かん}する itself is a verb meaning 'to relate'.
に{関|かん}する will be followed directly by a second noun, while に{関|かん}して creates a pause in the sentence, before (B) will be explained in the second half of that sentence.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にかけては (N2, When it comes to, Regarding, Concerning): Both show a relationship, but differ in nuance. に関する・に関して means 'about/concerning (A)' and attaches to nouns, e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('a book about history') or 歴史に関して書く ('write about history'). In contrast, にかけては means 'when it comes to (A)' and highlights strength or excellence in an area, e.g. 料理にかけては彼が一番だ ('When it comes to cooking, he's the best').

を巡って (N2, Concerning, In regard to, About, (Split) over): These phrases are similar in that both can be translated as 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)', but they differ in nuance. に関する・に関して is a more neutral and general-purpose expression that can be used to express 'about (A)' in a wide variety of contexts, while を巡って is more formal and often implies differing opinions or viewpoints surrounding a topic, and is therefore used more narrowly.

について (N3, Concerning, About, Regarding): Both patterns mean 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)' and show a relationship between (A) and the following phrase, but with some differences. について is neutral in formality and attaches to verb phrases, e.g. 歴史について学ぶ ('Learn about history'), while に関する・に関して is somewhat more formal and can modify verbs (in に関して form) or nouns directly, e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('A book about history'), which について cannot do.

において・における (N3, In, On, At, Regarding, In terms of): These patterns are similar in that both follow nouns, then attach to either another noun (に関する and における) or the rest of the sentence (に関して or において), but differ in meaning. に関する・に関して means 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)', while において・における can be considered a more formal/literary equivalent of で indicating a context, place, or setting.

に対して (N3, In contrast to, While, In regard to, Whereas): Both patterns show a relationship, but differ in nuance and usage. に関する・に関して attaches to a noun to mean 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)', e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('a book about history'). In contrast, に対して (or に対する before nouns) implies a directional or oppositional relationship like 'toward (A)', e.g. 彼に対する気持ち ('feelings toward him').

関係がある (N3, (Not) involved with, (Not) concerned with, (No) connection with, (No) relationship with, (Not) related to): Both express the idea of connection, but differ in usage and nuance. に関する・に関して attaches to nouns to mean 'about (A)' or 'regarding (A)', e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('a book about history') or 歴史に関して勉強する ('study about history'). 関係がある conveys a looser connection, meaning 'is related to (A)', and unlike に関する・に関して, can be used with と as well as に, in sentence-final position, or with ない to express a lack of connection.

にかかわる (N2, To relate to, To have to do with, Concerning, Depends on): Both follow nouns to express the idea of being related to or having to do with something, but they differ in nuance and structure. に関する・に関して attaches to a noun to mean 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)', e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('a book about history'). にかかわる also connects to nouns but often implies a more serious or impactful relationship, e.g. 命にかかわる問題 ('a life-threatening issue').
