sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に対して
text: に{対|たい}する and に{対|たい}して are two grammar patterns in Japanese that are regularly used to show when (B) is 'opposed to' or 'in contrast with' (A). {対|たい}する itself is a verb meaning 'to oppose'. Although this feeling of 'opposition' may be negative, in most circumstances, it just means 'toward' in the sense of targeting something.
に{対|たい}する will be followed directly by a second noun, while に{対|たい}して creates a pause in the sentence, before (B) will be explained in the second half of that sentence.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にひきかえ (N1, In stark contrast, In comparison, On the other hand, While, In sharp contrast): Both にひきかえ and に対して set things side by side, but they differ in purpose and tone. にひきかえ is used specifically to make a contrast between two situations or people, often highlighting a difference in evaluation or outcome, as in 父が厳しすぎるのにひきかえ、母は優しすぎる (‘My father is too strict, whereas my mother is too kind.’). に対して can be used similarly, but is also a broad and neutral expression meaning “toward,” “regarding,” or “in response to,” and is used for attitudes, actions, or opinions directed at a target without implying comparison or evaluation, as in 彼はみんなに対して優しい人だ (‘He is kind toward everyone.’).

に関する・に関して (N3, Related to, About, Regarding): Both patterns show a relationship, but differ in nuance and usage. に関する・に関して attaches to a noun to mean 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)', e.g. 歴史に関する本 ('a book about history'). In contrast, に対して (or に対する before nouns) implies a directional or oppositional relationship like 'toward (A)', e.g. 彼に対する気持ち ('feelings toward him').

について (N3, Concerning, About, Regarding): Both に対して and について express a relationship between (A) and (B), but differ in nuance and usage. について means 'about (A)' and marks the topic of a statement, e.g. 日本について学ぶ ('Learn about Japan'), while に対して means 'toward (A)' and expresses direction or stance, e.g. 親に対する気持ち ('Feelings toward parents') or 優しい人に対して ('Toward kind people').

にかけては (N2, When it comes to, Regarding, Concerning): While both can be used for comparison, their nuance differs. に対して typically contrasts two things in terms of opposing qualities, e.g. 田中先生が厳しいのに対して、鈴木先生は優しい ('Whereas Prof. Tanaka is strict, Prof. Suzuki is lenient'). In contrast, にかけては highlights strength or excellence in a specific area, e.g. 料理にかけては彼が一番だ ('When it comes to cooking, he's the best').

において・における (N3, In, On, At, Regarding, In terms of): Both patterns connect to nouns to show a relationship, but differ in nuance. に対して (which also appears before nouns as に対する) implies a directional or oppositional relationship, like 'toward (A)', e.g. 彼に対する気持ち ('feelings toward him'). In contrast, において・における is a more formal/literary equivalent of で, indicating a context, place, or setting, e.g. 現代社会における宗教 ('religion in modern society').

反面 (N2, While, On the other hand, Although, However, On the flip side): Both express contrast, but their nuance differs. に対して typically compares two things with opposing qualities, e.g. 田中先生が厳しいのに対して、鈴木先生は優しい ('Whereas Prof. Tanaka is strict, Prof. Suzuki is lenient'). 反面 focuses on two sides of the same situation, e.g. 都会の生活は便利な反面、お金がかかる ('Life in the big city is convenient, but expensive'). に対して also has a 'toward (A)' usage, which 反面 does not.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About くらい ②
text: Often, the noun くらい is used as an adverbial particle. This use of くらい (or ぐらい) expresses the limit of something, in a similar way to ほど. This means that it can be translated as 'about (A)', 'so (A) that (B)', or '(A) to the extent of (B)'. Let's take a look at a few examples.

Despite translating in the above ways, we can see that this use of くらい is similar to the standard kanji use {位|くらい}, which literally means a 'rank', or 'grade' of something. What this means is that (A) will usually be considered to be at the 'grade' of something that was required in order to cause/allow (B).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: くらい and ぐらい may be used 100% interchangeably, but ぐらい is far more common in speech

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: くらい ① (N5, About, Approximately): くらい (often ぐらい in speech) expresses an approximate degree or extent. It's commonly used with number + counter expressions (the くらい① form), as in 100円くらい = 'about 100 yen.' It can also be used like ほど to express extent or degree, as in 足が動けなくなるくらい走った = 'I ran so much my legs couldn't move anymore.'

ほど (N3, The more, About, To the extent that, So much… that): Both くらい and ほど can express extent in the sense of 'so much that (A)' or 'to the extent of (A)', and are often interchangeable, e.g. 驚くくらい静かだった / 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.') くらい (also written as ぐらい) tends to sound slightly more colloquial, and each word has other uses where they may not be interchangeable.

まで (N4, Even, To even, To the extent of): Both まで and ほど share the core meaning of 'to the extent of,' but are used differently. まで emphasizes inclusivity or a surprising limit, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.'). In contrast, くらい② means 'to the point of' and often expresses degree, e.g. 叫びたいくらい怖かった ('It was so scary I wanted to scream.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About は～くらいです
text: は～くらいです is an expression in Japanese used to convey that '(B) is all that exists within (A)'. As with other grammar points that use くらい, this nuance will be shown in the form of an 'extent'. In は～くらいです, both は and くらい are being used as adverbial particles. This structure is often translated as '(B) is about the extent of (A)'.

To use this grammar pattern, (A) will come before は, highlighting the situation, place, thing, or person within which a limit exists. The (B) part of the sentence will then describe what that limit is, followed by くらいです (or だ).
In order to add extra emphasis, のもの or なもの may follow くらい.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ほど (N3, The more, About, To the extent that, So much… that): Both relate to expressing extent, but with different emphasis. は～くらいです highlights something as the only or most notable case, like 'about the only (A) is (B)', e.g. できるのは田中さんくらいです ('Mr. Tanaka's about the only person who can do it.') ほど expresses extent or intensity, e.g. 驚くほど静かだった ('It was quiet to a surprising degree.')

くらい ① (N5, About, Approximately): くらい (or ぐらい in speech) expresses an approximate degree or amount, like the English 'about.' It's commonly used with numbers and counters (the くらい① form), e.g. 100円くらい = 'about 100 yen.' A related pattern, は～くらいです, means 'just about the only X is Y.' For example, 食べ物で嫌いなのはピーマンくらいです = 'The only food I dislike is peppers.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さ - Interjection
text: さ is a {感動詞|かんどうし} (interjection) in Japanese that has three primary uses. These are as follows:
{誘|さそ}い、{促|うなが}し - To invite, incite, or draw attention to something.
{驚|おどろ}き、{当惑|とうわく} - To express surprise, confusion, or bewilderment.
{話|はなし}の{流|なが}れを{抑|おさ}える - To control or keep in check the flow of a conversation.

In this lesson, we will be focusing on the first meaning (to invite or draw attention). In English, this is usually translated as 'there we go', 'ok then', or 'well you see'. さ (or sometimes さあ) will come at the beginning of a sentence, before the point that the speaker would like to highlight is explained.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Generally, the lengthened “さあ” is used more often than the shorter “さ”

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: では・それでは・じゃあ (N3, If so, Well (then), In that case): Both can appear at the beginning of a sentence to mark a transition. では・それでは・じゃあ signal a shift or next step based on context, e.g. じゃあ、行こうか ('Well then, shall we go?') さ (often extended as さあ) adds an encouraging or prompting tone, e.g. さあ、そろそろ行こうか！ ('Come on, let's get going!')

さ - Casual よ (N3, Casual よ): Both can be used to express emotion in casual conversation. The interjection さ is often used at the beginning of sentences and can express encouragement, e.g. さあ、行こう！ ('All right, let's go!'), or hesitation/uncertainty, e.g. さあ、分かりません ('Let's see... I don't know.'). The other usage appears at the end of phrases and functions like a casual よ, e.g. できるさ！ ('You can do it, I'm telling you!').

さて (N3, Well, Well then): These are two similar-looking interjections with different uses. さて is a transitional phrase often used at the beginning of sentences to change the topic or move the conversation into a new phase, like 'well then' or 'now then'. In contrast, さ is a casual interjection that serves multiple functions, such as encouragement (e.g. 'all right!', 'come on!') or hesitation ('well, you see...').

さ - Filler (N3, Like, You know, You see, Listen, Uhh): さ is a common expression in casual speech with multiple distinct usages. One is as an interjection for encouragement, e.g. さあ、行こう！ ('All right, let's go!'), or hesitation, e.g. さあ、分かりませんね ('Let's see... I don't know.'). The other is as a filler that ties parts of a sentence together, e.g. 昨日さ、図書館に行ったらさ、ケンジくんがいたよ ('Yesterday, like, I went to the library, right? And Kenji was there!').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さ - Filler
text: さ is a {感動詞|かんどうし} (interjection) in Japanese that has three primary uses. These are as follows:
{誘|さそ}い、{促|うなが}し - To invite, incite, or draw attention to something.
{驚|おどろ}き、{当惑|とうわく}し - The express surprise, confusion, or bewilderment.
{話|はなし}の{流|なが}れを{抑|おさ}える - To control or keep in check the flow of a conversation.

In this lesson, we will be focusing on the second meaning (to express surprise, confusion, or bewilderment). In English, this is used in a very similar way to 'like', 'you know', 'uhh', and other short phrases that are employed when a speaker is searching for the right thing to say, and is filling the silence. This さ may be used in any position within a sentence, simply to create thinking time.
The 'confusion' that this さ expresses is not necessarily a bad thing, and is used by many people to simply express that they have not finished talking yet.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: さ - Casual よ (N3, Casual よ): Both uses of さ are characteristic of casual conversation. The 'casual よ' usage comes at the end of sentences and, like よ, often emphasizes or confirms something to the listener, like 'I'm telling you'. The 'filler' usage of さ appears mid-sentence and ties phrases together, similar to English expressions like 'like' or 'you know', e.g. 昨日さ、ケンジ君に会ったよ ('So yesterday, like, I saw Kenji!').

さ - Interjection (N3, All right, There we go, Now, You see, Well (I don't know, let me see)): さ is a common expression in casual speech with multiple distinct usages. One is as an interjection for encouragement, e.g. さあ、行こう！ ('All right, let's go!'), or hesitation, e.g. さあ、分かりませんね ('Let's see... I don't know.'). The other is as a filler that ties parts of a sentence together, e.g. 昨日さ、図書館に行ったらさ、ケンジくんがいたよ ('Yesterday, like, I went to the library, right? And Kenji was there!').

meaning: Casual よ
summary: A short, casual interjection used either to fill silence, or to express that new information has been conveyed.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さ - Casual よ
text: さ is a {感動詞|かんどうし} (interjection) in Japanese that has three primary uses. These are as follows:
{誘|さそ}い、{促|うなが}し - To invite, incite, or draw attention to something.
{驚|おどろ}き、{当惑|とうわく}し - To express surprise, confusion, or bewilderment.
{話|はなし}の{流|なが}れを{抑|おさ}える - To control or keep in check the flow of a conversation.

In this lesson, we will be focusing on a specific feature of the first meaning (to draw attention). Unlike other types of drawing attention that さ is able to be used for (see this grammar point), this さ will only appear at the end of sentences. Here, さ is almost identical in meaning to that of よ, with a slight added nuance of high confidence in what one is saying.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Used only at the end of a sentence

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: さ - Filler (N3, Like, You know, You see, Listen, Uhh): Both uses of さ are characteristic of casual conversation. The 'casual よ' usage comes at the end of sentences and, like よ, often emphasizes or confirms something to the listener, like 'I'm telling you'. The 'filler' usage of さ appears mid-sentence and ties phrases together, similar to English expressions like 'like' or 'you know', e.g. 昨日さ、ケンジ君に会ったよ ('So yesterday, like, I saw Kenji!').

さ - Interjection (N3, All right, There we go, Now, You see, Well (I don't know, let me see)): Both can be used to express emotion in casual conversation. The interjection さ is often used at the beginning of sentences and can express encouragement, e.g. さあ、行こう！ ('All right, let's go!'), or hesitation/uncertainty, e.g. さあ、分かりません ('Let's see... I don't know.'). The other usage appears at the end of phrases and functions like a casual よ, e.g. できるさ！ ('You can do it, I'm telling you!').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About それぞれ
text: それぞれ is a noun in Japanese that is used similarly to 'each' in English. Like other nouns that can be used adverbially (ほとんど, {沢山|たくさん}, and かなり for example), それぞれ regularly comes before a whole sentence, or before a specific noun preceded by の.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: それぞれ comes from the same kanji as {其|それ}, the word used to highlight 'that' (close to the listener) in Japanese. Due to this, the literal meaning of それぞれ is 'that and that' (interpreted simply as 'everyone', or 'each).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 当たり (N3, Per~, A~, Apiece, Each): 当たり and それぞれ can both convey a sense of 'each', but their nuances are different. 当たり attaches to numbers to mean 'each' in the sense of 'apiece', e.g. １個当たり１００円 ('100 yen each' / '100 yen apiece'). In contrast, それぞれ means 'each' in the sense of 'to each their own', e.g. 人はそれぞれ個性がある ('People each have unique traits').

各 (N4, Each, Every, Respective, Various): Both 各 and それぞれ express the idea of 'each' or 'every', but they differ in usage. 各 always goes before a noun, for example, 各部屋 'each room', 各階 'each floor', and so on. それぞれ, on the other hand, can stand alone at the start of a sentence or be attached to a noun with の. For example, 人はそれぞれ違う意見がある ('People each have differing opinions.').

～ずつ (N3, One at a time, Per, Each, Gradually): Both convey the meaning of 'each', but differ in structure. ～ずつ attaches to quantity expressions to mean 'each' or 'little by little', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' or ちょっとずつよくなってきた 'It's gotten better a little at a time.' それぞれ appears before a phrase or with の and emphasizes individuality, e.g. 人はそれぞれ個性がある 'People each have unique qualities.'

meaning: As is, While remaining, Left in a state
summary: A grammar point that expresses something left as is, often in some unchanging state.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About まま(に)
text: まま, coming from the kanji {儘|まま}, which means 'as it is', is a noun in Japanese that is used for describing the 'unchanged state' of something. This expression may be translated as 'while remaining (A)', 'as (A) is', or 'left in the state of (A)'. It can be used after any word in its attributive form. However, when used with verbs, it has a tendency to be used with the た (past) form most frequently.
まま often expresses that something should be left alone, or undisturbed. This is generally seen with verbs in the ない form.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Occasionally written as まんま

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: れる・られる + ままに (N1, Do as (one is told or ordered…), In accordance with, In compliance with, Just like): Both patterns use まま, but れる・られる + ままに expresses acting in line with orders or circumstances, e.g. 言われるがままにする ('Do exactly as told'). In contrast, standalone まま(に) is used in a wider range of contexts to express an unchanged state, e.g. 窓が開けたままになっている ('The window is still open'). The compound implies passivity; the base form, a persistent state.

っぱなし (N3, Leaving something in a certain state, Left as is, Keep on -ing): まま(に) and っぱなし both describe something left in a certain state, but differ in tone. まま(に) can be neutral or passive, e.g. 電気をつけたまま寝た ('I fell asleep with the light on'). っぱなし adds a careless or irresponsible nuance, as in ドアを開けっぱなしにしないで ('Don't leave the door wide open').

ずじまい (N1, Ended up not, Did not (in the end), Never did): Both relate to a state continuing without change. まま describes a condition or state that remains as it is, neutral in tone, and when used as ないまま it means an action did not happen and that non-action continued, as in 行かないままだった ('I remained in a state of not going.'). ずじまい is especially close to ないまま but emphasizes the outcome that, after time or circumstances, the action never happened at all, often with regret or resignation, as in 結局行かずじまいだった ('In the end, I never went.').

きり (N3, Only, Just, Since): きり often marks an action done once and left that way, as in 去年会ったきり連絡がない ('I haven't heard from them since we met last year'). まま(に) marks an ongoing unchanged state, as in 靴を履いたまま入らないで ('Don't enter with your shoes on'). Both can imply continuation, but きり emphasizes a cutoff point.

たなり・なり (N1, While... ~ing, Remaining, Not or ever since, Keep or leave): Both expressions refer to a persisting state, but differ in nuance. With たなり・なり, there's often (but not always) an implication that the situation is undesirable or unexpected, as in 部屋に入ったなり出てこない ('Ever since going in his room, he hasn't come out'). まま(に) also marks an unchanged state, e.g. 窓が開けたままになっている ('The window is still open'), but is more neutral in tone.

如く・如き・如し (N1, Like, Similar to, As if, The same as): まま(に) can suggest a condition continuing unchanged or doing something exactly a certain way, e.g. 指示されたままに動く ('Act exactly as instructed'). 如く・如き・如し express resemblance, e.g. 夢の如く消えた ('It vanished like a dream'). Both can involve comparison, but only 如く emphasizes similarity, and is far more formal/literary than まま(に).

てある (N4, Something is done, Has been done, Remaining state): てある and まま(に) both describe continuing states, but differ in nuance. てある implies an action was done for a reason and that the result remains. For example, 窓が開けてある ('The window has been opened.') implies that it has been left open for a purpose. In contrast, まま(に) emphasizes that the state remains unchanged, without implying purpose, e.g. 窓を開けたまま家を出てしまった ('I left the house with the window open.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そこで
text: そこで (very rarely seen as {其処|そこ}で) is a combination of そこ 'there', and the case marking particle で. It is often translated as 'to that end', or 'accordingly'. Literally, it just means 'at that place', with で's use as 'with' or 'by' highlighting that something will be done there ('there' often being a situation). This phrase behaves very similarly to 'as such' in English.
Usually, a first sentence will highlight what the 'situation' is, before そこで goes on to explain how that situation was or will be resolved.
As で implies the 'use' of something, this expression should only highlight actions that are controllable.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: したがって (N2, Therefore, Thus, As a result): そこで and したがって are both used at the beginning of a sentence to express one action following another, but differ in nuance and tone. そこで is a general-purpose expression usable in various situations and contexts, like the English 'so' or 'as such'. In contrast, したがって is more formal and has a stricter 'following from that' or 'thus' nuance.

すると (N3, Having done..., If...is done..., (And/just) then, Thereupon, If so): Both describe what follows from a previous situation, but with different nuance. そこで introduces an intentional response to a situation, e.g. 雨が降ってきた。そこで傘をさした ('It started raining, so I opened my umbrella.') すると shows a natural or immediate result, e.g. 雨が降ってきた。すると子供が泣き出した ('It started raining. Then the child started crying.')

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): Both are typically used at the beginning of a sentence to show what follows from a certain cause or situation. そのため(に) more clearly states the relation and can mean either 'due to that' or 'for that purpose', while そこで is less clear about the relationship between the previous thought and what follows, similar to the English 'as such' or 'in light of that'.

その結果 (N3, As a result): These expressions are similar in that both are used at the beginning of a sentence and can express the outcome of a situation, but they differ in nuance. そこで is relatively vague about the connection between the two events, like the English 'as such' or 'accordingly', while その結果 more specifically conveys that a situation or condition results from the previously mentioned cause.

meaning: Have no choice but, Only, Just
summary: A structure that specifically expresses that no action apart from (A) is possible.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About しかない
text: しかない is a commonly used expression in Japanese that is partnered with verbs. It is a combination of しか, the adverbial particle, and the い-Adjective ない. This structure may be translated as 'to have no choice but (A)', or 'there is only (A)'. しかない regularly emphasizes the point that nothing apart from (A) is possible.
To use しかない, simply attach it directly to the non-past form of whichever verb you would like to highlight as being the 'only' possible action.

Unlike だけ, which implies that one particular option was chosen (out of several), しか always insinuates that (A) is the only option, and therefore will sound much stronger than だけ. Also, as only one option exists, it will often be assumed by the listener that some particular circumstances resulted in (A) being all that can be done.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In more casual language or manga/anime, しかない is sometimes shortened to っきゃない

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しか～ない (N4, There's only, Nothing but): When used with a noun and a negative verb, しか～ない expresses the idea of 'only' (literally, 'nothing but'), e.g. １００円しかない ('I only have / have nothing but 100 yen.') and バナナしか食べなかった ('I only ate / ate nothing but a banana.'). When used at the end of a sentence following a verb in the affirmative form, しかない has the related meaning of 'there's no choice but to do (A)', e.g. 行くしかない ('I have no choice but to go.').

よりほかない (N2, To have no choice but, No other way than, Have to): しかない and よりほかない are similar in that both mean 'there's no choice but to (A)', but よりほかない is considerably more formal than the colloquial しかない, and can carry a nuance that other options exist but aren't feasible due to external pressure or circumstance.

よりしかたがない (N2, There is no choice but, Can't be helped, Inevitable): While しかない and よりしかたがない both express having no choice, しかない is more neutral and conversational, while よりしかたがない is more literary and formal, often adding a nuance of resignation. Compare: そうするしかない ('We have no choice but to do that') and 待つよりしかたがない ('There's nothing to be done but wait').

ざるを得ない (N2, Can't help doing, Have no choice but): しかない and ざるを得ない both express having no choice, but しかない is more neutral and conversational, e.g. やるしかない ('I have no choice but to do it'). ざるを得ない has a similar meaning but is more literary, and is found mostly in writing or formal speech, as in 行かざるを得なかった ('I was forced to go').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About てもかまわない
text: ても{構|かま}わない is often used to express that something 'doesn't matter', or that the speaker 'doesn't mind'. This structure is a combination of ても (with verbs and い-Adjectives), or でも (with nouns and な-Adjectives) grouped with the negative conjugation of the う - Verb {構|かま}う, which means 'to brace'. Literally, this expression can be thought of as being similar to 'to not be uptight'. However, it is almost always simply used to convey that there is no issue with something.
ても{構|かま}わない may be used with any type of word that appears in its ても or でも conjugation form.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: {構|かま}う is usually translated as 'to brace', but the kanji {構|かま} often has the nuance of 'to posture', or 'to pose' (into some type of strong/resistant shape). In the ても{構|かま}わない grammar structure, this translates as (A) simply being something that will not cause the speaker to 'posture', 'position', or 'pose' themselves in a resistant way.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てもいい (N5, It is alright/fine/okay even if, Can/may, ~ is also okay): Both てもいい and てもかまわない are used to give or ask for permission, but with slight differences in nuance and tone. てもいい is a straightforward way to say 'It's okay' or 'Is it okay to (do this?)' On the other hand, てもかまわない adds a nuance of 'Do you mind if…' or 'it doesn't matter if…' てもかまわない sounds more polite, especially in it's かまいません form.

でよければ (N3, If it is alright, If you don't mind, If you would like, If possible): でよければ and てもかまわない both express acceptance, but from different perspectives. でよければ is most often used to modestly present something as an option, e.g. 私でよければお手伝いします ('If I'm acceptable, I'll help'). In contrast, てもかまわない is used to allow or grant permission, e.g. 使ってもかまわない ('I don't mind if you use it').

Verb + てもいい (N5, It's okay to, It's alright to, Can/may): Both Verb + てもいい and てもかまわない are used to give or ask for permission. The difference is tone and formality. てもいい is a basic, everyday expression, while てもかまわない is slightly more formal and often used in writing or professional contexts to mean 'It doesn't matter if…' or 'It's fine if…'

text: Like かどうか, another way that Japanese conveys 'whether or not' is through the use of ～ても～なくても. This grammar structure literally means 'even if (A), even if not (A)', to show that whatever the result is will not change, regardless of (A).
～ても～なくても is used primarily with verbs, and will always have the same verb appearing both before ても and なくても.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないまでも (N1, May not … but (at least), Even though not, Even if not): Both express that something holds regardless of degree, but the framing differs. ないまでも means ‘even if not to that extent’ and concedes a weaker case while still affirming the main point, often implying partial satisfaction, as in 完璧ではないまでも、十分だ ('Even if it’s not perfect, it’s good enough.'). ～ても～なくても states full irrelevance of the condition, meaning the result is the same whether it happens or not, as in 言われても言われなくても私はやる ('I’ll do it whether I'm told or not.').

ようが～まいが (N1, Even if, No matter what, Whether or not, [Emphatic], Volitional + が): ～ても～なくても and ようが～まいが are identical in meaning, both expressing the idea of 'whether or not', with the difference that ～ても～なくても is more casual and colloquial, while ようが～まいが is more formal/literary and emphatic. For example, 行っても行かなくても and 行こうが行くまいが mean the same thing but differ in tone.

を問わず (N2, Regardless of, Whether or not, No matter, With or without): ～ても～なくても and を問わず both express 'regardless of', but ～ても～なくても contrasts doing something with not doing it, e.g. 雨が降っても降らなくても ('whether it rains or not'), while を問わず states that something holds true regardless of category or attribute, e.g. 年齢を問わず ('regardless of age').

〜でも 〜でも (N4, Whether ~ or, Neither ~ or): 〜でも〜でも and ～ても～なくても both express 'whether or not'. 〜でも〜でも shows multiple possibilities, e.g. クッキーでもケーキでも甘いものは食べたい ('I want sweets, whether it's cookies or cake.'). ～ても～なくても shows opposition, e.g. 行っても行かなくても大丈夫 ('It's okay whether you go or not.').

にしろ～にしろ (N2, Whether… or): ～ても～なくても and にしろ～にしろ can both mean 'whether it's (A) or (B)', but ～ても～なくても contrasts something with its negative, e.g. 食べても食べなくても ('whether you eat or not'), while にしろ～にしろ typically contrasts two opposing words or ideas, e.g. 勝つにしろ負けるにしろ ('whether we win or lose').

かどうか (N4, Whether or not, If...or not): かどうか expresses uncertainty, like 'whether or not', as in 行くかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll go.'). ～ても～なくても presents two opposite possibilities and says the result is unchanged, like 降っても降らなくても行く ('Whether it rains or not, I'm going.').

やら～やら (N2, Whether or, Things like, And … so on): ～ても～なくても and やら～やら both present multiple possibilities, but ～ても～なくても contrasts something with its negative, e.g. 行っても行かなくてもいい ('Go or don't, it's fine'), while やら～やら loosely lists alternatives, which may include opposites, e.g. 行くのやら行かないのやら ('whether he'll go or not'), or not, e.g. 本やら辞書やら ('things like books and dictionaries').

にしても～にしても (N2, Regardless of whether): ～ても～なくても and にしても～にしても are similar in that both can mean 'regardless of whether it's (A) or (B)'. The difference is that ～ても～なくても contrasts doing something with not doing it, e.g. 行っても行かなくても ('whether you go or not'), while にしても～にしても contrasts two opposing words or expressions, e.g. 勝つにしても負けるにしても ('whether we win or lose').

にかかわらず (N2, Regardless of, Whether or, No matter, With or without): ～ても～なくても and にかかわらず both express that something holds regardless of condition. ～ても～なくても contrasts an action with its negative, e.g. 行っても行かなくても ('whether you go or not'), while にかかわらず can attach to a single noun, e.g. 天気にかかわらず ('regardless of the weather'), or a pair of opposing concepts, e.g. 早いか遅いかに関わらず ('whether early or late').

meaning: Don't, Mustn't, Shouldn't have
summary: A slightly slangy expression used to prohibit an action by framing it as something that is not done.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About んじゃない
text: んじゃない is a slightly slang grammar pattern used with verbs to prohibit or request that something not be done. It will usually just be translated as 'don't do (A)', or 'you mustn't (A)'. んじゃない is almost always used from a higher position toward someone of a lower status. It may be used when the speaker is angry, but not always.
んじゃない is a combination of the case-marking particle の, and the abbreviated form of ではない, じゃない. It will connect to the dictionary form of verbs.

Despite being slang, the slightly more formal version んじゃありません can also be seen occasionally. This variation is common when the speaker wants to forbid something, but not sound angry, such as when an adult is talking to a child.

The more literal translation of Verb + んじゃない is just 'it's not (verb)'. This sounds a bit strange in English, but might be similar to something like 'you're not (verb)', where a person is directly telling another what they shouldn't do.
It is also common to see the abbreviated ている form, てん, before じゃない.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About わけがない
text: One of the strongest ways to use the noun わけ in Japanese, is in the expression わけがない. This is regularly translated as 'there is no way that (A)', or 'it is impossible that (A)'. However, as mentioned in other わけ lessons, わけ is used very similarly to 'so' in English, so may also be thought of as 'it is SO not (A)', with 'so' being used for emphasis. In this structure, わけ is combined with the case marking particle が, and the い-Adjective ない.
わけがない may be used with verbs, or adjectives in their attributive form.

text: そうもない (N3, Very unlikely to, Does not seem that, Does not appear that): そうもない and わけがない are similar in that both express the unlikelihood of an event. そうもない suggests low probability based on observation, e.g. 雨が降りそうもない ('It seems unlikely that it'll rain'), while わけがない is an emphatic denial based on the speaker's logical conclusion, e.g. 勝てるわけがない ('There's no way we can win').

わけではない (N3, It doesn't mean that, It is not the case, It's not like): Both of these patterns with わけ express negation, but with different nuances. わけではない denies a possible interpretation or assumption, e.g. 'it's not the case that (A)', while わけがない is a stronger, categorical denial, meaning 'there's no way that (A)' or '(A) is impossible'.

はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): はずがない and わけがない are similar in that they both express a strong denial of a possibility, similar to the English 'There's no way that (A)', but with slightly different nuances. はずがない gives the sense that the speaker is drawing a conclusion based on their own reasoning, often with a sense of surprise or disbelief. In contrast, わけがない expresses an even stronger denial, as if the impossibility is an obvious fact.

ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): These expressions are similar in that both emphatically express negation, but they differ in nuance. ことはない implies something never happens, or literally 'there are no cases of (A)', e.g. 二度と会うことはない ('I'll never talk to him again / a second time.'). In contrast, わけがない expresses strong denial or impossibility, e.g. 負けるわけがない ('There's no way I can lose.')

ようがない・ようもない (N2, There's no way to, It's impossible to): わけがない and ようがない・ようもない are similar in that both express impossibility. わけがない rejects something as logically unthinkable, e.g. 彼がそんなことをするわけがない ('There's no way he'd do that'). ようがない emphasizes that there is no way or means to do something, e.g. 助けようがない ('There's no way to help').

slug: としたら-とすれば-とすると
pattern: としたら・とすれば・とすると
meaning: If it were the case that, Assuming that...
summary: A structure that goes off the assumption that (A) were true, and then expresses some hypothetical result.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About としたら・とすれば・とすると
text: When partnered with several of the assumption based expressions that are used in Japanese, the case marking particle と may be used to show a hypothesis about a certain result. This is one of the result highlighting uses of と. Structures that may be seen are as follows:
(A) としたら (B) - When (A) is the result, (B).
(A) とすれば (B) - If the result is (A), (B).
(A) とすると (B) - A result of (A) will be (B).

Although these nuances are slightly different, realistically they are used in almost exactly the same way, to express a possible (undetermined) result. This can be translated to 'assuming that (A)', or 'if it were the case that (A)'.
To use these expressions, simply attach と and your chosen variation of したら to the end of any verb/い-Adjective, or noun/な-Adjective followed by だ.

text: ばあいは (N4, In the event of, In the case of): ばあいは and としたら・とすれば・とすると both express the idea of 'in the case of' or 'in the event that'. In general, ばあいは (often written in kanji as 場合は) is more concrete and used for specific situations that might arise. For example, 行く場合 'in the event that you go'. In contrast, としたら・とすれば・とすると is typically used to discuss more hypothetical scenarios.

としても (N2, Even if (we assume), Assuming, Also as): としたら・とすれば・とすると and としても both introduce hypothetical situations. The former typically presents a scenario as worth considering, e.g. 留学するとしたら ('If I were to study abroad'). The latter introduces an unlikely or extreme case and implies that something will happen regardless, e.g. 行くとしても一人では行かない ('Even if I go, I won't go alone').

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): Both としたら・とすれば・とすると and なら express 'if,' but with different nuance. としたら (and its variants) emphasize a strongly hypothetical condition, like the English 'if we suppose that (A)'. In contrast, なら can imply that the speaker believes the condition likely to happen, e.g. 'if it's true that (A)', or 'if it's the case that (A)'.

summary: A grammar point that expresses something, considering either the viewpoint or role of (A). Going off that it's (A), (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About として
text: When the case marking particle と is used to highlight a result, it regularly translates to 'as' in English. This nuance of 'as' simply assumes that (A) is a plain or unchanging fact from which something (usually an opinion or evaluation) is based. Combining this nuance of と with して (the conjugation form of する), として will present (A) as the base point from which (B) can be determined.

Despite being a combination of several individual parts, として is often considered to be a {副助詞|ふくじょし} (adverbial particle) by itself, meaning that it will most often be seen connected directly to nouns.
As として works in the same way as a {副助詞|ふくじょし}, it may be connected directly to a second noun to express that (B) is something functioning as (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たる (N1, To be (in a position of), As a, For): たる and として both mean 'as (A)' or 'in the role of (A)', but たる is formal and often used when describing what someone in that position should be or do, e.g. 指導者たる者 ('a person in the role of leader'). として is more neutral and can be found in everyday speech, e.g. 学生として ('as a student').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にしては
text: Like として, にして highlights an aspect of something from which another thing happens. The primary difference being that と implies that (B) results from (A), while に implies that (B) happens/exists at the same time as (A). This reflects the case marking particle に's use as a location. The adverbial particle は presents the entire (A) phrase as something that will be compared.

にしては is regularly translated as 'considering (A), (B)', or 'even for (A), (B)', and may be used with both verbs and nouns. Like として, にして is often considered as a stand-alone adverbial particle, despite stemming from several parts.

Despite the 'considering (A), (B)' translation, にしては is closer in meaning to 'while (A), (B)'. This expresses that (A) and (B) share a simultaneous relation, but also that (B) is not necessarily a result of (A) at all.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からして (N2, Even..., Judging from, Based on): にしては and からして both use a reference point, but にしては highlights a result that defies expectations, e.g. 子供にしては詳しい ('He knows a lot for a child'), while からして draws a conclusion from one part that suggests the whole, e.g. みんなの感想からして面白そう ('From everyone's impressions, it seems interesting').

からすると・からすれば (N2, Judging from, Considering): にしては and からすると・からすれば both express judgment, but にしては highlights a state or result that departs from expectations, e.g. 初心者にしては上手だ ('He's good for a beginner'), while からすると・からすれば shows reasoning from a standpoint, e.g. 私の経験からすると ('Based on my experience').

に取って (N3, To, For, Concerning): に取って (often written in kana as にとって) and にしては both involve perspective, but にとって expresses personal relevance, e.g. 子供にとっては大問題だ ('It's a big issue for a child'), while にしては shows that a certain quality or characteristic defies expectations, e.g. 子供にしてはおとなしい ('He's quiet for a child').

から見ると (N2, From the point of view of, By the look of): にしては and から見ると both reflect viewpoint, but にしては highlights a result that departs from expectations for a category or role, e.g. 新人にしては落ち着いている ('She's calm for a newcomer'), while から見ると gives a neutral assessment from a given perspective, e.g. プロから見ると ('From a professional's viewpoint').

に比べて (N3, Compared to, When compared to): Both are used in making comparisons, but にしては expresses when something is unexpectedly different from what one would assume based on a certain condition, e.g. 子供にしては大人しい ('He is quiet for a child'), while に比べて simply compares or contrasts, e.g. この問題は前のに比べて簡単だ ('This problem is easier than the previous one'). にしては implies something contrary to expectations, while に比べて does not.

にしてみれば (N1, For (A), In the case of (A), From (A)'s point of view, In the eyes of (A)): Though both express a sort of contrast, they are used quite differently in practice. にしてみれば expresses a hypothetical from the point of view of another, e.g. 初心者にしてみればなかなか難しい implies that one might expect something to be simple, but it's difficult from the perspective of a beginner. にしては expresses a surprising or unexpected result given the basis or condition, eg. 初心者にしては上出来だ ('That's a great job for a beginner.')

としては (N2, As a, For a, As for): にしては and としては both relate to judgment, but にしては highlights a state or result that departs from what one might expect, e.g. 子どもにしてはおとなしい ('He's quiet for a child'), while としては simply shows perspective, e.g. 親としては反対だ ('As a parent, I'm against it').

割に (N3, Although, Despite, Rather...for, Unexpectedly, Comparatively, Considering): 割に and にしては both express something contrary to expectations, but 割に suggests mild contrast with what was assumed, e.g. 高いわりに美味しくなかった ('For how expensive it is, it wasn't tasty'), while にしては more clearly emphasizes how something defies expectations for its role or class, e.g. 初心者にしてはうますぎる ('He's too good for a beginner').

summary: A phrase that expresses that even if you go off the assumption that (A), (B) is still true.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にしても
text: In the same way that にしては highlights a point to be considered about (A), or simply 'while (A)', the replacement of は with the adverbial particle も will put further emphasis on (B) being a surprising or unexpected thing that accompanies (A). This continues to reflect the case marking particle に's use as a location.

にしても may be translated as 'even considering (A), (B)', or 'even while (A), (B)', and may be used with any word in its plain form. にして by itself is often considered as a stand-alone adverbial particle, despite stemming from several parts.

にしても is very regularly used with Japanese's equivalent of WH-words, like どこ, どの, だれ, なに, etc. In these cases, it highlights that 'even considering (A) is undetermined (in location, number, amount, etc), (B)'.

text: どんなに〜ても (N3, No matter how): Both どんなに〜ても and にしても introduce conditions contrary to results, but with different focuses. どんなに〜ても emphasizes an unchanging outcome despite extreme conditions, e.g. どんなに高くても買います ('I'll buy it no matter how expensive it is'), while にしても is used more flexibly to acknowledge a point while suggesting a contrast or reservation, e.g. 行くにしても、今日は無理だ ('Even if I go, today's not possible').

にしろ～にしろ (N2, Whether… or): にしても and にしろ～にしろ are similar in that both express 'whether', but にしても tends to focus on a single case and convey contrast or concession, e.g. 遅れるにしても連絡はしてほしい ('Even if you're late, I want you to contact me'). にしろ～にしろ pairs two options and stresses that the result remains the same, e.g. 勝つにしろ負けるにしろ ('Whether we win or lose').

たって (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter how): にしても and たって are related in that たって is a more casual form of ても, meaning 'even if'. にしても could be rephrased as にしたって, which sounds more informal and emotional. For example, どこに行くにしても ('No matter where you go') can also be expressed as どこ行くにしたって.

何しろ (N2, No wonder, After all, In fact, Because, At any rate): 何しろ and にしても are similar in that both have a general sense of 'no matter' or 'regardless', they are used quite differently. 何しろ comes at the beginning of a sentence to express 'after all, (A)', while にしても follows a noun or phrase to specifically state 'even if (A), still (B)'.

かどうか (N4, Whether or not, If...or not): かどうか expresses binary uncertainty, like 'whether or not', as in 行くかどうか分からない ('I don't know whether or not they'll go.'). にしても adds a tone of concession or contrast, like 'even if'. For example, どこに行くにしても 'no matter where (you) go'. The former asks a yes/no-type question, the latter implies acceptance of a situation.

～と言っても (N3, Although ~ might say that ~): Both ～と言っても and にしても can be translated as 'even though' or 'even if', but they differ in nuance. ～と言っても is used to downplay or soften expectations, e.g. 運動と言ってもウォーキング程度です ('Even though I say exercise, it's just walking'), while にしても has the nuance of 'even considering (A), (B)' or 'no matter if (A), (B)', e.g. 忙しいにしても連絡してほしい ('Even if they're busy, I'd at least like to be contacted').

としても (N2, Even if (we assume), Assuming, Also as): にしても and としても both mean 'even if', but にしても can introduce a judgment that doesn't directly follow from the condition, e.g. 行くにしても不安だ ('Even if I go, I'm uneasy'). としても implies that the result stems logically from the assumption, e.g. 行くとしても一度だけだ ('Even if I go, it'll be only once').

とも (N2, Even if, No matter): にしても and とも both express 'even if', but differ in formality and structure. にしても follows the plain, non-past form and is more common in daily language, e.g. どこに行くにしても ('No matter where you go'). とも follows the volitional form and is more formal and emphatic, often found in set expressions like 何があろうとも ('No matter what happens').

てでも (N2, Even if I have to, By any or all means, No matter what): にしても and てでも both express determination in hypothetical or extreme situations. にしても presents a condition with contrast or concession, e.g. 行くにしても気が進まない ('Even if I go, I don't feel like it'). てでも emphasizes doing something even if it requires an extreme measure, e.g. 会うためなら借金してでも行く ('I'd even go into debt just to see them').

ながらも (N3, But, Even while, Even though, Despite, Although): にしても and ながらも both express contrast. にしても introduces something counter to the condition, e.g. 難しいにしてもやってみたほうがいい ('Even if it's hard, you should try doing it'). ながらも shows two opposing facts that coexist, e.g. 忙しいながらも楽しんでいる ('I'm busy, but still enjoying it').

たとえ〜ても (N3, Even if…is the case, Supposing that): にしても and たとえ〜ても both mean 'even if', but にしても leans toward conditions that are reasonably likely, e.g. 難しいにしてもやってみたほうがいい ('Even if it's difficult, you should give it a try'). たとえ〜ても is far more hypothetical, e.g. たとえ失敗してもあきらめない ('Even if I fail, I won't give up').

にせよ・にしろ (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter, Whether… or): にしても and にせよ・にしろ both mean 'even if' or 'regardless of', but にせよ・にしろ are stronger and more formal, often used in instruction or insistence, e.g. 行くにせよ行かないにせよ連絡してほしい ('Whether you go or not, I want you to let me know'). にしても is softer and more reflective, e.g. どこに行くにしても携帯は持っていったほうがいい ('Regardless of where you go, you should bring your cell phone').

のに (N4, Despite, Although, Even though): Both にしても and のに express contrast, but with different nuances. のに is a general contrastive expression, like 'although.' にしても often presents a hypothetical or assumed condition, followed by an unexpected result. Like other ～ても forms, it's commonly used with Wh-words, e.g. どこに行くにしても 'no matter where you go'.

ても (N4, Even if, Even though): Both forms can mean 'even if' or 'even though,' but differ in nuance. ても is more versatile and often appears in expressions like てもいい 'it's okay to (A)' for asking or giving permission. にしても carries a stronger hypothetical tone, like 'Even supposing that...' which ても alone doesn't necessarily convey. Both are used with question words, e.g. どこに行っても and どこに行くにしても 'no matter where you go', with the latter sounding more hypothetical.

reading: と{言|い}うのは{事実|じじつ}だ
meaning: It is a fact that ~, There is no doubt that
summary: A structure highlighting that that which can be said is (A), is the truth.
formation: Phrase + (という) + のは事実（じじつ） + だ
Phrase + (という) + のは事実（じじつ） + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～というのは事実だ
text: ～というのは{事実|じじつ}だ is a phrase used to strongly express that (A) is something that is 'true', 'a fact', or has 'no doubt'.
というのは may be used after almost any phrase, before the noun {事実|じじつ} 'truth', paired with the auxiliary verb だ (or です) will determine that phrase to be a fact.

The literal translation というのは{事実|じじつ}だ is 'that which is (A) is true', as (A) is just a nominalized phrase. It is also quite common to see this expression with という omitted, the only difference being that it sounds slightly weaker.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 何といっても (N2, By any account, All the same, No doubt): Both phrases assert something strongly, but from different angles. ～というのは事実だ affirms something as a literal fact, e.g. 負けたというのは事実だ ('It's a fact that we lost'). 何といっても expresses what the speaker feels is most important, e.g. 何といっても家族が大事だ ('No matter what you say, family is important').

もさることながら (N1, It is a fact that, But, Even more than, It goes without saying, Not only but also,): Both emphasize a truth, but differ in nuance and tone. ～というのは事実だ explicitly affirms something as a fact, e.g. 彼がやったというのは事実だ ('It's a fact that he did it'). もさることながら highlights one point while further stressing another, e.g. 見た目もさることながら味も最高だ ('Not only the appearance, but the taste is excellent'). Both are formal, but the former is more clinical, while the latter sounds more literary or poetic.

に違いない (N3, There is no doubt that, I'm sure): Both ～というのは事実だ and に違いない make confident statements, but differ in implied certainty. ～というのは事実だ affirms something as a fact, e.g. 負けたというのは事実だ ('It's a fact that we lost'). に違いない expresses strong conviction, but not absolute certainty, e.g. 彼は疲れているに違いない ('He must be tired').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About から言うと
text: からいうと (appearing with or without kanji) is a phrase in Japanese that is used to express a particular viewpoint or standpoint from which some type of evaluation, conclusion, or opinion can be drawn. The と that appears here is one of the assumption uses of this particle, meaning that から{言|い}えば may also be used.

からいうと will always follow a noun (or noun phrase), before the (B) part of that same sentence will describe some kind of evaluation/opinion/etc. This structure closely reflects phrases like 'speaking in terms of (A), (B)', or 'what can be drawn from (A) is that (B)'.
Occasionally, the use of particles such as と or ば may be skipped entirely, with から{言|い}って being used instead.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The preceding noun cannot identify a person. However, Personの立場 + からいうと/からいって/からいえば are allowed.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からすると・からすれば (N2, Judging from, Considering): から言うと and からすると・からすれば are similar in that both introduce perspective. から言うと explicitly means 'speaking from (A)', offering a basis for opinion, e.g. 経験から言うと簡単ではない ('Speaking from experience, it's not easy'). からすると・からすれば has a broader 'based on (A)' meaning, often implying inference, e.g. 態度からすると反省していない ('Judging from his attitude, he isn't sorry').

上 (N2, From the standpoint of): から言うと and 上 both indicate viewpoint, but から言うと introduces a subjective opinion from a specific angle, e.g. 学生の立場から言うと反対だ ('Speaking from a student's viewpoint, I'm against it'). 上 expresses evaluation based on a defined category, e.g. 法律上問題はない ('There's no problem in terms of the law').

にしたら (N2, From the point of view of): から言うと and にしたら both express perspective, but differ in nuance. から言うと gives an opinion or evaluation from a stated viewpoint, e.g. 医者から言うとこれは異常だ ('From a doctor's perspective, this is abnormal'). にしたら puts the speaker in someone else's position to make a subjective judgment, e.g. 子供にしたら怖かっただろう ('It must have been scary from the child's perspective').

ことから (N3, From the fact that): ことから and から言うと both express basis or reasoning, but differ in tone and usage. ことから is generally used for factual inference or deduction, e.g. 電気が付いていないことから、誰もいないと分かった ('Judging from the fact the lights are off, I could tell no one is there'). から言うと provides a basis for a stated opinion, e.g. 経験から言うと注意が必要だ ('Speaking from experience, caution is required').

から見ると (N2, From the point of view of, By the look of): から言うと and から見ると both express viewpoint, but differ in nuance. から言うと emphasizes interpretation or judgment from language or opinion, e.g. 経験から言うとそれは無理だ ('Speaking from experience, that's impossible'). から見ると highlights observation or appearance, e.g. 外国人から見ると奇妙に見える ('From a foreigner's perspective, it appears strange').

で言うと (N3, In, Of, According to): で言うと and から言うと both present a frame of reference, but differ in nuance. で言うと highlights category or classification, often for comparison, e.g. 車で言うとポルシェみたいなものだ ('If we speak in terms of cars, it's like a Porsche'). から言うと gives a basis for a stated opinion, e.g. 私の経験から言うと、もうどうしようもない ('Speaking from my experience, there's nothing to be done').

meaning: To, For, Concerning
summary: A phrase that often gives someone's opinion, or their take on (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に取って
text: にとって (or に{取|と}って when appearing as kanji) is a structure in Japanese that is used to convey opinions, or just generally to discuss something from a particular perspective. This expression regularly appears after names/pronouns, but may also be used with regular nouns. にとって is often translated as 'to (A)', 'for (A)', or 'concerning (A)'. However, it is used in almost exactly the same way as から{見|み}て 'from the perspective of (A)'.
To use にとって, simply attach it to the end of a noun (or noun phrase) that you would like to express a certain viewpoint, judgment, or opinion from.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: において・における (N3, In, On, At, Regarding, In terms of): に取って (usually written in kana as にとって) expresses viewpoint or concern, e.g. 私にとって大切な人だ ('She's an important person to me'). において・における is a formal equivalent of で, conveying setting, context, or means, e.g. 歴史において重要な出来事だ ('It's an important event in history'). Unlike にとって, the latter can directly modify nouns in the における form, e.g. 教育における問題 ('Problems in education').

にかけては (N2, When it comes to, Regarding, Concerning): に取って (usually written in kana as にとって) shows viewpoint or relevance, often translated as 'to/for (A)' or 'as far as (A) is concerned', e.g. 子供にとって有害だ ('It's harmful to children'). にかけては highlights someone's strength or skill, e.g. 歌にかけては彼が一番うまい ('When it comes to singing, he's the best').

には (N2, In order to, In regard to, For): に取って (usually written in kana as にとって) indicates a perspective or viewpoint, e.g. 私にとって大切なことだ ('It's something important to me'). には can be used this way too, e.g. 私には分からない ('It's not understandable to me'), but also has broader uses like indicating purpose, target, or scope, e.g. 成功には努力が必要だ ('To succeed, effort is necessary').

にしては (N3, (Even) considering, (Even) for): に取って (often written in kana as にとって) and にしては both involve perspective, but にとって expresses personal relevance, e.g. 子供にとっては大問題だ ('It's a big issue for a child'), while にしては shows that a certain quality or characteristic defies expectations, e.g. 子供にしてはおとなしい ('He's quiet for a child').

について (N3, Concerning, About, Regarding): These two phrases appear similar but are used quite differently. について means 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)' and indicates the topic of a speech, discussion, etc., e.g. ゲームについて話す ('Speak about games'), while に取って (often written in hiragana as にとって) means 'to/for (A)' or 'as far as (A) is concerned' and is typically used to express perspective or point of view, e.g. 私にとって大切な人 ('An important person to me').

にしてみれば (N1, For (A), In the case of (A), From (A)'s point of view, In the eyes of (A)): にしてみれば and にとって are similar in that both express that something is true from the perspective of a certain person or group. にしてみれば is more hypothetical, e.g. 初心者にしてみればなかなか難しい implies that one might expect something to be simple, but it's difficult from the perspective of a beginner. にとって is a more neutral 'to’ or 'from the perspective of', e.g. 私にとって宝物だ ('To me, it's a prized possession.').

にしたら (N2, From the point of view of): に取って (usually written in kana as にとって) indicates a perspective or viewpoint, e.g. 社会にとって必要な制度だ ('It's a necessary system for society'). にしたら also means 'for (A)', but often implies a more subjective or emotional stance, e.g. 親にしたら心配だろう ('For a parent, it must be worrying').

としては (N2, As a, For a, As for): に取って (usually written in kana as にとって) marks relevance or effect from a certain standpoint, e.g. 学生にとって分かりにくい説明だ ('It's a hard-to-understand explanation for students'). としては expresses viewpoint based on role or identity, e.g. 留学生としては反対だ ('As an exchange student, I disagree').

ばあいは (N4, In the event of, In the case of): ばあいは (often written in kanji as 場合は) and に取って (often written in kana as にとって) can overlap in some cases, but not all. For example, 私の場合は and 私にとって can both mean 'as far as I'm concerned' or 'in my case'. However, since にとって simply means 'concerning', it can't replace ばあいは for the meaning of 'in the event that', e.g. 行く場合は気をつけたほうがいい ('In the event that you go, you should be careful.').

meaning: From the fact that
summary: A phrase that expresses the thing which is (A) as a fact, and then explains further from that.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことから
text: In order to come to a logical conclusion about something in Japanese, sometimes strong expressions like ことから will be used. This is a combination of the noun こと, and the case marking particle から. ことから literally means 'from that which is (A), (B)', but is generally simply translated as 'from the fact that (A), (B)'.
ことから may be connected to the end of any phrase, so long as the word before it is in its attributive form.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からして (N2, Even..., Judging from, Based on): ことから and からして both express reasoning, but in different ways. ことから means 'from the fact that (A)' and is used to explain a cause or basis, e.g. 声がふるえていることから緊張していると分かる ('From the fact their voice is trembling, I know they're nervous'). からして highlights a telling detail as evidence, e.g. 見た目からして運動していそう ('Judging from her appearance, it looks like she exercises').

から言うと (N3, Speaking in terms of, From the point of view of): ことから and から言うと both express basis or reasoning, but differ in tone and usage. ことから is generally used for factual inference or deduction, e.g. 電気が付いていないことから、誰もいないと分かった ('Judging from the fact the lights are off, I could tell no one is there'). から言うと provides a basis for a stated opinion, e.g. 経験から言うと注意が必要だ ('Speaking from experience, caution is required').

からすると・からすれば (N2, Judging from, Considering): ことから and からすると・からすれば both describe drawing conclusions, but differ in tone and focus. ことから shows cause and effect based on a fact, e.g. 足音がしたことから誰かがいると分かる ('From the fact we heard footsteps, we know someone is there'). からすると・からすれば show judgment from a certain viewpoint, e.g. 足音からすると一人の女性だったみたい ('Judging from the footsteps, it seems like it was one woman').

ことだから (N2, It is exactly because): ことから and ことだから both express reasons, but differ in usage. ことから explains a fact-based conclusion, e.g. 顔が赤いことから熱があると分かった ('From the fact their face is red, I knew they had a fever'). ことだから gives a reason based on someone's known traits, e.g. 田中さんのことだから、もう宿題は終わっているだろう ('Since we're talking about Tanaka, he's probably finished his assignment already').

点 (N3, Aspect, Respect, Point, Way, In terms of, In that, From the point of view): ことから is used to draw a logical conclusion from a fact or observation, e.g. 顔色が悪いことから風邪を引いていると分かった 'From the fact that his face was pale, I could tell he had caught a cold.' 点 comments on a specific point without implying a conclusion, e.g. 安さという点でこのスマホのほうがいい 'This smartphone is better from the perspective of low price.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About というより
text: When combining the quotation use of the case marking particle と with the う - Verb {言|い}う 'to say', and the case marking particle より 'comparing', というより presents a phrase that is being compared through further evaluation/reconsideration. This may be thought of as similar to 'rather than saying (A), (B)' in English.
というより
may be used after any type of word. However, due to phrase that comes before it 'determining' something that will then be compared, nouns and
な-Adjectives
will require
だ
(despite being omitted in casual speech).
だ
may also be omitted if the sentence finishes with a
だ
that is describing the same thing in a different light.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: より (N4, More than, Over): より expresses a general comparison, like 'more than (A)' or '~er,' e.g. 月曜日より水曜日がいい ('Wednesday is better than Monday.') or 走るより野球をするのが好き ('I prefer playing baseball to running.'). In contrast, というより specifically means 'more/rather than saying (A)' and is used primarily when rephrasing or clarifying something.

といおうか (N1, How to put it, How shall I put it, How should I put it, Or perhaps, Or maybe, Call it … or): Both といおうか and というより are used to adjust or refine what the speaker is saying, but they differ in how that adjustment works. といおうか is used when the speaker hesitates and offers an alternative way of describing something, often softening the statement or showing uncertainty, as in 優しいというか、少し甘い人だ (‘He’s kind, or rather, maybe a bit naive.’). In contrast, というより is used to correct or replace the first expression with a more accurate one, clearly shifting to what the speaker considers the better description, as in 忙しいというより疲れている (‘Rather than saying I'm busy, I’m tired.’).

むしろ (N3, Rather, Instead, Over): むしろ and というより can both be used when clarifying or rewording something, but function differently. というより attaches to a word or phrase to suggest a more appropriate expression, while むしろ introduces the clarified or preferred wording. Because of this, they often pair together, e.g. 可愛いというより、むしろ美しい ('Rather than cute, she's beautiful').

meaning: Not only but also, Let alone, Not to mention, Of course

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About はもちろん
text: はもちろん, or occasionally は{勿論|もちろん}, is a phrase in Japanese that presents (A) as being something obvious, while (B) should still be considered/mentioned. In this expression, the adverbial particle は presents (A) as being a stand-alone topic, before the adverb もちろん 'naturally' emphasizes that (A) is what it is. After this, the (B) part of the sentence will describe some other factor that is worth mentioning.

はもちろん will be used directly after noun (A), before the sentence will go on to discuss noun (B). This construction can be translated as 'not only (A), but (B)', 'not to mention (A), (B)', and other similar English expressions.
In many cases, despite (A) being the obvious factor, (B) is being highlighted as sharing similar qualities to (A). This means that in はもちろん sentences, も will almost always be seen after (B).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: While quite similar in meaning to だけでなく, はもちろん is quite a bit more formal. Due to this, it may sound quite stiff in friendly conversation, unless particularly emphasizing something.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だけでなく (N4, Not only… but also): だけでなく and はもちろん both express non-exclusivity, but differ in nuance and emphasis. だけでなく simply means 'not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 英語だけでなく、日本語も話せる ('He can speak not only English, but also Japanese.'). In contrast, はもちろん implies the first thing is obvious, while the second is more notable, e.g. 英語はもちろん、日本語も話せる ('He can speak English of course, but also Japanese.').

ばかりでなく (N3, Not only…but also, As well as): はもちろん highlights an obvious example together with a more unexpected addition, e.g. 子供はもちろん大人も楽しめる ('Not only kids, but adults too can enjoy it'). ばかりでなく is more neutral, simply listing two things, e.g. 雨ばかりでなく雪も降った ('It not only rained, but also snowed').

はもとより (N2, Not only... but also, Let alone, Of course): はもちろん and はもとより both mean 'not only... but also'. はもちろん adds the nuance of 'of course (A), and also (B)', e.g. 学校はもちろん家でも勉強する ('He studies at home, not just at school'). はもとより is more formal and emphasizes that (A) goes without saying, e.g. 親はもとより先生も反対した ('Not only his parents but also his teacher opposed it').

に加えて (N2, Not only...but also, In addition, Not to mention): はもちろん emphasizes the obviousness of the first item before adding another, e.g. 英語はもちろん中国語も話せる ('He speaks not only English but also Chinese'). に加えて simply adds one thing to another without that emphasis, e.g. 雨に加えて風も強い ('In addition to the rain, the wind is also strong').

をはじめ (N3, Not only...but also..., Starting with): はもちろん highlights an obvious example together with a more unexpected addition, e.g. 寿司はもちろん納豆も食べる ('He eats not only sushi, but also natto'). をはじめ is used to give a leading example from a larger group, e.g. 校長先生をはじめ多くの人が来た ('Many people came, starting with the principal').

に限らず (N2, Not just, Not only… but also): はもちろん emphasizes something obvious before adding another case, e.g. 日本人はもちろん留学生も来た ('Not only Japanese people but also exchange students came'). に限らず expands the scope of a statement, implying 'not limited to (A), also (B)', e.g. 子供に限らず大人も楽しめる ('Not only children, but also adults can enjoy it').

だけでなく(て)～も (N3, Not only ~ but ~ also, Not just ~ but ~ also): Both express 'not only (A), but also (B)', but the nuance differs. はもちろん stresses (A) as obvious, e.g. 寿司はもちろん納豆も食べる ('He eats not only sushi, but also natto'). だけでなく gives equal weight to both, e.g. 映画だけでなくドラマも好きだ ('I like not only movies, but also TV dramas').

meaning: Not only...but also..., Starting with
summary: A phrase that expresses logical or planned progressions that start from (A).
formation: Noun + をはじめとする + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About をはじめ
text: When presenting a topic in Japanese as a 'starting point', を{始|はじ}め will often be used to show any logic (or planned) progressions from that point. This is often translated as 'not only (A), but (B)', or 'starting with (A), (B)'.
To use を{始|はじ}め, one noun will be highlighted as the starting point, before another (or several others) will appear in part (B) of the sentence.

Due to sentences featuring をはじめ placing emphasis on (A) as a starting point, additional expressions such as として (or とする) will sometimes be paired with it. These structures function to further emphasize (A), and are similar to 'with (A) as the starting point, (B)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だけでなく (N4, Not only… but also): だけでなく and をはじめ both express non-exclusivity, but differ in nuance. だけでなく simply means 'not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 英語だけでなく、日本語も話せる ('He can speak not only English, but also Japanese.'). In contrast, をはじめ implies that something is the first in a list of many, e.g. 日本語をはじめ、様々な外国語が話せる ('He can speak many foreign languages, starting with Japanese.').

ばかりでなく (N3, Not only…but also, As well as): ばかりでなく and をはじめ both introduce additional items, but their focus differs. ばかりでなく is neutral and treats both elements as equal, e.g. 彼は英語ばかりでなく日本語も話せる ('He speaks not only English but also Japanese'). をはじめ highlights the first item as the most representative, e.g. 校長先生をはじめ、先生たちが全員参加した ('Starting with the principal, all the teachers joined').

に加えて (N2, Not only...but also, In addition, Not to mention): をはじめ introduces a prominent example from a group, e.g. 学生をはじめ多くの人が参加した ('Many people participated, starting with students'). に加えて simply adds another element to the first, e.g. 雨に加えて風も強い ('In addition to the rain, the wind is also strong').

はもちろん (N3, Not only but also, Let alone, Not to mention, Of course): はもちろん highlights an obvious example together with a more unexpected addition, e.g. 寿司はもちろん納豆も食べる ('He eats not only sushi, but also natto'). をはじめ is used to give a leading example from a larger group, e.g. 校長先生をはじめ多くの人が来た ('Many people came, starting with the principal').

を皮切りに (N1, Beginning of, Starting with): を皮切りに marks the beginning of a sequence of events, e.g. 東京公演を皮切りに全国ツアーが始まった ('With the Tokyo performance as the start, their national tour began'). をはじめ lists a representative example from a group, focusing on inclusion rather than sequence, e.g. 田中先生をはじめ、皆さんに感謝している ('Beginning with Prof. Tanaka, I'm grateful to everyone').

に限らず (N2, Not just, Not only… but also): をはじめ highlights one example among similar ones, e.g. 日本をはじめ多くの国で使われている ('It's used in many countries, starting with Japan'). に限らず expands the scope beyond the first item, e.g. 学生に限らず誰でも参加できる ('Not limited to students, anyone can participate').

だけでなく(て)～も (N3, Not only ~ but ~ also, Not just ~ but ~ also): をはじめ gives a representative example and implies that others follow, e.g. 東京をはじめ、全国でイベントが行われた ('The event was held across the country, starting with Tokyo'). だけでなく(て)～も lists multiple elements without suggesting one is more representative, e.g. 東京だけでなく大阪でも人気だ ('It's popular not only in Tokyo but also in Osaka').

meaning: For the first time, Not until, Only after, Only when, Only because
summary: An expression that highlights that not until after the first time of (A), did (B) happen.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About て初めて
text: て{初|はじ}めて is an expression in Japanese that highlights one verb as being the catalyst for some particular result/state. Verb て{初|はじ}めて literally means 'with (A) done, for the first time (B)'. Often, this translates similarly to 'only after I (A) did I (B)', or 'not until (A) did I (B)'.
In this structure, it should be noted that the (A) verb is not necessarily being done for the first time ever, just that this time resulted in the speaker's first experience of (B).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てから (N5, Once...is done, Once...happens, After doing): て初めて and てから both use the Verb + て form to show actions happening in sequence, but with different nuances. てから simply shows that one event happened after another, while て初めて emphasizes that the second action happened 'only after' or 'not until' meaning 'for the first time after' the previous event.

にして① (N1, At, Over, In, Only (after, when, or because)): These expressions are often found together because their meanings complement each other. にして suggests a significant occasion or example of something, while て初めて describes something happening for the first time 'only after' a certain event. Together, they can express an idea like 結婚10年目にして初めて二人で旅行した ('They vacationed together for the first time in their 10th year of marriage.').

てからでないと (N2, (Not) unless ~ cannot, (Not) until ~ cannot): Both imply 'only after (A) did (B) happen', but differ in nuance. て初めて is typically used in a positive sense, often conveying realization or discovery, e.g. 大人になって初めて分かった ('I first understood after becoming an adult'). In contrast, てからでないと focuses on the negative—the inability to do something until a condition is met, e.g. パスポートを取ってからでないと申し込めない ('You can't apply unless you get a passport first').

まず (N4, To start with, Firstly): まず means 'first' or 'to begin with' and is used to express something that happens or should happen before something else. In contrast, て初めて means 'not until (A) did (B) happen' or 'for the first time after (A), (B)', e.g. 大人になって初めて分かった ('I understood for the first time after becoming an adult.').

上で (N3, After, Upon): Both show one action leading to another, but with different focus. て初めて marks a first experience or realization, e.g. 大人になって初めて分かった ('I only understood after becoming an adult.') 上で shows a necessary step before the next action, e.g. 社長に相談した上で決めましょう ('Let's decide after consulting the president.')

meaning: Even
summary: A structure that shows that the very surprising (A) can even be included in a group.
formation: Verb + こと(1) + さえ + (する)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さえ
text: さえ is an adverbial particle in Japanese that is used to place emphasis on something existing in certain state. It is often translated as 'even'. さえ has three primary meanings, which are as follows:
Analogical Reasoning: {類推|るいすい} - Analogy, (A) is an outstanding example of something.
Limit: {限定|げんてい} - Limit, (A) is all that is needed for something.
Addition: {添加|てんか} - (A) compounds something that is pre-existing.

さえ is regularly paired with other particles and is often followed by verbs in negative form, with the overall meaning usually being determined by what part (B) of the sentence is conveying. Let's look at a few examples.
In each of these cases, we can see how さえ is showing that (A) is an extreme example of something.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: すら (N1, Even): すら and さえ are both somewhat formal intensifiers that can be used in similar ways. For example, 子どもですらできる and 子どもでさえできる are both emphatic ways to say 'even a child could do it'. Though they can overlap in some usages, one difference is that さえ can be used with ば conditionals in expressions such as これさえすれば 'as long as you do this', while すら is not used in this way.

割に (N3, Although, Despite, Rather...for, Unexpectedly, Comparatively, Considering): Both さえ and 割に convey, in some sense, a characteristic or event contrary to expectations. さえ is a strong 'even' that shows emphatic extremity or surprise, e.g. 子どもさえ分かる ('Even a child understands'). 割に expresses contrast with expectations, e.g. 年の割に元気だ ('He's energetic for his age').

まで (N4, Even, To even, To the extent of): Both さえ and まで mean 'even,' but with different nuances. さえ is often used with negatives to express 'not even X,' e.g. 食べることさえできなかった ('I couldn't even eat.'). まで is usually affirmative and highlights something surprising or extreme, e.g. 骨まで食べた ('He even ate the bones.').

さえ〜ば (N3, If only…then, As long as..., Provided..., Only thing ... needs for ... is ...): Both expressions use さえ, but their usages and nuances differ. さえ〜ば shows that one condition is sufficient, like 'as long as (A)', e.g. お金さえあれば何とかなる ('As long as I have money, things will work out'). さえ alone emphasizes extremity, surprise, or unexpectedness, e.g. 彼さえ知らない ('Even he doesn't know').

ても (N4, Even if, Even though): さえ and ても can both express the meaning of 'even' and sometimes overlap, especially with nouns. For example, 子どもでもできる and 子どもさえできる both mean 'Even a child can do it.'. However, they diverge when ても expresses permission, such as in 行ってもいい ('You can go.') or when さえ means 'if only', e.g. お金さえあれば 'as long as you have money'. In these cases, the two expressions are not interchangeable.

meaning: If only…then, As long as..., Provided..., Only thing ... needs for ... is ...
summary: A strong, hypothetical phrase that expresses (A) as being all that is required for (B).
formation: Verb［て］+ さえ + いれば

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さえ〜ば
text: As a set expression, さえ～ば is a combination of the adverbial particle さえ, and the conjunction particle ば. It is used to highlight assumption, and presents (A) as a extreme limitation that is required to achieve (B), hypothetically. This structure may be translated as 'if only (A), then (B)', 'the only thing needed for (B) is (A)', or 'as long as (A), (B)'.
さえ may be grouped with any word, but will require the conjunctive form, or て form before it when grouped with verbs. It also regularly appears after other particles, forming a dual-particle meaning.

This use of さえ is an example of limit, with (A) being a hypothetical limit presented by the ば particle. It is also possible to see さえ with other hypothetical indicators (such as たら), but is quite rare in modern Japanese, as さえ～ば is considered a set pattern.
This limitation is also sometimes referred to as a 'stipulation', or 'condition'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: たら can be used instead of ば form, but it is rarely the case.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: からには (N2, As long as, Since, Given): These expressions both connect a condition to a result, but in different ways. さえ〜ば emphasizes that the condition alone is enough, e.g. お金さえあれば大丈夫 ('As long as I have money, I'll be fine'). からには highlights an obligation or natural consequence once a condition is true, e.g. 仕事を引き受けたからには最後までやる ('Since I took on the task, I'll see it through').

限り (N2, As long as, While… is the case, Limited to): Both expressions can be translated as 'as long as (A)', but they differ in nuance. さえ〜ば indicates that a single condition is sufficient, e.g. 努力さえすればうまくいく ('As long as you try, things will go well'). 限り means 'as long as' in the sense of duration or ongoing state, e.g. 生きている限り夢を追いたい ('As long as I live, I want to chase my dream').

さえ (N3, Even): Both expressions use さえ, but their usages and nuances differ. さえ〜ば shows that one condition is sufficient, like 'as long as (A)', e.g. お金さえあれば何とかなる ('As long as I have money, things will work out'). さえ alone emphasizes extremity, surprise, or unexpectedness, e.g. 彼さえ知らない ('Even he doesn't know').

meaning: Used to
summary: A strong expression that says that which is (A) used to be a certain way in the past, often with a nuance of being nostalgic or reminiscing.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たものだ
text: As mentioned in the ものだ lesson, the combination of the noun {物|もの} 'thing', with the auxiliary verb だ forms a strong determination about whatever comes before it as being 'the way it is'. As an extension of this nuance, ものだ can be paired with verbs in the past tense, creating a phrase similar to 'I used to (A) in the past'. However, the literal meaning is closer to '(A) was the way it used to be'.

Due to ものだ being a strong determination of something's existence/truth, this expression quite often carries the nuance that the speaker is nostalgic about (A), reminiscing about (A), or being introspective about (A). This means that it will not sound natural when describing things that are seemingly inconsequential, or have no meaningful significance.
When highlighting things in the past that are not particularly important, たことがある will be used instead.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たことがある (N5, Have done before): Both expressions describe past experiences but with different nuances. たことがある states that something has happened before, as in 日本に行ったことがある ('I've been to Japan'). たものだ adds a nostalgic tone and refers to things done regularly in the past, as in 子どもの頃、よくこの公園で遊んだものだ ('I often played at this park when I was a child').

meaning: Well, Well then
summary: A short sentence starter typically used to change topic, or start talking about more important matters.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About さて
text: Acting as a conjunction, さて is a word used when one wants to change the topic of conversation, or is ready to move on to a new point. Usually it is translated as 'well', or 'well then'.
さて will appear at the beginning of a sentence, before the speaker highlights what the new topic is.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: では・それでは・じゃあ (N3, If so, Well (then), In that case): Both mark transitions, but with slightly different nuance. さて is used to shift to a new topic or proceed to the next step, e.g. さて、次の話題に入りましょう ('Now then, let's move on to the next topic.') では・それでは・じゃあ reference the previous context and often lead into a decision or conclusion, similar to 'well then' or 'in that case', e.g. それでは、始めましょう ('Well then, let's begin.')

さ - Interjection (N3, All right, There we go, Now, You see, Well (I don't know, let me see)): These are two similar-looking interjections with different uses. さて is a transitional phrase often used at the beginning of sentences to change the topic or move the conversation into a new phase, like 'well then' or 'now then'. In contrast, さ is a casual interjection that serves multiple functions, such as encouragement (e.g. 'all right!', 'come on!') or hesitation ('well, you see...').
