meaning: Rather, Instead, Over
summary: A phrase used to say rather than (A), (B), often with the nuance that (B) is preferable.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About むしろ
text: When a speaker is making a determination about something in Japanese, the adverb むしろ is often used to express a more accurate depiction of what has already been said. This is regularly translated as 'rather', or 'instead'.
むしろ will mostly appear at the beginning of new sentences, or the beginning of a second clause within a sentence, before information about (A) will be clarified.
As むしろ seeks to give a more accurate description about something, it will often be paired with grammar patterns such as より, to show where the comparison is being made.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それとも (N2, Or, Or else, Rather): Both むしろ and それとも involve choices, but in different ways. むしろ is used to clarify or emphasize a preferred option, e.g. ワインよりむしろビールが飲みたい ('I'd rather have beer than wine'). それとも offers neutral choices in questions, e.g. ワインにする？それともビール？ ('Will you have wine? Or beer?').

に反して (N2, Go against, Contrary to): むしろ and に反して both express contrast, but differ in usage. むしろ emphasizes preference or clarification, e.g. 雨でもむしろ外に出たい ('Even in the rain, I'd rather go out'). に反して highlights contradiction or opposition, e.g. 期待に反して失敗した ('He failed, contrary to expectations').

代わりに (N3, Instead of, In place of, In exchange for): Both expressions involve alternatives, but with different meanings. 代わりに indicates a direct substitution or exchange, often physical or role-based, e.g. 泳ぐ代わりに走った ('I ran instead of swimming'). むしろ introduces a more suitable or preferred option, e.g. 泳ぐよりむしろ走りたい ('I'd rather run than swim').

割に (N3, Although, Despite, Rather...for, Unexpectedly, Comparatively, Considering): むしろ and 割に both involve contrast, but from different perspectives. むしろ introduces a preferred or more accurate option, e.g. 寝るよりむしろ本を読みたい ('Rather than sleep, I'd rather read'). 割に shows discrepancy between expectation and reality, e.g. 安い割に美味しい ('It's good for how cheap it is').

というより (N3, ...is more of a... than a..., Rather than saying that...): むしろ and というより can both be used when clarifying or rewording something, but function differently. というより attaches to a word or phrase to suggest a more appropriate expression, while むしろ introduces the clarified or preferred wording. Because of this, they often pair together, e.g. 可愛いというより、むしろ美しい ('Rather than cute, she's beautiful').

逆に (N2, On the contrary): むしろ and 逆に both express contrast, but with different nuances. むしろ presents a preference or clarification, e.g. 話すよりむしろ相手の話を聞きたい ('I'd rather listen than talk'). 逆に highlights an outcome opposite to what was expected, e.g. 喜んでくれると思ったが逆に怒られた ('I thought they'd be happy, but they got mad instead').

却って (N3, All the more, On the contrary, Conversely): Both むしろ and 却って express contrast with expectation, but differ in nuance. むしろ introduces a preferred or clearer option, e.g. ワインよりむしろビールが飲みたい ('Rather than wine, I'd rather drink beer'). 却って highlights ironic reversal, e.g. 手伝ってあげたのに却って怒られた ('I helped, but they got angry instead').

meaning: In short, To sum up, In other words
summary: A phrase used for summarizing that packs information into something smaller.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About つまり
text: つまり (or {詰|つ}まり) is a word in Japanese that is often used as an adverb. It takes a previous statement (said either by the speaker or by someone else) and summarizes it. This translates as 'in short', 'in other words', and similar expressions in English.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ということは (N2, That means, That is to say): つまり and ということは both rephrase earlier information, but differ in usage. つまり restates or explains something just said, e.g. つまりできないってこと？ ('So you're saying you can't do it?'). ということは introduces a logical inference or consequence, e.g. ということは、試合は中止だね ('So that means the game is canceled').

即ち (N3, In other words, That is, Namely): Both つまり and 即ち mean 'in other words', but differ in tone and context. つまり is casual and used in conversation, e.g. つまりしょうがないってこと ('In other words, it can't be helped'). 即ち is formal and often used in academic or written contexts, e.g. 生きることは即ち戦いである ('To live is, in other words, a battle').

要するに (N2, To sum up, In summary, In short): つまり and 要するに both signal a rephrasing or summary, often translated as 'in other words' or 'to sum up'. つまり is more casual and common in conversation, e.g. つまり、行かないってこと？ ('So, you're not going?'). 要するに is more formal and often used in writing or speeches, e.g. 要するに無理だということです ('To sum up, it's impossible').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 即ち
text: In a similar way to つまり, {即|すなわ}ち is another grammar pattern in Japanese that is often translated as 'in other words'. It may also be translated as 'namely', or 'that is to say'. While {即|すなわ}ち is an adverb, it is often used as a conjunction, linking two sentences via some sort of reasoning.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つまり (N3, In short, To sum up, In other words): Both つまり and 即ち mean 'in other words', but differ in tone and context. つまり is casual and used in conversation, e.g. つまりしょうがないってこと ('In other words, it can't be helped'). 即ち is formal and often used in academic or written contexts, e.g. 生きることは即ち戦いである ('To live is, in other words, a battle').

ということは (N2, That means, That is to say): 即ち and ということは both rephrase information, but differ in tone and function. 即ち is formal and used to define or clarify precisely, often in writing, e.g. 日本の首都、即ち東京 ('The capital of Japan—namely, Tokyo'). ということは is conversational and introduces a conclusion, e.g. 明日は休み？ということは、今日は早く帰れるかもね ('Tomorrow's a holiday? So that means we might get to leave early today').

要するに (N2, To sum up, In summary, In short): 即ち and 要するに both help clarify or summarize a statement, but they differ in function. 即ち gives a formal restatement or definition, e.g. 日本の首都、即ち東京 'the capital of Japan, that is to say Tokyo'. 要するに summarizes the main point and can be used in speech or semi-formal writing, e.g. 要するに時間がない ('To sum it up, we have no time.').

meaning: All the more, On the contrary, Conversely
summary: A word used to express that rather than (A), (B). Can be seen as revoking or taking back the initial (A), due to (B) being more correct.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 却って
text: In order to revoke, or take a step back from a statement that has already been made, {却|かえ}って will often be used. {却|かえ}って can translate as 'rather', or 'all the more'. If a sentence consists of '(A) {却|かえ}って, (B)', what it means is 'putting aside (A), (B)'. {却|かえ}って is an adverb.

{却|かえ}って itself translates most closely to 'instead'. However, this is not the 'instead' used for phrases like '(B) was chosen over (A)', but the 'instead' used for phrases like '(A) couldn't be achieved, so (B)'. This shows that (A) is usually the intention or aim of the speaker, but (B) was the result instead.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 逆に (N2, On the contrary): 却って and 逆に both express something being counter to expectations, like the English 'on the contrary'. 却って is more formal, and occurs primarily in writing in the context of a full sentence or explanation. In contrast, 逆に is quite casual, and can be used in the same way as 却って, but also as an interjection at the beginning of a sentence or phrase, e.g. 逆にたかし君はどう思いますか？ ('On the contrary, what do you think, Takashi?').

ところが (N3, Even so, However, Even though, But): Both introduce unexpected outcomes, but differ in type of surprise. 却って means the result was the opposite of what was intended or expected, e.g. 謝ったら却って怒られた ('When I apologized, I was yelled at instead.') ところが highlights a surprising turn of events, though not necessarily the exact opposite, e.g. 田中さんに電話をかけた。ところがもう出発していた ('I called Tanaka. But he had already departed.')

むしろ (N3, Rather, Instead, Over): Both むしろ and 却って express contrast with expectation, but differ in nuance. むしろ introduces a preferred or clearer option, e.g. ワインよりむしろビールが飲みたい ('Rather than wine, I'd rather drink beer'). 却って highlights ironic reversal, e.g. 手伝ってあげたのに却って怒られた ('I helped, but they got angry instead').

に反して (N2, Go against, Contrary to): Both convey contradiction, but they differ in usage and nuance. 却って connects to the rest of the sentence to emphasize unexpected results, e.g. 慌てて出ようとしたら、却って遅くなった ('I tried to rush out, and I actually ended up running later.'). In contrast, に反して connects to a noun and highlights going against norms or expectations, e.g. 親の期待に反して、大学に進学しなかった ('Against his parents' expectations, he didn't go to college.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About まるで…ようだ
text: まるで～ようだ is an expression in Japanese that combines the adverb まるで (sometimes written as {丸|まる}で), and combines it with a description of (A) followed by the auxiliary verb よう (with or without either だ or です after it). {丸|まる}で can be translated as 'entirely', or 'completely', while the whole expression may be understood as 'it seems entirely as though (A)'.
まるで will be used at the beginning of a sentence, before the description of what (A) seems to be like.
Instead of ようだ, other expressions of conjecture may also be used, such as みたい.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: のように・のような (N4, Like (Noun), Similar to (Noun)): These are two closely related grammar points that both use 様 to make an explicit comparison. まるで～様だ is an emphatic expression that makes a statement that one thing is almost exactly comparable to something else (despite actually being different). In comparison, のように is used adverbially, likening a particular state or action to a similar one.

かのようだ (N2, As if, Just like): These are minor variations of the same basic expression meaning 'as if it were (A)'. まるで adds an emphatic nuance, implying it's 'just like' the thing it's being compared to, e.g. まるで夢のようだ 'It's just like a dream.' If the question particle か is present, it adds a nuance of uncertainty, highlighting that though it seems like that thing, the speaker doubts it is (or knows it is not) that thing, e.g. 日本にいるかのようだ 'It's like I'm in Japan (though I'm not).'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ような気がする
text: ような{気|き}がする is a phrase that takes the base meaning of {気|き}がする 'to have a feeling that (A)', or 'to give off a vibe that (A)', and adds an extra layer of uncertainty through use of the auxiliary verb よう. This can be understood as meaning 'to have a funny feeling that (A)', or 'to kinda have a feeling that (A)'.
As always, よう must be attached to the attributive form of any word that comes before it.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: {気|き}がする is quite a bit stronger than ような{気|き}がする, so the latter will often be used when the speaker is not 100% sure about something, and does not want to sound rude.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): ように・ような follows the plain form of a verb or adjective, and expresses similarity in a general sense. For example, 春が来たような日 'a day that is like as if spring had come'. ような気がする is a common idiom that uses this pattern, meaning 'have a feeling.' For example, 誰かが来たような気がする ('I have a feeling that someone came.').

気 (N2, Feel like ~, Spirit): Both ような気がする and 気 use 気 'spirit' expressions to convey subtle states or impressions, but with different nuance and usage. ような気がする follows a phrase to express a subjective hunch like 'Have a feeling that (A)', e.g. 来るような気がする 'I have a feeling they'll come.' 気 itself can be used after verbs mid-sentence or at the end of a sentence to express 'Feel like (doing) (A)', e.g. 行く気満々だよ 'I have a real mind to go!'

げ (N2, Seemingly, Giving appearance of, [Expresses emotions or feelings]): Both ような気がする and げ (from 気) use 気 expressions to convey subtle states or impressions, but with different nuance and usage. ような気がする follows a phrase to express a subjective hunch like 'Have a feeling that (A)', e.g. 来るような気がする 'I have a feeling they'll come.' げ attaches to emotion-related stems to describe appearance based on sensory perception, e.g. 悲しげな顔 'A face with a sorrowful air.'

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): ような気がする and そう both express impressions, but with different nuance. ような気がする conveys personal intuition or vague feeling, i.e. something you sense even without clear reason. On the other hand, そう is typically based on observable clues or appearance. In that sense, ような気がする is more subjective and less confident than そう.

ぎみ (N3, Looking, Feeling a little, Touch of, Tending to, Slightly): Both ような気がする and ぎみ (from 気味) use 気 expressions to convey subtle states or impressions, but with different nuance and usage. ような気がする follows a phrase to express a subjective hunch like 'Have a feeling that (A)', e.g. 来るような気がする 'I have a feeling they'll come.' ぎみ attaches to nouns to express a slight tendency or hint of something observable, often (but not always) negative, e.g. 疲れ気味だ 'I'm feeling a bit tired.'

meaning: Not ~ at all, Cannot ~ at all
summary: An expression meaning not at all (A), or (A) is impossible. Literally, in every way, not (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とても～ない
text: When seen in sentences containing verbs negated with the auxiliary verb ない, とても carries the nuance of 'not (A) at all', or 'cannot (A) at all'. とても is supposed to only be used when expressing 'impossibility', {不可能|ふかのう}. Due to this, it will primarily appear alongside the potential form of verbs.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Strong sense of impossibility

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): とても～ない is an emphatic negative used to show that something is far beyond one's ability. For example, とてもできない ('I can't do that at all.'). In contrast, すこしも～ない means 'not even a little bit (A)' and isn't limited to ability. For example, すこしも面白くない ('It's not interesting at all.'). Unlike すこしも, とても can be used without ない if the meaning is still negative, e.g. とても無理だ ('It's completely impossible.').

全く～ない (N3, Not~at all): 全く～ない and とても～ない both express strong negation, but differ in nuance. 全く～ない is used to completely deny or negate something, indicating total absence or lack. とても～ない, on the other hand, implies an extreme state or condition that makes something impossible, adding a nuance of implausibility or incapability.

ぜんぜん (N4, (Not) at all): Both ぜんぜん (with a negative form) and とても～ない can mean 'not at all', but differ slightly in nuance. とても～ない emphasizes impossibility, e.g. とてもできない and ぜんぜんできない both mean 'I absolutely can't do it.'. With adjectives like 美味しくない, where there is no sense of potential, 全然 is preferred, e.g. 全然美味しくない ('It's not tasty at all.').

meaning: Not really, Not particularly, It's not like...
summary: An expression that shows that (A) is not really the case, or not exclusively the case.
formation: 別（べつ）に + ［な］Adjective + ではない(1)
別（べつ）に + Noun + ではない(1)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 別に〜ない
text: When paired with ない (either the い-Adjective or the auxiliary verb), the adverb {別|べつ}に 'separately' changes slightly in definition to that of {特|とく}に 'especially'. Let's have a look at a few examples.

This 'especially' nuance of {別|べつ}に comes from 'separately' being negated. The literal meaning of {別|べつ}に～ない is something like '(A) cannot be separated/differentiated'. This comes across as 'maybe it is a little (A), maybe a lot (A), but in any case, it cannot be said that it IS (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): Both 別に〜ない and あまり〜ない are used to qualify negative statements, but differ in nuance. あまり〜ない expresses a lesser degree, e.g. あまり痛くない ('It doesn't hurt much.'). In contrast, 別に〜ない adds a tone of indifference or dismissal, e.g. 別に痛くない ('It's not like it hurts.', implying that there is no need to worry, etc.).

なかなか～ない (N3, Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from): Both negate expectations, but in different ways. 別に〜ない downplays something as not particularly important, e.g. 別に怒ってないよ ('I'm not especially mad.') なかなか〜ない indicates that something doesn't happen easily, e.g. なかなか怒らない人だね ('He's not someone who gets angry easily.')

meaning: Not only…but also, As well as
summary: A slightly formal way to express that something is not just (A), but also (B).
formation: ［な］Adjective + な + ばかりではなく(1)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ばかりでなく
text: ばかりでなく is a combination of the adverbial particle ばかり, with the conjugated (and negated) form of the auxiliary verb だ. It can be translated as 'not only (A), (B)', or 'not limited to (A), (B).
As ばかり is an adverbial particle, it may be paired with the attributive form of other words.

Like all other grammar points that negate だ, several forms may be seen. でなく, でなくて, ではなく, ではなくて, じゃなく, じゃなくて. However, it is important to remember that the addition of the は particle will place further emphasis on ない.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だけでなく (N4, Not only… but also): だけでなく and ばかりでなく convey the same essential meaning of 'not only'. Both expressions are often followed by another noun + も, which gives the added meaning of 'not only (A), but also (B)'. The main difference is that ばかりでなく is more formal and appears primarily in written or academic language. In everyday speech, the だけ version is more common, particularly in the variant form だけじゃなくて.

はもちろん (N3, Not only but also, Let alone, Not to mention, Of course): はもちろん highlights an obvious example together with a more unexpected addition, e.g. 子供はもちろん大人も楽しめる ('Not only kids, but adults too can enjoy it'). ばかりでなく is more neutral, simply listing two things, e.g. 雨ばかりでなく雪も降った ('It not only rained, but also snowed').

をはじめ (N3, Not only...but also..., Starting with): ばかりでなく and をはじめ both introduce additional items, but their focus differs. ばかりでなく is neutral and treats both elements as equal, e.g. 彼は英語ばかりでなく日本語も話せる ('He speaks not only English but also Japanese'). をはじめ highlights the first item as the most representative, e.g. 校長先生をはじめ、先生たちが全員参加した ('Starting with the principal, all the teachers joined').

に加えて (N2, Not only...but also, In addition, Not to mention): Both are formal patterns which add new information or elements, but they differ in nuance. ばかりでなく is a relatively straightforward 'Not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 日本語ばかりでなく、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' In contrast, に加えて has a more specific nuance of 'In addition to (A)', e.g. 日本語に加えて、文学も勉強することになった 'In addition to Japanese, I'll also study literature.'

のみならず (N2, Not only...but, Not just...but, What is more): ばかりでなく and のみならず are both expressions used to convey the meaning of 'Not only (A)'. While both are formal, のみならず is even more literary. Both patterns can also be followed by noun + も to express 'But also (B)'. For example, 日本語のみならず、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' vs. 日本語ばかりでなく、韓国語も話せる (Same meaning, but slightly less literary in tone).

に限らず (N2, Not just, Not only… but also): Both are fairly formal patterns which convey that something applies to more than one item, but they differ in nuance. ばかりでなく is a relatively straightforward 'Not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 日本語ばかりでなく、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' In contrast, に限らず has a more specific nuance of 'Not limited to (A)', e.g. 学生に限らず誰でも入場できます 'Not limited to students, anyone can enter.'

だけでなく(て)～も (N3, Not only ~ but ~ also, Not just ~ but ~ also): ばかりでなく and だけでなく(て)～も are nearly identical in meaning, both meaning 'Not only (A), but also (B)'. ばかりでなく is the more formal expression, while だけでなく (especially in the alternate form だけじゃなくて) is more common in everyday speech. For example, 日本語ばかりでなく、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' vs. 日本語だけじゃなくて、韓国語も話せる (Same meaning, but more casual in tone).

ばかり (N3, Just, Only, Nothing but): ばかり means 'only' or 'nothing but', emphasizing exclusivity, e.g. 甘いものばかり食べている ('He eats nothing but sweets.'). ばかりでなく means 'not only…but also', adding inclusivity, e.g. 甘いものばかりでなく野菜も食べなさい ('Don't eat only sweets, but vegetables too.').

はもとより (N2, Not only... but also, Let alone, Of course): Both formally express that something applies to more than one item, with different nuance. ばかりでなく is a neutral 'Not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 日本語ばかりでなく、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' はもとより is more literary in tone, and implies that the first item is obvious and the second more noteworthy, e.g. 親はもとより先生にも感謝しています 'I'm grateful not only to my parents, but also to my teachers.'

slug: ではなくて-じゃなくて
pattern: ではなくて・じゃなくて
meaning: Not A but B, Conjunctive
summary: A phrase used to express that in general, it is not (A), but actually (B).
formation: Verb + の + ではなく（て）(1)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ではなくて・じゃなくて
text: When the auxiliary verb だ is seen in its negative conjugated form, it states that (A) is not correct, but (B) is. This form is ではなく, and may appear either with or without the conjunction particle て attached to the end.
ではなくて is commonly seen grouped with nouns, or other words that have been nominalized through the use of の or こと.

In ではなくて, the adverbial particle は is not strictly required. However, as this expression is comparing what (A) is 'not' to what (B) 'is', the contrast that は provides means that the phrase will sound far more natural with its inclusion.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: なくて = casual・colloquial, なく = formal・written

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なくて (N4, Not ~ and, Not so, Because not (Examples)): ではなくて (formal) and じゃなくて (casual) are used with nouns and な-adjectives, while なくて is used with verbs and い-adjectives. Both connect negative forms to another idea and can express cause or reason. For example, 便利じゃなくて残念です ('It's unfortunate it's not convenient.') vs. 行けなくて残念です ('It's unfortunate I couldn't go.').

連用形 (N3, Formal Conjunctive): 連用形 is a more formal way to connect phrases or clauses, often used in writing. It shares the same basic meaning as the て form. In the case of ではなくて・じゃなくて, the 連用形 becomes ではなく・じゃなく, e.g. 病院ではなく、図書館です 'It's not a hospital, but a library.' (Same meaning, just more formal in tone.)

なくて (N4, To not ~ and ~, Not ~ and ~ (Conjugations)): ではなくて (formal) and じゃなくて (casual) are used to connect negative forms of nouns and な-adjectives, while なくて is used with verbs and い-adjectives. For example, 先生ではなくて、学生です ('He's not a teacher, but a student.') and 弟にはあげなくて、妹にあげた ('I didn't give it to my brother, but to my sister.').

meaning: Not only ~ but ~ also, Not just ~ but ~ also
summary: An expression which states that not only (A), but also (B), when emphasizing (B).
formation: Noun + だけ + でなく（て）(1) + Noun + も

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だけでなく(て)～も
text: As an extension of the standard だけでなく, meaning 'not only, but also', adding the adverbial particle も to the (B) part of a sentence will place extra emphasis on the thing that is being included in the same category as (A).
だけ itself is an adverbial particle, so will primarily follow nouns. After this, the negative conjunctive form of the auxiliary verb だ (でなく) will create the 'not only' meaning.
て is not strictly required as part of this structure, but will help to create a far more natural 'separation' between (A) and (B) when it is used.
Either じゃなく or じゃなくて may also be used, as is the case with all でなく and ではなく based grammar structures.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: なくて = casual・colloquial, なく = formal・written

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: だけでなく (N4, Not only… but also): だけでなく (or だけでなくて, だけじゃなくて, etc.) is a common expression that means 'not only'. It is often followed by another noun + も in the expression だけでなく(て)～も, which has the meaning of 'not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 肉だけでなく、魚も食べる ('I eat not only meat, but also fish.'). In other words, だけでなく(て)～も is an extension of the だけでなく pattern when you want to specify the additional thing or quality.

はもちろん (N3, Not only but also, Let alone, Not to mention, Of course): Both express 'not only (A), but also (B)', but the nuance differs. はもちろん stresses (A) as obvious, e.g. 寿司はもちろん納豆も食べる ('He eats not only sushi, but also natto'). だけでなく gives equal weight to both, e.g. 映画だけでなくドラマも好きだ ('I like not only movies, but also TV dramas').

をはじめ (N3, Not only...but also..., Starting with): をはじめ gives a representative example and implies that others follow, e.g. 東京をはじめ、全国でイベントが行われた ('The event was held across the country, starting with Tokyo'). だけでなく(て)～も lists multiple elements without suggesting one is more representative, e.g. 東京だけでなく大阪でも人気だ ('It's popular not only in Tokyo but also in Osaka').

ばかり (N3, Just, Only, Nothing but): ばかり emphasizes exclusivity, meaning 'only' or 'nothing but', e.g. 肉ばかり食べている ('He eats nothing but meat'). だけでなく～も expresses inclusion, meaning 'not only…but also', e.g. 肉だけでなく野菜も食べている ('He eats not only meat but also vegetables'). Compared to だけ, ばかり often carries a stronger nuance of excess or doing something too much.

ばかりでなく (N3, Not only…but also, As well as): ばかりでなく and だけでなく(て)～も are nearly identical in meaning, both meaning 'Not only (A), but also (B)'. ばかりでなく is the more formal expression, while だけでなく (especially in the alternate form だけじゃなくて) is more common in everyday speech. For example, 日本語ばかりでなく、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' vs. 日本語だけじゃなくて、韓国語も話せる (Same meaning, but more casual in tone).

はもとより (N2, Not only... but also, Let alone, Of course): Both express that something applies to more than one item, but differ in nuance and tone. だけでなく(て)～も is a neutral 'Not only (A), but also (B)', e.g. 日本語だけでなく、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' はもとより is more literary and formal, and suggests the first item is obvious, e.g. 親はもとより先生にも感謝しています 'I'm grateful not only to my parents, but also to my teachers.'

のみならず (N2, Not only...but, Not just...but, What is more): のみならず and だけでなく(て)～も are nearly identical in meaning, both meaning 'Not only (A), but also (B)'. のみならず is by far the more formal expression, while だけでなく (especially in the alternate form だけじゃなくて) is more common in everyday speech. For example, 日本語のみならず、韓国語も話せる 'He can speak not only Japanese, but also Korean.' vs. 日本語だけじゃなくて、韓国語も話せる (Same meaning, but far more casual).

sections.heading: About だけしか
text: だけしか is a combination of two adverbial particles, だけ 'only', and しか 'nothing but'. This structure primarily follows nouns, before part (B) of the sentence will have a corresponding ない based word.
Despite all of these possibilities, it should be noted that だけしか～ない is an expression that appears with negative verbs, far more than any of the other combinations.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しか～ない (N4, There's only, Nothing but): だけしか is essentially an emphatic version of しか～ない, combining だけ 'only' and しか～ない 'nothing but' to strongly emphasize that there is nothing else. For example, １００円だけしかない ('I only have / have nothing but 100 yen.) is a more emphatic version of 100円しかない (same meaning), and 日本語だけしか話せない ('I can only speak / can speak nothing but Japanese.') is a more emphatic version of 日本語しか話せない (same meaning).

きり (N3, Only, Just, Since): きり and だけしか both express limitation, but with different nuance. きり often implies that something has happened only once or hasn't changed since, e.g. 去年会ったきり一度も連絡が来ない 'I haven't heard from them even once since we met last year.' だけしか means 'Nothing but', typically in a way that emphasizes lack or even disappointment, e.g. 千円だけしか持っていない 'I only have 1000 yen.'

ばかり (N3, Just, Only, Nothing but): ばかり and だけしか are similar in that both can express limitation, but ばかり emphasizes the idea of excessiveness of a single thing, e.g. 漫画ばかり読む 'do nothing but read manga', while だけしか emphatically stresses insufficiency, e.g. 千円だけしかない ('I have only 1,000 yen.').

だけ (N5, Only, Just): だけ conveys the meaning of 'only' or 'just.' だけしか is a more emphatic expression, comparable to the English 'nothing but.' In addition to the increased emphasis, だけしか has more limited usage. While だけ can be used after nouns, verbs, and adjectives, だけしか is typically used only after nouns and is almost always followed by a negative verb (similar to the base しか～ない pattern).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About は言うまでもない ①
text: は{言|い}うまでもない is a structure that combines the adverbial particle は, the う - Verb {言|い}う, two (2) additional adverbial particles まで and も, and the い-Adjective ない. This is regularly translated as 'it goes without saying that (A)', or 'it is needless to say (A)', where (A) is whatever comes before は.
This expression may be preceded by almost any phrase, but is often emphasized even further by the inclusion of こと (or の), or ということ (or の).
Literally, this expression is a combination of the meanings of its individual parts.
は - Presents the topic.
{言|い}う - Presents that topic as something that can be said.
まで - Presents 'being said' as an extent.
も - Emphasizes the extent set by まで.
ない - Expresses that extent as not existing.Fun FactThis grammar pattern will often be followed by structures such as が, to add a 'but' nuance.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 言うまでもない ② (N3, It goes without saying, It is needless to say, Of course, Obviously): These are slight variations of the same expression meaning 'to go without saying'. は言うまでもない① follows a topic to say '(A) goes without saying'. 言うまでもない②, often seen in forms like 言うまでもないことだけど or 言うまでもなく, comes at the start of a phrase to mean 'Needless to say, (A)' or 'It goes without saying, but (A).'

meaning: Never, By no means
summary: A grammar point that strongly implies that something is decisively not the case.
formation: 決（けっ）して + ［な］Adjective + ではない(1)
決（けっ）して + Noun + ではない(1)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 決して〜ない
text: {決|けっ}して by itself is the て form of the verb {決|けっ}する 'to determine'. However {決|けっ}して is special in that it is considered to be a stand-alone adverb. As an adverb, it carries the meaning of 'decidedly', or 'assuredly', and is used in sentences that contain ない, in order to convey 'never (A)', 'under no circumstances (A)' or 'by no means (A)'.
Like many other adverbs in Japanese, {決|けっ}して can appear at the beginning of a sentence, or directly before the word it is modifying (which will be in its ない form).
While the translation is 'never', the literal meaning of {決|けっ}して is 'decidedly not (A)', or 'assuredly not (A)', simply emphasizing the negative point within a sentence.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ことはない (N3, There is no need to, Never happens): Both express negation, but differ in tone and nuance. ことはない suggests that something never happens, or literally that 'there are no cases of (A)', e.g. 忘れることはない ('There's no way I'll forget'), while 決して〜ない adds strong emphasis, meaning 'never' or 'by no means', and could even be used together with ことはない, e.g. 決して忘れることはない ('I will by no means forget').

すこしも～ない (N4, Not even a little, Not at all, Not in the least, Never): 決して〜ない and すこしも～ない are both emphatic negatives, but differ in nuance and formality. 決して〜ない is more formal and mainly used in writing, with the sense of 'by no means' or 'never'. For example, 決して危険ではない ('It is by no means dangerous.'). すこしも～ない is less formal and emphasizes absence of degree or amount, e.g., 少しも危険ではない ('It's not even a little bit dangerous.').

全く～ない (N3, Not~at all): While both 決して〜ない and 全く〜ない express negation, their nuances differ. 決して〜ない is a stronger, more emphatic expression meaning 'never' or 'by no means', and often carries an emotional or resolute tone. 全く〜ない translates as 'not at all' and conveys a more general or objective negation. The choice between them depends on context and the speaker's emotional stance.

meaning: Cannot afford to, No way, Impossible to do
summary: A strong expression that states (A) as being impossible, or unable to proceed if so.
formation: Verb + わけにはいかない
Verb + わけにはいきません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About わけにはいかない
text: わけにはいかない is a statement that combines わけ 'to be so', 'reason', or 'cause', with the case marking particle に, the adverbial particle は, and the 'cannot go' meaning of {行|い}かない. It can be translated as 'cannot afford to (A)', or 'impossible to (A)'. However, the literal meaning is much closer to 'it cannot be so that (A)'.
This structure will be used directly after the non-past form of verbs, in order to highlight them as being either highly undesirable, or highly unattainable.

Although わけにはいかない primarily highlights things that are undesirable, it may also highlight something that is desirable, but impossible for some reason. This will depend largely on the speaker's tone of voice, and context of the conversation.
In these types of sentences, the expression is quite similar to the 'I guess it's just not meant to be so' nuance that can be conveyed in English, highlighting regret.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ずにはいられない (N3, Cannot help doing something, Cannot resist doing something): These express internal conflict, but from opposite angles. わけにはいかない implies being unable to act due to duty or social constraint, e.g. 断るわけにはいかない 'I just can't refuse.' ずにはいられない expresses an inability to stop oneself from acting, e.g. 笑わずにはいられない 'I couldn't help but laugh.'

てはいられない (N2, Can't afford to, Unable to): Both express that an action can't be taken, but for different reasons. わけにはいかない implies restraint due to strong internal or societal reasons, e.g. 泣くわけにはいかない 'I can't very well cry.' てはいられない conveys urgency or pressure, suggesting that one can't allow a situation to continue, e.g. 怠けてはいられない 'I can't afford to slack off.'

ないわけにはいかない (N2, Can't not, No way to avoid): These are opposites in meaning. わけにはいかない expresses an inability to do something, often out of obligation or social pressure, e.g. 行きたくないけど、断るわけにはいかない 'I don't want to go, but I can't refuse.' ないわけにはいかない means the opposite: 'I have no choice but to (A),' e.g. 助けないわけにはいかない 'I can't not help them.'

ずにはすまない (N1, Won't get away without, Won't get off without, Have to, Have no choice but to, Can’t not): Both express that an action cannot be avoided for similar but slightly different reasons. ずにはすまない means ‘cannot avoid doing’ due to moral obligation, responsibility, or consequences, often implying inner pressure or remorse, as in 迷惑をかけた以上、謝らずにはすまない ('Since I caused trouble, I can’t avoid apologizing.'). わけにはいかない also means ‘cannot do,’ but focuses on social rules, common sense, or one’s position making the action inappropriate, rather than moral necessity, as in 今日は大事な会議があるから休むわけにはいかない ('I can’t take the day off because there is an important meeting.').

かねる (N2, Cannot, Be unable to, Hard to, Hesitant to): Both express inability to do something, but differ in tone and usage. わけにはいかない follows the non-past form of a verb and implies a moral or social reason for being unable to act, e.g. 約束を破るわけにはいかない 'I can't break my promise.' かねる attaches to the verb stem and is more formal, often used in business settings for polite refusals or hesitations, e.g. 私には分かりかねます 'I'm afraid I'm not sure.'

reading: う・よう + としない
meaning: Not willing to, Not make an effort to, To not attempt or try to, Volitional + としない
summary: A phrase that highlights that someone does not have the strong will to attempt (A), or will not make an effort.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 〜ようとしない
text: Like ～ようと思う 'I think that I shall do (A)', ～ようとしない is a combination of a verb that has been grouped with the auxiliary verb う (or よう), followed by the case marking particle と, and then another verb. In this case, する. ～ようとしない is often translated as 'shall not (A)', but with emphasis on a lack of effort, or willingness.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): ようにする (literally, 'do things in such a way as to X') can express the idea of taking care to perform a certain action and often describes intentions or habits. 〜ようとしない conveys the opposite, not making an effort to do something. For example, 毎日野菜を食べるようにしている ('I'm making a habit of eating vegetables every day.') vs. うちの子どもは野菜を食べようとしない ('My child doesn't even try to eat vegetables.').

Verb[volitional]とする (N3, Try to, Attempt to, To be about to): These two expressions are opposite uses of the same structure. Verb[volitional]とする means 'Try to do (A)' or 'Make an attempt at (A)', often with the nuance that the attempt may fail, e.g. 食べようとしたけど、無理だった 'I tried to eat it, but I couldn't.' In contrast, 〜ようとしない means 'Not even try to (A)', e.g. うちの息子は、野菜を食べようとしない 'My son doesn't even try to eat vegetables.'

Verb[よう] (N4, Let's, I shall (Casual volitional)): Both of these use Verb [よう], the volitional form. By itself, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat'.). Combined with としない, it means 'doesn't even try to,' e.g. 野菜を食べようとしない ('He/she doesn't even make an effort to eat vegetables.'). The key difference is between making a proposal vs. showing a lack of intent or effort.

meaning: Perhaps, Maybe, Possibly
summary: A strong way to further emphasize a hypothetical situation.
formation: もしかしたら(1) + Phrase +（かもしれない）
(1) もしかして、もしかすると

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About もしかしたら
text: もしかしたら and its alternatives are usually treated as stand alone {副詞|ふくし} (adverbs) in Japanese that are used to present hypothetical situations, and what could happen within those situations. These expressions are a combination of the adverb {若|も}し, the case marking particle か, and one of several combinations of する (したら, して, or すると). It is often translated as 'perhaps', 'maybe', or 'possibly'.

As with many other Japanese adverbs, it will often appear at the beginning of sentences. Due to もしかしたら presenting hypothetical situations, かもしれない will regularly appear in the same sentence (although it is not required).

As もしかしたら is a combination of もし 'if', か (presents a question), and したら 'so happens that', the literal translation is close to 'does it so happen that', or 'should it so happen that', with past or present tense being controlled more so by the following statement.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: かもしれない (N4, Might, Maybe, Probably): かもしれない and もしかしたら both express possibility, but differ in placement and nuance. かもしれない appears at the end of sentences or phrases and means 'might' or 'may', e.g. 行くかもしれない ('I might go.'). もしかしたら comes at the beginning to emphasize the uncertainty, e.g. もしかしたら行くかもしれない ('Perhaps I might go.').

おそらく (N2, Probably, Perhaps, (Most) likely, (I) fear that): Both express possibility, but differ in how likely something seems. おそらく suggests a high chance and is often used with だろう or でしょう, e.g. おそらく来るでしょう 'Most likely, he will come.' もしかしたら suggests a lower chance or speculation, and pairs with かもしれない or かもしれません, e.g. もしかしたら雨が降るかもしれない 'Perhaps it will rain.'

あるいは (N3, Or, Possibly, Maybe, Perhaps, Or possibly): あるいは and もしかしたら can overlap in one usage. あるいは is usually used mid-sentence to present alternatives, e.g. 月曜日あるいは火曜日 'Monday or Tuesday.' However, it can also appear at the start of a sentence to mean 'Perhaps,' e.g. あるいはそうかもしれない 'Perhaps that might be so.' もしかしたら can be used the same way, as in もしかしたらそうかもしれない, though あるいは carries a stronger nuance of weighing other possibilities.

meaning: Even if…is the case, Supposing that
summary: A phrase that presents that even if one supposed that (A) were true, (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たとえ〜ても
text: たとえ, coming from {仮令|たとえ}, an adverb meaning 'supposing that', is a word in Japanese that is often used with ても (or でも), in order to present possible circumstances, and their contradictory and/or (usually) undesirable outcomes. たとえ is primarily seen at the beginning of a sentence, before some kind of possibility, comparison, or supposition will be stated.

たとえ tends to be used to present situations where 'even if (A) were true, (B) still may/may not happen'. This is called a 'contrastive' example. もし on the other hand tends to be used for examples in which (A) will directly result in (B). This is called a 'resultative' example.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Sometimes seen as「たとい」

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): もし and たとえ are similar in that both can be used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize a hypothetical situation or condition. The primary difference is that while もし can be followed by a wide variety of conditionals, including なら, たら, ば, and ても, たとえ is almost always followed by a ても expression, giving it the meaning of 'even if (A)' or 'even supposing that (A)'.

ても (N4, Even if, Even though): たとえ～ても is a stronger and more limited version of ても used in hypothetical situations. For example, たとえどこに行っても 'no matter where you might go' is a more emphatic version of どこに行っても 'wherever you go'. However, in cases where ても expresses permission, e.g. てもいい 'you can (A)', たとえ would not be used, since the meaning is not strongly hypothetical.

とも (N2, Even if, No matter): Both express strong contrary hypotheticals, similar to 'Even if (A), still (B)'. たとえ〜ても is less formal and more common in speech, e.g. たとえ一人でも、ちゃんとやる 'Even if it's just me, I'll do it right.' とも is more literary and formal, and takes the volitional form, e.g. 死のうとも構わない 'Even if I die, I don't mind.'

たって (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter how): Both express contrastive conditionals. たとえ〜ても is neutral or formal, e.g. たとえ雨に降られても気にしない 'Even if I get rained on, I won't care.' たって is casual and conversational, often used with emotional insistence, e.g. そんなこと言ったってしょうがないよ 'Even if you say that, there's nothing we can do.'

としても (N2, Even if (we assume), Assuming, Also as): Both express hypothetical conditions, but with different implications. たとえ〜ても presents contrast, like 'Even if (A), still (B)', e.g. たとえ雨が降っても行きます 'Even if it rains, I'll go.' としても assumes (A) as a premise for argument or stance, e.g. 行くとしても一人では行かない 'Even if I go, I won't go alone.'

もしも～なら・もしも～でも (N3, If, Supposing): Both introduce hypothetical situations, but with different nuances. たとえ〜ても sets up contrast, like 'Even if (A), still (B)', e.g. たとえ負けても悔いはない 'Even if I lose, I'll have no regrets.' もしも～なら・～でも expresses a basic hypothetical and its result, e.g. もしも彼が来たら、話します 'If he comes, I'll talk to him.'

にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): にしても and たとえ〜ても both mean 'even if', but にしても leans toward conditions that are reasonably likely, e.g. 難しいにしてもやってみたほうがいい ('Even if it's difficult, you should give it a try'). たとえ〜ても is far more hypothetical, e.g. たとえ失敗してもあきらめない ('Even if I fail, I won't give up').

にせよ・にしろ (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter, Whether… or): Both show that something remains unchanged regardless of conditions. たとえ〜ても presents a contrasting hypothetical, e.g. たとえ雨に降られても気にしない 'Even if I get rained on, I won't care.' にせよ・にしろ is more concrete and neutral, often listing options, e.g. 行くにせよ行かないにせよ、連絡してほしい 'Whether you go or not, I want you to contact me.'

meaning: Extremely, Especially, To my ...
summary: A phrase that expresses the extremely or particularly high emotional response of (A), caused by something unexpected.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことに
text: When {事|こと} 'thing' is combined with the case-marking particle に following a statement, it highlights that something is of a 'great extent'. Common translations include 'particularly', 'especially', or 'to my (A)'. This grammar pattern almost always describes some kind of feeling or emotion.
ことに is regularly seen after verbs, い or な-Adjectives.
In most situations, '(A) ことに (B)' can be translated quite literally as 'to a particularly (A) extent, (B)'.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: ことに may sometimes be seen before descriptions rather than following them. In these cases, it comes from the kanji {殊|こと}, and is being used adverbially in the same way as {特|とく}に to mean 'particularly' or 'especially'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: ことに only carries this meaning with words that describe 'feelings'

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てしょうがない (N2, Extremely, Very, Really, It can't be helped): Both can express emotion, but ことに highlights the emotional tone of a situation, e.g. 嬉しいことに、試験に合格しました 'To my delight, I passed the test.' てしょうがない expresses a strong, almost uncontrollable personal feeling, e.g. 帰りたくてしょうがない 'I want to go home so badly I can't help it.'

そうにない (N2, Unlikely to, Showing no signs of): ことに emphasizes a strong emotional or subjective reaction to an event, while そうにない expresses objective improbability. For example, 驚いたことに、巨人が負けた 'To my surprise, the Giants lost.' expresses emotional impact, whereas 雨は降りそうにない 'It doesn't look like it will rain.' simply states an unemotional likelihood.

てならない (N2, Very, Extremely, Can't help but do): ことに and てならない both express emotional intensity, but differ in focus. ことに emphasizes the emotional tone of the situation itself, e.g. 悔しいことに、負けてしまった 'Regretfully, I lost.' てならない expresses a deeply felt, uncontrollable emotion, e.g. 心配でならない 'I can't help but worry.'

幸い・幸いなことに (N2, Luckily, Fortunately): 幸いなことに (sometimes shortened to just 幸い) means 'Fortunately', and is a fixed phrase, e.g. 幸い(なことに)、大事には至らなかった 'Fortunately, it didn't become serious.' It's a variation of ことに, which highlights emotional reactions. While 幸い expresses a positive outcome, ことに can also appear with other emotion words, like 驚いたことに 'To my surprise' or 悲しいことに 'Sadly'.

てたまらない (N2, Can't help but want to, Very, Extremely): Both ことに and てたまらない express emotion, but in different ways. ことに highlights the speaker's emotional response to a situation, usually following an adjective or verb, e.g. 悲しいことに、誰も来なかった 'Sadly, no one came.' てたまらない conveys an overwhelming personal feeling, often physical or emotional, e.g. 会いたくてたまらない 'I want to see you so badly I can't stand it.'

meaning: How…, What..., God knows...
summary: A phrase that expresses (A) as being a particularly large amount that shocks even the speaker.
formation: Noun + である + ことか

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ことか
text: ことか is a combination of こと 'thing', and the case marking particle か, used to present a question.

In sentences with ことか, words that highlight some particular number or extent are often used, before ことか comes at the end of the statement, expressing that 'extent' as being particularly unusual, or even unbelievable (thanks to the addition of か). This is often translated simply as 'how (A)', 'what (A)', or even 'god knows (A)'. Let's look at a few examples.

Literally, ことか can be translated as 'to what particular (A) is (B)!?', as the enquiry is often not directed at anyone specifically, but instead presents itself as a question simply to emphasize its magnitude.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: いくたび・いくど

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものか (N2, Definitely not, Absolutely not, Impossible, Do you really think~?): Both ことか and ものか express strong emotion, but differ in purpose and tone. ことか is a rhetorical exclamation used to convey deep feelings like admiration or regret, e.g. どんなに嬉しかったことか 'How happy I was!' ものか expresses emphatic denial or rejection, e.g. 行くものか 'As if I'd go!' ものか can also appear as the casual contraction もんか, while ことか is typically more formal or literary.

一体 (N3, (What) the heck?, (Who) in the world?, (Where) on earth?, (How many) f*ing...): 一体 and ことか both add emphasis to questions, but differ in nuance. 一体 strengthens genuine questions with a tone of surprise or frustration, like 'What in the world?', e.g. 一体何があったんですか？ 'What in the world happened?' ことか appears in rhetorical questions or exclamations to express strong emotion, e.g. 彼がどんなに努力したことか 'How hard he worked!'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～かというと ①
text: ～かというと is a phrase that has two primary functions. The first is used in conjunction with 'why' and 'how' words, like どうして or なぜ, while the other is used with 'who', 'when', 'where', and 'what'. We will focus on the former in this lesson. かというと is a combination of the case marking particle か in its use as a question marker, the case marking particleと in its citation use, the う - Verb {言|い}う 'to say', and the case marking particle と in its result use.
This is quite a few particles combined together, but the literal meaning is more simply 'if (A) were to be asked', before the speaker will go on to highlight their reasoning in (B).
As ～かというと will come before some sort of explanation, から will also regularly be used at the end of the sentence as 'because', emphasizing the speaker's reasoning.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: In casual speech, の can be changed to ん and と to って

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なぜなら〜から (N3, Because, The reason is, That is because): These phrases are related in that they can be used similarly, as なぜなら〜から could be rephrased as なぜかというと. They are different in that なぜなら〜から always states the reason for something previously said, like 'as for why that is, it's because (A)', while ～かというと① can be used to clarify what you are explaining, for example by saying なぜ嫌いかというと 'as for why I dislike it'.

～かというと ② (N3, If you ask me..., If I had to say, If I were to say, If I were to choose one, I'd rather): The pattern ～かというと has two main uses. ～かというと① introduces reasoning or a cause mid-sentence by echoing a question, e.g. なぜ行かなかったかというと 'If you're asking why I didn't go...' ～かというと② qualifies a personal opinion in response to an implied question, like 'If I were asked' or 'If I had to say,' e.g. どこに住みたいかというと、やっぱり大阪がいい 'If you're asking where I'd like to live, I have to go with Osaka.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～かというと ②
text: ～かというと is a phrase that has two primary functions. The first is used in conjunction with 'why' and 'how' words, while the other is used with 'who', 'when', 'where', 'which' or 'what'. We will focus on the latter in this lesson. かというと is a combination of the case marking particle か in its use as a question marker, the case marking particle と in its citation use, the う - Verb {言|い}う 'to say', and the case marking particle と in its result use.

This is quite a few particles combined together, but the literal meaning is more simply 'if (A) were to be asked', before the speaker will go on to highlight their reasoning in (B). {何|なん}で, {何|なに}, どちら, {誰|だれ}, どの, and similar words often appear as the 'who', 'where', or 'which' words in these sentences.
As ～かというと will come before some sort of explanation, から will also regularly be used at the end of the sentence as 'because', emphasizing the speaker's reasoning.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なぜなら〜から (N3, Because, The reason is, That is because): These phrases are related in that they can be used similarly, as なぜなら〜から could be rephrased as なぜかというと. They are different in that なぜなら〜から always explicitly states a reason for something, like 'as for why, it's because (A)', while ～かというと② can simply be used to comment on something, e.g. 好きか嫌いかというと 'if I were to say whether I like it or dislike it'.

～かというと ① (N3, Why? Well..., Why? Because..., If you ask me why..., The reason why is..., It is because...): The pattern ～かというと has two main uses. ～かというと① introduces reasoning or a cause mid-sentence by echoing a question, e.g. なぜ行かなかったかというと 'If you're asking why I didn't go...' ～かというと② qualifies a personal opinion in response to an implied question, like 'If I were asked' or 'If I had to say,' e.g. どこに住みたいかというと、やっぱり大阪がいい 'If you're asking where I'd like to live, I have to go with Osaka.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About で言うと
text: でいうと is an expression in Japanese that is commonly used to ask questions, or to give information about how one thing corresponds with another. It is a combination of the case marking particle で meaning 'with', and {言|い}うと meaning 'if said', or 'if we say'.
This structure will be seen after nouns, and can be translated as 'if said with (A), (B)'.
でいうと will often be seen in sentences with に{当|あ}たる 'to be equivalent to', another common grammar structure used for drawing connections between things.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Lit. “if you were to say... in (terms of)/as”

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: から言うと (N3, Speaking in terms of, From the point of view of): で言うと and から言うと both present a frame of reference, but differ in nuance. で言うと highlights category or classification, often for comparison, e.g. 車で言うとポルシェみたいなものだ ('If we speak in terms of cars, it's like a Porsche'). から言うと gives a basis for a stated opinion, e.g. 私の経験から言うと、もうどうしようもない ('Speaking from my experience, there's nothing to be done').

meaning: One at a time, Per, Each, Gradually
summary: A suffix which indicates each (A), with the nuance of (A) being an individual allotment of something.
formation: 2. 少（すこ）し(1) + ずつ (Little by little)
3. いくらか + ずつ (Some … every)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～ずつ
text: ずつ, or {宛|ずつ} in its kanji form, is a suffix in Japanese that is used to highlight things that occur/exist in specific amounts. It is often translated simply as 'each', 'per', or 'at a time'. Depending on the source, ずつ may also be considered to be an adverbial particle. However, this will not change the way that it is utilized.
ずつ is used directly after the number/amount of something that it is highlighting as being the 'at a time' grouping.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ごとに (N4, Each, Every): Both express regular repetition, but in different structures. ～ずつ attaches to quantity phrases to mean 'each' or 'little by little', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' ごとに follows nouns and means 'every (A)', often time-based, e.g. ３０分ごとに体を動かす 'I move my body every thirty minutes.'

おきに (N3, Repeated at intervals, Every other, Every, At intervals of): Both deal with repetition or intervals, but in different ways. ～ずつ means 'each' or 'at a time' and attaches to quantity expressions, e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' おきに follows time or distance intervals to mean 'every (A)', e.g. ５分おきに電車が来る 'Trains come every five minutes.'

それぞれ (N3, Each, Respectively): Both convey the meaning of 'each', but differ in structure. ～ずつ attaches to quantity expressions to mean 'each' or 'little by little', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' or ちょっとずつよくなってきた 'It's gotten better a little at a time.' それぞれ appears before a phrase or with の and emphasizes individuality, e.g. 人はそれぞれ個性がある 'People each have unique qualities.'

各 (N4, Each, Every, Respective, Various): Both mean 'each', but with different usage. ～ずつ follows quantity expressions to mean 'each' or 'at a time', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' or ちょっとずつよくなってきた 'It's gotten better a little at a time.' 各 appears before nouns and means 'every' or 'each', e.g. この電車は各駅にとまります 'This train stops at every station.'

当たり (N3, Per~, A~, Apiece, Each): Both express the idea of 'each', but with different nuance and usage. ～ずつ attaches to quantity expressions like numbers or 少し to mean 'each' or 'at a time', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' or ちょっとずつよくなってきた 'It's gotten better a little at a time.' 当たり also attaches to Number + Counter, but means 'per' or 'apiece', e.g. １個当たり５００円です 'They're 500 yen apiece.'

summary: A casual expression highlighting that (A) is far more than anything else, due to its degree continuing on and on, unwaveringly.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ずっと ②
text: In addition to the ずっと used to mean 'always', or 'non-stop', this adverb may also convey that one thing is 'by far (A)', or 'much more (A)' than something else. In these phrases, ずっと usually comes at the beginning of the sentence, before some form of comparison will be made between (A) and (B).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ずっと ① (N4, Continuously, All throughout, Entire time, Ever (since), The whole time, All the way): ずっと is an adverb with two main uses that are related but differ in nuance. ずっと① emphasizes a continuous action or state over time, for example, ずっと好きだった ('I always liked you/her/etc.'). In contrast, ずっと② is used in comparisons to show degree, for example, バスケより野球のほうがずっと好き ('I like baseball much more than basketball.').

meaning: Completely covered in, Full of
summary: A grammar point expressing that (A) is covered in (B), often lots of individual small things.
formation: Noun + だらけ + の + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About だらけ
text: だらけ is a suffix that is used in Japanese to express when one thing is 'covered in', or 'filled with' another thing.

だらけ will be attached to the end of nouns, before (sometimes) being followed by the case marking particle の and a second noun. The second noun is frequently omitted if the place or thing that is 'covered in' something is obvious.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しか～ない (N4, There's only, Nothing but): だらけ and しか～ない are used differently and express contrasting meanings. だらけ follows nouns and expresses the idea of 'covered with' or 'full of', e.g. 泥だらけ 'covered in mud'. In contrast, しか～ない is used with a noun and negative verb to mean 'only' or 'nothing but', e.g. １００円しかない ('I have only 100 yen.'). They are similar in that both can often carry a negative or undesirable nuance.

塗れ (N1, Stained, Covered in, Smeared, Dirty with, Soaked in): だらけ and 塗れ (often written in hiragana as まみれ) both describe being covered in something, but differ in nuance. だらけ suggests an overwhelming or chaotic abundance of unpleasant things, e.g. 傷だらけの手 'Hands full of cuts.' 塗れ emphasizes being soaked or stained, either physically or figuratively, e.g. 泥まみれの靴 'Mud-covered shoes' or 借金まみれの男 'A man drowning in debt.'

にほかならない (N2, Nothing but, None other than, Simply): Both express a strong characterization, but differ in tone and focus. だらけ implies a negative excess of something undesirable, e.g. ミスだらけのレポート 'A report full of mistakes.' にほかならない expresses emphatic certainty or identity, e.g. 犯罪にほかならない 'It is nothing less than a crime.'

ずくめ (N1, Completely, Entirely, All in, Nothing but, A real streak of, Without exception, Jet): Both indicate that something is filled with many similar elements, but the evaluation differs. だらけ means ‘full of’ with a negative or undesirable nuance, used when the items are unwanted or messy, as in ゴミだらけの部屋だ ('The room is full of trash.'). ずくめ means ‘nothing but’ with a positive or favorable nuance, used when the elements are all good or fortunate, as in いいことずくめの旅行だった ('It was a trip full of good things.').

meaning: Although, But, However, For all that, Provided that
summary: An expression that highlights the previous statement as being reasonably or plausibly true, but (B) is the whole truth.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About もっとも
text: もっとも, sometimes also seen as {尤|もっと}も, is a conjunction that is used to clarify when (A) is not the only important thing to be considered. This expression is usually translated as 'although'. However, 'for all that', or 'with that said' are also accurate translations, depending on the context. Let's look at a few examples.
Due to もっとも offering clarification about something, the (B) phrase will often end with が, けど, けれども, and other similar expressions.

When もっとも is used, the speaker is agreeing that (A) is true, but not the whole picture. As a noun itself, {尤|もっと}も can be described as {道理|どうり}に{適|かな}う, which means 'to stand to reason'. This nuance is kept, and may also be used as an accurate translation for もっとも as a conjunction.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それなのに (N2, And yet, Despite this): Both can begin a sentence to introduce contrast, but differ in tone and nuance. もっとも is more formal and adds a condition that qualifies the previous statement, e.g. 全員来ました。もっとも、田中さんは遅れましたが 'Everyone came. That said, Tanaka was late.' それなのに is more casual and expresses surprise at an unexpected outcome, e.g. 雨だった。それなのに、試合は行われた 'It rained. And yet, the match was held.'

しかしながら (N2, However, Nevertheless, But): Both もっとも and しかしながら are formal expressions that can begin a sentence to convey contrast, but differ in nuance. しかしながら is a literary and emphatic variant of しかし, e.g. 'しかしながら、例外があります' ('Nevertheless, there are exceptions'). もっとも adds a qualification to the previous statement, e.g. '全員来ました。もっとも、田中さんは遅れましたが' ('Everyone came. However, Tanaka was late').

meaning: Again, Once more, A second time
summary: A somewhat formal way to express that (A) will be done again, or for a second time.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 再び
text: {再|ふたた}び is an adverb that means 'to repeat'. It is regularly translated as 'again', 'once more', or 'a second time'. Usually, {再|ふたた}び will appear at the beginning of a sentence, before some sort of request or statement will be made about what needs to be repeated.

Despite meaning 'to repeat', {再|ふたた}び specifically has the nuance of repeating something 'for the second time'. Because of this, it will not be used to highlight things that need to be repeated over and over again.

CautionUnlike また, which is frequently used to express 'again', {再|ふたた}び is quite formal, and will be seen far more often in books/articles, than it will be spoken.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 更に (N2, Even more or further, Again, More and more): Both 再び and 更に can involve repetition or continuation, but they differ in meaning. 再び means 'again' or 'once more', and is used when something is done a second time after a pause, e.g. '再び会う' ('to meet again'). 更に means 'further' or 'more', and emphasizes intensification or accumulation, e.g. '更に深まる' ('to deepen further').

また (N4, Also, As well, Moreover, Again, Additionally): また and 再び both mean 'again', but differ in nuance and formality. また is common in speech and writing, used for repetition or to add information, like 'again' or 'additionally'. 再び is more formal and literary, often with a stronger sense of 'for the second time'.

meaning: ~ness, Used to indicate conditions or nature
summary: A suffix used to indicate the conditions or innate nature of an adjective, rather than the amount.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About み
text: み is a common suffix in Japanese that has the role of transforming adjectives into nouns. This is often translated as '(A)ness' in English, but has a few small differences.
To use み, attach it to the stem form of either い-Adjectives or な-Adjectives. The {語幹|ごかん} (stem form) being the form with い removed (for い-Adjectives), or な removed (for な-Adjectives).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: げ (N2, Seemingly, Giving appearance of, [Expresses emotions or feelings]): み and げ are adjective endings that serve different roles. み turns adjectives into abstract nouns that describe a quality, e.g. '深み' ('depth') or '苦しみ' ('suffering'). げ turns adjectives or verbs into な-adjectives with the nuance of seeming to possess an emotion, e.g. '嬉しげな顔' ('a happy-seeming face') or '意味ありげな表情' ('a seemingly meaningful expression').

さ (N4, Converting adjectives to nouns): さ and み both nominalize adjectives, similar to '~ness' in English, but differ in nuance and usage. さ works with both い and な-adjectives and expresses measurable degree, e.g. 高さ 'height' or 大変さ 'difficulty'. み is typically used with い-adjectives and focuses on quality or characteristics rather than degree, e.g. 面白み 'that which makes (something) interesting'.

meaning: About the same as, About as, No less
summary: A structure highlighting that something is approximately or about the same as (A).
formation: Noun + と同（おな）じ + くらい(1)
Noun + と同（おな）じ + くらい(1) + の + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と同じくらい
text: As a combination of the case marking particle と, the noun {同|おな}じ 'the same', and the adverbial particle くらい. と{同|おな}じくらい is an expression used to highlight that something is 'about the same as (A)'.

To use と{同|おな}じくらい, attach it to the end of a noun that you want to highlight as being the prime example, with whatever is comparable to it coming later in the sentence, or directly attached through the case marking particle の.
If you want to express that an action is being performed in 'almost the same way' as (A), に may replace の, after くらい.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 並み (N1, As, On par with, Worthy of): Both expressions are similar in that this refer to something being equivalent to something else. 並み in particular refers to measuring up to a certain standard, e.g. 彼の歌はプロ並みだ ('His singing is on par with a pro.'), while と同じくらい simply expresses an equivalence without implying a certain standard, e.g. 息子と同じぐらいの年 'around the same age as my son'.

reading: とおなじで・とちがって
meaning: Like, Similar to, Unlike, Dissimilar to
summary: One of two phrases which may express something being like or similar to (A), or unlike or differing from (A).
formation: Noun + と + 同（おな）じで
Noun + と + 違（ちが）って

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と同じで・と違って
text: Two regular expressions that are used in Japanese for conveying similarity, and dissimilarity are と{同|おな}じで 'the same as (A)', and と{違|ちが}って 'different to (A)'. While both of these structures use the case marking particle と to mark (A), {同|おな}じ is a noun, while {違|ちが}って is the て form of the う - Verb, {違|ちが}う. Due to this, the auxiliary verb だ is required after {同|おな}じ, in order to link (A) and (B). だ will appear in its conjunctive form.
Both と{同|おな}じで and と{違|ちが}って will be preceded by a noun or noun phrase, before the (B) part of the sentence will describe the similarity/dissimilarity.

In this structure, as the conjunction particle て, has a similar role to the conjunctive form of だ (で), both expressions are simply stating that (B) is existing in a state of 'having sameness', or 'having difference' with (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: みたいに・みたいな (N4, Like, Similar to, Resembling): みたいに・みたいな and と同じで both express comparison but differ in nuance. みたいに・みたいな suggests similarity or resemblance, e.g. ‘like’ or ‘seems like'. と同じで states something is explicitly the same, showing a stronger degree of similarity. Conversely, と違って means ‘unlike’ or ‘different from'.

meaning: In line with, Comparable with, Along with, Just like, As … as
summary: A formal expression showing that something is comparable to (A), due to being in line with it.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と並んで
text: Often, when the case marking particle と is used alongside the conjunction particle て containing form of the う - Verb {並|なら}ぶ 'to line up', the meaning of 'to be comparable with (A)', or 'to be in line with (A)' will be conveyed.
と{並|なら}んで will be preceded by nouns, or noun phrases.
Occasionally, the plain form of {並|なら}ぶ can be seen alongside ほど, to show that (B) is 'at the extent of being in line with (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: に沿って (N2, Along, In accordance with, In line with): While both と並んで and に沿って indicate some kind of coordination, their core meanings differ. と並んで highlights equivalence or joint status, e.g. 'ドラえもんと並んで人気のアニメ' ('an anime as popular as Doraemon'). に沿って means 'in line with' or 'according to', emphasizing adherence to a path, rule, or guideline, e.g. '規則に沿って行動する' ('act in accordance with the rules').

と共に (N3, Together with, At the same time, As well as): と並んで and と共に both suggest pairing, but with different focuses. と並んで stresses equal footing or value, e.g. '村上春樹と並んで人気の日本人作家' ('a Japanese author as popular as Haruki Murakami'). と共に emphasizes accompaniment or simultaneity, e.g. '友人と共に旅に出る' ('go on a trip with a friend') or '厳しいと共に優しい' ('kind as well as strict').

に伴って・に伴い (N2, As, Due, Along with, Hand-in-hand with, Resulted in, Be consequent upon): Both に伴って and と並んで connect two elements, but differ in meaning. に伴って expresses a causal or accompanying relationship where one thing changes in response to another, e.g. '経済の成長に伴って、生活水準も上がった' ('As the economy grew, the standard of living also rose'). と並んで indicates comparable qualities without implying cause, e.g. 'ドラえもんと並んで人気のアニメ' ('an anime as popular as Doraemon').

summary: An expression that highlights that there is no mistaking (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に違いない
text: When the case marking particle に is combined with the noun {違|ちが}い 'difference', and the い-Adjective ない, an expression similar to 'there is no doubt that (A)', or 'I'm sure that (A)' is created.
に{違|ちが}いない may be used with any verbs, い-Adjectives, な-Adjectives or nouns in their plain form.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It should be noted that {違|ちが}いない is a combination of a noun and an い-Adjective, and not the negative form of the う - Verb {違|ちが}う, which would be {違|ちが}わない. {違|ちが}いない translates as 'there is no difference', while {違|ちが}わない would translate as 'it is not different'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 確かに (N2, Surely, Certainly): 確かに and に違いない both signal confidence in a statement, but with different structures and emphasis. 確かに is an adverb used to affirm a fact, sometimes paired with a following contrast, as in 確かにそうだ (That’s certainly true). に違いない is a grammatical pattern attached to phrases to express logical certainty or strong inference, as in 彼は犯人に違いない (He must be the culprit).3

に決まっている (N2, Surely, Bound to, Certainly, Be decided): に違いない and に決まっている both express strong conviction, but differ in tone and basis of judgment. に違いない implies a strong conclusion drawn from evidence or context, e.g. '何かあったに違いない' ('Something must have happened'). に決まっている conveys more assertive confidence, often based on common sense or the obvious, e.g. '美味しいに決まっている' ('Of course it tastes good').

に相違ない (N2, Without a doubt, Certainly, Surely, Not mistaken): Both に相違ない and に違いない express a high degree of certainty, often translated as 'no doubt' or 'surely', but differ in tone and formality. に相違ない is more formal and used in writing or official contexts, e.g. '彼が犯人に相違ない' ('There is no doubt he is the culprit'). に違いない is more common in conversation and conveys strong personal conviction, e.g. 'あの人は日本人に違いない' ('That person must be Japanese').

～というのは事実だ (N3, It is a fact that ~, There is no doubt that): Both ～というのは事実だ and に違いない make confident statements, but differ in implied certainty. ～というのは事実だ affirms something as a fact, e.g. 負けたというのは事実だ ('It's a fact that we lost'). に違いない expresses strong conviction, but not absolute certainty, e.g. 彼は疲れているに違いない ('He must be tired').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 当たり
text: When attached to the end of numbers or counters, the noun {当|あ}たり 'to hit' will be used as a suffix. In these cases, the meaning is usually translated as 'per (A)', or 'each (A)'. Let's take a look at some examples.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: に当たる (N3, Correspond to, Amounts to, Equals to, Is appropriate): Both phrases derive from 当たる, but are used in very different ways. に当たる means 'corresponds to' and often functions as a more formal, indirect way of saying 'is', e.g. '父親に当たる人' ('a person who is [lit. corresponds to] their father'). 当たり is used after number + counter expressions to mean 'per' or 'apiece', e.g. '１個当たり１００円' ('100 yen apiece').

それぞれ (N3, Each, Respectively): 当たり and それぞれ can both convey a sense of 'each', but their nuances are different. 当たり attaches to numbers to mean 'each' in the sense of 'apiece', e.g. １個当たり１００円 ('100 yen each' / '100 yen apiece'). In contrast, それぞれ means 'each' in the sense of 'to each their own', e.g. 人はそれぞれ個性がある ('People each have unique traits').

～ずつ (N3, One at a time, Per, Each, Gradually): Both express the idea of 'each', but with different nuance and usage. ～ずつ attaches to quantity expressions like numbers or 少し to mean 'each' or 'at a time', e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' or ちょっとずつよくなってきた 'It's gotten better a little at a time.' 当たり also attaches to Number + Counter, but means 'per' or 'apiece', e.g. １個当たり５００円です 'They're 500 yen apiece.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に当たる
text: As mentioned in our {当|あ}たり lesson, {当|あ}たる often has a meaning that is similar to に{対|たい}して 'to be in regard to'. Due to this, when combined with the case marking particle に, に{当|あ}たる will be translated as 'to correspond to', 'to amount to', 'to be appropriate for', or 'to be in regard to'. These may seem quite different, but we will examine the similarities shortly.

To use に{当|あ}たる, attach it to the end of an (A) noun that you would like to mark as being the 'point of reference'. (B) may come directly after に{当|あ}たる, or earlier in the sentence, so long as it is clearly separated from (A).

As for the link between に{対|たい}して and に{当|あ}たる, it is as follows. In に{対|たい}して, (A) and (B) exist simultaneously, but (B) opposes something about (A). In に{当|あ}たる, (A) and (B) exist simultaneously, but (B) matches something about (A). Due to this, unless the speaker is specifically trying to highlight something that is 'opposing', or 'matching', the base meaning of '(A) and (B) existing simultaneously' may be the standard translation.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 当たり (N3, Per~, A~, Apiece, Each): Both phrases derive from 当たる, but are used in very different ways. に当たる means 'corresponds to' and often functions as a more formal, indirect way of saying 'is', e.g. '父親に当たる人' ('a person who is [lit. corresponds to] their father'). 当たり is used after number + counter expressions to mean 'per' or 'apiece', e.g. '１個当たり１００円' ('100 yen apiece').

にあたり・にあたって (N2, When, When doing something, On the occasion, At the time): Both derive from 当たる, but are used in different ways. に当たる means 'corresponds to' and functions as an indirect way of saying 'is', e.g. '父親に当たる人' ('a person who is [lit. corresponds to] their father'). にあたり・にあたって follows nouns or verb phrases and means 'when' or 'on the occasion of', e.g. '就職に当たり' ('on the occasion of getting a job'). Note that に当たる can also appear as に当たり in formal conjunctive form.

meaning: Nothing better than, There's nothing like, Limited to
summary: An expression showing that something is limited to being within or in (A). Highlighting that there's nothing like (A).
formation: Verb［る］(1) + に限（かぎ）ります (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に限る
text: に{限|かぎ}る is a combination of the case marking particle に (marking a location), and the う - Verb {限|かぎ}る 'to limit'. This expression can be translated as 'there's nothing better than (A)', or 'there's nothing like (A)'.
に{限|かぎ}る may be paired with verbs in their base form, or with nouns.

に{限|かぎ}る may also appear with verbs that have been negated with the auxiliary verb ない. Care will need to be taken with translating these sentences, as they will express that 'there is nothing better than -not- doing (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 限り (N2, As long as, While… is the case, Limited to): に限る and 限り both relate to boundaries or constraints, but serve different functions. に限る expresses the speaker's judgment that something is the best or most suitable, e.g. '寒い日は鍋に限る' ('Nothing beats hot pot on a cold day'). 限り sets a condition or scope, meaning 'as long as' or 'while', e.g. '知っている限り' ('as far as I know').

に越したことはない (N2, There is nothing better than, It is the best, Would be the best): Both に限る and に越したことはない express preference, but differ in certainty and nuance. に限る asserts that something is clearly the best option, e.g. '本は紙に限る' ('Books are best on paper'). に越したことはない is softer and suggests a desirable but not essential option, e.g. '安いに越したことはない' ('Inexpensive would be best').
