sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とは限らない
text: とは{限|かぎ}らない is regularly used to convey the meaning of '(A) is not necessarily so', or 'there is no guarantee that (A)'. This expression utilizes the case marking particle と in its use for highlighting results, the adverbial particle は, and the negated form of the う - Verb {限|かぎ}る 'to limit'.
This structure may be used with verbs, い-Adjectives, な-Adjectives, or nouns. However, だ will be required after な-Adjectives and nouns.
{限|かぎ}らない literally means 'to not be bound', or 'to not be limited'. Therefore, despite と highlighting a result, that result is then being clarified as 'not the only possibility'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: というわけではない (N2, It is not that, It doesn't mean that, It is not always the case): Both expressions deny absolutes, but differ in usage. とは限らない expresses that something isn't necessarily the case, e.g. '留学すれば英語が上手になるとは限らない' ('Studying abroad doesn't always mean your English improves'). というわけではない clarifies previous statements or assumptions, e.g. '嫌いというわけではない' ('It's not the case I dislike it').

ことにはならない (N2, Just because… doesn't mean…): While both deny expected conclusions, ことにはならない expresses that one thing doesn't necessarily lead to another, e.g. '話し合ったからといって解決したことにはならない' ('Just talking about it doesn't mean it's resolved'). とは限らない expresses that something isn't necessarily the case, e.g. '高いものが必ずしも良いとは限らない' ('Expensive things aren't always good').

というものでもない (N2, There is no guarantee that…, Not necessarily): These two expressions are similar in meaning, but with a slightly different nuance. とは限らない says that something isn't necessarily the case, e.g. '高いものが必ずしも良いとは限らない' ('Expensive things aren't always good'). というものでもない says that something cannot be stated as a general truth, e.g. '努力すれば必ず成功するというものでもない' ('It's not necessarily true that effort always leads to success').

ないことはない (N3, Is not impossible, It doesn't mean that it isn't): Both introduce nuance and uncertainty, but with opposite slants. とは限らない expresses that something isn't necessarily the case, e.g. '有名だからといって面白いとは限らない' ('Just because it's famous doesn't mean it's interesting'). ないことはない uses a double negative to express a less confident positive statement, e.g. '行けないことはない' ('It's not that I can't go').

必ずしも (N3, Not always, Not entirely, Not necessarily): 必ずしも and とは限らない often appear together as a pair in statements expressing that something isn't necessarily always the case, e.g. 必ずしも努力が報われるとは限らない ('Effort doesn't always pay off.'). とは限らない alone can express the same meaning without 必ずしも, but the pairing goes together naturally.

に限ったことではない (N1, Not limited to, Not restricted to, Not only): Both express that something is not exclusive, but with a different nuance. に限ったことではない means ‘not limited to this case’ and is used to say that a problem or tendency applies more broadly than the topic at hand, often generalizing from an example, as in 若者に限ったことではない ('It’s not something limited to young people.'). とは限らない means ‘not necessarily’ and is used to deny certainty about an assumption or conclusion itself, as in 成功するとは限らない ('It won’t necessarily succeed.').

限り (N2, As long as, While… is the case, Limited to): These two expressions derived from 限る contrast in meaning. とは限らない expresses that something is not necessarily the case, e.g. '雨だからといって中止とは限らない' ('Just because it's raining doesn't mean it will be canceled'). 限り indicates a bounded condition or extent, e.g. '知っている限り' ('as far as I know').

わけではない (N3, It doesn't mean that, It is not the case, It's not like): Both とは限らない and わけではない challenge assumptions, but in different ways. わけではない denies a specific inference or interpretation, e.g. 'it's not the case that (A)', while とは限らない emphasizes exceptions, e.g. 'just because (A), it's not always (B)'.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About めったに〜ない
text: めったに～ない is an expression that may be translated as 'hardly', 'seldom', or 'rarely'. Originally, {滅多|めった} is a な-Adjective that means 'thoughtless', or 'reckless'. Due to this, as an adverb, {滅多|めった}に literally means 'thoughtlessly' or 'recklessly'.
めったに～ない will usually be paired with a verb in the negative form, or following a noun, and the adverbial particle は.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: It is far more common to see めったに written without kanji, than with. However, both are used.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 陸に～ない (N2, Not well or properly, Not much or enough, Barely, Hardly): Both ろくに〜ない and めったに〜ない express the idea of scarcity, but differ in nuance and context. めったに〜ない refers to the rarity of an action or event, e.g. 'めったに外出しない' ('rarely go out'). ろくに〜ない emphasizes inadequacy or insufficiency, often judging something as not measuring up, e.g. 'ろくに話せない' ('barely able to speak').

なかなか～ない (N3, Not really, Hardly, Not easily or readily, By no means, Far from): めったに〜ない and なかなか〜ない both express rarity, but with different nuance. めったに〜ない means something rarely happens and carries a neutral or negative tone. なかなか〜ない, while also indicating rarity, emphasizes difficulty or persistence, often despite effort. It suggests that the situation is hard to bring about, rather than simply uncommon.

あまり～ない (N4, Not very, Not much, Not really, Hardly): Both めったに〜ない and あまり〜ない are used to qualify negative expressions, but differ in nuance. めったに〜ない means 'rarely' or 'almost never' and focuses on frequency, e.g. めったに行かない ('I rarely go.'). あまり〜ない is less strong, e.g. あまり行かない ('I don't go often.'). It can also qualify a degree or amount, e.g. あまり寒くない ('It's not very cold.'), while めったに cannot.

ほとんど (N4, Almost all, Most, Hardly any, Few (Adverbial noun)): めったに〜ない and ほとんど can be used similarly, but with key differences. めったに〜ない means 'rarely', much like ほとんど with a negative verb. For example, めったに行かない ('I rarely go.') and ほとんど行かない ('I almost never go.') are close, though めったに suggests even lower frequency. Unlike めったに, ほとんど can also be positive, as in ほとんどみんな 'almost everyone'

meaning: Although, Despite, Rather...for, Unexpectedly, Comparatively, Considering
summary: A phrase that shows that something is unexpected, proportionately to what the norm of (A) is.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 割に
text: As an adverb, {割|わり}に is usually used in a similar way to 'although', 'despite', or 'comparatively' in English.
{割|わり}に may be used at the beginning of a sentence, or after any word/phrase that it is highlighting as being 'comparative'. When following な-Adjectives or nouns, な or の will be required.
{割|わり} itself is a noun meaning 'proportionate', and is primarily used as a suffix. {割|わり}に may be thought of as a direct extension of this use, as 'proportionately' is its closest literal meaning.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: While {割|わり}に is often thought to make comparisons between things, it actually only ever compares something to itself (or things within the same category). The 'proportion' that is then highlighted is something that is not common within the category of (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものの (N2, Although, But, Even Though): Both ものの and 割に express contrast, but in different ways. ものの links two opposing facts to mean 'despite', e.g. '話せるものの、字は読めない' ('Despite the fact that he can speak, he can't read characters'). 割に describes a quality being out of proportion with something else, e.g. '高い割にはあまり美味しくない' ('For being expensive, it's not very tasty').

さえ (N3, Even): Both さえ and 割に convey, in some sense, a characteristic or event contrary to expectations. さえ is a strong 'even' that shows emphatic extremity or surprise, e.g. 子どもさえ分かる ('Even a child understands'). 割に expresses contrast with expectations, e.g. 年の割に元気だ ('He's energetic for his age').

むしろ (N3, Rather, Instead, Over): むしろ and 割に both involve contrast, but from different perspectives. むしろ introduces a preferred or more accurate option, e.g. 寝るよりむしろ本を読みたい ('Rather than sleep, I'd rather read'). 割に shows discrepancy between expectation and reality, e.g. 安い割に美味しい ('It's good for how cheap it is').

に比べて (N3, Compared to, When compared to): Both are used in making comparisons, but に比べて is used to directly compare and contrast two things, e.g. このスマホはあのスマホに比べて安い ('This smartphone is cheaper than that one'), while 割に expresses a gap between expectation and reality, e.g. 値段の割に美味しい ('It's tasty considering the price'). The former makes a neutral comparison; the latter evaluates something against an assumed standard.

にしては (N3, (Even) considering, (Even) for): 割に and にしては both express something contrary to expectations, but 割に suggests mild contrast with what was assumed, e.g. 高いわりに美味しくなかった ('For how expensive it is, it wasn't tasty'), while にしては more clearly emphasizes how something defies expectations for its role or class, e.g. 初心者にしてはうますぎる ('He's too good for a beginner').

meaning: Try to, Attempt to, To be about to
summary: A structure that highlights the strong will to attempt, or be about to perform an action.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[volitional]とする
text: When combined with the auxiliary verb う (or よう), とする carries the meaning of 'to try to do (A)', or 'to be about to do (A)'. The case marking particle と in this expression highlights a 'result'.
To use おうとする, modify the (A) verb into its う or よう receiving form, and then add とする.

As う and よう mark volition (the express intent to do something), とする adds the nuance that the express intent has been decided, and all that remains is to 'do' the action. This translates quite closely to 'to endeavor to do' in English, where the past form 'endeavored to do' will suggest that the attempt was unsuccessful.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Verb[Volitional]としても(even if someone attempts to) can be contracted to Verb[Volitional] + たって/ったって。

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: Verb[volitional] + としたが (N3, Tried to ~ but ~, Was about to ~ but ~, Was going to ~ but ~): Both structures use the volitional verb form to show intent, but differ in whether the outcome is explicitly expressed. 'Verb[volitional]とする' expresses an attempt or intention to do something, e.g. '食べようとする' ('try to eat'). 'Verb[volitional]としたが' implies the attempt was interrupted or failed, e.g. '食べようとしたが、無理だった' ('I tried to eat it, but couldn't').

ようにする (N4, To try to, To make sure to, To endeavor to): ようにする (literally, 'do things in such a way as to X') expresses taking care to perform a certain action and often indicates a habitual effort. In contrast, Verb[volitional] + とする implies a one-time attempt to do something, often implying the attempt may not succeed. For example, 毎朝走るようにしている ('I'm making a habit of running every morning.') vs. １０キロ走ろうとしたけど ('I tried to run 10k, but...' implying 'but I couldn't finish', etc.).

〜ようとしない (N3, Not willing to, Not make an effort to, To not attempt or try to, Volitional + としない): These two expressions are opposite uses of the same structure. Verb[volitional]とする means 'Try to do (A)' or 'Make an attempt at (A)', often with the nuance that the attempt may fail, e.g. 食べようとしたけど、無理だった 'I tried to eat it, but I couldn't.' In contrast, 〜ようとしない means 'Not even try to (A)', e.g. うちの息子は、野菜を食べようとしない 'My son doesn't even try to eat vegetables.'

るところだ (N4, About to, On the verge of): Both can describe actions about to happen, but with different nuance. るところだ simply states that something is on the verge of occurring. Verb[volitional] + とする adds a sense of intent or effort, and is often used when the action may not actually happen, e.g. 子どもはなんでも食べようとする ('Kids will try to eat anything.'), where 食べるところだ wouldn't be appropriate.

Verb[よう] (N4, Let's, I shall (Casual volitional)): Both of these use Verb [よう], the volitional form. On its own, it expresses a suggestion, e.g. 食べよう ('Let's eat.'). When combined with とする, it shows an attempt to do something, often one that fails, e.g. 食べようとしたけど ('I tried to eat it, but...'). The key difference is suggestion/proposal vs. attempted action.

てみる (N4, To try to): Verb[volitional]とする and てみる are both translated as 'try', but the former implies attempting something that may not succeed, e.g. 話そうとした ('I tried to speak.'), which implies that maybe the attempt was unsuccessful. In contrast,てみる focuses on trying something to see the result, as in 話してみた ('I tried speaking.'), which has the nuance of doing so to see what it was like.

まだ～ていません (N5, Still haven't done (something)): The grammar point 'Verb[volitional]とする' expresses the speaker's decision or intention to do something, often indicating a plan or goal. In contrast, 'まだ～ていません' is used to express that an action has not yet occurred or a state has not yet been reached, emphasizing the ongoing absence of the action or state.

meaning: Tried to ~ but ~, Was about to ~ but ~, Was going to ~ but ~
summary: A phrase which indicates that someone had the will or intent to do (A), but was unable to complete the action for some reason.
formation: Verb［おう］ + としたが(1) + Result
Verb［おう］ + としたら + Result

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About Verb[volitional] + としたが
text: As mentioned in our ようとする lesson, when combined with the auxiliary verb う (or よう), とする carries the meaning of 'to try to do (A)', or 'to be about to do (A)'. The case marking particle と in this expression highlights a 'result'.

However, the addition of structures like the conjunction particles が, or たら, to the past tense of する will indicate that something interrupted (A), and therefore it was unable to be completed. In these cases, the translation becomes 'to have tried to do (A), but (B)', 'was about to (A), but (B), or 'was on the verge of (A), but (B)'.

う and よう mark volition (the express intent to do something), while とする adds the nuance that the express intent has been decided, and all that remains is to 'do' the action. Due to this, when something interrupts a ようとする verb, it strongly suggests that (B) is/was highly unanticipated.

text: Verb[volitional]とする (N3, Try to, Attempt to, To be about to): Both structures use the volitional verb form to show intent, but differ in whether the outcome is explicitly expressed. 'Verb[volitional]とする' expresses an attempt or intention to do something, e.g. '食べようとする' ('try to eat'). 'Verb[volitional]としたが' implies the attempt was interrupted or failed, e.g. '食べようとしたが、無理だった' ('I tried to eat it, but couldn't').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 言うまでもない ②
text: Unlike は{言|い}うまでもない, which usually comes after other phrases, {言|い}うまでもない tends to come at the beginning. It is a structure that combines the う - Verb {言|い}う, two (2) adverbial particles まで and も, and the い-Adjective ない. This is regularly translated as 'it goes without saying that (A)', or 'it is needless to say (A)', where (A) is whatever comes later in the sentence.
{言|い}うまでもない is often followed directly by ことだが, が, けど, and similar expressions, to add the nuance of 'but'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: は言うまでもない ① (N3, It goes without saying (that), (It is) needless to say, I don't need to remind you): These are slight variations of the same expression meaning 'to go without saying'. は言うまでもない① follows a topic to say '(A) goes without saying'. 言うまでもない②, often seen in forms like 言うまでもないことだけど or 言うまでもなく, comes at the start of a phrase to mean 'Needless to say, (A)' or 'It goes without saying, but (A).'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About そうもない
text: そうもない is an expression used with verbs in Japanese, to indicate that some particular action is very unlikely. It is a combination of the auxiliary verb そう, the adverbial particle も, and the い-Adjective ない.
To recap, one of the primary uses of そう is to highlight appearance. Therefore, そうもない literally means 'to not even appear like (A)'. This structure will be used after verbs in their conjunctive form.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: そうもない is very similar to そうにない. The primary difference being that そうもない is stronger. This is due to も expressing something that is surprising (or for emphasis), while に simply marks a location (or state) within which something does or does not exist. The difference can be understood as follows:
(A) そうもない - To not even look like (A), where 'even' emphasizes (A).
(A) そうにない - To not be looking like (A), where 'be' marks where (A) is 'not' existing.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Less likely than そうにない

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): そうもない and はずがない both express the improbability of something happening. そうもない is the less confident of the two and carries the nuance that something seems unlikely, e.g. 雨が降りそうもない ('It doesn't appear that it's going to rain.'). In contrast, はずがない is a stronger denial, with a nuance of disbelief or surprise, e.g. 負けるはずがない ('There's no way / It's highly unlikely [we] will lose.').

わけがない (N3, There is no way, There is no reason, It is impossible, Cannot be): そうもない and わけがない are similar in that both express the unlikelihood of an event. そうもない suggests low probability based on observation, e.g. 雨が降りそうもない ('It seems unlikely that it'll rain'), while わけがない is an emphatic denial based on the speaker's logical conclusion, e.g. 勝てるわけがない ('There's no way we can win').

ようがない・ようもない (N2, There's no way to, It's impossible to): While both express impossibility, そうもない focuses on visual or situational cues suggesting unlikelihood, e.g. '雨が降りそうもない' ('It doesn't look like it'll rain'). ようがない・ようもない implies there is no method or way to perform the action, e.g. '連絡のしようがない' ('There's no way to contact them').

っこない (N2, There is no chance of, There is no way of, Impossible): Both そうもない and っこない express unlikelihood, but differ in intensity and tone. そうもない implies doubt but leaves room for possibility, e.g. '間に合いそうもない' ('It doesn't seem like we'll make it in time'). っこない is stronger and more absolute, suggesting impossibility, e.g. 'そんなことできっこない' ('There's no way I could do that'). っこない is also more casual and colloquial, while そうもない is more neutral.

そうにない (N2, Unlikely to, Showing no signs of): そうもない and そうにない are extremely similar, both expressing that something is unlikely or shows no signs of happening. The difference is that そうもない feels stronger and more confident due to も adding emphasis, e.g. '雨が降りそうにない' vs. '雨が降りそうもない' (same meaning, but the latter sounds more confident).

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): そう is used to express that something seems likely based on perception or indirect signs, e.g. 雨が降りそう ('It looks like it's going to rain.'). In contrast, そうもない (or そうにない) indicates that there are no signs of something happening, e.g. 雨が降りそうもない ('It doesn't seem like it'll rain at all.').

ないことはない (N3, Is not impossible, It doesn't mean that it isn't): Both そうもない and ないことはない express uncertainty, but in opposite directions. そうもない shows strong doubt or improbability, e.g. '雨が降りそうもない' ('It doesn't look like it will rain'). ないことはない uses a double negative to express a less confident positive, e.g. '行けないことはない' ('It's not that I can't go'), which implies that while not impossible, it might be with some difficulty.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ないことはない
text: ないことはない is an expression that utilizes either the auxiliary verb ない, or the い-Adjective ない, depending on what type of word it is used with. This structure may literally be translated as something similar to 'not (A) is not all there is'. However, the common translations are '(A) is not impossible', or 'it doesn't mean that it isn't (A)'.
This expression may be used with the ない form of any verb, い-Adjective, or な-Adjective. Let's have a look at a few examples before exploring the meaning further.

By itself, ことはない highlights something that is unneeded, or never happens. This is partly due to the adverbial particle は expressing something as being 'complete'. In this way, 'there is no situation in which (A)', is quite an accurate translation of ことはない. By adding ない to the (A) verb, all ないことはない is doing is simply changing this nuance to 'there is -not- no situation in which (A)', a double negative expressing that (A) is actually possible.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とは限らない (N3, Not necessarily so, Is not always true, There is no guarantee that): Both introduce nuance and uncertainty, but with opposite slants. とは限らない expresses that something isn't necessarily the case, e.g. '有名だからといって面白いとは限らない' ('Just because it's famous doesn't mean it's interesting'). ないことはない uses a double negative to express a less confident positive statement, e.g. '行けないことはない' ('It's not that I can't go').

はずがない (N4, Hardly possible, Cannot be, Highly unlikely, Improbable): はずがない strongly denies something, as in そんなことがあるはずがない ('That can't possibly be true.'). In contrast, ないことはない suggests that something is technically possible, but maybe unlikely or difficult, as in 行けないことはない ('It's not that I can't go.').

～ない～はない (N4, There is not ~ that is not/does not): Both forms use a double negative to convey a positive meaning, but differ in nuance and usage. ～ない～はない means 'There is no (A) that isn't (B).', e.g. 書けない漢字はない ('There are no kanji he can't write.'), strongly affirming his ability. In contrast, ないことはない softens a statement, implying 'It's not that (A) isn't true,' e.g., 書けないことはないけど ('It's not that I can't write.', i.e. I can, but perhaps not easily or well.).

そうもない (N3, Very unlikely to, Does not seem that, Does not appear that): Both そうもない and ないことはない express uncertainty, but in opposite directions. そうもない shows strong doubt or improbability, e.g. '雨が降りそうもない' ('It doesn't look like it will rain'). ないことはない uses a double negative to express a less confident positive, e.g. '行けないことはない' ('It's not that I can't go'), which implies that while not impossible, it might be with some difficulty.

というわけではない (N2, It is not that, It doesn't mean that, It is not always the case): Both というわけではない and ないことはない introduce nuance or partial disagreement, but in opposite directions. というわけではない denies a conclusion or assumption, e.g. '好きというわけではない' ('It's not that I like it'). ないことはない uses a double negative to express a less confident positive, e.g. '行けないことはない' ('It's not that I can't go'), implying it may be possible but difficult.

meaning: Such as, Things like, Emphasis
summary: A casual expression used for emphasis or pointing out similar things. Often used simply to fill in the silence in sentences.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なんか・なんて
text: なんか is an expression in Japanese that is frequently associated with the adverbial particle など. They are thought to have overlapping meanings in many circumstances, and なんか itself may be considered an adverbial particle. なんて is an extension of this, and may be considered an abbreviation of などという 'to say something like'.

Both なんか and なんて are used in the same way as など, having translations like 'such as', and 'things like' in English. The primary difference between なんか and なんて is that なんて is far more common after {用言|ようげん} (conjugatable words). This includes verbs, い-Adjectives, and な-Adjectives. On the other hand, なんか is almost exclusively used after {体言|たいげん} (unconjugatable words). In other words, nouns.

Despite the {体言|たいげん} and {用言|ようげん} tendency, most native speakers will not consider it incorrect to use either なんか or なんて with any type of word.

Fun FactBoth なんか and なんて are often used to show a low evaluation of the word that they follow. This can come across as humility when used in relation to oneself, or as an insult when used in relation to others.
Don't let this point stop you from using なんか or なんて though, as many native speakers use it simply to fill the silence in modern Japanese.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Notice that なんか generally follows nouns

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: など (N4, Such as, Things like, Etc., And so on): Both なんか・なんて and など can be used to give examples, like '(A) and so on' or 'things like (A)', but they differ in nuance and formality. など is neutral and used in both speech and writing. なんか・なんて are more casual and often carry a dismissive or belittling tone, like '(A) and whatever' or 'unimportant things like (A)'.

こそ (N3, For sure, For certain, Even more so, Underlined or bolded text): Both add emphasis, but with opposite nuance. なんか・なんて often downplays or dismisses, while こそ highlights importance or exclusivity. The former can feel self-deprecating or casual, while the latter stresses that something uniquely applies. Compare 私なんかできるのかな？ ('I wonder if someone like me could do it?') versus 彼こそできる ('Him, if no one else, can do it.')

まさか (N3, I never dreamed, Never, No way, Don't tell me, You don't say): まさか and なんか・なんて are both used to express surprise, but function in different ways. まさか comes at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize that what follows goes against the speaker's expectations, while なんて appears at the end of a sentence or phrase to express the same. Because they fill different roles, they are often used together. For example, まさか勝てるなんて！ ('To think we could win!' / 'I never thought we could win').

って (N3, As for, Speaking of, Casual は (Sentence topic marker)): って casually introduces or refers back to a topic, e.g. あの人って優しいよね ('That person is really kind, huh?') なんか・なんて adds a dismissive or emotional tone, often implying downplaying or surprise, e.g. 私なんかにできるかな ('Can someone like me really do it?')

とか～とか (N4, Among other things, For example, Such as): なんか・なんて and とか～とか both give examples, but differ in tone and usage. なんか・なんて usually follows a single noun to imply 'things like (A)', often with a dismissive or belittling nuance. とか～とか is used after each item in a list and simply means 'things like (A), (B), and so forth' without any negative implication.

とは (N1, That..., (Surprised) that..., (Never expected) that..., (Shocked) that...): なんて can overlap in meaning with とは when used in phrases like 優勝できる（とは）・（なんて）夢にも思わなかった ('Never even in my dreams did I think we could win the championship.'). なんて however has a variety of usages that do not apply to とは, such as to comment (often negatively) on 'things like (A)', e.g. 嘘なんて大嫌い ('I hate things like lies.').

といった (N2, Such as, Like, So much as): Both express that something is one example of a larger group, but differ in usage. といった is neutral and often used to classify or exemplify within a broader group, e.g. 'ピアノやギターといった楽器' ('musical instruments such as the piano and guitar'). なんか・なんて is more casual and implies a dismissive attitude, e.g. '宿題なんかしたくない' ('I don't want to do homework or anything like that').

meaning: Moreover, Additionally, And also, In addition, Furthermore, Or
summary: An expression indicating that in addition to (A), (B). Branching off from (A), also (B). Usually (A) and (B) are equally important.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 又〜も
text: {又|また}～も is a combination of the adverb {又|また}, a noun, and the adverbial particle も. It can be translated as 'moreover', 'additionally', or 'furthermore'. As も is being used, whatever is being said in (B) will usually be new information.
To use {又|また}～も, an (A) phrase will be stated, before {又|また} will open the (B) phrase, and then be followed by a noun + も.
Instead of も, でも or ても may be used for extra emphasis.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The kanji {又|また} and {叉|また} share an interesting relationship. {又|また} is used to refer to things that reach a point of separation, but then fold back on themselves (being translated as 'again', or 'in addition'). On the other hand, {叉|また} refers to things that reach a point of separation, and then split (being translated as 'a fork in the road', or 'crotch').

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: また + ても・でも adds more emphasis

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しかも (N2, Moreover, Furthermore): Both express addition like the English 'moreover', but differ in usage. しかも starts a sentence to add information that emphasizes the previous point, e.g. '彼は優秀だ。しかも努力家だ' ('He's talented. Moreover, he's hardworking'). 又〜も, because of も, must be used with another noun that also applies and adds to the previous statement, e.g. '姉はピアノが弾ける。また、歌も歌える' ('My older sister can play piano. She can also sing songs').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ついでに
text: {序|つい}でに is an adverb in Japanese that is used in a similar way to 'while you're at it', or 'on the occasion of (A)' in English. {序|つい}で itself is a noun that means 'precedence' (in terms of being the first thing to happen). Due to this, the literal meaning of {序|つい}でに may be thought of as 'with (A) as the precedence, (B)'.
{序|つい}でに is commonly used with verbs, or nouns. In the case of nouns, it will need to be preceded by the case marking particle の.

text: Just like 'precedence' in English, {序|つい}でに implies that (A) is the instigator for (B). Because of this, {序|つい}でに is a good way to convey that something is not urgent, but, if (A) is happening, it is the perfect chance to do (B) as well.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つつ (N2, While, And): Both ついでに and つつ involve performing multiple actions together, but differ in nuance. ついでに expresses performing a second action while it's convenient or appropriate, e.g. '買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った' ('I stopped at the post office while shopping'). つつ is a formal expression indicating simultaneous actions or states, e.g. 'レシピを見つつ料理をする' ('cook while looking at a recipe').

がけに (N2, On the way to, As you go): ついでに and がけに both relate to doing something while engaged in another action. ついでに expresses a second action done while convenient, e.g. '買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った' ('I stopped at the post office while shopping'). がけに is used with movement verbs and emphasizes doing something during a transition, e.g. '帰りがけに電話した' ('I called on my way home').

ているところだ (N4, In the process of doing ~ right now/at this moment): ているところだ and ついでに both relate to ongoing actions but differ greatly in usage. ているところだ describes an action in progress at that moment, with the nuance that the speaker is currently occupied (e.g. 昼ご飯を食べているところだ = 'I'm in the middle of eating lunch'). In contrast, ついでに describes performing an 'extra' action on the same occasion as another (e.g. 散歩のついでに昼ご飯を買ってきた = 'While on a walk, I bought lunch').

際に (N2, When, At the time of, In case of, On the occasion of): Both ついでに and 際に refer to additional actions tied to another event, but differ in tone. ついでに is an everyday expression for when something is done while convenient, e.g. '買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った' ('I stopped at the post office while shopping'). 際に is more formal and emphasizes a particular occasion, e.g. '来日の際にご連絡ください' ('Please contact us when you come to Japan').

の間に (N3, While, During, Between, Period): ついでに and の間に can both express the idea of 'while', but are used in different contexts. ついでに implies taking advantage of one action to do another, e.g. 買い物のついでに銀行に寄った ('I stopped by the bank while shopping.') の間に, by contrast, means 'during/while (A), (B)' without the added nuance of 'while you're at it' that comes with ついでに.

ながら (N4, While ~ing, During, As): ながら attaches to verb stems to express performing one action simultaneously with another, e.g. 音楽を聴きながら走る 'listen to music while running'. In contrast, ついでに follows various words or phrases to convey the idea of taking advantage of the opportunity to do another thing at the same time, e.g. 買い物に行くついでに走ってきた ('On the occasion of going shopping, I went for a run.').

うちに (N3, While, During): Both can be translated as 'while', but with different implications. ついでに means 'while you're at it' and adds a convenient extra action, e.g. 買い物のついでに銀行に寄った ('I stopped by the bank while shopping.') うちに emphasizes doing something before a condition changes, e.g. 熱いうちに食べてね ('Eat it while it's hot.')

にあたり・にあたって (N2, When, When doing something, On the occasion, At the time): Both connect actions to a larger context, but with different emphasis. ついでに expresses performing a second action while it's convenient, e.g. '買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った' ('I stopped at the post office while shopping'). にあたり・にあたって is more formal and used for actions on a certain occasion, e.g. '開会にあたり、ご挨拶申し上げます' ('On the occasion of the opening, I extend my greetings').

ているあいだに (N4, While, During the time that ~): Both can mean 'while,' but the nuance differs. ついでに implies doing something extra during another task, e.g. 買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った ('While shopping, I stopped at the post office.'). ているあいだに just marks that something happened during another action, as in 買い物しているあいだに電話がかかってきた ('I got a call while shopping.').

～ところに・～ところへ (N2, At the time, When, While, Timing): Both ついでに and ～ところに・～ところへ relate to timing, but from different angles. ついでに expresses performing a second action while it's convenient, e.g. '買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った' ('I stopped at the post office while shopping'). ～ところに・～ところへ focuses on when something happens, often unexpectedly, e.g. '出かけようとしたところに電話がかかってきた' ('Just as I was about to leave, the phone rang').

がてら (N1, On the occasion of, While … as well, While … (one is) at it, During, Along the way): Both express simultaneous actions, but differ in nuance. ついでに implies convenience, e.g. '買い物のついでに郵便局に寄った' ('I stopped at the post office while shopping'). がてら implies doing something while moving, e.g. '散歩がてら郵便を出した' ('I mailed a letter while taking a walk'). They also differ grammatically: がてら connects directly to nouns, while ついでに requires の.

summary: A grammar point that shows two or more things happening or existing in unison, or as one.
formation: ［な］Adjective + である + と共（とも）に

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About と共に
text: {共|とも} is a noun in Japanese that is frequently used as a either a prefix, or a suffix. In the case of と{共|とも}に, it is used in conjunction with the case marking particle と as an adverb. と{共|とも}に expresses that (A) will happen 'together with (B)', or 'at the same time as (B)'.
と{共|とも}に may be used after verbs, い-Adjectives, な-Adjectives or nouns. With な-Adjectives, it will sometimes be preceded by である.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と並んで (N3, In line with, Comparable with, Along with, Just like, As … as): と並んで and と共に both suggest pairing, but with different focuses. と並んで stresses equal footing or value, e.g. '村上春樹と並んで人気の日本人作家' ('a Japanese author as popular as Haruki Murakami'). と共に emphasizes accompaniment or simultaneity, e.g. '友人と共に旅に出る' ('go on a trip with a friend') or '厳しいと共に優しい' ('kind as well as strict').

と同時に (N3, At the same time as, The instant, The moment, As well as): と同時に and と共に can both mean 'together with' or 'at the same time as', but their nuance differs. と同時に emphasizes temporal simultaneity in neutral or factual contexts, while と共に often conveys shared action, emotional resonance, or development over time.

と (N5, And): と is a basic particle used to connect nouns, similar to 'and' in English, commonly appearing in both speech and writing. と共に, however, is a formal expression meaning 'along with' or 'at the same time as,' and is used with verbs, adjectives, or nouns. It often suggests a mutual or deeper connection, unlike と, which simply connects items without implying additional nuance.

と (N5, With): Both と and と共に express mutual action or relation, similar to the English 'with.' と is more common and used in everyday speech and writing, but it only follows nouns (e.g., 友だちと遊ぶ = 'play with a friend'). In contrast, と共に is more formal, appearing in written Japanese or structured speech, and can follow verbs, adjectives, and nouns.

合う (N3, To do for one another, Mutually, With): Both relate to the idea of doing something 'together', but with different nuances and usage. 合う attaches to verb stems to convey mutual interaction, e.g. 助け合う ('help each other'), while と共に means '(A) happens together with (B)' in the sense of co-existence or simultaneity, e.g. 年を取ると共に考え方も変わった ('My thinking changed as I grew up').

につれて (N3, As…then, In proportion to, (Along) with): と共に and につれて are similar in that both can be translated as 'together with', but differ in nuance. と共に can express simultaneous actions or states, or the idea of accompaniment, e.g. '厳しいと共に優しい' ('kind as well as strict'). につれて highlights proportional change over time, e.g. '年を取るにつれて体力が落ちる' ('As I get older, my stamina declines').

に伴って・に伴い (N2, As, Due, Along with, Hand-in-hand with, Resulted in, Be consequent upon): に伴って・に伴い and と共に both express things happening in connection with another event. と共に emphasizes simultaneity or shared experience, e.g. '成長と共に責任も増える' ('Responsibility grows along with maturity'). に伴って・に伴い emphasizes causality or consequential change, often in formal contexts, e.g. '経済の発展に伴って生活水準が向上した' ('As the economy developed, living standards improved').

summary: A phrase that shows that (B) will be taken along with (A), and act in proportion or equivalence to it.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About につれて
text: につれて, or に{連|つ}れて when using kanji, is an expression that may be translated as 'as (A), then (B)', or 'in proportion to (A), (B)'. It is formed through the use of the case marking particle に, the る - Verb {連|つ}れる 'to take along', and the conjunction particle て. Literally, the translation is similar to 'being taken along with (A), (B)', or 'in tow with (A), (B)'.
につれて will be used after the plain, non-past form of verbs, or nouns.

As {連|つ}れる is a transitive verb, (A) につれて (B) implies that (A) is causing (B) to happen simultaneously. This does not have to be something that (A) is purposely doing (although it may be), just a 'domino' type effect, where (A) is considered the instigator.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: と (N5, And): につれて describes changes that occur in proportion to each other, as one progresses, the other does too. と, on the other hand, is a conditional particle used when one event naturally or habitually leads to another. Unlike につれて, と does not imply a proportional relationship between the events.

にしたがって (N2, As, Following, As then, According to, In accordance with): Both express change in tandem and can often be used interchangeably. にしたがって frames it as happening 'in accordance with' another, while につれて emphasizes gradual, proportional change. For example, '話すにしたがって、だんだん打ち解けてきた' and '話すにつれて、だんだん打ち解けてきた' have nearly the same meaning.

に伴って・に伴い (N2, As, Due, Along with, Hand-in-hand with, Resulted in, Be consequent upon): につれて and に伴って・に伴い both express one thing happening as a result of or alongside another. につれて emphasizes gradual and proportional change, e.g. '年を取るにつれて体力が落ちる' ('As I age, my stamina declines'). に伴って・に伴い can also be used with one-time or habitual events, e.g. '津波は地震に伴い発生する' ('Tsunamis occur together with earthquakes').

ともなると・にもなると (N1, When, If, Once, As): Both につれて and ともなると・にもなると describe changes that arise with conditions, but differ in nuance. につれて describes gradual, parallel change over time, e.g. '年を取るにつれて体力が落ちる' ('As I age, my stamina declines'). ともなると・にもなると marks a turning point or elevated situation, e.g. '社長ともなると責任が重い' ('Once you become a company president, the responsibility is heavy').

と共に (N3, Together with, At the same time, As well as): と共に and につれて are similar in that both can be translated as 'together with', but differ in nuance. と共に can express simultaneous actions or states, or the idea of accompaniment, e.g. '厳しいと共に優しい' ('kind as well as strict'). につれて highlights proportional change over time, e.g. '年を取るにつれて体力が落ちる' ('As I get older, my stamina declines').

summary: An expression meaning that (A) will intentionally be done immediately, with the nuance of directly, or straight away.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 直ちに
text: The adverb {直|ただ}ちに is commonly used in Japanese to convey that something is happening 'immediately', or 'at once'. Like many adverbs, it will regularly appear at the beginning of a sentence.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: か〜ないかのうちに (N2, Right after, As soon as, Just when, Barely): Both express immediacy between actions, but with different focus. 直ちに stresses promptness, often used for direct commands or instructions, e.g. '直ちに医者を呼んでください' ('Call a doctor immediately'). か〜ないかのうちに highlights how closely two actions occur in time, e.g. 'ドアを開けるか開けないかのうちに猫が飛び出した' ('No sooner had I opened the door than the cat jumped out').

たとたんに (N3, The instant or moment, As soon as, Just as): 直ちに and たとたんに both indicate swift timing, but differ in tone and structure. 直ちに is formal and emphasizes urgency, e.g. '直ちに避難してください' ('Please evacuate immediately'). たとたんに conveys something happening instantly after another event, often with surprise, e.g. '顔を見たとたんに泣き出した' ('She started crying the moment she saw his face').

次第 (N3, As soon as): Both 直ちに and 次第 can imply prompt timing, but differ in grammatical usage and nuance. 直ちに is used before phrases and emphasizes urgency, e.g. '直ちに避難してください' ('Please evacuate immediately'). 次第 attaches to verb stems to suggest one action happening immediately after another, e.g. '準備ができ次第、出発します' ('We'll leave as soon as we're ready').

たちまち (N2, Immediately, Quickly, Suddenly, In a moment or flash): Both 直ちに and たちまち mean 'immediately', but differ in tone and context. 直ちに is formal and emphasizes urgency, often used in official or written language, e.g. '直ちに避難してください' ('Please evacuate immediately'). たちまち suggests a spontaneous change out of the speaker's control, e.g. '空がたちまち暗くなった' ('The sky suddenly turned dark').

かと思ったら・かと思うと (N2, Then again, Just when I thought, No sooner than): Both involve rapid transitions, but differ in usage. 直ちに is formal and emphasizes urgency, often used in official or written language, e.g. '直ちに避難してください' ('Please evacuate immediately'). かと思ったら・かと思うと is more colloquial and marks an abrupt or surprising change just after a perceived moment, e.g. '転んだかと思ったらすぐ立ち上がりました' ('Just when I thought he'd fallen, he got right back up').

meaning: The instant or moment, As soon as, Just as
summary: A phrase that indicates something happening the instant that (A) does, or on the tip of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たとたんに
text: たとたんに, frequently seen using its kanji form た{途端|とたん}に is a structure used to convey that something happens 'the instant', or 'the moment' that something else occurs. It is a combination of the auxiliary verb た (indicating the completion of a verb), and the noun {途端|とたん} 'on the tip of' used adverbially (with に).
(A) た{途端|とたん}に (B) is used to express (B) things that are beyond the control of the speaker, and may be considered strange, or unexpected.
As {途端|とたん} literally means 'on the tip of', any (B) action is considered to happen either directly upon (A), or even simultaneously with (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: かと思ったら・かと思うと (N2, Then again, Just when I thought, No sooner than): Both express actions occurring in close sequence, but differ in focus. たとたんに emphasizes the precise moment with suddenness, e.g. 'ドアを開けたとたんに猫が飛び出した' ('The moment I opened the door, the cat jumped out'). かと思ったら・かと思うと marks a quick change with surprise, e.g. '晴れたかと思ったら、すぐに雨が降り出した' ('Just when I thought it cleared up, it started raining again').

たところだ (N4, Just finished doing, Was just doing): たところだ and たとたんに are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but with different usage and nuance. たところだ simply describes the timing, e.g. 家に帰ってきたところだ ('I just got home.'). In contrast, とたんに expresses that something else happened immediately at that moment. For example, 家に帰ってきたとたんに雨が降ってきた ('The instant I got home, it started to rain.').

直ちに (N3, At once, Immediately, As soon as): 直ちに and たとたんに both indicate swift timing, but differ in tone and structure. 直ちに is formal and emphasizes urgency, e.g. '直ちに避難してください' ('Please evacuate immediately'). たとたんに conveys something happening instantly after another event, often with surprise, e.g. '顔を見たとたんに泣き出した' ('She started crying the moment she saw his face').

たばかり (N4, Just did, Something just happened): Both refer to something that just happened, but differ in nuance. たばかり describes the state after completion, e.g. 帰ってきたばかり 'just got home'. とたんに means something happened the moment another did, e.g. 帰ってきたとたんに雨が降った ('The moment I got home, it started to rain.').

と同時に (N3, At the same time as, The instant, The moment, As well as): Both と同時に and たとたんに describe closely linked events, but they differ in focus. と同時に emphasizes simultaneity or coordination, while たとたんに conveys a sudden, often unexpected result following a completed action. Their grammar structure also differs: と同時に follows the non-past form, while たとたんに follows the past tense.

次第 (N3, As soon as): Both describe sequences where one action quickly follows another, but differ in tone and formality. 次第 is formal and indicates that an action will follow as soon as another is completed, e.g. '会議が終わり次第、報告します' ('I'll report as soon as the meeting ends'). たとたんに emphasizes sudden or unexpected results, often in conversation, e.g. 'ドアを開けたとたんに猫が飛び出した' ('The moment I opened the door, the cat jumped out').

なり (N1, As soon as, The moment, When): Both express immediacy following another action, but differ in nuance and tone. たとたんに stresses suddenness or unexpectedness, sometimes with emotion, e.g. '立ち上がったとたんに倒れた' ('He collapsed the moment he stood up'). なり also marks instantaneousness, but feels more formal or literary, and implies a natural cause-effect link, e.g. '席に着くなり、食べ始めた' ('As soon as he sat down, he started eating').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About おきに
text: {置|お}きに is a combination of {置|お}き, a suffix meaning 'opening' or 'interval', and the case marking particle に. Primarily written without kanji, it is an expression used to show that something happens 'every (A)', or 'at intervals of (A)'.
The difference between something being interpreted as 'every', or 'at intervals of' can be tricky though, so we'll look at both.
Due to おきに being a suffix, it will be attached to the end of numbers, counters, or any 'space' that it is highlighting as being an 'opening' or 'interval'.

Looking at these sentences, we can see that the 'interval' is a bit difficult to understand even in English. However, the easier way to think of おきに in this sense is 'leaving a space of (A), (B)'. So if we say 'leaving a space of two days, (B)', it becomes a bit clearer that something is happening during the third day.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: This is a topic that native speakers frequently get wrong themselves, so don't worry if it takes a while to understand! If you are unsure about which one to use, think of {置|お}きに as 'leaving intervals of (A), (B)' for most purposes. {一時間|いちじかん} tends to be the upper limit of time that most people disagree about whether the meaning is 'every hour', or 'every second hour'. This makes sense, as the time frame is short, but still sort of long, so whether someone takes it as the beginning of the hour or some point during that hour being the important information, their opinions may differ. Remember though, おきに itself only ever points to the beginning of the space after (A), it doesn't care when/where (B) happens afterward.

sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: につけ (N2, Whenever, Every time something happens): Both おきに and につけ describe repeated occurrences, but are used differently. おきに attaches to time expressions to mean 'at intervals of (A)', e.g. '５分おきに電車が来る' ('Trains arrive every five minutes'). につけ is used with verbs and nouns to express a habitual response, e.g. '彼の声を聞くにつけ' ('whenever I hear his voice').

に (Frequency) (N4, Times (In each time period), Every, Frequency of): Both expressions show frequency, but in different ways. The に (frequency) construction combines a time period with a number to mean '(A) times per (B),' e.g. 一週間に２回 'twice a week'. おきに attaches to a number + counter to mean 'at intervals of (A),' e.g. 二日おきに学校に行く ('I go to school every three days.' meaning 'every third day').

たびに (N3, Each time, Every time, Whenever): Both おきに and たびに describe repeated occurrences, but are used differently. おきに attaches to time expressions to mean 'at intervals of (A)', e.g. '５分おきに電車が来る' ('Trains arrive every five minutes'). たびに describes a response that recurs whenever a particular thing happens, e.g. '見るたびに笑ってしまう' ('I end up laughing every time I see it').

ごとに (N4, Each, Every): ごとに and おきに both express regular intervals, but with a key difference. ２日ごとに means 'every two days', i.e. the event happens on the second day. ２日おきに means 'at intervals of two days', or in other words every third day. A helpful tip: おきに comes from 置く, which can have the meaning of leaving a gap or space.

まい～のように (N4, Almost every ~, Nearly every ~, On a ~ basis): Both まい～のように and おきに express frequency, but in different ways. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, おきに attaches to a number + counter expression to mean 'at intervals of (A),' e.g. 一日おきに 'every other day' or 'at intervals of one day'.

～ずつ (N3, One at a time, Per, Each, Gradually): Both deal with repetition or intervals, but in different ways. ～ずつ means 'each' or 'at a time' and attaches to quantity expressions, e.g. 一つずつください 'Give me one of each.' おきに follows time or distance intervals to mean 'every (A)', e.g. ５分おきに電車が来る 'Trains come every five minutes.'

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たびに
text: {度|たび}に is the adverbial form of the noun {度|たび}, meaning 'time' (as in 'at the time of'). たびに is frequently paired with either verbs, or nouns, in order to show that something happens 'whenever (A)', or 'each time (A)'.
After nouns, the case marking particle の will be required before たびに.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: たびに is often pronounced as たんびに in casual conversation.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: おきに (N3, Repeated at intervals, Every other, Every, At intervals of): Both おきに and たびに describe repeated occurrences, but are used differently. おきに attaches to time expressions to mean 'at intervals of (A)', e.g. '５分おきに電車が来る' ('Trains arrive every five minutes'). たびに describes a response that recurs whenever a particular thing happens, e.g. '見るたびに笑ってしまう' ('I end up laughing every time I see it').

ごとに (N4, Each, Every): ごとに and たびに both express frequency, and can be interchangeable in cases like 失敗するたびに／ごとに 'every time (you) fail'. However, ごとに can directly follow time or distance expressions (e.g. ３時間ごとに), while たびに requires a verb indicating an action or event, e.g. ３時間が経つたびに 'every time 3 hours pass'. Their noun forms also differ, e.g. 発表の度に vs. 発表ごとに (both meaning 'with every announcement').

まい～のように (N4, Almost every ~, Nearly every ~, On a ~ basis): Both まい～のように and たびに express frequency and the idea of 'every,' but with different nuances. まい～のように is used with 'every~' time expressions to mean 'almost every (A)', e.g. 毎日のように 'almost every day'. In contrast, たびに follows verbs or noun phrases to mean 'every time (A)', e.g. 彼に会うたびに 'every time I see him' or 旅行のたびに 'every time I take a trip'.

につけ (N2, Whenever, Every time something happens): These are similar expressions that both express the idea that every time one thing happens, so does something else. While they are interchangeable in some cases, につけ can only be used for naturally occurring events, e.g. '見るにつけ笑ってしまう' ('I laugh every time I see it'). たびに can also be used for volitional actions, e.g. '出張に行くたびにお土産を買う' ('I buy souvenirs every time I go on a business trip').

meaning: Or, Possibly, Maybe, Perhaps, Or possibly
summary: An expression used to say or, possibly, or maybe, literally indicating (A) or a certain (B) which is like (A).
formation: あるいは + Phrase + かもしれない
あるいは + Phrase + かもしれません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About あるいは
text: あるいは is a construction in Japanese that is used as a {接続語|せつぞくご} (conjunction). It usually appears after statements that have been marked with the adverbial particle か. あるいは may be loosely translated as 'possibly', 'maybe', or 'or'.

Although usually being treated as a single word, あるいは is actually a combination of the attributive form of {或|あ}る, a verb meaning 'a certain', the suffix character い (used for making い-Adjectives), and the adverbial particle は. Due to this, the literal meaning of あるいは is just 'another possibility', as it highlights a certain something existing within the same area/category as (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もしかしたら (N3, Perhaps, Maybe, Possibly): あるいは and もしかしたら can overlap in one usage. あるいは is usually used mid-sentence to present alternatives, e.g. 月曜日あるいは火曜日 'Monday or Tuesday.' However, it can also appear at the start of a sentence to mean 'Perhaps,' e.g. あるいはそうかもしれない 'Perhaps that might be so.' もしかしたら can be used the same way, as in もしかしたらそうかもしれない, though あるいは carries a stronger nuance of weighing other possibilities.

か (N5, Or): Both か and あるいは present alternatives. か is casual and follows nouns to mean 'or' (e.g., 今日か明日休みます = 'I'll take off today or tomorrow'). あるいは is more formal, mainly used in writing or formal speech (e.g., 新品で買うか、あるいは中古で買うか、まだ決めていません = 'I haven't decided yet whether I'll buy it new or perhaps second-hand').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ながらも
text: ながらも is a combination of the conjunction particle ながら, and the adverbial particle も. Coming from the kanji {乍|なが}ら, with the meaning of 'while', ながら almost always keeps this nuance. Because of this, ながらも can be translated as 'even while (A), (B)', or 'although (A), also (B)'.
ながらも usually expresses surprise at the coexistence of (A) and (B), and may be used after い-Adjectives, な-Adjectives, nouns, or the conjunctive form of verbs.

ながらも is used to highlight a thing that comes after the existing state of (A) 'そのままで{後|あと}に{続|つづ}く{事|こと}'. Due to this, ながらも may only be used with verbs that highlight states of existence (like feelings), rather than ongoing actions.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Unlike ながら 、ながら(も) is preceded only by verbs that express state

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: それなのに (N2, And yet, Despite this): Both express contrast, but with different nuances and usage. ながらも attaches to verbs, adjectives, or nouns and conveys contradictory states, e.g. '緊張しながらもわくわくしている' ('While feeling anxious, I'm also excited'). それなのに is used at the start of a sentence to mean 'and yet', often with surprise, e.g. '８時間も寝た。それなのに眠い' ('I slept eight whole hours. But still, I'm sleepy').

にもかかわらず (N2, Despite, In spite of, Regardless, Nevertheless): ながらも and にもかかわらず both express contradiction, but differ in nuance and usage. ながらも conveys coexisting contradictory states, e.g. '緊張しながらもわくわくしている' ('While feeling anxious, I'm also excited'). にもかかわらず means 'despite' and is used when something occurs against expectations, e.g. '雨にもかかわらず出かけた' ('He went out despite the rain').

つつ(も) (N2, Even while ~ing, Even though ~ing, Despite ~ing, Although ~ing): Both mean 'while' or 'although' and are often interchangeable, e.g. '何度も休みつつ、ゴールまでたどりついた' ('While/although resting many times, I neared the goal'). This could also be expressed as '何度も休みながらも...'. However, ながらも requires the action to occur over time, so '手紙を開きつつ' ('while opening the letter') would typically not use ながらも.

くせに (N3, Even though, And yet, Despite): ながらも and くせに both express contradiction, but differ in nuance. ながらも simply expresses two seemingly contradictory states coexisting in a neutral fashion, e.g. 緊張しながらもわくわくしている ('While feeling anxious, I'm also excited.'). In contrast, くせに implies blame or criticism, e.g. 知っているくせに教えてくれない ('Even though he knows, he won't tell me.').

にしても (N3, Even though, Even if, Even when, Also): にしても and ながらも both express contrast. にしても introduces something counter to the condition, e.g. 難しいにしてもやってみたほうがいい ('Even if it's hard, you should try doing it'). ながらも shows two opposing facts that coexist, e.g. 忙しいながらも楽しんでいる ('I'm busy, but still enjoying it').

のに (N4, Despite, Although, Even though): Both のに and ながらも express contrast, but with different focuses. のに is more general and used widely, like the English 'although.' ながらも is mainly used with state-expressing verbs and conveys surprise that something happened despite that state.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About において・における
text: において is a combination of the case marking particle に in, and the {接続語|せつぞくご} (conjunction) おいて. Either {於|お}いて, or {於|お}ける may be used, with no difference in meaning. において itself is usually translated as 'at', 'in', 'on', or 'regarding'.
において (or における) will be used after nouns, or when connecting one noun to another. In the case of connecting one noun to another, における, or においての will be required.
においての (and における) are primarily used in formal language, and will not commonly be used in daily speech.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にて (N2, In, At, With, Using, By): Both are formal equivalents of で and can mark place of action, means, or method. において・における can also describe nouns, e.g. '現代社会における問題' ('problems in modern society') or '現代社会においての問題'. にて always connects to the rest of the sentence, not directly to a noun, e.g. '大会にて優勝する' ('win in the tournament').

に取って (N3, To, For, Concerning): に取って (usually written in kana as にとって) expresses viewpoint or concern, e.g. 私にとって大切な人だ ('She's an important person to me'). において・における is a formal equivalent of で, conveying setting, context, or means, e.g. 歴史において重要な出来事だ ('It's an important event in history'). Unlike にとって, the latter can directly modify nouns in the における form, e.g. 教育における問題 ('Problems in education').

について (N3, Concerning, About, Regarding): While they appear similar in form, these expressions have different nuance and meaning. について means 'concerning (A)' and often marks a topic of discussion, question, and so on, e.g. 日本文化について話す ('Talk about Japanese culture'), while において・における is a formal equivalent of で and often indicates the location or context something happens, e.g. 会議において発表する ('Announce at the meeting').

にかかわる (N2, To relate to, To have to do with, Concerning, Depends on): While both にかかわる and において・における describe relationships with nouns, their meanings differ. にかかわる expresses significant relevance or impact, often with serious subjects, e.g. '命にかかわる' ('a matter of life'). において・における simply marks context without implying influence, e.g. '歴史において重要な事件' ('an important event in history').

で (N5, At, In): Both で and において・における indicate the location where an action takes place, but differ significantly in formality. で is common in daily speech and informal writing, whereas において・における appear mainly in formal contexts or written language. Additionally, において・における can express meanings like 'in terms of' or 'with respect to.'

に関する・に関して (N3, Related to, About, Regarding): These patterns are similar in that both follow nouns, then attach to either another noun (に関する and における) or the rest of the sentence (に関して or において), but differ in meaning. に関する・に関して means 'about (A)' or 'concerning (A)', while において・における can be considered a more formal/literary equivalent of で indicating a context, place, or setting.

に対して (N3, In contrast to, While, In regard to, Whereas): Both patterns connect to nouns to show a relationship, but differ in nuance. に対して (which also appears before nouns as に対する) implies a directional or oppositional relationship, like 'toward (A)', e.g. 彼に対する気持ち ('feelings toward him'). In contrast, において・における is a more formal/literary equivalent of で, indicating a context, place, or setting, e.g. 現代社会における宗教 ('religion in modern society').

meaning: Start, First (point), Foremost, To begin with
summary: A structure showing that (A) is first, or the most important, due to it being the first number or position in a series.
formation: 第一（だいいち） + の + Noun
Phrase + 第一（だいいち） + だ
Phrase + 第一（だいいち） + です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 第一
text: {第一|だいいち} is an expression in Japanese which may be used either as an adverb, or as a noun. As a noun, it will carry the meaning of 'foremost', or 'most important'. As an adverb, it can mean 'first', or 'above anything'.

To use {第一|だいいち} adverbially, pair it with に. As a noun, it will usually be followed by の (when connecting nouns), or by the auxiliary verb だ, when at the end of a sentence. に will often be omitted when there is no need to put specific emphasis on a time.
Occasionally, まず 'first of all' will be paired with {第一|だいいち}. This may seem redundant, but is like saying 'the very first' in English.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: {第|だい} is a kanji that is often translated as 'number'. However, the literal meaning is a bit closer to 'position', as it refers to the place that something has within a sequence of numbers. As such, {第一|だいいち} simply means '1st position'.

meaning: Increasingly, More and more, Decreasingly, Less and less, Keep -ing
summary: A word which indicates (A) happening or trending more and more, or to keep doing (A). May signify changes in either volume or intensity.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ますます
text: When using the adverb ますます, it will have the meaning of 'increasingly', 'more and more', or even 'to keep (A)ing'. It is used to emphasize continuous trends, and will regularly be seen at the beginning of a sentence.
Occasionally, the kanji form {益々|ますます} will be used. This will not change the nuance at all. The kanji {益|えき} simply means 'gain'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 一方だ (N3, More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er): Both 一方だ and ますます express progressive change, but differ in usage. 一方だ follows verbs, often in formal or objective contexts to describe trends, e.g. '物価は上がる一方だ' ('Prices keep rising'). ますます has a similar nuance, but precedes the phrase or sentence, e.g. '彼の人気はますます高まっている' ('His popularity is increasing more and more').

更に (N2, Even more or further, Again, More and more): 更に and ますます both suggest addition or progression, but with different nuances. 更に emphasizes adding something on top of what already exists, e.g. '更に三人が参加した' ('Three more people joined'). ますます highlights a state intensifying over time, e.g. 'ますます寒くなってきた' ('It's gotten colder and colder').

どんどん (N4, Progressively, Rapidly increasing, More and more): どんどん and ますます are both adverbs used to describe change over time. どんどん emphasizes rapid progress or sudden development, often in leaps and bounds. ますます focuses on something already in a certain state becoming even more so, and is often used in polite expressions like wishes for continued health or success.

ば〜ほど (N3, The more…the more): They are similar in that both describe change, but ば〜ほど specifically expresses a proportional relationship between two things, like the English 'the more (A), the more (B)', e.g. 見れば見るほど好きになる ('The more I look, the more I like it.'). In contrast, ますます simply emphasizes continued intensification, e.g. 彼の人気はますます高まっている ('His popularity is steadily rising.')

meaning: More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er
summary: A grammar point that expresses the way that a certain trend is continuing, regarding either intensity or number.
formation: Verb + 一方（いっぽう）で + Phrase
Verb + 一方（いっぽう）です (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 一方だ
text: {一方|いっぽう} is a noun that is often seen after verbs, in order to convey the meaning of 'more and more (A)', 'continuing to (A)', or 'getting (A)er and (A)er'.
{一方|いっぽう} will be paired with the auxiliary verb だ (at the end of sentences), or で, だ's conjunctive form when it will be followed by some sort of explanation.
As the literal meaning of {一方|いっぽう} is 'single direction', it may be used with things that are increasing, decreasing, intensifying, or weakening, so long as the shift is all in a single direction.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The verb must express change (e.g. 増える、下がる、or verbs ending with …なる、…てくる、…ていく etc.)

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 一方で (N3, On the other hand, At the same time, While): While they look similar, 一方で and 一方だ serve different functions. 一方で shows contrast between two ideas or situations, e.g. '一方で反対する人もいる' ('On the other hand, some people are against it'). 一方だ follows verbs to describe trends, e.g. '物価は上がる一方だ' ('Prices keep rising').

つづける (N4, To continue): つづける and 一方だ both indicate continuation but differ in tone. つづける means a simple ongoing action, e.g. 減り続けている 'is still decreasing'. 一方だ follows dictionary-form verbs and adds a sense of progression in one direction, often negatively, e.g., 減る一方だ 'is getting worse and worse'.

ますます (N3, Increasingly, More and more, Decreasingly, Less and less, Keep -ing): Both 一方だ and ますます express progressive change, but differ in usage. 一方だ follows verbs, often in formal or objective contexts to describe trends, e.g. '物価は上がる一方だ' ('Prices keep rising'). ますます has a similar nuance, but precedes the phrase or sentence, e.g. '彼の人気はますます高まっている' ('His popularity is increasing more and more').

どんどん (N4, Progressively, Rapidly increasing, More and more): どんどん is an adverb that implies rapid or dramatic change, often in leaps and bounds, and is common in everyday speech. In contrast, 一方だ is more formal and used to describe ongoing change that continues beyond the speaker's control. Structurally, 一方だ follows the verb, unlike どんどん, which appears before it.

いよいよ (N2, At last, Finally, More and more): Both 一方だ and いよいよ express change, but differ in usage. 一方だ follows verbs, often in formal or objective contexts to describe trends, e.g. '物価は上がる一方だ' ('Prices keep rising'). いよいよ suggests something is finally or imminently happening, often with anticipation, e.g. 'いよいよ試合が始まる' ('The match is about to begin').

ば〜ほど (N3, The more…the more): Both can be used to describe change, but with different patterns. ば〜ほど expresses a proportional relationship between two things, like 'the more (A), the more (B)', e.g. 練習すればするほど上手になる ('The more you practice, the better you get.') 一方だ shows a continuous, one-way change in a single direction, e.g. 物価は上がる一方だ ('Prices just keep rising.')

ばかりだ (N3, (Only) continue to, Keep on -ing, More and more): ばかりだ and 一方だ are similar in that both express continuous or progressive change. However, ばかりだ is typically used with negative developments and often carries a more subjective tone, e.g. 状況は悪くなるばかりだ ('The situation keeps getting worse'). 一方だ, on the other hand, sounds more neutral or objective, and doesn't necessarily imply a negative trend, e.g. 人口は増える一方だ ('The population keeps increasing').

summary: A phrase that highlights one direction, before expressing that another way could differ.
formation: ［な］Adjective + な(1) + 一方（いっぽう）（で）
Noun + の(1) + 一方（いっぽう）（で）

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 一方で
text: {一方|いっぽう}で is a combination of the noun {一方|いっぽう} 'one direction', and the case marking particle で, in its nuance as 'at'. Together, they are used in a similar way to a conjunction particle, carrying the meaning of 'on the other hand', 'at the same time', or 'while'.
{一方|いっぽう}で may be used after the attributive form of other words, or at the beginning of new phrases.
As {一方|いっぽう}で has a literal meaning similar to 'at the (A) side', or 'in the (A) direction', it is expressing that another direction also exists, which may then be compared or contrasted with (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 一方だ (N3, More and more, Continue to, Keep on, -er and -er): While they look similar, 一方で and 一方だ serve different functions. 一方で shows contrast between two ideas or situations, e.g. '一方で反対する人もいる' ('On the other hand, some people are against it'). 一方だ follows verbs to describe trends, e.g. '物価は上がる一方だ' ('Prices keep rising').

反面 (N2, While, On the other hand, Although, However, On the flip side): 一方で and 反面 both show contrast, but differ in tone. 一方で is neutral and presents parallel or opposing facts, e.g. '一方で経済は成長している' ('On the other hand, the economy is growing'). 反面 highlights a downside or contradiction, e.g. '便利な反面、依存しやすい' ('While convenient, it's also easy to become dependent').

かたわら (N1, While, Besides, In addition to): かたわら and 一方で both describe two actions or conditions, but differ in nuance. かたわら implies doing something secondary alongside a main activity, e.g. '彼は本業のかたわら小説を書いている' ('He writes novels alongside his main job'). 一方で marks contrast or coexistence between broader situations, e.g. '一方で都市化が進んでいる' ('Meanwhile, urbanization is advancing').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 遂に
text: Like とうとう, {遂|つい}に is an adverb that is frequently used to mean 'finally', or 'at last'. It will usually come at the beginning of a sentence.
{遂|つい}に may be seen equally as often with or without kanji. When compared to {到頭|とうとう}, ついに is slightly more formal.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: いよいよ (N2, At last, Finally, More and more): Both 遂に and いよいよ can mean 'finally', but with different focus. 遂に indicates that something has occurred at last, often after struggle or delay, e.g. '遂に大学に入った' ('I finally entered university'). いよいよ emphasizes an approaching climax or moment of anticipation, e.g. 'いよいよ卒業の日が来た' ('Graduation day has finally arrived').

とうとう (N4, Finally, After all): Both とうとう and 遂に mean 'finally', but with different nuances. とうとう emphasizes the long effort or struggle leading up to the result, while 遂に focuses more on the result itself and what may follow. In other words, both とうとう大学生になった and 遂に大学生になった mean 'I finally became a university student.', but the former is more backward-looking, while the latter is forward-looking.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About すでに
text: As a formal alternative to もう, the adverb {既|すで}に is used in Japanese as 'already'. Usually, {既|すで}に will come at the beginning of a phrase that it is clarifying as being 'already (A)'.
すでに has several nuances in Japanese beyond just 'already', let's take a look at a few of these possibilities:
のこらず - Nothing remaining.
あまねく - All around.
ことごとく - Altogether.
もはや - Already.
まぎれもなく - Beyond doubt.

These may all seem quite different, but together they show the full meaning of {既|すで}に very clearly. That meaning is 'to be completely unchanging'. Let's take a look at how すでに can be used with each of these nuances.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もう (N5, Already, Anymore): Both もう and すでに express the idea of 'already.' The difference is their level of formality and tone. While もう is commonly used in everyday conversation and can have a personal or emotional nuance, すでに is more objective and found primarily in writing or formal speech. もう can also be used alone as an expression of exasperation or frustration, while すでに cannot.

meaning: Without doing
summary: A somewhat old-fashioned way to express that something will be done, without doing (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ずに
text: Although it is not considered to be one of the primary 18 auxiliary verbs that are used in modern Japanese, ず is a classical auxiliary verb that has the same role as ぬ, and ない. This role is negating the verb that it is attached to. ずに is simply the addition of the case marking particle に to ず. Together, they mean 'without doing', in a similar way to ないで.
To use ずに, attach it to the indeterminate form of the verb that you wish to express as 'without doing (A)'. This is the same form used with ない.
ずに is quite a bit more formal than ないで, but still frequently used in modern Japanese. Especially as part of set phrases, like ずにすむ (which we will learn about in another lesson).

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: に can be omitted

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ずにはいられない (N3, Cannot help doing something, Cannot resist doing something): ずに has the core meaning of 'without doing', while ずにはいられない is an idiomatic form meaning 'I can't help but (A)'. Compare '宿題をせずに寝た' ('I went to bed without doing my homework'), which describes inaction, to '彼の話に笑わずにはいられなかった' ('I couldn't help but laugh at his story'), which expresses an uncontrollable response.

ずに済む (N2, Get by without doing something, To get away with): ずに has the core meaning of 'without doing', and ずに済む is an idiomatic usage of meaning 'not having to do (A)' (literally, 'it works out without doing it'). Compare 宿題をせずに寝た ('I went to bed without doing my homework.'), which simply describes lack of action, to e.g. 新しいスマホを買わずに済んだ ('It worked out so that I didn't have to buy a new smartphone.').

ことなく (N2, Without ~ing): Both ずに and ことなく mean 'without doing (A)' and can often be used interchangeably. ずに is more common and used in both writing and conversation, e.g. '宿題をせずに寝た' ('I went to bed without doing my homework'). ことなく is more formal and tends to appear in writing, e.g. '彼は休むことなく働き続けた' ('He continued working without rest').

ないで (N4, Without doing, Not ~ and ~): ないで and ずに both express the idea of 'without doing (A)' and are used in similar ways. For example, 朝ご飯を食べないで学校に行った and 朝ご飯を食べずに学校に行った both mean 'I went to school without eating breakfast.', but ずに has a slightly more formal or literary tone, while ないで is more conversational. Unlike ないで, ずに cannot be used as a negative request form to say 'Don't (A).'.

meaning: Cannot help doing something, Cannot resist doing something
summary: A somewhat old-fashioned way to show that not doing (A) cannot be lived with, or is unbearable.
formation: Verb［ない］+ ずにはいられない
Verb［ない］+ ずにはいられません (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ずにはいられない
text: As mentioned in our ずに lesson, ず is an auxiliary verb that is not commonly used in modern Japanese, except for in set expressions. It has the equivalent role of ない, in expressing that something 'has not', or 'will not' happen. The case marking particle に is then combined with the adverbial particle は, and the negative-potential form of いる, いられない. ずにはいられない may be translated as 'cannot help doing (A)', or 'cannot resist doing (A)'.
ずにはいられない will be attached to the indeterminate form of verbs. This is the same stem form as ない uses.
Although ずにはいられない is often translated as 'cannot resist (A)', the literal meaning is simply 'cannot be without (A)'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: する → せず

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ないわけにはいかない (N2, Can't not, No way to avoid): Both imply that something must be done, but differ in the nature of the obligation. ずにはいられない arises from emotional urgency, e.g. '泣かずにはいられなかった' ('I just couldn't help but cry'). ないわけにはいかない often reflects social duty or pressure, e.g. '謝らないわけにはいかない' ('I have to apologize').

わけにはいかない (N3, Cannot afford to, No way, Impossible to do): These express internal conflict, but from opposite angles. わけにはいかない implies being unable to act due to duty or social constraint, e.g. 断るわけにはいかない 'I just can't refuse.' ずにはいられない expresses an inability to stop oneself from acting, e.g. 笑わずにはいられない 'I couldn't help but laugh.'

ずに (N3, Without doing): ずに has the core meaning of 'without doing', while ずにはいられない is an idiomatic form meaning 'I can't help but (A)'. Compare '宿題をせずに寝た' ('I went to bed without doing my homework'), which describes inaction, to '彼の話に笑わずにはいられなかった' ('I couldn't help but laugh at his story'), which expresses an uncontrollable response.

ないではいられない (N2, Cannot help doing something, Cannot resist doing something): These are nearly synonymous expressions that both mean 'can't help but do (A)'. ずにはいられない feels slightly more formal or literary, while ないではいられない is more typical of speech. Compare '笑わずにはいられない' and '笑わないではいられない' (same meaning, but the latter sounds less literary).

ざるを得ない (N2, Can't help doing, Have no choice but): Both express uncontrollable actions or feelings, but differ in tone. ずにはいられない often has a more subjective or emotional feel, e.g. '泣かずにはいられなかった' ('I just couldn't help but cry'). ざるを得ない has a more objective tone and is used to express external necessity or obligation, e.g. '行かざるを得ない' ('I have no choice but to go').

てたまらない (N2, Can't help but want to, Very, Extremely): Both express uncontrollable actions or feelings, but differ in nuance. ずにはいられない is about being compelled to act (lit. 'unable not to act'), e.g. '彼を応援せずにはいられない' ('I can't help but root for him'). てたまらない emphasizes a state or feeling that overwhelms you, e.g. '暑くてたまらない' ('It's unbearably hot') or '会いたくてたまらない' ('I want to see you so much I can't bear it').

てならない (N2, Very, Extremely, Can't help but do): Both express uncontrollable actions or feelings, but differ in nuance. ずにはいられない is about being compelled to act (lit. 'unable not to act'), e.g. '彼を応援せずにはいられない' ('I can't help but root for him'). てならない emphasizes a state or feeling that overwhelms you, e.g. '暑くてならない' ('It's unbearably hot') or '会いたくてならない' ('I want to see you so much I can't bear it').

てしょうがない (N2, Extremely, Very, Really, It can't be helped): Both express uncontrollable actions or feelings, but differ in nuance. ずにはいられない is about being compelled to act (lit. 'unable not to act'), e.g. '彼を応援せずにはいられない' ('I can't help but root for him'). てしょうがない emphasizes a state or feeling that overwhelms you, e.g. '暑くてしょうがない' ('It's unbearably hot') or '会いたくてしょうがない' ('I want to see you so much I can't bear it').

meaning: Without, No
summary: A slightly formal word used to show that something is without (A). The existence of (A) is not included.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About なし
text: Although it is used almost exclusively as a suffix, なし is actually a noun that means ないこと 'thing without'. なし, or {無|な}し when using kanji, will be used after nouns that it is indicating as 'not having (A)'.

Depending on what the speaker wants to convey, なし is often partnered with the auxiliary verb だ, or its conjunctive form で. なしで will mean '(A) that is without (B)'. When connected directly to another noun, の will be required after なし. Again, this will mean '(A) that is without (B)'.

なし does not always need to be connected directly to another noun. Often, it can be used in reference to an event or thing that someone wants to skip, or avoid. In cases like this, it may be paired with the case marking particle に, to show determination to avoid something.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: あり (N3, Possibility, To have, With): These two phrases come from the existence verb ある and its negative form, and are opposites meaning 'with (A)' or 'without (A)', e.g. '字幕ありで観る' ('watch with subtitles') and '字幕なしで観る' ('watch without subtitles'). They also have opposite figurative meanings, with あり meaning 'possible' or acceptable, and なし used to reject something as an option.

抜きで (N2, Without, Unless): Both なし and 抜きで express the idea of 'without' in Japanese, but with a slight difference in nuance. なし indicates the absence or lack of something, e.g. '砂糖なしでお願いします' ('I'll have it without sugar'). 抜きで implies the exclusion of something that would typically be expected, e.g. 'ワサビ抜きのお寿司' ('sushi without wasabi') or 'ランチ抜きで仕事する' ('work without eating lunch').

summary: A common expression used to show that (A) is unimaginable. It cannot even be considered.
