sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 考えられない
text: {考|かんが}えられない is the negative potential form of the る - Verb {考|かんが}える 'to consider'. It will regularly be used after the adverbial particle など (なんか, or なんて), or any expression that nominalizes a phrase, like ということは.
{考|かんが}えられない is regularly translated as '(A) is unimaginable', or '(A) is unthinkable', which is quite close to the literal meaning.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とかんがえられている (N4, Is considered, Is thought of as): These two forms of the verb 考える express opposite sentiments. 考えられない (lit. 'one cannot think') expresses strong disbelief or the idea that something is inconceivable, e.g. 'そんなことは考えられない' ('I can't imagine such a thing'). In contrast, と考えられている indicates a commonly accepted or reasoned belief, often used in formal writing to make statements less direct, e.g. 'これは効果的だと考えられている' ('This is considered effective').

と考えられる (N2, Can be considered as, Is thought to be, One can think that, It is conceivable that): These two forms of the verb 考える express opposite sentiments. 考えられない (lit. 'one cannot think') expresses strong disbelief or the idea that something is inconceivable, e.g. 'そんなことは考えられない' ('I can't imagine such a thing'). と考えられる, on the other hand, expresses a reasoned or likely conclusion, e.g. 'これは自然な結果だと考えられる' ('This can be considered a natural result').

meaning: Possibility, To have, With
summary: A fairly casual expression that is used to highlight the inclusion or possibility of something.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About あり
text: あり itself is the literary form of the う-Verb {有|あ}る 'to be', and is used in a similar way to なし. However, rather than meaning that something is 'without (A)', it shows that something is 'with (A), amongst other things'. This 'amongst other things' is important, as あり will primarily be used when something is being presented as a single possibility among many possibilities.
あり can be and often is used simply as a reply to a statement to indicate agreement, or that the listener thinks that what the speaker is saying is possible.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Occasionally, the kanji {在|あ}る may sometimes also be used. Although the difference between these two kanji is slight, {有|あ}り indicates 'inclusiveness as part of a whole', while {在|あ}り focuses more on 'stand-alone existence'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なし (N3, Without, No): These two phrases come from the existence verb ある and its negative form, and are opposites meaning 'with (A)' or 'without (A)', e.g. '字幕ありで観る' ('watch with subtitles') and '字幕なしで観る' ('watch without subtitles'). They also have opposite figurative meanings, with あり meaning 'possible' or acceptable, and なし used to reject something as an option.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 必ずしも
text: Although it is often considered a stand-alone adverb, {必|かなら}ずしも is a combination of the adverb {必|かなら}ず 'invariably', or 'certainly', and the adverbial particles し and も. し and も are often combined in order to strengthen the meaning of the word before it. Due to this, {必|かならず}ずしも may be translated as something similar to 'absolutely certainly'.

However, {必|かならず}ずしも is an expression that is only used in negative sentences, so is commonly translated as 'not always (A)', 'not entirely (A)', or 'not necessarily (A)'. Despite this, the literal meaning is close to 'not absolutely certainly (A)'. {必|かならず}ずしも is often used at the beginning of a phrase, before expressing something that is not 100% certain.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とは限らない (N3, Not necessarily so, Is not always true, There is no guarantee that): 必ずしも and とは限らない often appear together as a pair in statements expressing that something isn't necessarily always the case, e.g. 必ずしも努力が報われるとは限らない ('Effort doesn't always pay off.'). とは限らない alone can express the same meaning without 必ずしも, but the pairing goes together naturally.

というものでもない (N2, There is no guarantee that…, Not necessarily): Both 必ずしも and というものでもない carry the meaning 'not necessarily', but are used in different ways. 必ずしも precedes a phrase or sentence to emphasize 'not always', and is often used with phrases like とは限らない, e.g. '必ずしもいいとは限らない' ('It's not necessarily good'). というものでもない appears at the end of a sentence and implies a general principle about how things are.

meaning: Formal Conjunctive
summary: A formal conjugation pattern used to say and, then, or several other meanings that could also be implied by て form.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 連用形
text: In Japanese, the conjunctive form is often called 'the ます form', or 'the conjunctive form'. 'The conjunctive form' is much more accurate, as it is used with more than just verbs. Basically, the conjunctive form is the form of any word that will be used in standard conjugation with other structures. For い-Adjectives, this is the form that uses く, for verbs, the ます stem.

The reason that conjunctive form is sometimes referred to as 'the formal conjunctive' is due to its use before a comma. Usually, the conjunction particle て would be used to separate clauses in sentences, however, the formal conjunctive allows this to be done without て. Let's look at some examples.
As we can see, although て is not required, a {読点|とうてん} (Japanese comma) will be required to prevent the sentence from becoming confusing.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: This type of conjugation is seen primarily in formal writing, and the standard て form will be heard much more frequently in daily speech.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Used primarily in written language

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ではなくて・じゃなくて (N3, Not A but B, Conjunctive): 連用形 is a more formal way to connect phrases or clauses, often used in writing. It shares the same basic meaning as the て form. In the case of ではなくて・じゃなくて, the 連用形 becomes ではなく・じゃなく, e.g. 病院ではなく、図書館です 'It's not a hospital, but a library.' (Same meaning, just more formal in tone.)

Verb + て (N5, And, Then (Linking events)): Both 連用形 and the て form connect sequential actions, but 連用形 sounds more formal and is often used in writing. For example, 起きて becomes 起き, e.g. ８時に起きて、朝ご飯を食べました 'I got up at 8 o'clock, then ate breakfast.' → ８時に起き、朝ご飯を食べました. (Same meaning, different register.)

Adjective + て・Noun + で (N5, And... (Conjunctive)): 連用形 also replaces て or で after adjectives and nouns in formal writing. For example, 優しくて becomes 優しく, e.g. とても優しくて、綺麗です 'She's very kind, and pretty.' → とても優しく、綺麗です. (Same meaning, but more formal and literary.)

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Suitable for, Facing
summary: A phrase that highlights something as facing (A), or suitable for (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 向き
text: {向|む}き is another noun in Japanese that is frequently used as a suffix. {向|む}き comes from the intransitive verb {向|む}く, meaning 'to face'. This word is often attached to the end of other nouns, in order to show that something is 'facing (A)', or 'suitable for (A)'.

Due to {向|む}き being intransitive, it usually implies that something is facing toward (A) naturally, or through chance. Because of this, it may convey that something is 'suitable for (A)', but not necessarily designed specifically for it.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 向け (N3, Intended for, Aimed at): Both 向け and 向き describe suitability or orientation, but differ in nuance and intent. 向け refers to something explicitly designed or intended for a specific group or purpose, e.g. '子供向けの番組' ('a program for children'). 向き describes natural suitability without implying deliberate targeting, e.g. '初心者向きのコース' ('a course suited for beginners').

に向かって・に向けて (N2, Towards, To face, To head to): These expressions all involve direction or suitability, but differ in usage. に向かって・に向けて describe motion or intent toward a goal or target, e.g. 'ゴールに向かって走る' ('run toward the goal'). 向き attaches directly to a noun and refers to the appropriateness or orientation of something for a group, without necessarily implying targeted action, e.g. '初心者向きのコース' ('a course suited for beginners').

ため(に) (N3, For, For the sake of, In order to): Both can be translated as 'for (A)', but differ in nuance. 向き attaches directly to a noun and suggests suitability, e.g. 子ども向きの本 ('A book suitable for children') ため(に) connects to nouns with の and suggests intended benefit or purpose, e.g. 子どものための本 ('A book for children [designed to benefit them]')

に合わせて・に合った (N3, In accordance with, Matching, Fitting, Suitable for, Adjust or tune to): Both relate to the idea of being suited to something else, but with different nuances. に合わせて・に合った implies active adjustment to suit a person or situation, e.g. 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ ('Choose clothes to match the season'), while 向き describes suitability or appropriateness by nature, e.g. 初心者向きの本 ('A book suitable for beginners').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Intended for, Aimed at
summary: A phrase that highlights something faced toward (A), or specifically intended for (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 向け
text: {向|む}け is a shortened form of the transitive verb {向|む}ける 'to aim at', and is considered to be a {造語|ぞうご} (neologism). This means a word that was created for a specific purpose, and may not necessarily be used for anything outside of that purpose. The purpose of {向|む}け is to attach to other nouns, in order to express that something is 'intended for (A)', 'aimed at (A)', or 'oriented toward (A)'.
{向|む}け may be seen followed by the case marking particle に (when followed by a phrase), or the case marking particle の, when linked with another noun.
In terms of products and similar items, although {向|む}け highlights that something has been intended for (A), it doesn't necessarily mean that it is limited to (A).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 向き (N3, Suitable for, Facing): Both 向け and 向き describe suitability or orientation, but differ in nuance and intent. 向け refers to something explicitly designed or intended for a specific group or purpose, e.g. '子供向けの番組' ('a program for children'). 向き describes natural suitability without implying deliberate targeting, e.g. '初心者向きのコース' ('a course suited for beginners').

に合わせて・に合った (N3, In accordance with, Matching, Fitting, Suitable for, Adjust or tune to): Both relate to the idea of being suited to something else, but with different nuances. に合わせて・に合った implies active adjustment to suit a person or situation, e.g. 季節に合わせて洋服を選ぶ ('Choose clothes to match the season'), while 向け describes being made for or targeted toward a certain group, e.g. 子供向けのアニメ ('A cartoon for children').

に向かって・に向けて (N2, Towards, To face, To head to): These expressions all involve direction or targeting, but their usage differs. に向かって・に向けて describe motion or intent toward a goal or target, e.g. 'ゴールに向かって走る' ('run toward the goal'). 向け attaches directly to a noun to describe something targeted at a particular group, e.g. '子ども向けのアニメ' ('an anime for children').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Something is finished, To finish something, Something has come to an end, To do something completely, To do something through
summary: A structure used for showing that a particular action has been finished up, or finished to completion.
formation: （Noun + が） + Verb ［stem］ + 上（あ）がります (polite)
（Noun + を） + Verb ［stem］ + 上（あ）げます (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 上がる・上げる
text: When used after the conjunctive form of a verb, either of the verbs {上|あ}げる 'to raise', or {上|あ}がる 'to rise' may be used. They will convey that something has been done 'to the limit'. {上|あ}がる will be used for actions that take place by themselves (intransitive), while {上|あ}げる will be used for actions that have an instigator (transitive).

Although {上|あ}げる and {上|あ}がる show that something has been done 'to the limit', the nuance is usually 'to do (A) to the point of completion', or 'to do (A) through to the end'. Therefore, the 'limit' that is being highlighted is usually a natural ending, and not due to running out of some kind of resource. Let's have a look at some examples.

{上|あ}げる and {上|あ}がる are most commonly used when some kind of effect or product is produced as a result of the (A) action. In these cases, the literal meaning of 'to (A) up' is very similar to 'to finish up (A)' in English.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: 上がる is intransitive, 上げる is transitive

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 抜く (N2, All~, Completely, See through, Overcome, To the bitter end): Both can attach to verb stems to express the completion of an action, but differ in nuance. 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in a finished product, e.g. '論文を書き上げる' ('finish writing a thesis'). 抜く highlights the effort or perseverance involved in following something through to the end, e.g. 'やり抜く' ('see it through').

切る (N3, To do something completely to the end, Utterly, Resolutely): Both can attach to verb stems to express the completion of an action, but differ in nuance. 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in a finished product, e.g. '論文を書き上げる' ('finish writing a thesis'). 切る expresses that something has been done thoroughly or completely, but doesn't necessarily imply a final product, e.g. '読み切る' ('read all the way through') or '使い切る' ('use up').

切れない (N3, Being unable to finish or complete): These phrases are opposites—one expresses a completed action, the other, incompleteness. 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in a finished product, e.g. '論文を書き上げる' ('finish writing a thesis'). 切れない expresses the inability to finish something fully, e.g. '食べ切れなかった' ('I couldn't finish eating it').

はじめる (N4, To start, To begin to): はじめる attaches to verb stems to express 'beginning to' do something, e.g. 作りはじめる 'to start making'. In contrast, 上がる・上げる also attach to verb stems but express completing an action, e.g. 作りあげる 'to finish making', often with a sense of effort or finality.

おわる (N4, To finish, To end): While おわる and 上がる・上げる both attach to verb stems to express finishing an action, their nuances differ. おわる can describe completing any action, e.g. ケーキを食べおわった ('I finished eating the cake.') or 映画を観おわった ('I finished watching a movie.'). 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in some completed product, e.g. 論文を書きあげた ('I finished writing the paper.').

てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): 上がる・上げる can express the idea of completing an action, which overlaps with てしまう・ちゃう, but they differ in nuance. てしまう・ちゃう can express regret or lack of control, while 上がる・上げる focuses on the act of producing a finished result. For example, 書き上げる 'finish writing'. In contrast, てしまう・ちゃう can be used with any verb, regardless of whether a tangible result is produced.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: To do something completely to the end, Utterly, Resolutely
summary: A grammar point that expresses (A) being done completely, or to the cutoff point.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 切る
text: Another verb that is often seen used after the conjunctive form of other verbs is the う - Verb {切|き}る 'to cut'. {切|き}る will give the (A) verb the nuance of being done 'to completion'. However, the 'completion' that is being conveyed with {切|き}る is usually caused by the running out of some kind of resource, like energy. Due to this, {切|き}る is often translated as 'to do (A) to the point of being unable to continue' (or not needing to continue), or 'to totally and utterly do (A)'.

Occasionally, {切|き}る may also be used to show that (A) is being done at 'full pelt', 'full steam', or 'full capacity'. In these cases, it is similar to 'to resolutely do (A)', and just means that 100% effort is being put into the action.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 上がる・上げる (N3, Something is finished, To finish something, Something has come to an end, To do something completely, To do something through): Both can attach to verb stems to express the completion of an action, but differ in nuance. 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in a finished product, e.g. '論文を書き上げる' ('finish writing a thesis'). 切る expresses that something has been done thoroughly or completely, but doesn't necessarily imply a final product, e.g. '読み切る' ('read all the way through') or '使い切る' ('use up').

抜く (N2, All~, Completely, See through, Overcome, To the bitter end): Both can attach to verbs to form compound words. 切る implies thorough completion and intensity, while 抜く emphasizes perseverance and sustained effort through to the end. For example, やり切る suggests 'do it thoroughly', while 考え抜く adds the nuance of overcoming difficulty in the thinking process.

おわる (N4, To finish, To end): Both 切る and おわる attach to verb stems to express finishing an action, but with different nuances. おわる simply marks completion, e.g. 使いおわった ('I finished using it.'). In contrast, 切る often implies using something up, e.g. バターを使い切った ('I used up all the butter.') or doing something to the very end with full effort, e.g. ゴールまで走り切った ('I ran all the way to the finish line.').

込む ② (N3, Remain, To do thoroughly, Deeply, Intensely): Both can attach to verbs to form compound words. 切る emphasizes full completion or decisiveness, e.g. '言い切る' ('say definitively') or '読み切る' ('finish reading'), focusing on doing something thoroughly to its end. 込む conveys depth or intensity of action, e.g. '考え込む' ('get lost in thought'), highlighting depth rather than finality.

切れない (N3, Being unable to finish or complete): These two expressions are opposite in meaning. 切る conveys resolution or the complete execution of an action, e.g. やり切る 'do it all the way' or 使い切る 'use up'. 切れない is its antonym, used to express not being able to see an action through to the end, e.g. 食べ切れない ('I can't finish eating it.').

てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): 切る conveys the idea of doing something completely, which overlaps with one nuance of てしまう・ちゃう, but their usage differs. てしまう・ちゃう can imply that the action was unintentional or against one's will, which 切る cannot. In other words, 食べ切った simply means 'I ate all of it.', while 食べてしまった・食べちゃった also can have the meaning of mean 'I ended up eating it (even though I didn't intend to).', which 食べ切った cannot.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Being unable to finish or complete
summary: A strong phrase expressing that (A) cannot be finished, or cannot reach the cutoff point.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 切れない
text: In the negative-potential form, {切|き}れない will attach to the conjunctive form of other verbs, to express that a particular action is 'unable to be completed'. Let's look at some examples.

Unlike {切|き}る, which usually attaches to verbs to show that something was done to the point of running out, {切|き}れない often implies the exact opposite. This means that the (A) verb cannot be completed specifically because there is too much/many of something in order to finish it.
{切|き}れない may also imply that something cannot be done 'to the point of satisfaction'. In this case, the feeling of dissatisfaction is what the speaker considers too much to overcome.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 上がる・上げる (N3, Something is finished, To finish something, Something has come to an end, To do something completely, To do something through): These phrases are opposites—one expresses a completed action, the other, incompleteness. 上がる・上げる is typically used when the action results in a finished product, e.g. '論文を書き上げる' ('finish writing a thesis'). 切れない expresses the inability to finish something fully, e.g. '食べ切れなかった' ('I couldn't finish eating it').

〜得ない (N2, Unable to, Cannot): Both 切れない and 得ない describe types of impossibility, but with different focuses. 切れない emphasizes physical or circumstantial inability to complete an action, e.g. '読み切れなかった' ('I couldn't finish reading it'). In contrast, 得ない expresses abstract or conceptual impossibility, e.g. '起こり得ない' ('impossible to happen'), and is used for events that cannot realistically occur.

かねる (N2, Cannot, Be unable to, Hard to, Hesitant to): Both 切れない and かねる express inability to do something, but differ in tone and nuance. 切れない describes physical or practical inability to complete an action, e.g. '食べ切れない' ('I can't finish eating it'). かねる conveys emotional or psychological reluctance and often appears in formal or polite refusals, e.g. '分かりかねます' ('I'm afraid I don't know').

切る (N3, To do something completely to the end, Utterly, Resolutely): These two expressions are opposite in meaning. 切る conveys resolution or the complete execution of an action, e.g. やり切る 'do it all the way' or 使い切る 'use up'. 切れない is its antonym, used to express not being able to see an action through to the end, e.g. 食べ切れない ('I can't finish eating it.').

てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): てしまう・ちゃう and 切れない can express opposite meanings. One nuance of てしまう・ちゃう is to do something completely, e.g. 食べてしまった has one potential meaning of 'I ate it all.'. In contrast, 食べ切れなかった would mean 'I couldn't eat all of it.'. Note that てしまう・ちゃう can also express regret or an unintentional action, which 切れない does not. For example, 食べてしまった could also mean 'I ate it (even though I didn't intend to).'.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Only, Just, Since
summary: A phrase that expresses the first and last time or limit for something as the cutoff point.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About きり
text: As an adverbial particle, きり may convey that 'upon (A)', where (A) is usually a verb, that action was the 'first and last time'. This is frequently translated as 'only', 'just', or 'since'. きり comes from the う - Verb {切|き}る 'to cut'. きり is often used after the plain past form of verbs, with nouns, or with counters. Let's look at verbs first.

With verbs, きり is primarily used to show that (A) occurring was all that was required for (B). Usually, this results in some permanent consequence, or permanent change of opinion. In almost every situation, (A) is something that has only happened once, and きり can be interpreted as 'ever since'.

When it comes to the use of きり with nouns or counters, it will express that something is happening with (A) as the limit 'nothing more, nothing less'. In other words, (A) is all that will be included in some particular situation/action.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: きり may also be seen as っきり or キリ. There is no specific change in nuance, but っきり is the most common casual form.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: っきり is more casual than きり

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: しか～ない (N4, There's only, Nothing but): きり and しか～ない can both express the idea of 'only,' but in different ways. きり is used primarily with number+counter expressions, like 一度きり 'only one time' or 二人きり 'only/just the two of us'. In contrast, しか～ない is used with a noun and negative verb to mean 'only' or 'nothing but', e.g. １００円しかない ('I have only 100 yen.'). In some cases, the two can be used together, e.g. 一度きりしか行っていない ('I only went just the once.').

を限りに (N1, As of (the end of), (Starting) from, (No longer) after, By (the), Ending with): Both を限りに and きり mark a point after which something stops or changes, but they differ in formality and nuance. を限りに is a fixed, formal expression used mainly in written or public contexts to indicate a clear and definitive final point, often for events, careers, or official actions, as in 本日を限りに閉店します (‘As of today, we will close for good.’). In contrast, きり is more casual and flexible, commonly used in everyday speech to say that something has not happened again since a certain point, and often used with number + counter expressions such as 一度きりしか会っていない ('I haven't met him except that one time.')

だけ (N5, Only, Just): だけ means 'only' or 'just,' while きり has a more specific nuance. After a past tense verb, きり suggests a permanent change after an event. For example, 日本に行ったきり、戻ってこなかった means 'Once (he) went to Japan, he never returned.' When used after a number + counter (e.g. 一人きり), it emphasizes 'nothing more, nothing less.'

たなり・なり (N1, While... ~ing, Remaining, Not or ever since, Keep or leave): たなり・なり and きり are very similar in meaning, both expressing that a certain state persists without the expected result occurring, and are often interchangeable. For example, in '東京に行ったきり地元に帰って来なかった' ('Once he went to Tokyo, he never came back to his hometown') and '東京に行ったなり地元に帰って来なかった' both convey the same lingering, unresolved situation.

だけしか (N3, To emphasize '~only', Nothing but): きり and だけしか both express limitation, but with different nuance. きり often implies that something has happened only once or hasn't changed since, e.g. 去年会ったきり一度も連絡が来ない 'I haven't heard from them even once since we met last year.' だけしか means 'Nothing but', typically in a way that emphasizes lack or even disappointment, e.g. 千円だけしか持っていない 'I only have 1000 yen.'

まま(に) (N3, As is, While remaining, Left in a state): きり often marks an action done once and left that way, as in 去年会ったきり連絡がない ('I haven't heard from them since we met last year'). まま(に) marks an ongoing unchanged state, as in 靴を履いたまま入らないで ('Don't enter with your shoes on'). Both can imply continuation, but きり emphasizes a cutoff point.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Half-, Not yet finished, About to, Begin to
summary: A word used to show that something is only half-done, or suspended in an unfinished state.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About かけ
text: Being an unofficial helper verb, かけ is what is known as a {造語|ぞうご} (neologism), and carries one specific meaning when used in conjunction with other words. This is similar to {向|む}け. かけ comes from the verb {掛|か}ける 'to suspend', and may be attached to the conjunctive form of other verbs, in order to convey that they are 'unfinished'. Usually this translates as 'half (A)', 'about to (A)', or 'not yet finished (A)'.
かけ behaves like a noun, so may be followed by the case marking particle の when attached directly to another noun, or by だ when at the end of a sentence.
Occasionally, the verb {掛|か}ける itself may be used instead of the noun form, かけ.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たて (N3, Freshly ~ed, Just ~ed): Both かけ and たて describe transitional states of actions, but with opposite timing. かけ refers to something that is incomplete or in progress, often implying interrupted action, e.g. 食べかけのパン 'half-eaten bread'. たて, by contrast, refers to something freshly completed, emphasizing newness and immediacy, e.g. 焼きたてのパン 'freshly baked bread'.

はじめる (N4, To start, To begin to): はじめる attaches to verb stems to mean 'to begin' or 'start' doing something, e.g. 食べはじめる 'to start eating'. In contrast, かけ also attaches to verb stems but indicates something incomplete or in progress, e.g. 食べかけ 'half-eaten'. Forms with かけ function grammatically as nouns, as in 食べかけのバナナ 'a half-eaten banana'.

だす (N4, To suddenly begin, To start doing): かけ and だす both attach to verb stems and can express the start of an action, but their nuance differs. かけ emphasizes that the action has begun but remains incomplete. For example, 書きかけの小説 'a partially written/incomplete novel.' In contrast, だす highlights the beginning of the action, often with a sense of suddenness. For example, 書き出した ('He suddenly started writing.').

るところだ (N4, About to, On the verge of): ところだ and かけ both express incomplete actions, but with a key difference. るところだ emphasizes that the action is just about to happen, e.g. リンゴを食べるところだ ('I'm about to eat an apple.'). かけ indicates the action has started but isn't finished, e.g. 食べかけのリンゴ ('a half-eaten apple').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Over (a period), From ~ until, Through
summary: An expression used to highlight a duration of time during which a certain action will be suspended in an ongoing state.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About にかけて
text: Coming from the る - Verb {掛|か}ける 'to suspend', にかけて conveys that something is happening 'over a period of time', 'from (A) until (B)', or 'all through (A)'. This grammar structure is a combination of the case marking particle に, and {掛|か}ける combined with the conjunction particle て. Literally, the meaning can be thought of as follows:
に - Marks (A) as the location/state.
{掛|か}けて - States that something is 'suspended' (in an ongoing process) in that location/state.
The 'something' that is an ongoing process will usually be indicated by a (B) part of the sentence. This expression will primarily be used with nouns.
にかけて is primarily used in written language, although it appears quite often in the news as well, indicating that some weather pattern is expected to continue for a set period of time.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: There is another use of にかけては that indicates that someone/something is remarkable in a certain field

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にわたって (N2, Across, Throughout, Extends, Over (a period of time or range)): にかけて and にわたって both describe range or extent, but differ in specificity. にかけて implies an approximate span in time or space, e.g. '九州から関西にかけて' ('from Kyushu through Kansai'). にわたって emphasizes coverage over a broad, often deliberate range, e.g. '三日間にわたって会議が開かれた' ('The conference was held over three days').

にかけては (N2, When it comes to, Regarding, Concerning): にかけては and にかけて share the same base expression but serve different functions. にかけて indicates a loose span of time or space, e.g. 九州から関西にかけて ('from Kyushu through Kansai'), while にかけては means 'when it comes to (A)' and introduces a topic that is evaluated positively. For example, 音楽にかけては自信がある ('when it comes to music, I'm confident').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Freshly ~ed, Just ~ed
summary: A word which indicates that (A) was just done, or freshly done. The finished product has just been established.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About たて
text: たて, coming from the verb {立|た}てる 'to stand' is a suffix in Japanese that is often used after the conjunctive form of verbs. たて conveys that something has 'just been finished', or is 'freshly finished'.
As a suffix, たて transforms verbs into nouns. This means that they may be followed by a (B) phrase, or followed directly by the case marking particle の and a noun.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たところだ (N4, Just finished doing, Was just doing): たところだ and たて are similar in that both refer to something that has just happened, but they differ in usage and nuance. たところだ uses the past tense of a verb and simply describes the timing, e.g. パンを焼いたところだ ('I just baked some bread.'). In contrast, たて attaches to verb stems and has the nuance of 'freshly done/finished', e.g. 焼きたてのパンが一番美味しい ('Freshly baked bread is the most delicious.').

かけ (N3, Half-, Not yet finished, About to, Begin to): Both かけ and たて describe transitional states of actions, but with opposite timing. かけ refers to something that is incomplete or in progress, often implying interrupted action, e.g. 食べかけのパン 'half-eaten bread'. たて, by contrast, refers to something freshly completed, emphasizing newness and immediacy, e.g. 焼きたてのパン 'freshly baked bread'.

たばかり (N4, Just did, Something just happened): Both express recency but differ in usage. たばかり follows た-form verbs to show something just happened, e.g. 焼いたばかり 'just baked'. たて attaches to stems and means 'freshly done', e.g. 焼きたてのパン 'freshly-baked bread'.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: To go into, To put into
summary: A structure expressing that the action of (A) will be done into something else. With the nuance of jamming or pressing through any obstacles.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 込む ①
text: In Japanese, the う - Verb {込|こ}む 'to jam into' is frequently used as a suffix to convey several different meanings. The primary meanings are as follows:
(A) {込|こ}む - To enter completely into doing (A), or the state of being in (A).
(A) {込|こ}む - To enter a state of doing (A) that will not be considered complete until 'success'.
(A) {込|こ}む - To enter a state of doing (A) that cannot be escaped from.

In this lesson, we will exclusively focus on the first meaning, which is usually translated as 'to put into (A)', or 'to go into (A)'. This form will be attached to the conjunctive form of other verbs.

Despite the multiple meanings, {込|こ}む can almost always be thought of as 'jamming (B) into (A)'. This means that whatever the (A) action is, will be something that is not easily entered, but also not easily escaped from.

sections.label: Compare

The second suggests intensity, depth, or duration of an action, as in 考え込む ('think deeply') or 座り込む ('sit down and refuse to move').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Remain, To do thoroughly, Deeply, Intensely
summary: A grammar point expressing that the action of (A) will be done deeply or thoroughly. With the nuance of jamming or pressing through any obstacles.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 込む ②
text: In Japanese, the う - Verb {込|こ}む 'to jam into' is frequently used as a suffix to convey several different meanings. The primary meanings are as follows:
(A) {込|こ}む - To enter completely into doing (A), or the state of being in (A).
(A) {込|こ}む - To enter a state of doing (A) that will not be considered complete until 'success'.
(A) {込|こ}む - To enter a state of doing (A) that cannot be escaped from.

In this lesson, we will exclusively focus on the second and third meanings, which are usually translated as 'to remain in (A)', 'to thoroughly do (A)', 'to do (A) deeply', or 'to do (A) intensely'. This form will be attached to the conjunctive form of other verbs.

Despite the multiple meanings, {込|こ}む can almost always be thought of as 'jamming (B) into (A)'. This means that whatever the (A) action is, will be something that is not easily entered, but also not easily escaped from.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 込む ① (N3, To go into, To put into ): 込む can be added to verb stems to express two nuances. The first is inward or inserted movement, as in 放り込む ('throw in') or 読み込む ('read in', such as reading data into a computer). The second suggests intensity, depth, or duration of an action, as in 考え込む ('think deeply') or 座り込む ('sit down and refuse to move').

切る (N3, To do something completely to the end, Utterly, Resolutely): Both can attach to verbs to form compound words. 切る emphasizes full completion or decisiveness, e.g. '言い切る' ('say definitively') or '読み切る' ('finish reading'), focusing on doing something thoroughly to its end. 込む conveys depth or intensity of action, e.g. '考え込む' ('get lost in thought'), highlighting depth rather than finality.

おわる (N4, To finish, To end): Both 込む and おわる attach to verb stems but express different nuances. おわる simply marks the end of an action, e.g. ケーキを食べおわった ('I finished eating the cake.') or 映画を観おわった ('I finished watching a movie.'). 込む adds the sense of doing something thoroughly and staying in that state, e.g. 黙り込んだ ('He fell completely silent and stayed that way.').

meaning: To pretend, To act as if
summary: A structure that implies that someone is pretending to do or be (A), by taking on its outward appearance.
formation: Verb［ている］(1) + ふりをする
Noun + の + ふりをする
Verb［ている］(1) + ふりをします (polite)
［な］Adjective + な + ふりをします (polite)
Noun + の + ふりをします (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ふりをする
text: ふりをする is an expression in Japanese that is used to show that someone is 'pretending to be (A)', 'putting on airs of (A)', or 'acting as if (A)'. This construction comes from a combination of the noun {振|ふ}り 'a shake', the case marking particle を, and する. It can be thought of as meaning 'to give off the impression of (A)', or 'to shake off the impression of (A)'.
As ふり itself is a noun, this expression may be used with the attributive form of any other word.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: The noun {振|ふ}り has several different nuances in Japanese, with only one of them being used in this particular expression. That meaning is 'to show a certain behavior pattern on the outside'. Due to this, ふり doesn't specifically mean 'to pretend', just that what is happening on the outside may be different to what is happening within a person (either mentally or physically).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): Both ふりをする and っぽい describe imitation or resemblance, but with a key difference in nuance. ふりをする implies pretending to be or do something one is not, as in 知ったふりをする ('pretend to know'). In contrast, っぽい conveys a natural resemblance or tendency, often unconscious or inherent, as in 子供っぽい ('childish').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: If possible
summary: A hypothetical construction which indicates that if (A) is doable, it should be done.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About できれば・できたら
text: Remembering that する has no potential form, the replacement る - Verb できる 'to amount to' will often be used in conjunction with particles, to indicate whether the possibility of amounting to something exists. The conjunction particles ば or たら will most frequently be used. できれば and できたら are usually translated simply as 'if possible'.
Both できれば and できたら will come at the start of a sentence, before the following statement will express some (desired) outcome.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: As ば and たら are the only 'hypothetical' indicators that can express the process toward potential outcomes, using なら or と would be be illogical. This can be visualized as follows:
(A) できると - Will express the result after achieving (A), not what is required to get there.

(A) できるなら - As なら is just the hypothetical form of だ, It is used to make guesses about what could happen if the situation of (A) exists, not how that situation can be used to produce some other result.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものなら① (N2, If, If one could, If something would be possible): できれば・できたら and ものなら both express possibilities, but differ in tone and implication. できれば・できたら is a relatively casual and neutral way to say 'if possible', often used for ordinary requests or wishes. ものなら sounds more formal and can convey a stronger emotional desire, often about something difficult or unrealistic, as in できるものなら ('if only it were possible').

なるべく (N4, As ~ as possible, Wherever practicable): なるべく and できれば・できたら both mean 'to the extent possible', but differ in nuance. なるべく implies doing something as much or as often as possible over time, e.g. 'whenever possible.' できれば・できたら typically are used when referring to a single situation or request, like 'if possible'.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: If it is alright, If you don't mind, If you would like, If possible
summary: A hypothetical phrase asking if (A) is good, or if proceeding with (A) will be good.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About でよければ
text: でよければ is an expression that is constructed with the case marking particle で, and the potential form of the い-Adjective いい, よければ. The literal meaning of 'if with (A) is good/fine', or 'if by (A) is good/fine' is quite similar to the standard translation, which is 'if (A) is ok'.
でよければ will always follow nouns or noun-phrases.
でよければ is a phrase that is often used in relation to oneself, in order to politely offer some sort of help, advice, or service.
As で is being used in its standard meaning of 'with' or 'by', でよければ implies that the speaker is enquiring whether the quality/ability of (A) is good enough to achieve some specific result.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てもかまわない (N3, It doesn't matter if, I don't mind): でよければ and てもかまわない both express acceptance, but from different perspectives. でよければ is most often used to modestly present something as an option, e.g. 私でよければお手伝いします ('If I'm acceptable, I'll help'). In contrast, てもかまわない is used to allow or grant permission, e.g. 使ってもかまわない ('I don't mind if you use it').

Verb + てもいい (N5, It's okay to, It's alright to, Can/may): The ても form means 'even if.' One common use is Verb + てもいい, which gives or asks for permission (e.g. 食べてもいい？ = 'Can I eat this?') A related pattern is でよければ, which uses the conditional form of いい (よければ) to mean 'if it's okay.' It's often used to make polite offers, like 私でよければお手伝いします ('If I'm okay [as a choice], I'll help').

examples.ja: {焼|や}き{肉|にく}**でよければ**、うちの{近|ちか}くに{美味|おい}しいところがあるから、そこに{行|い}かない？

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: As soon as
summary: An expression that states that as soon as (A), (B), with (A) determining the involuntary sequence of (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 次第
text: {次第|しだい} is a noun that is often translated in different ways, depending on what type of word it follows. In this lesson, we will look at the meaning associated with the conjunctive form of standard verbs, and the stem of する verbs. Although it is a noun, {次第|しだい} may also be classified simply as a suffix in many cases.
Basically,
{次第|しだい}
means 'next in sequence after (A)', and is often translated to 'as soon as (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: にかかわる (N2, To relate to, To have to do with, Concerning, Depends on): 次第 emphasizes timing or sequencing, used to express that one action is a condition for the next, which will follow immediately. For example, 準備ができ次第出発します ('As soon as preparations are done, we'll depart'). にかかわる focuses on relevance or importance, describing how something affects or relates to another matter. For example, 命にかかわる問題 ('a matter of life').

次第だ・次第で (N2, Depending on, So): Both of these expressions use 次第 but differ slightly in usage. 次第 alone attaches to verb stems to emphasize timing or sequencing, expressing that one action is a condition for the next. For example, 終わり次第連絡します ('I'll contact you as soon as I'm finished'). 次第だ・次第で, by contrast, introduces conditional relationships or dependence. For example, 努力次第で結果は変わる ('The results will depend on your effort').

直ちに (N3, At once, Immediately, As soon as): Both 直ちに and 次第 can imply prompt timing, but differ in grammatical usage and nuance. 直ちに is used before phrases and emphasizes urgency, e.g. '直ちに避難してください' ('Please evacuate immediately'). 次第 attaches to verb stems to suggest one action happening immediately after another, e.g. '準備ができ次第、出発します' ('We'll leave as soon as we're ready').

によって・による (N3, By means of, According to, Depending on, Because of, Due to): Both describe how one thing leads to another, but with different nuance. 次第 emphasizes immediacy, e.g. 方法が決まり次第連絡します ('I'll contact you as soon as the method is decided.') によって・による shows variation or dependence, e.g. 方法によって結果が変わる ('The result changes depending on the method.')

たとたんに (N3, The instant or moment, As soon as, Just as): Both describe sequences where one action quickly follows another, but differ in tone and formality. 次第 is formal and indicates that an action will follow as soon as another is completed, e.g. '会議が終わり次第、報告します' ('I'll report as soon as the meeting ends'). たとたんに emphasizes sudden or unexpected results, often in conversation, e.g. 'ドアを開けたとたんに猫が飛び出した' ('The moment I opened the door, the cat jumped out').

なり (N1, As soon as, The moment, When): Both なり and 次第 indicate immediacy but differ in tone and nuance. なり is a neutral expression suggesting a spontaneous or automatic reaction. For example, 布団に入るなり寝た ('He fell asleep as soon as he got in his futon'). 次第 has a more formal tone and is often used in business contexts to show that something happens immediately after a condition is met. For example, 終わり次第ご連絡します ('I'll contact you as soon as I'm finished').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: In that way, Exactly, Precisely, Just as
summary: A phrase that expresses agreement about (A), due to the logic following the same road.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About とおり
text: Often, the noun とおり carries the meaning of 'in that way', or 'just like that'. In its kanji form, とおり will be written as {通|とお}り, and literally means 'street', or 'way'. However, it is regularly used to indicate the level of 'sameness' one thing has with another. This 'sameness' meaning appears when とおり is used as a suffix.
とおり (or どおり) may be used with verbs or nouns. In the case of verbs, it is common to see it being used after both the plain form, and the simple-past form.
Both どおり and のとおり may be used directly after nouns. However, とおり will only be used when the case marking particle の comes between the noun and とおり.

While both of these structures may be used interchangeably, どおり is more common, especially in speech.

Fun FactConstructions like {言|い}った{通|とお}り and その{通|とお}り are used very frequently, simply as a polite way to agree with what has been said by another. In these cases, it translates similarly to 'that's exactly right', or 'that's it!'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ように・ような (N4, As・like, Just like): Both とおり and ように・ような can express doing something in a similar way, but their nuance differs. とおり implies doing something exactly as described, while ように・ような suggests general similarity. For example, 言われたとおりにした ('I did exactly as I was told.') vs. 言われたようにした ('I did it as I was told.'), where the latter is less precise and emphatic about how closely the speaker followed instructions.

れる・られる + ままに (N1, Do as (one is told or ordered…), In accordance with, In compliance with, Just like): Both convey the idea of doing something in precisely a certain way, but differ in nuance. れる・られる + ままに implies passivity or being compelled by external forces. For example, 言われるがままにやった ('I did as told'). とおり can be used similarly, as in 言われたとおりにやった ('I did it just as I was told'), but also appears in neutral contexts. For example, レシピのとおりに作った ('I made it exactly according to the recipe').

まま(に) (N1, As (one likes, feels or pleases), Spur of the moment, Wherever one fancies, Spontaneously, On a whim): Both まま(に) and とおり express doing something in a certain way, but differ in nuance. まま(に) emphasizes leaving things as they are or acting spontaneously. For example, 思うままに話す ('Speak as you feel'). とおり stresses replication or faithful adherence. For example, レシピのとおりに作った ('I made it exactly according to the recipe').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Be also, It also is
summary: A construction showing that while something is (A), it is also even (B). Also even exists as (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About でもある
text: As an extension of the formal version of the auxiliary verb だ, である, でもある simply conveys that something 'is also (B)'. However, as も often shows something that is surprising or unexpected, でもある will primarily be used to describe additional facts about (A) that may be unexpected. Due to this, でもある usually fills the (B) role in sentences like 'while (A), it is also (B)', or 'in spite of (A), it is also (B)'.
でもある may be used after nouns, or な-Adjectives.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: も (N5, Also, Too, As well, Even, Either, Neither): でもある and も can both express 'also' (the も of でもある is the same as the particle も), but there is a key difference to note. AもB means '(A) is also (B)', while Aでもある means 'it is also (A)'. For example, compare 田中さんは学生です。鈴木さんも学生です ('Tanaka is a student. Suzuki is also a student') vs. 田中さんは学生です。日本人でもあります ('Tanaka is a student. He is also Japanese').

と同時に (N3, At the same time as, The instant, The moment, As well as): でもある and と同時に can both express the idea of 'also' or '(A) as well as (B)', though they function differently. と同時に follows the first item of information, while でもある follows the additional information. Because they appear in different parts of a sentence, they can also be used together. For example, ピアニストであると同時に、作曲家でもあります ('In addition to being a pianist, he is also a composer').

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Regardless of, No matter what
summary: A construction stating that no matter how the issue of (A) is even handled, the result will not change.
formation: Verb + と + どうしても

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About どうしても
text: どうしても is a construction in Japanese that is often considered to be a stand-alone adverb meaning 'no matter how', or 'regardless of anything'. Originally, it is a combination of the adverb どう 'how', the て-form of する, and the adverbial particle も, meaning 'to even do'.
どうしても will regularly be used at the beginning of sentences before conveying something that is considered by the speaker to be 'absolutely true'.
Alternatively, どうしても may be used after verbs, following the conjunction particle と. This will express that 'if (A) happens, (B) is unavoidable'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: たって (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter how): どうしても and たって are similar in that both express ideas like 'even' or 'no matter', but they are used differently. どうしても appears at the beginning of a sentence to convey 'no matter what'. For example, どうしても勝ちたい ('I want to win no matter what'). たって is a casual verb ending that functions like ても. In fact, どうしても can be expressed more colloquially as どうしたって.

にしても～にしても (N2, Regardless of whether): どうしても and にしても～にしても both express the idea that something happens regardless of differing conditions. どうしても begins a sentence to show strong intent or inevitability, e.g. どうしても勝ちたい ('I want to win no matter what'). にしても～にしても is used to list contrasting cases and state that the outcome remains unchanged. For example, 上手にしても下手にしても ('Whether you're good or bad at it').

にかかわらず (N2, Regardless of, Whether or, No matter, With or without): どうしても and にかかわらず both mean 'no matter' or 'regardless of', but differ in usage. どうしても appears at the beginning of a sentence to express strong will or inevitability. For example, どうしても勝ちたい ('I want to win no matter what'). にかかわらず usually follows nouns or question phrases and shows that something remains unchanged regardless of conditions. For example, 年齢にかかわらず参加できます ('You can participate regardless of age').

にせよ・にしろ (N2, Even if, Even though, No matter, Whether… or): どうしても and にせよ・にしろ both express that something happens regardless of conditions, but differ in nuance and structure. どうしても comes at the start of a sentence to show persistence or inevitability, as in どうしても勝ちたい ('I want to win no matter what'). にせよ・にしろ presents hypothetical cases and emphasizes that the outcome won't change. For example, 雨にせよ雪にせよ中止しない ('We won't cancel whether it rains or snows').

どんなに〜ても (N3, No matter how): どんなに〜ても means 'no matter how' and emphasizes that an outcome remains unchanged even under extreme or difficult conditions, e.g. どんなに努力しても勝てない ('No matter how hard I try, I can't win'). On the other hand, どうしても expresses strong intent or inevitability, often meaning 'no matter what' or 'at any cost', e.g. どうしても行きたい ('I want to go no matter what'). It can reflect either persistence or a lack of alternatives.

いくら〜でも (N3, No matter how (much)): どうしても and いくら〜でも both express emphasis but in different ways. どうしても is used when something must happen or when the speaker is determined, e.g. どうしても行きたい ('I want to go no matter what'). いくら〜でも means 'no matter how much' or 'how many', often used with amounts or degrees to show that the outcome won't change, e.g. いくら頼んでも無理です ('No matter how much you ask, it's impossible').

を問わず (N2, Regardless of, Whether or not, No matter, With or without): どうしても and を問わず share the meaning of 'no matter' or 'regardless of', but are used differently. どうしても appears at the beginning of a sentence to express persistence or inevitability. For example, どうしても勝ちたい ('I want to win no matter what'). を問わず usually follows nouns or question words and shows that something holds true regardless of conditions. For example, 年齢を問わず参加できます ('You can participate regardless of age').

とも (N2, Even if, No matter): どうしても and とも both express the meaning of 'even if' or 'no matter', but differ in formality and placement. どうしても comes at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize determination, as in どうしても勝ちたい ('I want to win no matter what'). とも is a verb ending, often more formal or literary than ても. For example, 彼女が何と言おうとも ('No matter what she says') is equivalent in meaning to 彼女が何と言っても, but more formal.

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

slug: もしも～なら・もしも～でも
pattern: もしも～なら・もしも～でも
meaning: If, Supposing
summary: A strong hypothetical phrase which indicates that even supposing if (A), (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About もしも～なら・もしも～でも
text: もしも is an adverb in Japanese that strengthens the base meaning of もし 'a bit'. Therefore, the literal meaning of もしも is 'even a bit'. Despite this, as もし and もしも are almost exclusively paired with sentences that use some sort of assumption, or 'hypothesis' based expression, もしも will often be translated as 'supposing that'.
もしも will be used at the beginning of sentences that include almost any form of hypothesis expression. For example, ば, と, なら, or ても.
Although もしも is considered a stand-alone adverb, it is just a combination of もし, and the adverbial particle も.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: もし (N4, If (For emphasis)): もし is typically used at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize that what follows is a hypothetical situation or condition, similar to the English 'if' or 'supposing that (A)'. もしも is a more emphatic version of this, and sentences with もしも almost always contain a conditional expression, as seen in the もしも～なら・もしも～でも pattern. The specific meaning is determined by the conditional, e.g. もしも～なら 'if (A)' vs. もしも～でも 'even if (A)'.

でも (N4, Or something, Any... (with question words), No matter (who)): もしも～なら and もしも～でも emphasize a hypothetical situation, similar to 'supposing that (A)' or 'even if (A)' in English. Separately, でも can attach to question words to mean 'any~', e.g. 誰でも 'anyone' and なんでも 'anything', or follow regular nouns to suggest a casual option, as in お茶でも飲みませんか？ ('Want some tea or something?').

ても (N4, Even if, Even though): ても is a highly versatile structure meaning 'even if,' used widely in both speech and writing. In contrast, ようが～まいが is much more formal and mainly found in written or academic contexts. Both forms can express 'whether or not'. For example, 食べても食べなくても and 食べようが食べまいが both mean 'whether or not (you) eat', but the latter is more emphatic and formal.

たとえ〜ても (N3, Even if…is the case, Supposing that): Both introduce hypothetical situations, but with different nuances. たとえ〜ても sets up contrast, like 'Even if (A), still (B)', e.g. たとえ負けても悔いはない 'Even if I lose, I'll have no regrets.' もしも～なら・～でも expresses a basic hypothetical and its result, e.g. もしも彼が来たら、話します 'If he comes, I'll talk to him.'

なら (N4, Were it, If, If it's the case, As for (Conditional)): なら is a conditional that follows phrases to mean 'if it's the case that (A)', often implying the condition is likely or assumed. もしも adds emphasis to the hypothetical nature of a situation and is placed at the beginning, e.g. もしも雨なら 'if it were to rain'. It can also appear with でも, e.g. もしも雨でも 'even if it rains' (implying 'I'll still go', etc.).

chapterTitle: Do it this Way, Did it that Way

meaning: Fellow, With each other, Mutually, Between, Among, Together, With
summary: A word expressing that groups of people are in the same role, or (A) is being done between people in that same position.
formation: Noun + 同士（どうし） + の + Noun

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 同士
text: {同士|どうし} 'fellow' is a noun that may be used in the same way as a suffix. When used this way, it conveys things that are 'mutually (A)', 'fellow (A)', or '(A) together'.

To use {同士|どうし}, attach it directly to the end of another noun, before expressing further information about that 'mutual' relationship. Alternatively, (noun + {同士|どうし} + の + noun) is also common, and expresses that noun (B) is a grouped form of noun (A).
{同士|どうし} is used most often to express two different types of 'mutuality'. These are as follows:
{種類|しゅるい} - Type. (A) is the same type as (B).
{関係|かんけい} - Relationship. (A) shares the same relationship as (B).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ～のうち(で) (N2, Of the, Among(st)): Both ～のうち(で) and 同士 describe relationships within a group, but differ in nuance. ～のうち(で) indicates selection from a group, e.g. ３人のうちで誰が一番早い？ ('Who is the fastest among the three?'). 同士 emphasizes mutual relationships or shared characteristics, e.g. 学生同士で助け合う ('Help each other as students').

のなかで (N4, In, Among, Within): のなかで and 同士 can both refer to groups or relationships, but their meanings and usage differ. のなかで means 'among' and is used to highlight one or more members within a group, e.g. サッカー選手の中で誰が好き？ ('Among soccer players, who do you like?'). 同士, on the other hand, emphasizes mutual relationships, e.g. サッカー選手同士で話し合った means 'They talked as fellow soccer players.'.

meaning: Hard to, Difficult to
summary: A phrase that focuses on the difficulty of (A), in relation to the task itself being hard.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がたい
text: Coming from the same kanji as {難|むずか}しい 'difficult', {難|がた}い is a suffix that also means 'difficult'. However, in the case of がたい, it will be attached to the conjunctive form of verbs, and conveys that '(A) is difficult to do'. がたい is almost always written without kanji in this meaning.

Compared to にくい, which can simply imply that something is 'uncomfortable' to do, がたい refers almost exclusively to {困難|こんなん}であること 'things that involve a high degree of difficulty, distress, or infeasibility'. Due to this, がたい will come across as far stronger than にくい, and may imply that a certain task is almost impossible.
Summed up, these nuances basically translate as the following:
にくい - Something is difficult based on someone's opinion, experience, or general feeling.
がたい - Something is difficult based on the task itself having a high level of difficulty.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ようがない・ようもない (N2, There's no way to, It's impossible to): Both ようがない・ようもない and がたい express difficulty or unfeasibility of an action, but differ in nuance. ようがない・ようもない conveys that there is no way or means to do something. For example, 連絡のしようがない ('There's no way to contact him'). がたい, on the other hand, indicates that something is very difficult to do, often due to factors beyond the speaker's control. For example, 信じがたい話だ ('It's a story that is hard to believe').

にくい (N4, Difficult to, Hard to): がたい and にくい both attach to verb stems and express the idea of 'difficult to do', but with different nuance and formality levels. にくい is used in everyday speech and reflects the speaker's personal sense of difficulty or discomfort. がたい is more formal/written-style and implies something is nearly impossible or extremely difficult due to factors beyond the speaker's control.

meaning: I never dreamed, Never, No way, Don't tell me, You don't say
summary: A strong word which emphasizes the following phrase as being unbelievable, or shocking.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About まさか
text: Almost always written purely in hiragana, まさか is a combination of まさ, a noun meaning 'precise', or 'exact', and the adverbial particle か. In modern Japanese, まさか is thought of as a single adverb meaning 'it can't be true', 'no way', or 'don't tell me'.
As it is treated primarily as an adverb, まさか will most often appear at the beginning of a sentence, before some statement about what the speaker is shocked/surprised about.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: なんか・なんて (N3, Such as, Things like, Emphasis): まさか and なんか・なんて are both used to express surprise, but function in different ways. まさか comes at the beginning of a sentence to emphasize that what follows goes against the speaker's expectations, while なんて appears at the end of a sentence or phrase to express the same. Because they fill different roles, they are often used together. For example, まさか勝てるなんて！ ('To think we could win!' / 'I never thought we could win').

とは (N1, That..., (Surprised) that..., (Never expected) that..., (Shocked) that...): Both expressions can be used to convey shock and surprise, though how they function in a sentence differs. まさか precedes whatever the speaker is surprised about, e.g. まさか勝てるなんて ('To think they could win!'), or even on its own as an interjection, i.e. まさか！ ('No way!). In contrast, とは always follows what the speaker is surprised about, and can pair with まさか for further emphasis, e.g. まさか勝てるとは (same meaning as the above example).

reading: {前者|ぜんしゃ}は～{後者|こうしゃ}は
meaning: The former ~ the latter, The first ~ the second
summary: A slightly formal construction used for indicating the former and latter cases in a description of (A).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 前者は・後者は
text: Used in almost exactly the same way as 'the former' and 'the latter' in English, {前者|ぜんしゃ} and {後者|こうしゃ} are two nouns that appear frequently in Japanese. The adverbial particle は will appear after these words, to express contrast between the two.

{前者|ぜんしゃ} will be used for 'the former', while {後者|こうしゃ} will represent 'the latter'. Both {前者|ぜんしゃ} and {後者|こうしゃ} appear at the beginning of their own statements, with a specific comment about each being made after は.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: まえに (N5, Before, In front of): まえに is used to express the relative timing of actions and often follows a plain (non-past) verb to mean 'before doing A.' In contrast, 前者 (the former) and 後者 (the latter) refer to things previously mentioned. They're used to avoid repeating a word or phrase, similar to how we use 'the former' and 'the latter' in English.

あとで (N4, After, Later): 前者は and 後者は, like あとで, relate to sequence, but in different ways. あとで (also written in kanji as 後で) refers to the order of actions, like 'after doing (A)'. 前者 and 後者 mean 'the former' and 'the latter', pointing back to the previously mentioned items.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About つい
text: Appearing most frequently at the beginning of sentences, つい is an adverb that may be translated as 'accidentally', 'unconsciously', 'absentmindedly', or 'against one's better judgment'. つい will often be paired with statements that use てしまう, to emphasize that something was unintentional.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Usually ends with てしまう

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てしまう・ちゃう (N4, To do something by accident, To finish completely・totally, Unfortunately): つい and てしまう・ちゃう can both express doing something unintentionally or against one's better judgment. つい appears at the beginning of a sentence or phrase, while てしまう・ちゃう is a verb ending. They are often used together to emphasize the nuance of regret or unintentionally, e.g. つい食べてしまった・つい食べちゃった would imply 'I ended up eating it (even though I didn't mean to).'.

いつの間にか (N2, Suddenly, Unnoticed, Without noticing, Too soon): Both describe actions that occur without full conscious control, but they differ in nuance. いつの間にか emphasizes that something happened without the speaker noticing, e.g. いつの間にか春になっていた ('Before I knew it, spring had come.'). つい highlights that an action was done inadvertently or against one's better judgment, and often pairs with 〜てしまう or 〜ちゃう, e.g. つい甘いものを食べてしまった ('I ended up eating sweets without meaning to.').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About せいで
text: Although written almost exclusively in hiragana, せい is a noun that may be better understood from its kanji, {所為|せい}, meaning 'doings'. せい is used to convey negative results that occurred due to the behavior or actions of another person/thing. Because of this, common translations of せい are 'fault', 'due to', or 'because of'.

As せい is a noun, it may be used after the attributive form of any other word. The case marking particle で will also regularly be seen after せい, especially when conveying the (B) result that occurred 'with' or 'by means of' those 'doings'.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Can express blame or fault, で can be omitted at the end of a sentence

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: おかげで (N3, Thanks to, Because of): Both mean 'because of', but with opposite tone. おかげで expresses a thankful cause, e.g. 先生のおかげで合格できた ('Thanks to my teacher, I passed.') せいで places blame for something negative, e.g. 雨のせいで試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled because of the rain.')

ために (N3, Due to, Because of, As a result of): ために and せいで can both mean 'due to (A)', but with a difference in tone. せいで almost always implies a negative or undesirable result. ために can be used with either positive or negative nuance. Also, ために can mean 'for the purpose of (A)', which せいで cannot.

そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): Both せいで and そのため(に) show cause and effect, but せいで follows a word or phrase and implies a negative result or blame, e.g. 台風のせいで試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled because of the typhoon'), while そのため(に) is used at the beginning of the sentence and neutrally shows a logical result of whatever was previously stated. そのため(に) can also express 'for the purpose of (A)', which is a nuance せいで cannot have.

につき (N2, Due to, On account of, Each or every): Both せいで and につき express cause, but with different nuance and tone. せいで is more colloquial and typically introduces a cause for a negative result, e.g. 雨のせいで試合が中止になった ('The game was canceled because of the rain.'). につき states a reason more neutrally and is often used in formal written announcements, e.g. 工事中につき通行止め ('Closed to traffic due to construction.').

meaning: Even though, And yet, Despite
summary: A phrase that expresses contempt or criticism that despite (A), (B) did not occur.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About くせに
text: {癖|くせ} is a noun that means 'habit' or 'tendency'. However, as it usually refers to a negative thing, 'vice' is another accurate translation. くせに (usually appearing without kanji) is the combination of くせ, and the case marking particle に. This structure is often used to criticize the actions of others, and is used in a similar way to 'despite', 'even though', or 'and yet' in English.
As くせ is a noun, くせに may be used after the attributive form of any other word.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: {癖|くせ} is a word that has developed a 'negative' meaning over time. Originally, {癖|くせ} was used to convey a preference, or the side that someone or something tended to lean toward (due to it being favorable for some reason). When adding the case marking particle に to this, it merely expressed that (A) was the preferable state/location, so (B) not being/not acting in a way appropriate for (A) is less than desirable.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: つつ(も) (N2, Even while ~ing, Even though ~ing, Despite ~ing, Although ~ing): Both くせに and つつ(も) express contradiction, but differ in tone. くせに is a casual expression with a blaming or critical tone, e.g. 知っているくせに何で教えてくれないの？ ('You know, so why won't you tell me!?'). つつ(も) is neutral and used to describe conflicting simultaneous actions, e.g. 危険だと知りつつも行った ('I went despite knowing at the same time that it was dangerous.').

が (N5, But, However): くせに expresses disapproval, similar to 'in spite of' or 'although' in English. In contrast, が is a neutral connecting particle, often expressing contrast (like 'but') or adding information (like 'and'). Unlike くせに, which carries a negative nuance, が is neutral. After な-Adjectives and nouns, くせに requires な or の, while が requires だ or です.

ながらも (N3, But, Even while, Even though, Despite, Although): ながらも and くせに both express contradiction, but differ in nuance. ながらも simply expresses two seemingly contradictory states coexisting in a neutral fashion, e.g. 緊張しながらもわくわくしている ('While feeling anxious, I'm also excited.'). In contrast, くせに implies blame or criticism, e.g. 知っているくせに教えてくれない ('Even though he knows, he won't tell me.').

それでも (N4, But still, And yet, Even so, Nevertheless): それでも and くせに both express contrast, but differ in tone. それでも is neutral, like the English 'even so'. くせに adds a critical nuance, often pointing out something negative or unjustified, e.g. 若いくせにやる気がない ('Even though he's young, he has no motivation.'), which implies disapproval.

のに (N4, Despite, Although, Even though): Both のに and くせに express contrast, but with different nuance. のに is relatively neutral, like 'although', while くせに adds a strong negative or critical tone. For example, 頭がいいのにやる気がない and 頭がいいくせにやる気がない both mean 'Although (he's) smart, (he) has no motivation.', the のに version is just stating a fact, while the くせに version implies that his lack of motivation is a negative trait and not befitting of him.

にもかかわらず (N2, Despite, In spite of, Regardless, Nevertheless): Both くせに and にもかかわらず convey contradiction between two facts, but with different nuance and tone. くせに is a casual expression with a blaming or critical tone, e.g. 知っているくせに何で教えてくれないの？ ('You know, so why won't you tell me!?'). In contrast, にもかかわらず is a more neutral and formal way to say 'in spite of (A)', e.g. 雨にもかかわらず出かけた ('We went out despite the rain.').

それなのに (N2, And yet, Despite this): Both express contrast, but differ in usage and implication. くせに follows a phrase and has a critical tone, e.g. 知っているくせに教えてくれない ('He knows but won't tell me.'), implying that the speaker is angry at the person. それなのに comes at the beginning of a sentence, is neutral, and expresses simple contradiction, e.g. 彼は真実を知っている。それなのに、教えてくれない ('He knows. And yet, he won't tell me.') with an objective nuance.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About がち
text: がち is a suffix in Japanese that will be used after nouns, or the conjunctive form of verbs. It conveys that someone is 'apt to (A)', 'tends to (A)', or 'is prone to (A)'. Although not always negative, がち is most frequently used to express negative tendencies.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): Both がち and っぽい describe tendencies or characteristic qualities, but differ in nuance. がち is neutral and used for tendencies that happen often, e.g. つい忘れがちだ ('I tend to forget.'). っぽい expresses an inherent quality or the appearance of something, similar to the English '~ish', e.g. 子供っぽい性格 ('a childish personality').

きらいがある (N1, Have a tendency to, Tend to, Be slightly~): Both express tendencies or patterns of behavior, but they differ in tone and usage. がち attaches to verb stems, and is neutral, used for tendencies that happen often, e.g. つい忘れがちだ ('I tend to forget.'). きらいがある follows the plain form of verbs and is typically used only for undesirable tendencies. Unlike がち, it can also express a tendency to not do something, e.g. 人の話を聞かないきらいがある ('He tends to not listen to others.').

meaning: Looking, Feeling a little, Touch of, Tending to, Slightly
summary: A slightly casual word that expresses weak feelings or tendencies, often based on sensation.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ぎみ
text: Coming from the noun {気味|きみ} meaning 'sensation', ぎみ is a suffix that is used to convey weak signs of (A). ぎみ may be used with nouns, or the conjunctive form of verbs. Often, ぎみ is translated as 'looking (A)', 'a touch of (A)', 'feeling a little (A)', or 'slightly (A)'.
ぎみ refers to the senses of the person who is experiencing them, and therefore may be used to refer to feelings about other people/things, or feelings about oneself.
As ぎみ expresses 'weak signs of (A)', it is often used to soften a statement, so that the speaker does not appear overconfident.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Although it comes from {気味|きみ}, ぎみ will always be said with a ぎ, and not a き. This is a sound change used to distinguish the noun and the suffix.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: げ (N2, Seemingly, Giving appearance of, [Expresses emotions or feelings]): ぎみ (often written in kanji as 気味) and げ both describe observable states, but differ in focus. ぎみ suggests a slight or subtle tendency, often related to physical or emotional states, e.g. 疲れ気味 ('a bit tired') or 風邪気味 ('have a bit of a cold'). げ expresses perceived emotions of others, e.g. 寂しげな顔 ('a lonely-looking face').

っぽい (N3, -ish, -like, Characteristic of, Typical of, Tendency to): Both ぎみ (often written in kanji as 気味) and っぽい describe tendencies or characteristics, but with different nuance. ぎみ suggests a slight or subtle tendency, often related to physical or emotional states, e.g. 疲れ気味 ('a bit tired') or 風邪気味 ('have a bit of a cold'). っぽい implies a more innate trait that gives the appearance or impression of something, e.g. 子どもっぽい ('childish') or 忘れっぽい ('forgetful').

的 (N3, ~ly・~like・~al, Typical): 的 and ぎみ (気味) are similar in that both can be attached to nouns to turn them into adjectives, but they differ in nuance and usage. 的 has a wider range of uses, similar to English endings like '-al', '-ly', etc., e.g. 感情 'emotion' vs. 感情的 'emotional'. In contrast, ぎみ has the specific meaning of 'slightly (A)' or 'showing tendencies of (A)', and typically expresses a subjective judgment about a condition, e.g. 疲れ気味 'a bit tired'.

ような気がする (N3, Have a feeling that): Both ような気がする and ぎみ (from 気味) use 気 expressions to convey subtle states or impressions, but with different nuance and usage. ような気がする follows a phrase to express a subjective hunch like 'Have a feeling that (A)', e.g. 来るような気がする 'I have a feeling they'll come.' ぎみ attaches to nouns to express a slight tendency or hint of something observable, often (but not always) negative, e.g. 疲れ気味だ 'I'm feeling a bit tired.'

summary: A casual expression that shows that something appears or is acting in a way that is like (A), but not.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About っぽい
text: っぽい (occasionally also seen as ぽい) is a suffix that may be attached to many different types of words, in order to create new い-Adjectives. In all cases, っぽい indicates something that is 'exhibiting characteristics of (A)'. This is most often in reference to the way (A) is acting, or the way (A) looks. In English, っぽい may be translated as '(A)ish', '(A)like', or 'tendency to (A)'. っぽい quite often carries a negative connotation.
As っぽい creates い-Adjectives from other words, it may be used with the conjunctive form of verbs, or the {語幹|ごかん} (stem form) of any other word.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: The fundamental meaning of っぽい will change depending on what type of word it is being used with. The general rules are as follows:
Verb + っぽい - To have a tendency to do (A).
Adjective + っぽい - To exhibit all the signs of being (A).
Noun + っぽい - To obviously not be (A), although show signs of being (A).

From this, we can see that っぽい is generally based on the opinion of the speaker, rather than the innate qualities of what is being observed. Thus, with verbs, adjectives, and nouns, the speaker feels like (A) is in excess, compared to what would be expected. This 'being in excess of what is normal' in the opinion of the speaker is what creates the negative connotation.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: Often has negative connotation.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: がち (N3, Apt to do, Tend to do, Prone to do): Both がち and っぽい describe tendencies or characteristic qualities, but differ in nuance. がち is neutral and used for tendencies that happen often, e.g. つい忘れがちだ ('I tend to forget.'). っぽい expresses an inherent quality or the appearance of something, similar to the English '~ish', e.g. 子供っぽい性格 ('a childish personality').

げ (N2, Seemingly, Giving appearance of, [Expresses emotions or feelings]): Both っぽい and げ describe perceived qualities, but differ in nuance. っぽい refers to innate behaviors or traits that give a certain impression. For example, 子どもっぽい ('childish') or 怒りっぽい ('quick to anger'). In contrast, げ highlights perceived emotions in others. For example, 寂しげな顔 ('a lonely-looking face').

ふりをする (N3, To pretend, To act as if): Both ふりをする and っぽい describe imitation or resemblance, but with a key difference in nuance. ふりをする implies pretending to be or do something one is not, as in 知ったふりをする ('pretend to know'). In contrast, っぽい conveys a natural resemblance or tendency, often unconscious or inherent, as in 子供っぽい ('childish').

ぎみ (N3, Looking, Feeling a little, Touch of, Tending to, Slightly): Both ぎみ (often written in kanji as 気味) and っぽい describe tendencies or characteristics, but with different nuance. ぎみ suggests a slight or subtle tendency, often related to physical or emotional states, e.g. 疲れ気味 ('a bit tired') or 風邪気味 ('have a bit of a cold'). っぽい implies a more innate trait that gives the appearance or impression of something, e.g. 子どもっぽい ('childish') or 忘れっぽい ('forgetful').

らしい ② (N4, typical of, -ish・like, appropriate for, becoming of, befitting): っぽい and らしい② both express resemblance. っぽい is casual, like '-ish' in English, e.g. 子どもっぽい 'childish' (usually with a negative nuance). らしい② implies that someone or something embodies expected traits, e.g. 男らしい 'manly' with a nuance of fulfilling cultural expectations of what a man should be.

的 (N3, ~ly・~like・~al, Typical): 的 and っぽい are similar in that both can be attached to nouns to turn them into adjectives (or adverbs, in the forms 的に and っぽく). They differ grammatically (的 functions as a な-adjective, while っぽい is an い-adjective), and in nuance. 的 has a wider range of uses, similar to English endings like '-al', '-ly', etc., e.g. 感情 'emotion' vs. 感情的 'emotional'. っぽい is narrower in use, and often carries a derogatory meaning, e.g. 子供っぽい 'childish'.

らしい ① (N4, Seems like, Apparently, I heard): っぽい and らしい ① both describe being 'like' something, but with different nuances and formality. っぽい, similar to the English '-ish,' refers to having the characteristics of something without being that thing, and is very casual, e.g. 子どもっぽい態度 'childish behavior', e.g. from an adult. In contrast, らしい ① implies embodying a characteristic in a more fitting or expected way, e.g. 子どもらしい笑顔 'a smile just as you'd expect from a child'.

そう (N4, Look like, Appear, Seem, Have a feeling that): Both っぽい and そう express appearance or impression, but differ in nuance and usage. そう attaches to word stems and is neutral and often based on observation, e.g. 雨が降りそう ('It looks like it'll rain.'). っぽい is casual and attaches to nouns to mean '~ish' or '~like', e.g. 子供っぽい 'childish'. Unlike そう, it often carries a negative or demeaning tone.
