summary: A grammar point that expresses something left or released in an ongoing state, often negatively.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About っぱなし
text: っぱなし is a suffix that originally comes from the う - Verb {放|はな}す 'to let loose'. When attached to the conjunctive form of verbs, it is used to indicate that something has been 'left' in a certain state. っぱなし is almost exclusively used negatively.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: てある (N4, Something is done, Has been done, Remaining state): てある and っぱなし both describe ongoing states, but differ in tone. てある suggests something was done intentionally for future benefit. For example, 窓が開けてある means 'The window has been opened (for a reason).'. In contrast, っぱなし often implies carelessness. For example, 窓を開けっぱなしにして家を出た means 'I (carelessly) left the house with the window open.'.

まま(に) (N3, As is, While remaining, Left in a state): まま(に) and っぱなし both describe something left in a certain state, but differ in tone. まま(に) can be neutral or passive, e.g. 電気をつけたまま寝た ('I fell asleep with the light on'). っぱなし adds a careless or irresponsible nuance, as in ドアを開けっぱなしにしないで ('Don't leave the door wide open').

meaning: Expressly, Especially, Go out of one's way, Take the trouble to
summary: A phrase highlighting that someone has gone out of their way to do (A), or expressly done (A). Often with a positive nuance.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About わざわざ
text: わざわざ is an adverb that is used to express when someone has gone out of their way to achieve a certain result. It may be translated as 'expressly', 'especially', or 'to go out of one's way to (A)'.
わざわざ will usually be used at the beginning of sentences, before some statement will be made about an activity that was intentionally done.
わざわざ has a tendency to be used positively, although it may be used with negative connotations as well.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: Although almost never used, {態態|わざわざ} may be seen in this kanji form. {態|わざ} is a kanji used to express 'purpose', or 'intent'. Generally, it refers to someone's 'willingness' to do something. As such, わざわざ just expresses that (A) is something that the speaker has as a strong goal. How it will be translated depends more on whether the actual result is positive, negative, or undecided.
Positive result - To purposefully do (A), with the result of (A).
Negative result - To have every intention of (A), with the actual result of (B).
Undecided result - To be intent on (A), with (A) hopefully happening.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: わざと means "on purpose"

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 折角 (N3, With trouble, At great pains, Take the trouble, Might as well..., Rare/long-awaited occasion): 折角 and わざわざ both convey effort or intentionality, but differ in nuance. 折角 highlights the value of an effort or opportunity, often implying it would be wasteful not to use it. For example, 折角来たのだから食べましょう ('We came all this way, so let's eat it'). わざわざ emphasizes that someone deliberately went out of their way. For example, わざわざ届けてくれてありがとう ('Thank you for going out of your way to deliver it to me').

meaning: (What) the heck?, (Who) in the world?, (Where) on earth?, (How many) f*ing...
summary: An exclamation which shows the speaker's surprise, in a similar way to what the heck in English. Primarily used to ask questions.
formation: いったい + Question Word + Phrase

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 一体
text: In order to convey the feeling of 'what the heck', with any 'how', 'what', 'where' or 'why' type question, the adverb {一体|いったい} will be used in Japanese. いったい appears frequently both with, and without kanji.
いったい will usually be seen at the beginning of sentences, before some statement about what the speaker finds unbelievable.

The literal meaning of いったい is 'one body', or 'one form'. In this way, when paired with questions, いったい can be thought of meaning 'in a way that can be understood, what is (A)', or 'in a way that makes sense, what is (A)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ことか (N3, How…, What..., God knows...): 一体 and ことか both add emphasis to questions, but differ in nuance. 一体 strengthens genuine questions with a tone of surprise or frustration, like 'What in the world?', e.g. 一体何があったんですか？ 'What in the world happened?' ことか appears in rhetorical questions or exclamations to express strong emotion, e.g. 彼がどんなに努力したことか 'How hard he worked!'

meaning: With trouble, At great pains, Take the trouble, Might as well..., Rare/long-awaited occasion
summary: An expression which shows that (A) has been long awaited, or arrived at after great mental or physical effort.
formation: せっかく + の + Noun (of Event)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 折角
text: {折角|せっかく} is an idiomatic adverb that is often used to express doing something 'with trouble', 'at great pains', or 'to be a rare/long-awaited occasion'. Being an adverb that often modifies the meaning of a whole sentence, it will commonly appear at the beginning of a statement. When {折角|せっかく} is nominating an event as being long awaited, it will appear directly before the event, separated only by the case marking particle の.

sections.label: Fun Fact
sections.heading: Fun Fact
text: There are several guesses for where {折角|せっかく} originates. One of the most common is that it is an abbreviation for {頭巾|ずきん}の{角|つの}を{折|お}る 'to fold the horn (tail) of a hood'. This was something that a famous confucian did intentionally to protect his hood from getting wet in the rain. The people of the time started to copy the act, and {折角|せっかく} also came to be used as an idiom to mean 'intentionally', or 'to go out of one's way to do something'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: わざわざ (N3, Expressly, Especially, Go out of one's way, Take the trouble to): 折角 and わざわざ both convey effort or intentionality, but differ in nuance. 折角 highlights the value of an effort or opportunity, often implying it would be wasteful not to use it. For example, 折角来たのだから食べましょう ('We came all this way, so let's eat it'). わざわざ emphasizes that someone deliberately went out of their way. For example, わざわざ届けてくれてありがとう ('Thank you for going out of your way to deliver it to me').

meaning: What is…again?, Was it... that... ?, Did you say...?
summary: A short sound often used to indicate something the speaker should know, but has been forgotten.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About っけ
text: け is a sentence ending particle in Japanese that is used to convey when the speaker is trying to either remember, or confirm information that they have forgotten. In this way, it is very similar to the 'again' in 'what is (A) again?'
け may only be used after the past form of the auxiliary verbs だ or た. This means that け (should) only be seen as だっけ or たっけ.
It is also common to see のだ and んだ utilized to make verb tenses a possibility.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: While Verb[る] + ん/の + だ/だった + っけ should be used, younger generation of Japanese simply uses Verb[る] + っけ

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: か (N5, Question marking particle): か is the standard question particle, used at the end of sentences to ask questions (e.g., どんな本が好きですか？ = 'What kind of books do you like?') and also within other grammar patterns. っけ, on the other hand, is a casual sentence-ending particle used when trying to recall something (e.g., 名前はなんだっけ？ = 'What was his name again?').

meaning: Instead of, In place of, In exchange for
summary: A phrase that shows that (B) is acting as a substitute or replacement for (A).
formation: Noun + の + 代（か）わりに

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 代わりに
text: {代|か}わり 'a substitute' is a noun that is used to convey when (B) is acting as a replacement or substitute for (A). The case marking particle に will come after {代|か}わり, before a (B) statement will highlight who the replacement is, and possibly what they are doing.
As {代|か}わり is a noun, it may be used after the attributive form of any word.
Occasionally, {替|か}わり 'to exchange' may be used instead of {代|か}わり 'to substitute'. However, within the context of this particular grammar structure, there is little to no change in nuance.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: に代わって (N3, In place of, On behalf of, To succeed): Both phrases use 代わる ('to replace') and express substitution or replacement, but differ in usage. 代わりに emphasizes doing something in place of another thing or action. For example, ご飯の代わりにパンを食べた ('I ate bread instead of rice'). に代わって is used when taking over someone's role or acting in their place, often in formal contexts. For example, 部長に代わってご挨拶します ('On behalf of the department head, I greet you').

むしろ (N3, Rather, Instead, Over): Both expressions involve alternatives, but with different meanings. 代わりに indicates a direct substitution or exchange, often physical or role-based, e.g. 泳ぐ代わりに走った ('I ran instead of swimming'). むしろ introduces a more suitable or preferred option, e.g. 泳ぐよりむしろ走りたい ('I'd rather run than swim').

meaning: In place of, On behalf of, To succeed
summary: An expression used to show when (B) will substitute for (A) in some specific role, often in succession.

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About に代わって
text: に{代|か}わって is an expression that will only appear with nouns, conveying that (B) is doing something 'in place of (A)', or 'on behalf of (A)'. This is a combination of the case marking particle に, the う - Verb {代|か}わる 'to substitute', and the conjunction particle て.
に代わり may also be used, as this is the formal conjunctive. Also known as the conjunctive form.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: 代わりに (N3, Instead of, In place of, In exchange for): Both phrases use 代わる ('to replace') and express substitution or replacement, but differ in usage. 代わりに emphasizes doing something in place of another thing or action. For example, ご飯の代わりにパンを食べた ('I ate bread instead of rice'). に代わって is used when taking over someone's role or acting in their place, often in formal contexts. For example, 部長に代わってご挨拶します ('On behalf of the department head, I greet you').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About どころか
text: どころか is a combination of the noun ところ 'place', and the sentence ending particle か. The change from ところ to どころ is a consistent sound change that is seen regularly in sentences that use {所|ところ} negatively.
どころか may be translated as 'far from', 'let alone' or 'anything but'. It strongly negates any statement before it, while also emphasizing what comes after it.
どころか may be paired with the attributive form of any other word. However, this is not a strict rule, as it can also be seen with the {語幹|ごかん} stem form of な-Adjectives, and directly attached to nouns.
Sentences that use どころか must always have a part (B) that emphasizes some type of far more important information (in the speaker's opinion).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: ものか (N2, Definitely not, Absolutely not, Impossible, Do you really think~?): Both ものか and どころか convey strong denial or contrast, but differ in tone. ものか expresses emphatic denial, often with indignation or disbelief. For example, 負けるものか ('As if I could lose!'). どころか highlights an opposite or unexpected result compared to an initial expectation. For example, 優勝どころか、一回戦で負けた ('Far from winning the championship, they lost in the first round').

どころではない (N2, This is not the time for…, Far from, Out of the question): Both contain どころ and express contrast, but differ in nuance. どころか emphasizes an extreme or surprising contrast. For example, 痩せるどころか、太ってしまった ('Far from slimming down, I actually gained weight'). どころではない conveys that something is completely out of the question due to circumstances. For example, 忙しすぎて年休を取るどころではない ('I'm so busy this is no time to take a day off').

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About という理由で
text: という{理由|りゆう}で is a phrase that is used when giving reasons for (A). (A) may be a range of different things, from what happened, to what one's opinion is. Due to という quoting the previous statement as being the 'reason', という{理由|りゆう}で puts quite a bit of emphasis on the reason itself. Because of this, the expression is quite similar to 'being that' in English.
The case marking particle で will be used after {理由|りゆう} to show that 'with' or 'by means of' that reason, (B).

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: そのため(に) (N3, For that reason, Because of that, To that end): Both introduce reasons, but そのため(に) shows a direct consequence or effect from what was previously stated, while という理由で introduces a reason more abstractly and with a greater degree of formality. They also differ in how they connect the reason to the consequence, with そのため(に) always appearing at the beginning of a sentence, and という理由で being able to appear either at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence.

meaning: It is (has been), Have/has become, Happen to be, Has been established
summary: An expression highlighting that in general, (A) happens to be (B), or has been established as (B).

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About ～は～となっている
text: (A) は (B) となっている is a common expression used to show that '(A) is becoming (B)', or (more commonly) '(A) has become (B)'. This expression will only appear with nouns, or な-Adjectives in their {語幹|ごかん} (stem form). (A) は (B) となっている is often translated as '(A) happens to be (B)', '(A) has been established as (B)', or 'it has been decided that (A) is (B)'.
Let's have a look at some examples, and then how this structure is formed.
Despite the different translations, (A) は (B) となっている always has the same meaning, which can be understood as follows:
(A) は - (A) is a constant unchanging thing.
(B) と - (B) is a result. (coming from the case marking particle と's role in highlighting results.)
なっている - (A) is existing in the state 'having arrived at the result of (B)'.

sections.label: Compare
sections.heading: Similar grammar
text: とかんがえられている (N4, Is considered, Is thought of as): ～は～となっている and と考えられている both express current states or views, but differ in tone. ～は～となっている describes some sort of established fact that is now 'the way things are', e.g. 店は日曜休業となっている ('The store is closed on Sundays'). と考えられている expresses a generally held belief or reasoning and is often used to make a statement sound less direct, e.g. 彼は天才だと考えられている ('He is thought to be a genius').

とされている (N4, To be considered, To be deemed, Be regarded as, Be accepted as, To be said, To be accredited with): Both present an accepted state or fact, but differ in nuance. ～は～となっている describes that something has been established and is now 'the way things are', e.g. 朝礼は毎朝１０時開始となっている ('The morning meeting is set to start every day at 10 a.m'). とされている conveys that it is generally regarded in a certain way or as something, e.g. この神社は最古のものとされている ('This shrine is considered the oldest one').

meaning: Influence, Impact, Control
summary: A phrase highlighting that something is being controlled or affected. (A) is being maneuvered left and right freely.
formation: 左右（さゆう） + する(1) + Noun
左右（さゆう） + します(1) (polite)
左右（さゆう） + する(2) + Noun (polite)

sections.label: About
sections.heading: About 左右する
text: {左右|さゆう} is a noun that may literally be translated as 'left and right'. This particular noun is quite often used as a する verb, in order to convey the level of control someone or something has over a specific situation. This control may be translated as 'influence', 'impact', 'dictate' or simply 'control'.
{左右|さゆう}する may be used by itself, when describing a whole clause, or it may be followed directly by another noun, to show exactly what is being controlled/influenced.

{左右|さゆう}する is frequently seen in the passive form {左右|さゆう}される. This is due to {左右|さゆう} usually indicating something that is out of one's control, so rather than the sentence focusing on what actually is causing the result, it will focus on what is being controlled or affected.

sections.label: Caution
sections.heading: Caution
text: {左右|さゆう}する implies (A)'s direct control of (B), and is far stronger than to affect '{影響|えいきょう}'. Due to this, {左右|さゆう} may be thought of as being closer to 'to dominate' in English. In Japanese though, the most basic description is {思|おも}うままに{動|うご}かす 'to move exactly as one wishes'.
